chapters.label: Prologue
chapters.title: The Wound in the Ledger
paragraphs: Two autumns after the ridge named Open Continuance, a wrong began that nobody could see, because it looked exactly like good arithmetic. The stranger in the loft with the sticking window had walked four hundred miles from the country that invented it. This time the road would run the other way.
Seasons had turned since that ridge. The world had spent them learning how to be one country.

That was the work of the Dawns, and it was less like a coronation than a harvest. The Broken Moon was no more. It had gone up into the sky as rivers of silver light, with threads of shadow glinting among them like new stars. Anyone looking west at dusk saw the old wound doing the work of a constellation. Shadow had been reconciled instead of beaten. The Forgotten Seal was back where it belonged. The Eleven had become Twelve. The Eternal Haven had been forged on the ground, on a plain, out of stone and argument and a great deal of bread.

Haven and Aurethys were no longer two realms with a veil between them. They were the same ground, and the trouble with one piece of ground is that everybody has to agree about the fence. The Twelve came down out of the sky to farm, argue, apologise, and be corrected in public. They took it better than anyone expected and worse than they thought they were taking it.

Aureon spent a whole winter learning that beans do not care who you used to be. Sancora walked the coast with her satchels and a reputation for doing necessary harm to people who needed it. Orphiel walked between the vaults, carrying memory the way other people carry grain. Nahl’s carriers taught the first law as a trade skill, which is the highest honour this world knows how to give anything.

Emberion hung low in the west: a dragon of sixteen stars, where the shepherds had counted him for five hundred years. They kept the count by pointing at the joints of his wing, so that a child could learn it before learning letters. The scarred moon kept its scars. The other moon kept its dignity, and did not mind being the ordinary one.

The tower above Vellum Reach still stood, dulled and unremarkable on purpose. It kept a school of blanks on the third floor and a soup club on the first. Item 41 still had no door. The road east of the village was gold in the mornings, because the world had learned to lay the invitation into the stones, and most people walked it with witnesses when they could.
The great work of that age was not the war. The war was over. The great work was the ordinary business of not becoming what you had fought.
That was the world the trouble came into. It came in through a market, on a bright day, in the smell of bread.
Riss had been in the loft with the sticking window for a year and eleven days.

They counted the turning in loaves and frosts, because that is how you count in a village that refuses to weigh its own time. Four hundred and twelve mornings of the fountain singing its cracked note on purpose. It had sounded like a mistake for the first two months and like weather by the fifth. A year and eleven days of the open temple keeping its open throat. Mill-dust the colour of breadcrust hanging in the light. Cracks left in the walls by policy and affection. Nobody ever explained to Riss why the policy and the affection were the same thing, and that was how Riss learned that they were.

Riss had arrived on river-ash boots, with a Seal on a cord of braided copper wire and a story they told in as few words as possible. The village made room. It gave them a season. When the season ended it reassessed them in public, extended it, and required two witnesses. Nobody ever asked them to be grateful in a way that cost anything.

They had work. Mornings, they sorted blank leaves with Halwen in the temple portico. Paper came up from the western mill and down from the coast, and one bad crate came from a river town that had used reed, which would not take ink. Halwen sorted by hand and by hem. He flapped each sheet once, as if listening to it. In the first month Riss thought he was mad. By the sixth month they thought he was a colleague, which is a different kind of respect.

The Listening Leaf lay open on the low table between them. It had goat-nose in the margins, and a child’s curve from a year ago, and a note that said amend me in three different hands. When Halwen found a sheet he could not classify, he did not throw it away. He put it in the back of the Leaf. His theory was that a stubborn sheet would tell you what it was, if you let it be nothing for a while. He said this as if quoting somebody with better sense than himself.

Evenings belonged to the Interval. At dusk the village stopped what it was doing and sang two notes that refused to fit together: close enough to be a mistake, held long enough to be a question. The notes never resolved, and that was the whole point of them. It annoyed certain birds. Nobody in the village minded the birds.

Riss had hated it for the first month and joined in by the sixth, badly, which was the only way the village allowed anyone to do it. There was a bell for people who sang it too well. It had rung twice in eleven years.

Children played doorstop in the square. One child stood in a doorway with their arms stretched across it. Another child had to walk through slowly. Both of them giggled, and neither was fooled. Riss once asked a girl of about nine what she was practising for. The girl gave them the patient look you give an idiot. *For the people who can’t be stopped.* Which people? *Any of them.* Then she went back to holding the doorway.

There were nine rules, and the village kept them the way it kept the plaster. No kneeling. An empty stool in the small ring, for the absent and the unready and whoever has not arrived yet. Miracles do housework, or wait outside until the soup is on. Bad singing is civic infrastructure. Correct a god in public. Tiredness is not treason. Riss learned the last three the way you learn grammar: by being corrected, in front of everybody, without cruelty, by people who had no interest in their own authority.

Under the bed in the loft was a crate. Inside it were a year of unburned rags, tied in bundles of sevens and twos; a spectacle-screw whose lenses had shattered in the heat; a hinge-pin; and a six-sided die that had come out of an oven blackened and unreadable. Riss had kept the die because nobody else wanted a die that argued about its own faces.

At the bottom of the crate, in a cloth, lay a copper plate the size of a hand. It was thin enough to bend, and it had never once bent. A glyph was cut into it that no school in the world recognised. The plate was warm on one side and cold on the other, and it was always cold on the side that had faced the fire.

The plate had a habit. When Riss was afraid, it hummed a low fifth. It was not the Interval’s fifth and not the fifth of any song the village sang. It was a fifth that had been divided and had not come back whole. Across the square, whenever it sounded, Kael Riven’s scar answered it. The two of them never discussed this. They had agreed, without a word, not to mention it to the village until they understood it.
Two years in, Riss had four things they had never said out loud.
The first was that they had pulled the plate out of a public fire, in a country that called the smoke hygiene.
The second was that the form wrapped around it had carried their own name, ticked in a box printed REMAINDER.

The third was that they had a sister named Ness. Ness was better at columns than Riss would ever be. Riss had left her downriver. The leaving had been done carefully, in arithmetic, with a promise to send for her *when the year divides better*. Ness had written back on the back of a form, three lines in the best handwriting in the family. The last line was: *Years don’t divide better. Come back when you can say what you took.*

The fourth thing Riss had never put into a whole sentence, even in their own head: that they had been happy in Vellum Reach for about seven months, and had spent the five months since waiting for the bill.
On the ninth day of the harvest month, in the second autumn, the bill began with a woman’s name.

She kept the bread-stall by the fountain. She was sixty-one. Her laugh made customers hand over their coins before they had chosen anything. She had a grandson of eleven who lived up the valley and came down on market days to carry her trays. She had sold bread on the ninth day of the harvest month every year for thirty years.
She was there all day. Her bread sold. She laughed at the salt-argument, which two farmers had been conducting without missing a day for eleven years. She took their money and gave change.
At noon, the market slate that listed the day’s sellers showed her line blank. Nobody noticed, because nobody reads a slate when they can see the stall.

On the second day she was slower with names than she used to be. Not forgetful. Just late, the way people are late when they have stopped hurrying. On the third day Maris leaned over her counter and said, warmly, *Morning, you.* The woman answered the greeting without using Maris’s name, and Maris told herself it was early.
On the fourth day Maris said her name across the counter, plainly, the way you say the name of somebody you have known for eleven years.

Maris heard it arrive in her own ear and nowhere else. She heard it, and understood it, and could not set it down anywhere behind her eyes. It was like shouting into a room after the door has shut. The sound goes out and comes back, and there is no room left behind it. Maris said the name again. The same thing happened, in the same place, in the same way. She went into the back of her own stall and cried where nobody could see, and came out with her face fixed, and sold bread all day, and called the woman *love* instead.
The woman never complained about it once. That was the worst part.
On the seventh day, she became even.

Her hands stopped shaking. She had had a tremor in her right hand since her husband died, and it had been part of her the way a knot is part of a plank. Riss had watched her pour tea with it for two years and had never seen her spill. Now the hands were steady. The laugh came at the same height every time. When the two farmers brought their salt-argument to her, the way they brought it to everyone, she ended it kindly in four sentences, using the actual numbers, which nobody had managed in eleven years. Both men agreed with her. They went back to their stalls and stood there. Afterwards, both of them described a feeling they could not name. It was the feeling of having been settled.

That evening Halwen wrote in the Listening Leaf: *She is exactly as she should be, which she was not before.* He underlined it twice. He did not sleep, and in the morning the sentence had not improved.
On the tenth day the stall was swept. It was salted, the way the market salts a plot after a fire. A printed card was tacked to the post. The card said STALL AVAILABLE in a good clean type.

Maris took the card down and carried it to the market-clerk. He was a patient young man with ink on his third finger and two years in the post, and he had never once raised his voice. He checked the day-slate. He said, pleasantly, that there was no line for that stall and never had been. Then he asked, pleasantly, whether she had eaten, because she looked pale.
Maris said, “She sold here for thirty years.”
The clerk said, “Then it will be in the slate.”

It was not in the slate. Maris stood in the market with the card in her hand for a long time. Then she went back to her own counter, put both hands flat on the wood, and looked at them. They were her hands. She knew them. It did not help as much as she had expected.
On the eleventh day, a boy of eleven came down from the upper valley with a tray to carry. It was a market day. That was the arrangement.

He stood in the square for a while, looking at the swept stall and the card. Then he went from counter to counter and described his grandmother to strangers. Sixty-one. Short. A laugh you could hear across the square. A tremor in the right hand. Keeps the bread-stall by the fountain. He described her perfectly. He described her so well that Maris had to put down her knife.

He could not say her name. It was in his mouth and it did not arrive anywhere. He knew what she looked like. He knew what she smelled like, and the tune she hummed when the dough was slow, and the shape of her hands on a tray. But when he reached for the word that was her, there was nothing behind it. He stood in the middle of the market at eleven years old and said, twice, “She’s my … she’s my …”

Nobody in the square could help him. They had all lost the same word on the same day. The only person in the market who understood exactly what had happened to the boy was a stranger on river-ash boots who had crossed four hundred miles of country to get away from that arithmetic. Riss stood at Halwen’s table with a crate of blank leaves and could not make themselves cross the square.

Riss did not cross the square. That is in the record, because Halwen wrote it down as it happened. It is also the first thing Riss said out loud afterwards, sitting in the portico with their head in their hands: *I knew what it was, and I said nothing, because if I said it out loud in that square I would have to be the person who knows. I have spent two years trying not to be that person.*

The village did not tell them it was all right. That is not one of the nine rules. Mira sat down on the step beside them and drew the boy’s face in the corner of the Wound-Chart. That was her way of saying that the boy existed, and that somebody had seen him, and that the seeing was now on a map. Nahl stood in the doorway and said nothing at all. That was the doorstop, and it was what Riss needed, and it took two hours.
After that, the symptoms came the way symptoms come: a thing had learned the shape of a country.

On the twelfth day, a caravan out of the river counties sold grain in the lower square. The grain was cheap. Every sack carried a small printed mark: a tick inside a circle, and under the tick, one word. CLEAN.

Two farmers from up the valley asked how grain got clean. The carter was a mild man with a good coat and three pens in his pocket. He explained, in the voice of somebody quoting a fair rule, that clean grain came from clean holdings, that clean holdings kept clean books, and that there was a small fee for the assessor and a stamp for the sacks. This was not a threat, he said. It was an opportunity.
Grain with the tick sold a penny under the market, and the poorest bought it first. That was the design of it. The poorest are the ones who cannot afford to ask what a stamp costs.

By the end of that fortnight, nine farmsteads in the valley had burned their unfinished tallies in their own yards at night. They did it quietly, without telling their neighbours. The smoke went up thin and guilty over the orchards. It smelled like the thing Riss had crossed a country to get away from: not woodsmoke, not lampblack, but a dry patient smell, like a sickroom cleaned too well. Riss smelled it from the loft window on the third night. They did not sleep. In the morning they told no one, and hated themselves for a week.

On the thirteenth day, a customs-clerk came through the market to take names for the river counties’ register. The counties were compiling a list of residents for the clean grain reckoning. It was administrative, and ordinary, and dull, and nobody in Vellum Reach thought twice about giving a name to a man with a ledger.
He wrote the names down in figures.

Riss stood at the water-trough and watched him work: a name, a number, and a second number after it. The thumb of his writing hand ran down the column the way a reader marks a place. When Riss’s turn came, they gave their name, because refusing would have been an event. The clerk wrote it in figures. Riss asked what the second number was for.
*Division,* the clerk said. He smiled, and moved on to the next stall.

He was polite. His coat was good. He smelled of mint and polished wood, which has no business in a market that also smells of fish. Riss stood by the trough for a while after he had gone, with that smell sitting in the roof of their mouth like a tuning-fork held against a table. They were thinking about how a country takes a thing. It does not come in one piece, with shouting, at a gate. It comes politely, with a fee and a smile and a form, and a queue of neighbours who are only giving their names.
On the fourteenth day, at dusk, the village set the Scar-Interval.

It was the practice the world had learned from the war: two tones a hair too close together, a third and a fourth, held until the ear gave up wanting them to resolve. It annoyed certain birds. It was the sound of a thing staying unfinished on purpose. The village called it the third rule, bad singing is civic infrastructure, and the whole point of it was that the ear never got what it wanted.
That evening, the two tones came together into a clean fifth.

It was the first true resolution that square had ever heard. Three people wept and could not say why. Children clapped, which had never happened in the history of the practice. Harmonix stood at the edge of the amphitheatre with open hands and a shut mouth. Afterwards, Harmonix said the sentence the village would repeat for a season: *The refusal was the amen. Something has made us agree.*

Old Den had lost a brother in the Ascension War and had a low opinion of anything that comforted. He said the practice had gone soft, and went home. Then he came back, and stood at the edge of the square listening to the silence with his arms folded, like a man listening to a well.
On the fifteenth day, the bad-singing bell rang at noon in an empty square. Nobody had sung and nobody had been stingy.
On the sixteenth day, Kael Riven came home from the eastern road.

He had spent two seasons as a roving trace-witness. He went where carriers and carriers’ families needed a second pair of eyes that had been trained not to seize. He came back with a coat that had seen weather and a way of standing that had stopped being a boy’s. He heard about the bread-woman in the square, in the middle of a sentence, from two people at once. He put his bag down where he stood. He went to the swept stall and stood in front of it, and then he took out his slate.

He tried to trace her, because that is what he was for. Three marks. Each one came out clean and complete, with no remainder hanging off it anywhere. Not a loose end. Not a frayed edge. Not the small untidiness that every honest trace has somewhere, because every honest person has some. He checked the marks against each other. He checked them again with his eyes shut, which Halwen had taught him and which he did not like doing in public.
Then he sat down on the low wall and held up his own burned hand and looked at it as though it had been caught lying to him.

“I’ve traced the missing before,” he said. To Mira, who had come up beside him, and to nobody in particular. “Missing has a shape. A hole has edges. You can put your hand on the edge of where somebody isn’t.” He turned the slate over. “This is not a hole. This is a clean page.”
And the goat walked to the swept stall and stood in front of it, and would not be moved, for two days.

This was the goat that had inherited the title from a better goat two winters before. It had no ethics, no shame, and no discernible use. Children fed it. Adults reasoned with it. Maris put a stool out and sat with it for an hour at a time. Nobody could read what it was doing, except that a goat which has decided something on behalf of everybody stands very still. This one did. The whole village knew that goats have veto. No one had yet worked out what the veto was for.
Then the shepherds came down with the other news.
It was worse than the bread-woman, because of the arithmetic in it, and because it had a date.

Emberion’s constellation had come up over the western ridge every dusk since the Dawns: a dragon of sixteen stars, low in the west. The shepherds kept a count for it, five hundred years old, taught by pointing at the joints of the wing, because a count you can teach a child is a count that survives. In the second week of the harvest, the count came to fifteen.

They counted again. They made the children start from the other end of the sky, which is the oldest check there is. Fifteen. They walked the ridge with the oldest shepherd in the valley, who was blind in one eye and had been counting that constellation since before the war. He stopped in the middle of the count. He stood there, and then he said, “It is not dim. It is not fallen. It has been got rid of.”

Nobody had seen a star go out. Nothing had moved. The other fifteen stood in the sky in the right places, at the right distances. The pattern still read as a dragon. A child could still point at it and say the name. One joint of the wing was not there, and the sky had been arranged so carefully around the gap that from the ground nothing looked wrong at all.

The sky had begun to be audited. Something had gone through it, found a star it did not need, taken it, and left the rest exactly as they were. The shepherds stood on the ridge in the dark and agreed that this was precisely the sort of thing a careful man does when he is tidying.
That was the state of things when Halwen chalked the ring.

He did it at noon, so nobody would mistake it for a summons. He did it badly, so nobody would mistake it for a court. Vellum Reach had learned long ago that a village which does not think out loud does not think. A chalk-ring at the end of a bad harvest is not a council. It is a room with no roof, which is another way of saying witnesses.
Everyone came, which was new for a chalk-ring at harvest.

Maris brought bread, because Maris brought bread. She set the loaves on the low wall with a cloth over them, and went back for the salt and the knife. Watching her, Riss understood that Vellum Reach had arrived at a civilization in which a serious conversation about the end of the world required a knife.

Nahl came and stood three paces from the ring’s edge, with the Bearer’s Seal quiet at their chest. They wore the cloak the colour of wet ash, and they were as still as Riss had once mistaken for sleep. Riss had watched them for two years, and could see them already counting the doors.

Mira came with the Wound-Chart across her knees. There were two marks on it now: one where the bread-stall stood, and one where the mill tally hung. She had drawn no line between them, and was not willing to.

Corvath came over from the smithy with the plowshare still in his hand. He had told Riss once, flatly, standing in his own doorway, that among neighbours he would rather be seen carrying a tool than a title.
Aureon came down off the ridge with dirt already under his nails, and stood with the ordinary neighbours. He had done that for two years and had never once made it into a gesture.

Halwen brought the Listening Leaf and laid it open on the low table. The goat came and stood at the ring’s edge with its head down. The boy of eleven came and sat on the wall. Old Den came last and stood at the back, because a village needs one person who will not be comforted.
Halwen asked the four questions. They are ordinary questions. Who has been harmed? What was seen? What was done about it, and by whom? What does the village intend to do next?
The village answered them honestly, and none of the answers were worth anything. That is the moment at which a ring becomes necessary.

“Say it’s a counting error,” said Old Den. “Villages have them every harvest. Somebody’s tally slips. Or a woman goes to her sister’s for a month, or a bell rings because a bell rings. The bread-woman’s gone off. The boy will remember her name by Yule. If he doesn’t, he’ll have a grandmother-shaped hole, and he’ll grow up around it the way a tree grows around a fence-post. That is how people have always lived. It is not a war. It does not need a ring.”

“Maps lose roads,” Mira said. “They do not lose names. I want to say this carefully, because it is the only thing I am sure of. When a road goes, the paper where it was is different. Thinner. Drier. That is how paper goes when ink has been lifted out of it. I have drawn two hundred roads. I know what a road leaving looks like. This is not a road leaving. There is a name-shaped dryness in the paper where a person was, and the paper around it has been left neat.” She put her charcoal down. “I do not know what leaves a name behind and takes the paper.”
“Then we send to the Twelve,” said Aureon.

The square went quiet. Lightfather had said out loud what half of them were thinking, and none of them had wanted it said. The reason they had not wanted it said is that it was not a stupid thing to say. It was a reasonable thing to say, and reason was the whole of the trouble.

“One reading,” Aureon said. “One measure, taken by people who cannot be lied to, at a cost the Ledger cannot argue with. We have the Twelve. We have Seals that can hold a country’s worth of truth. Let it be settled and done with before it spreads past three villages. If it spreads, it will not be three villages. It will be a market. Then we will spend a generation arguing about it while it buys one village a year.” He said it without heat, which was the frightening part. “This is what the Accord is for.”

Riss stood at the edge of the ring, holding Maris’s salt, because Maris had handed it to them on the way past. They watched the word settled go round the square like a coin looking for a hand to be spent from. It found several. Two farmers nodded. The miller nodded. A woman Riss did not know said, quietly, that she had a cousin downriver, and that if one measure would keep her cousin nameless no longer, and then she stopped, because she had said nameless, and the word sat in the ring and looked at everybody.
Corvath set the plowshare down an inch. That was his way of standing up.
“I have smelled this before,” he said, “and I do not smell it now, and that is what frightens me.”

He tasted the air a second time. He did it out of habit now, the way a man who has broken a leg checks the road before he steps off a curb. He described it to strangers as a disability, which was Corvath’s version of manners.

“The old hunger stank of closed rooms and filing-cabinets. It stank of ledgers waiting for names the way traps wait for soft feet. It was honest, in its way. It wanted a finished world and it said so, and it took everything in one motion, so that we could see it coming and hate it in the open.” He looked at the swept stall, and the card, and the salted stones. “This does not smell at all. This smells of a bright market and a man being polite about a fee.”
He straightened up. Nobody in the square had ever seen him do that in daylight.

“I was the thing under the world for a century. I know what it is to be made into a shape that suits somebody else’s arithmetic. Whatever is doing this does not want our fear. It does not want our obedience. Those were my instruments, and they are far too expensive.” He set the plowshare down flat. “It wants our books to balance.”
“What does it want?” Nahl said.
Nobody answered, so Nahl answered it themselves. Their voice was quiet, and it was the voice of somebody who had once been filed and had walked out of the file with their name still attached.

“Everything that ever took names wanted something. Hunger wants feeding. Fear wants safety. The Hollow Index wanted a finished world, and was honest enough to say so. It lost three times. It went quiet two years ago. I want it placed on the record that I do not think this is it.” Nahl looked at the swept stall and the printed card. “This takes nothing. It keeps nothing. It lets the bread sell. So it is keeping something. And I want to know where, because whatever is kept can be carried back out.”
“It balances.”
Everyone turned. Riss had set the salt down on the wall.

They had not planned to speak. They could feel the shape of the room, though, the way you feel a door in the dark. A square of neighbours. A ring. A question. A stranger standing at the edge of it with a crate of blank leaves and a copper thing under their shirt, holding a knife for a woman who had handed it over because she trusted their hands.

There is a point in every ring where not speaking becomes a lie. Riss had crossed that point twelve days earlier, in a market, when a boy of eleven stood in front of them and reached for his grandmother’s name and found nothing behind it. Riss had stood still and said nothing, because saying nothing was safer.
They were done being safe. It had not made them safe.

“It doesn’t take, and it doesn’t keep. Not the way you mean,” Riss said. “It divides. Every name in this village is written down twice. Once for the market, once for the mill. The market and the mill have to agree, or the tally is a lie. The counties have done it that way for a hundred years, and nobody remembers where they learned it.”
Riss picked up Halwen’s stylus. The square leaned in, not knowing what it was looking at.

“Two offices. Two columns. One name. And the two columns around that woman’s name agree too well. Not close. Well. They agree the way two clerks agree when they are both reading off the same paper, and the paper has one figure in the middle that both columns were built around.” Riss drew two short columns in the margin of the Leaf, put a single dot between them, and drew a line from the dot to each. “That figure is a shared factor. Two accounts of the same person, sharing one factor, agreeing too well. That is the whole small craft of it. It is not magic. It does not need a mind to want anything.

“When two accounts of a person share a factor, you can know everything the columns knew about her. You can never add her back up. Not with witnesses. Not with Seals. Not with song. The leftovers cannot be recombined, because the accounts never had the parts. And a thing that cannot be recombined can be tidied. Tidying is cheap. It is legal. It is exactly the kind of work that careful men do, in good coats, before they go home and kiss their children.”
The square was quiet. Maris had stopped cutting bread.
“In my country,” Riss said, “we do it to the year.”
They said it flatly, in the voice of a person reading a duty roster, because that is where the voice comes from and there is no other voice that would hold the words.

“Every year, the Ledger gives the year a number. Which box you land in depends on that number. There are two boxes on the form. REMAINDER and SEED. One gets a lower grain allowance and a stamp that follows you to school, to the hiring table, to the customs post. The other gets spoken to kindly in the square. Same person. Different year. Different box.

“Nobody has to hate you for it. That is the point of it. Nobody has to hate you, and it never stops, and it is fair, and they mean that word when they say it. The men who keep the columns are careful men who go home and kiss their children. Every one of them will tell you, truthfully, that the system is only arithmetic, and that arithmetic has no favourites.”
Halwen’s thumb had stopped in the margin of the Leaf.

“It is not a beast to be slain,” Riss said. “It is a sum. And it has to be answered by a wider column than the one it was written in. That is the only thing that has ever worked. I know it because my country has been winning at the other way for sixty years. It beat us with forms. It beat us so completely that we stopped noticing it was happening. The ones who noticed went quiet. The ones who went quiet got a box.”

Riss’s hands were ordinary on the wall, and their voice was ordinary. Only the thing under their shirt was not. It had begun to hum, low, in the fifth that was not the Interval’s fifth: the fifth that had been divided and had not come back whole. Across the square, in front of everybody, Kael Riven’s scar answered it. The two of them looked at each other over the heads of the village and said nothing. That was the third of the four things Riss had never said out loud.

“I have a sister,” Riss said. “Her name is Ness. She is better at columns than I ever was. She has the best handwriting in the family, and it leans very slightly left at the base, the way soldiers stand at ease. When we were children, I used to make her write my name on my slate for me, because mine looked like a wasp had fallen in ink. I left her downriver. I told her I would send for her when the year divides better.”
The post-boat had come in while Riss was talking.

That is how post-boats work. The bundle sat on the mill step in its oiled cloth. Halwen opened it, because Halwen opened things, and had opened other people’s post in front of witnesses for thirty years without once having it held against him.
The top sheet was a form.

It was pale grey county stock, printed with a grid. Column one held names: ninety-one of them, small and exact, written by a clerk’s hand that had been taught to write names the way a mason is taught to cut stone. Column two held figures, one beside each name, in a hand Riss had not seen in two years and would have known in a crowd of a thousand. Column three held a heading in a language nobody in the square could read. At the foot of the sheet was a box, ticked. Beside the box was a signature that was not Ness’s. Above the signature was a title, three words in the county tongue, which Halwen read out slowly, because he read everything out slowly: ASSESSOR OF HYGIENE.
**Ness Riss** was the thirty-first name on the list.
Nineteen of the ninety-one names were ticked.

Riss looked at it for a long time. Their sister’s hand in the clerk’s column, filling in figures for other people’s sons and mothers, doing the work carefully, correcting one figure with a small neat stroke. Ness had never in her life been able to do a column badly. Riss looked at the figure beside their sister’s name, and at the tick in the box at the foot of the page.
“That’s my sister’s hand,” Riss said. Nobody asked how they could tell.
Then they understood the whole of it, and said so, in the flat voice, because there was no other voice that would hold it.
“She is inside it. They did not make her a remainder, and they did not make her a seed. They made her the clerk.”
Riss folded the form along its creases, twice, and put it in the pocket with the plate.

“That means it is not a raid, and not a storm, and not a thing you fight at a gate. It is a country. It has been practising on the poor for two generations, where nobody with a voice could see it. Now it has come up the river, selling clean grain to farmers who burn their own tallies at night for a stamp, and taking names in figures in markets, and taking one star out of a constellation so neatly that the sky still reads as a dragon. It has a market, a fee, a title, a signature, and a queue.

“It will arrive in this village the way a road arrives. Politely. One field at a time. The first thing it will do when it arrives is ask to see our books, because it cannot do anything to us until our books agree with each other too well.”
Nahl stepped into the ring. Three paces from Riss and one from the panic. Doorstop. Nobody had to be told, and nobody had to be thanked.
“Then you are not going alone,” Nahl said.

“I want to see the country that does this to a name and calls it cleanliness,” said Kael Riven. He turned his slate face-down on the low wall, which he had not once done in two years, and left it there.
“I will draw the road,” Mira said, “and when the road lies to me, I will draw that too, and I will label it a liar, because somebody has to.”
“I am coming,” said Corvath, “because I know exactly what it is to be rounded down and left standing. And because once in my life I would like to be the doorstop instead of the danger.”
Old Den stood at the back with his arms folded. “I will come as well. Somebody has to say no in front of witnesses. I have had my hand up for eleven years, and nobody has ever once taken it.”

And out of the dusk, along the coast road, Sancora arrived with two satchels and dust to the knee. She had heard. She always heard, and the village had stopped asking how. She said the sentence the square had been waiting for without knowing it: “Ugly healing. My specialty.”

Behind her, in the door of the open temple, Veylan Perfectscribe stood with a crate of seedlings under one arm and a trowel in the other hand. He had spent a lifetime being corrected and had made a discipline out of it. “I dig badly,” he said. “It is a method. It takes four hands, and it is the only way to find out what is under a floor without breaking what is above it. I am coming.”
Aureon rose last.

“I will take the ridge road and put this in front of the Twelve before it reaches their villages and mine,” he said. “If they will give one measure and one reading freely, then good. The roads will be safer for it, and I will have been wrong about nothing. If they will not, I will not take it by myself.”
He looked at Nahl while he said it. Nahl looked back for a long moment, and then nodded once. That is not the same as agreeing. Everyone in the square knew it. That, too, is one of the rules.

The living road at the square’s edge brightened as dusk came down. Gold threads rose in the cold air: the old invitation, the colour the village had walked on for two generations and had taught Riss to read in their first week. *This way, with witnesses, in daylight if you can.*
Under the gold, thin as a scratch on glass, a second line came up out of the stones and ran the other way. West. Downriver. The colour of wet ash.

Nobody in Vellum Reach had ever seen the second colour. Mira was already on her knees with charcoal, and she did not draw it. She had drawn two hundred roads in her life, and she knew a line that pointed at a person when she saw one, and she was not going to be the first to put it on paper. The goat walked to the edge of the square, put its crooked head down, and stood squarely on the grey line. That is what a goat does when it has decided something on behalf of everybody. Nobody had ever seen it do that about anything else.

In the loft with the sticking window, Riss sat on the floor with the crate open. A year of unburned rags, tied in sevens and twos. A spectacle-screw. A hinge-pin. A blackened die that argued about its own faces. The plate lay in its cloth on the sill, humming its low divided fifth in the dark. Beside it lay a leaf Halwen had torn out of the Listening Leaf and handed over without a word. On it, in his bad hand, he had written: *amend me.*
They did not sleep. Neither did the goat.
At dawn, the company went downriver.

Riss went with the plate under their shirt and the form folded in their pocket. Nahl went with the Bearer’s Seal and the first law, and the cloak the colour of wet ash, and a bag of carrier’s gear, because they would rather arrive able to work than able to impress.

Kael went with the slate face-down under his arm, and did not turn it over once, all the way to the river. Mira went with the Wound-Chart and forty feet of blank parchment, because the blank part was the point. Corvath went with a smith’s hammer and no shadow to sit down for him. Old Den went with his hand up. Sancora went with her satchels. Veylan went with seedlings in a crate and a trowel on his belt, hopeless and useful.

Maris walked the first mile with them, carrying bread, salt and a knife. Then she turned back, because the village had learned long ago that a speech is a way of keeping somebody from leaving, and the whole of the nine rules is that a person who can leave makes a stronger room.

Halwen walked out to the square before they were over the ridge, and turned Nahl’s stool to face west. The nine rules permit it, for those who are travelling. Vellum Reach had never once needed it before.

Ahead of them, the grey road ran down to the river. The river ran down to the counties. Somewhere past the counties were ninety-one names in a column, nineteen ticks in a box, a third heading nobody could read, and a girl with the best handwriting in the family, doing the sums carefully for strangers while her own brother’s name stood in the same column, waiting its turn.
And beyond the river, above the western peaks that had not been flown in two hundred years, something enormous turned over in its sleep at the smell of the wrongness in the arithmetic.
It had been asleep since the Ascension War. It was not one of the Twelve. It had never been to the Circle. The last thing it had done before it slept was refuse to be counted.
It shifted. It settled. It opened one eye. It considered the smell of a careful man tidying a sky, and did not care for it at all.
Riss did not know that yet.

What Riss knew, walking into the grey morning with a company and a plate and a sister’s handwriting in their pocket, was the thing the village had taught them across a year and eleven days without ever once making it into a speech. A remainder is not a wound to be healed, and it is not a crime to be tidied.
A remainder is a person who has not yet been asked what they are for.

The fire was out. That was the official position. Downriver, in a room that smelled of mint and polished wood, a clerk on night duty copied a market column into a long book, initialled the row, and marked it clean.
Everything had been read, and counted, and closed.
And the road came up out of the stones anyway, grey, west, and pointing at the only person in the world who could read it.

chapters.label: Chapter 1
chapters.title: The River
paragraphs: After the grey road came up out of the stones, they went down to the water, and the water did not care about any of it.

That was the first comfort of the journey, and Riss took it. Rivers go the way rivers go. You can put a company on a barge, and a copper plate under a coat, and a sister’s handwriting in a pocket, and the river carries all of it at the same weight, and asks nothing.

They had left Vellum Reach at dawn. Maris walked the first mile with them, carrying bread, salt, and a knife. At the bend she handed the bread over, and the knife to Nahl, and the salt to Riss, and she did it the way a woman hands tools to people she expects to come back. Then she turned around and went home to her stall, because there was bread to sell, and because a long goodbye is a way of asking somebody to stay.

The barge was called the *Tin Kettle*. The name was painted on the bow in letters that had been repainted so often they looked as if they were arguing with each other. The barge-master was a woman named Becks. She had one eye, two poles, and a great many opinions. She took their coin, looked them over one at a time, and said she did not carry goats.
The goat was already aboard.

Nobody had seen it come on. Becks said the goat had to go. The goat stood on the cargo, put its crooked head down, and looked at her. Becks looked back. Something passed between them that Riss did not see and that Becks never explained. She spat over the side, picked up her pole, and went to work. The goat stayed. Goats have veto. Everyone in the company had learned that in a different village, and none of them had learned what to do about it.
So they went downriver with a goat, which Becks mentioned to every lock-keeper they passed for the next three days.

There were four things in the company that were not objects and had been packed anyway, and Riss had carried all four out of the loft in the crate with the sticking window, and had not once written any of them down.
The first was the square, on the night the grey road came up out of the stones.

The second was what they had been holding when they walked out of it, which was a plate of copper, wrapped in a cloth, humming a fifth that was split down the middle and had no business being two notes.
The third was the sister downriver, whose handwriting was in Riss’s pocket on the back of a county form, in three lines, the last of which said *come back when you can say what you took*.
The fourth was that they had been happy in Vellum Reach for about seven months, and had spent the five months since waiting for the bill.

Nobody in the company had asked about any of the four. That was not a courtesy and it was not a conspiracy. It was the same reason nobody asked Corvath what he smelled or Old Den what he had done with ten thousand men: a company that is going to walk four hundred miles together has to give each other somewhere to keep the worst thing, or the road turns into a series of confessions and nobody gets any distance.

The river counties came up slowly, in the way of a country that has never needed to hurry. The near bank was willows and wet grass, and the far bank was barley going gold, and every mile or so there was a lock with a keeper’s house and a garden and a child on the gate. At the first lock, a girl of about seven recited the carrier’s rule at them from the top of the gate, all in one breath, the way a child recites a thing to prove she can.
*Two hands, two eyes, no names in the pot.*
Nahl raised one hand to her, which the rule allows, and she looked pleased and then suspicious, because she was seven and had not yet decided what adults were for.
At the second lock the keeper kept a book.

He was a small, exact man of about sixty with his sleeves rolled and his hands wet, and the book was on a lectern by the gate, because the county required every lock-keeper to enter every boat: the barge, the master, the cargo, and the number of persons aboard. He had been entering boats in that book for thirty-one years. The pages were ruled in four columns and the ink was good.
He wrote the *Tin Kettle* and Becks and the cargo, and then he asked, without looking up, for the names of the persons aboard.
Nobody answered him.
He looked up. He looked along the deck: a company in ordinary clothes, one goat, a crate of seedlings, a roll of blank chart, a plowshare laid along the gunwale like a tool somebody meant to use.
“I need the names,” he said. “It’s the form. It goes to the county and the county counts the crossings.”
“There aren’t any names,” said Riss.
“There are always names.”

And there were, and that was true, and the company stood on the deck of the *Tin Kettle* in the sun and did not give him one. It was not a plan they had agreed and it was not a refusal they had thought about. It happened the way the goat happened. Somebody had asked for a name and nobody in the party had one they were willing to put in a column.
The keeper waited. He had the patience of a man with a wet lock and a ledger, and he had clearly done this before with other people, and he had clearly won those arguments, and this time he did not.
“Then I’ll enter it as it is,” he said, at last, and wrote something short in the fourth column in a neat hand, and shut the book, and took the coin, and opened the gate.
Mira went and looked at the page over his shoulder while the water came up, because she was a mapmaker and could not help it.
“What did you write?”
“*Party of no account,*” the keeper said. “*No names given.*”
“That’s a description, not a name.”

“That’s what I have,” said the keeper, and it was the first time in the book that anybody said a sentence that Riss would still be thinking about four months later, standing in the west of the world. “It’s not my book. I just keep it.”

Nahl wrote it in the Leaf that evening, in the small hand they used for things that were not arithmetic: *the first man to ask us for a name wrote nothing, and he had a form, and the form required it, and there was no second column for a party of no account to go into.*

They worked the barge the way Becks told them to and no other way. Mira sat at the stern with the Wound-Chart across her knees and forty feet of blank parchment rolled beside her like a sleeping animal. She had drawn the river to the first bend and no further, and when Riss asked why, she said the blank part was the point. You cannot lie about a road you have not drawn yet.

Veylan kept his crate of seedlings tied where the spray would not reach it. He watered them twice a day from a jug Becks called a nuisance and then stopped calling a nuisance after the third day, when one of them came up. Sancora sat with her two satchels and watched the banks like a woman reading a list of things that could go wrong. Corvath poled when Becks let him, which was most of the time, with the plowshare laid along the gunwale where he could see it. Old Den stood at the bow with his arms folded and said very little, which was usual, and watched the water ahead, which was not.
Kael sat near the middle of the barge with the slate on his knees and did not open it. That was the first day. On the first night he opened it.

They made camp on the towpath where Becks tied up for the night. Bread came out, and the salt, and the knife. Becks told a story about a lock-keeper who had tried to charge her for the sound of her own bell. Everyone laughed except Old Den, who said the man had probably needed the money. That was also true. The two of them looked at each other and did not argue. That was how the company had learned to handle Old Den.
Riss took the first watch, because they usually did, and because the first watch was the one where you were left alone with the fire and the river and whatever you had brought with you.

Nahl came and sat down beside them without being asked; that was what Nahl did. The Bearer’s Seal sat quiet at their chest in the dark, not glowing, not asleep, just present, the way a good tool is present. The cloak the colour of wet ash took the firelight and gave nothing back.
They sat for a while. The river went on with its work.
“Ask me,” Riss said at last, because Nahl had been sitting there for a quarter of an hour and had not asked anything, and the not-asking had a shape to it.
“All right.” Nahl looked at the fire, not at Riss. “The plate. What does it want?”
Riss did not answer.

It was not that they did not have an answer. They had four answers, and all of them came out wrong. The plate wanted to be carried. The plate wanted to be read. The plate wanted to be put back in the fire where it belonged. The plate wanted nothing, because it was a piece of copper, and the wanting was Riss’s.

Nahl waited. Nahl was very good at waiting. Nahl had once been filed, Riss knew, and had walked out of the file with their name still attached, and had never once said what it cost. Waiting was part of the trade.
“I don’t know,” Riss said, which was one of the four answers and the least useful.
“Good,” said Nahl.
Riss looked at them.

“You keep expecting me to be disappointed when you don’t know a thing,” Nahl said. “I’m not. I’m the Bearer. I carry what people hand me. When somebody hands me a wrong answer, that’s worse than a hole.” They turned their hands over in the firelight. “I asked so you’d know the question can be asked. That’s all. The plate can stay under your coat.”
Riss put a hand flat over the coat, over the plate, and felt it not hum. It was quiet tonight. That was almost worse than the humming. The humming at least meant something was happening.
“Does yours do that?” Riss said. “Go quiet.”

“Mine is always quiet,” Nahl said. “That’s the whole work. It’s quiet and it stays. That’s the promise.” They were silent a moment. “I’ll tell you a thing I’ve never put in a report. When they filed me, I didn’t lose anything I could point to. I lost the shape of what I would have been if they’d let me be it. A hole you can draw. This was more like a room they carried away and left the floor.”
Riss said nothing. There was nothing to say that was not smaller than the thing.
“That’s why I ask about the plate,” Nahl said. “Because you keep it under your coat like it might hear you.”
They sat a while longer. Down the bank, Corvath’s shadow lay in the firelight, and did not sit down, and nobody had commented on it in two years.
Then Kael made a sound, and Riss looked up.

Kael was at the edge of the firelight with the slate open on his knees. He had a piece of charcoal in his burned hand, which he used when he wanted to feel the mark as well as see it. He was trying to trace the bread-woman.
He had tried it in the square, the day he came home. He had tried it on the road. He was trying it again, on the first night out, because that is what a man does with a thing he cannot put down.

Kael’s trade was looking. He was the best trace-witness on the eastern road. He could find the edge of a thing that was gone, and mark it, and leave a place where the next person could put their hand. Missing had a shape, he always said. A hole has edges.

He worked for a while. He did not hurry. He made three marks and checked them the way he had been taught. Then he made a fourth. Then he sat back and looked at the slate for a long time, and Riss watched the firelight move on his face, and could see the exact moment he understood that it was going to be the same as it was in the square.
There was no edge. There was nothing to put a hand on.

Kael closed the slate. He did not snap it shut or throw it. He closed it the way you close a book you have finished to your own dissatisfaction, and he wrapped the cord, and he put it under his pack, and he did not take it out again.
“Nothing,” he said, to nobody in particular.
“There’ll be something else,” Mira said, from the dark, because she had not been asleep either.
“There’ll be something else,” Kael agreed. He did not sound convinced.

Riss thought he had done the braver thing. Not the trace. The putting away. A trace-witness who cannot find an edge and will not manufacture one is worth more than a company of men who can find edges they put there themselves. But they did not say so. It would have sounded like praise, and Kael had not done anything but refuse to lie. That should not need praising. It should be ordinary.
Riss took the second watch too, and gave the third to Nahl, and did not sleep, and watched the fire, and thought about a room they had carried away.
In the morning the grey road was ahead of them.

Mira found it. She had walked the towpath at dusk the night before, the way she walked every new road, because a mapmaker who does not walk the ground she is about to draw is just a woman with opinions. There had been no line on the towpath. She had checked twice, once with the lamp and once without, and she had drawn nothing, because there had been nothing to draw.
Now, in the grey light before the sun, there was a line.

It ran along the bank at the water’s edge, thin and even, and it was the colour of wet ash. It was not a path: no ruts, no stones, no wear. It lay on the ordinary ground the way a scratch lies on glass, as if the ground had been there first and the line had been put in afterward by someone who was not quite done.
Riss got off the barge and stood over it. The plate was cold under their coat (cold on the side that had faced the fire), and otherwise quiet.

“It wasn’t there last night,” Mira said. She was already down on one knee with charcoal, and then she stopped, because she had promised herself something in a village a long way back about the lines she would not draw.
“It’s the colour of the grey road,” Riss said. “From the square.”
“It’s the same colour,” Mira said. “I don’t know if it’s the same line.”

They tested it the obvious way, because they were practical people. Becks poled the *Tin Kettle* out into the current and went on downriver, the way the barge was going anyway. The line stayed on the bank for a hundred paces. Then it came out onto the water.

Not a bridge. Not a ford. It lay on the surface of the river like a scratch on glass, and it ran downstream, and the barge went downstream, and the line kept pace. When Becks slowed, the line slowed. When she stopped, it stopped, a little ahead of them, waiting, the way a dog waits for a walker who has stopped to tie a boot.

Nobody said anything for a while. Veylan put his trowel down. Sancora’s hands went still on her satchels. Old Den came back from the bow, which he had not done all the first day, and looked at the line, and then looked at his own boots, which were standing on the deck beside it, on the ordinary barge, on the ordinary river.
“What does it want?” Kael said.
“That,” said Nahl, “is the wrong question, and we should stop asking it.”
They all looked at Nahl. The Bearer’s Seal was quiet at their chest.

“Ask what it’s for,” Nahl said. “A road is for going somewhere. This one came to us. It didn’t have to. That means it was sent, or it means it’s following, and either way somebody upstream of it thinks we’re going the right way.” They looked down at the grey line keeping pace along the water. “Or they think we should be.”

Corvath made a low sound, not quite a word. He was standing at the gunwale with the plowshare in his hand. He had tasted the air twice since dawn, the way he did, and had said nothing about what he found.

“It smells of nothing,” he said, when they looked at him. “Same as the market. Same as the square.” He set the plowshare down. “I would very much like to smell something. Even a bad thing. A bad thing is a thing.”

The goat walked to the gunwale, put its crooked head over the water, and looked at the grey line for a long moment. Then it turned around and lay down on Veylan’s seed crate, which Veylan did not protest, because he had learned that a goat which has decided something does not negotiate.

Riss stood at the rail with one hand on the plate and one on the warm wood, and did the thing they had come four hundred miles to stop doing and had not yet managed to stop: they counted. One line in the square, on a night in Vellum Reach. One line on the towpath, on the first night out. One line on the water, going the way they were going.
Not a road home. Not the gold. The other one.
“Becks,” Riss said. “How far to the first big market?”
“Two days,” Becks said. “If the river’s kind.”
“It won’t be,” said Old Den, from the stern, with his arms folded, because someone had to say something true before breakfast.

Becks laughed, which she did rarely and loudly, and pushed off, and the *Tin Kettle* went downriver with the company on its deck and the goat on the seedlings and the grey line running alongside, keeping pace, patient as arithmetic.

chapters.label: Chapter 2
chapters.title: The First Village
paragraphs: After two days on the river, the *Tin Kettle* came to a village called Collow, and Collow had already taken the stamp.

Veylan saw it from the water before he saw anything else. The landing stage was new. You could tell by the planks: cut square, laid even, no rot in them, no repairs. A village does not build a stage like that with its own money. It builds one like that when somebody pays.
There was a signboard at the head of the stage, painted in good clean letters, and under the village name were two words. *Collow. Clean.*
“They’ve got a sign,” Mira said.
“A sign,” said Veylan.
“With the word on it.” Mira looked at the signboard longer than a sign is worth looking at. “*Clean.*”
Veylan did not laugh. He had spent a lifetime being corrected and had made a discipline out of it, and one of the disciplines was knowing when a joke was being used to carry something heavy.

They tied up. Becks took their coin for the last leg and said she would be going back upriver at dawn, and that she did not intend to wait for anybody. She said it kindly. She also said, looking at the signboard, that she had been bringing goods to Collow for nine years and had never once seen a sign on that stage.

They walked up from the water into the market. Riss walked with one hand flat over the coat, where the plate lived, and did not take it out. The goat had got off the barge without being asked and was already ahead of them, standing in the middle of the lane as if it had been sent.

The market was busy. That was the first surprise, and Veylan made himself notice it properly, because a busy market is not what a frightened village looks like. There were stalls. There was bread. Two women were arguing about the price of thread in the good-natured way that means the argument is a habit and not a quarrel. A boy was minding a goat. A man was mending a net.

The second surprise was the sacks. They were stacked along the north wall of the square, forty or fifty of them, and every one carried the same small printed mark: a tick inside a circle, and under the tick, one word. CLEAN.

The third surprise was the drinking fountain. It stood in the middle of the square where a fountain should be, and it was covered with boards, and tacked to the boards was a printed notice. *Held for testing.* The boards had been there long enough to have gone grey at the edges.
Children used to drink at that fountain. Veylan could tell, because there were worn places on the stone rim, two of them, at exactly the height of small hands.

He stood in the square and did the thing his trade had taught him, which was to look at the ground. Under the flagstones around the fountain, the earth was dark and loose. Somebody had been digging there, and not long ago, and then had put the stones back.
He wrote nothing down. He did not want to be seen writing.

Mira had the chart out before they were an hour in the village, because Mira could not help it. She sat on the low wall at the market’s edge with the Wound-Chart across her knees and drew what she saw: the square, the fountain, the stages, the north wall with its sacks, the lane to the mill.
Then she wrote one word beside it.
Veylan came and looked over her shoulder. *Amended.*
“Why that word?” he said.

“Because it’s the honest one.” She kept drawing. “A map of Collow sixty years ago would have had a fountain runnin’ and no sign on the stage. A map of it now has to have the boards and the ticks and the sign. So the village got amended. That’s what you call a document that’s been changed by somebody who wasn’t the person who wrote it.” She put the charcoal down. “I’ll draw the village as it is. But I’ll label it as what was done to it.”
“That’s a mapmaker’s quarrel,” Veylan said.
“It’s a mapmaker’s job,” said Mira.
The assessor’s table stood in the shade of the north wall, and it was, Veylan thought, the most ordinary table he had ever seen.

That was the thing about it. He had expected something else, he realised: a bench, a guard, a man in a heavy coat. Instead there was a light trestle with a green cloth over it, and a young clerk behind it with a ledger open and a brass rule laid square against the paper’s edge, and a queue of about a dozen people standing quietly in the shade, waiting their turn.

The queue was the part that unsettled him most, and it took him the walk across the square to understand why. The people in it were not afraid. They were patient. Two of them were talking about a wedding. A woman near the back was dandling a baby and letting it hold her finger. This was not a punishment queue. It was a market queue. It was as ordinary as bread. Nahl stood three paces from the table with the Bearer’s Seal quiet at their chest, did not join the queue, and was not asked to, which was its own kind of information.
The clerk saw the two of them come, and looked at their boots and their packs and their coats, and said, pleasantly, “Morning. Passing through, or here for the tally?”
“Passing through,” Mira said.

“Then you won’t need to be counted.” He smiled and turned to the woman at the head of the queue, who put a paper on the cloth, and the clerk squared his brass rule against it and began to read down the figures with his finger.
Veylan watched four tallies being taken. It took about the length of a song.

The clerk was not unkind. When one old man could not find his second page, the clerk waited. When a young woman’s figures did not add up, the clerk showed her where the slip was and corrected it in pencil for her, and told her to bring the clean copy next week. When the woman with the baby reached the front, the clerk asked after the child’s cough, and the woman told him it was better, and he said he was glad.

The fee was two pennies a tally. The clerk took the pennies, and stamped the paper, and handed it back, and the people went away with their stamped papers held carefully, and put them in pockets or sleeves or inside their coats.
“Why the stamp?” Veylan asked, when they were out of earshot.

Mira had been watching the queue too. “To prove which column you’re in,” she said. “Same as the grain. Same as the form. You show the stamp at the mill, and the mill gives you the allowance, or it doesn’t.”
“And if you don’t bring the tally at all?”
Mira looked at him. “Then you’re not in a column,” she said. “And a person who isn’t in a column isn’t anything yet. And anything is easier to move than something.”
The farmer’s name was Drem Mallow, and he had burned his tally in the spring.

He told them so himself, an hour later, when they found him outside his own barn on the lane past the mill. He was mending a harrow. He was a big man gone grey, with hands like a man who had worked every day of his life. He looked at their company (three of them had come up the lane) and then he straightened. It was the slow kind of look that prices you out of politeness and into honesty.
“You’re the ones off the barge,” he said.
“We are,” said Mira.
“You’ve come a long way to look at a stamp.”
“We have,” said Mira, “come a long way to look at what the stamp does.”

Drem Mallow considered that. Then he waved them into the barn, which was a thing Veylan had not expected, and it was there, in the cool and the dark and the smell of good dry hay, that the farmer told them about the spring.

“The assessor said bring your pages,” he said. “All of them. Every year, every line, and they’d read them and give us the count.” He picked up a piece of harness and turned it over. “And I did it, first year. I did it second year. Third year I looked at my pages and thought, that’s not a count, that’s an inventory. They’re not counting my grain. They’re counting me.” He set the harness down. “So in the spring I burned them. All of them. In my own yard, at night, quiet.”
“And what did they do?” Veylan asked.

“Nothing.” Drem said it flatly. “That’s the thing I want you to understand. Nothing at all. The clerk was very pleasant. He said, ‘Then it will be in the slate.’ He said it the way you’d say it about rain.”
Veylan had heard that sentence before, and it had not been in this village. He heard it again, and it sat in his chest like a swallowed stone.
“But you keep a copy,” Mira said.
Drem Mallow’s face did not change. That was how Veylan knew it was true.

In the hay, under three boards, in a tin box no bigger than a bread crock, Drem Mallow kept a copy of every page he had burned. Not written. He could not write, he said. Kept in his head, in the shape of a song he had made when he was young to remember the sheep, because a man who tends sheep learns early that the way to keep a count you cannot write down is to put it in a tune.
“How many years?” Mira said.
“Forty-one.”
“Say one.”
And Drem Mallow, in his own barn, in front of three strangers, sang a year of his farming.

It was not a good song. It had a bad tune and worse rhyming and a chorus about a wet spring. It listed the sowing and the reaping and the frost and the two ewes lost in the twelfth month and the price his father got for the wool. It took him about a minute and a half. When he finished, he stood with his hands on the harness, and he did not look at any of them, and there was water in his eyes that he ignored the way a man ignores rain.
“That’s the tally,” he said.
“That’s the tally,” said Mira.
They brought him to the square that evening, because Mira said they should, and because Veylan agreed, and because Kael said nothing at all, which in Kael’s case meant yes.

Drem Mallow did not want to. That was plain. He stood at the edge of the square with his hat in his hands and watched the assessor’s table with the queue thinning out in front of it, and he said, twice, that the man had always been decent to him.
“Then he can hear it too,” said Mira.
The clerk was packing his ledger when they came. He looked up, and he was pleasant, and he said it was past the hour, and the queue was closed.
“I burned my pages,” Drem Mallow said.
“Then it will be in the slate,” said the clerk.
“That’s what you said in spring. I’ve got a copy.”

The clerk stopped packing. He looked at the farmer for a moment, and then he did the thing that Veylan would remember longer than anything else that happened in Collow. He did not argue, and he did not call for anybody, and he did not look surprised. He looked *interested*. He sat back down, and he opened the ledger, and he said, “Recite it, then.”

So Drem Mallow recited a year of his farming, standing in the square of his own village, in the failing light of a good evening, out loud, to a clerk with a ledger, while eleven people who should have been at their suppers stopped in the lanes and listened.

He got to the second month. The clerk took it down. He got to the sixth month, the frost, the two ewes, and the clerk took that down too, and his brass rule stayed square against the paper the whole time.
At the end, the clerk read his figures back. They were right.

Across the square, Kael Riven’s burned hand closed slowly into a fist. The scar answered the way it always answered arithmetic it did not like, and Riss, standing back with the plate cold under their coat, felt it too.
“Very good,” the clerk said. He inked the last figure. “Now you’re in both columns.”
And he stamped the page, and offered it to Drem Mallow, and waited, pleasant as ever, while the farmer stood in the square and looked at the paper in the clerk’s hand and understood what he had done.

Veylan understood it too, one half-step behind, and understood that the man had walked them all into it. A tally that is burned is not a tally. A tally that is recited in front of witnesses, taken down in figures, initialled and stamped, is a tally twice over, and a name that is entered in two columns is a name that shares a factor.
Drem Mallow did not take the paper. He turned around and went home.
That night Veylan could not sleep, and neither, he found, could Nahl.

The oldest man in Collow was named Senn, and he was not hard to find, because he was the only person in the village who sat on the north wall and watched the assessor’s table with his arms folded and his jaw set, and had done it, Veylan gathered, for most of his life.

He was eighty-one. He had opinions about weather, daughters, and the price of nails, and he gave all three freely to Mira when she sat down beside him with the chart, which is how she got a conversation out of a man who did not do conversations.
*Did the stamps come in his lifetime?*
Not in his. In his da’s.

“When I were a boy of nine,” Senn said, “a man come from the county with a green table and a book, same as that lad down there. And he said, we’re going to write everybody down, so the towns can send us what we need and no more waste. And everyone said, that’s a good idea. And it *were* a good idea.” He spat, without malice, at a crack in the wall. “My da were one of the four that said no.”
“What happened to him?”

“Nothing.” Senn looked at Mira sideways, to see if she would not believe him. “Nothing at all happened to him. That’s what nobody understands about it. The man with the book were *polite*. He said, that’s your right, Senn. And then the allowance come down a quarter, because the allowance is for holdings that are counted, and we weren’t, and that were all.” He folded his arms again. “We ate less for three year. My brother went to the coast and never came back. And in the fourth year my da put his thumb on the paper, and the man with the book thanked him for it.”
Veylan was standing at the end of the wall, and he asked the question that had been in him since the barn.
“Did your father ever say why he changed his mind?”
Senn was quiet for a while.

“He said the village had got tired of being hungry on his account,” he said at last. “And that were true. And that’s the whole of the trick, son. They don’t need to break you. They need the village to get tired. Get five villages tired, and you’ve got a county, and the county does the work for you, and everyone in it thinks they chose.”
Mira wrote nothing for a long moment, and then she wrote one line under the word *amended*, and put her charcoal down.
“Two generations,” she said.
“Two generations,” Senn said. “And where’s your company from, that you find that surprising?”
Veylan dug the next morning, because that was the only thing he could offer that the village actually wanted.

The fountain was the village’s sorest subject. Senn’s granddaughter, a brisk woman named Halla who ran the mill’s office and had no patience for anybody, including, especially, her grandfather, had asked, when she heard there was a digger with the company, whether he might look at the boards and tell them whether the stone was sound. The village wanted its fountain back. She said it in a very level voice, the way people say things they have given up hoping for.
Veylan lifted the boards with Kael’s help and looked at the stone, and the stone was sound. The pipe was sound. There was nothing wrong with the fountain except the notice.

Then he did the thing he was for. He dug badly. He took the earth out in layers instead of in scoops, and looked at what came up out of each layer before he went on to the next. That is a discipline. It takes four hands, and it is the only way to find out what is under a floor without breaking what is above it.
He found the tin two hours later, eighteen inches under the fountain’s western footing, in the dark loose earth where somebody else had dug before him and had put the stones back.

It was flat and long and rusted at the seams, and it held paper. Forty or fifty sheets, wrapped in oiled cloth and tied with cord, and every sheet was a tally: names, years, grain, births, deaths, debts, the small untidy arithmetic of a village. The oldest sheet was dated sixty-one years earlier, in a careful hand, and signed at the bottom with a thumbprint instead of a name.

Senn’s father. The four who said no. He had buried the village’s real books under the fountain the year the man came with the green table, and had never told anyone, and had died without telling them.
Halla the mill-clerk knelt down in the mud in her good apron and looked at the sheets for a long time without touching them.
“These are ours,” she said.
“These are yours,” said Veylan.
She looked up at him, and she was not crying, and she was very angry, and she said, “What are they *for*?”
Nahl answered that, from the edge of the hole, in the voice of somebody who had once been filed and had walked out of the file with their name still attached.

“For a wider column,” Nahl said. “They wrote you down in two columns and left out the parts they didn’t need. This is the parts they didn’t need. Keep them. Add to them. Write everything: marriages, songs, quarrels, the names of the dead, the price of nails. The more of you there is on paper, the harder you are to round.”
Halla wiped her hands on her apron. “And who’s going to write it?”
“Your grandfather,” said Nahl. “He’s got the arms folded for it.”

They left Collow at first light, and the company’s packs were heavier by the weight of one flat tin box, lent to them by a village that had voted, in the square, that same evening, by raised hands and one abstention, to let the strangers carry a copy of their books downriver.
Drem Mallow came to see them off, and said nothing about the tally, and put four apples in Veylan’s seed crate without asking, which is the highest honour a farmer gives anybody.

Mira stopped at the edge of the village where the lane met the county road, and looked back at the square with the boarded fountain and the notice on it, and the north wall with the sacks, and the sign on the stage. She took out the chart and looked at the word she had written, and then, in front of them all, she wrote a second word under the first, and closed the roll.
“What did you put?” Veylan asked.
“*Amended*,” she said. “*Again.*”
They walked on. Behind them, two boys were already up ladders, taking the boards off the fountain, because the village had decided that morning that the water had been tested long enough.
Nobody sang the Interval in Collow at dusk. That had been the arrangement for eleven years.

But the children were at the fountain by mid-morning, and one of them, a girl of about six, Halla’s youngest, stood on the rim, and sang two notes at the top of her voice that did not fit together, and then laughed, and did it again.
The assessor’s clerk wrote the company’s names into his ledger that morning, in figures, and noted their direction, and sent a boy on a fast horse down the county road an hour before they left.
They did not see the rider. They saw the grey line, though: it was waiting for them beyond the last field, patient, keeping pace, running alongside the road the way it had run alongside the water.

And that evening, when they stopped, Kael Riven took out his slate for the first time since the river. He did not trace the bread-woman. He sat with the tin box open on his knees and traced Senn’s father’s thumbprint on the oldest sheet, and this time, because the man had put something down and kept it, the trace found an edge.
Kael sat looking at it for a long time. Then he closed the slate, and wrapped the cord, and put it away, and said, to nobody and to all of them:
“There’s an edge. There’s always an edge on a thing that was kept.”
Nahl looked down the road at the grey line.
“Then we keep everything,” Nahl said.

chapters.label: Chapter 3
chapters.title: The Interval
paragraphs: After the tin under the fountain, they walked north along the grey line for four days, and on the fourth evening they came to a village called Nettleford, where the people still sang the Interval, and where it no longer worked.

Riss heard it before they saw the village. That was the first wrong thing, because the Interval is not a thing you hear by accident. It is two tones that refuse each other, held by a lot of people at once, and it carries a long way across flat country at dusk.
What came across the fields to them was a clean fifth.
Riss stopped walking. Nahl stopped beside them, which is what Nahl did. Behind them, Corvath put his head up and tasted the air, and said nothing.
“That’s the Interval,” Mira said.
“That’s not the Interval,” said Riss.

Nettleford was a bigger village than Collow, with a mill and a market cross and two streets going up a hill. The people were friendly in the way of people who have decided that everything is all right.

It had taken the stamp as well. There was an assessor’s table at the market cross, smaller than Collow’s, and a queue that came and went all day with the ordinary patience of people buying bread. Nobody in Nettleford found the table remarkable. Riss watched a woman put her tally down, take her stamped paper, and tuck it into her sleeve without looking at it, the way you put away a coin.

They sang at dusk in the square. It was the ordinary practice, and Riss watched it done properly for the first time since Vellum Reach. A woman with a good voice set the two tones. The square took them up. Every person there, old and young, reached for the two notes that do not fit together.
And the notes fitted.
