Not because anybody sang them wrong. The woman pitched them a hair apart, exactly as they should be, and the whole square held them, and the air took the two and closed them into one clean chord, and the chord was beautiful, and it resolved, and it was finished.

People smiled. A man said, “There, that’s a good one.” Children were sent to bed. The square emptied in four minutes. Nobody stood around afterwards the way people stand around after the Interval in Vellum Reach, slightly shaken, checking each other’s faces.
Riss watched them go, and could not have said what was wrong with any of it.

That was the worst part of the evening, and they only understood it later when they were trying to get it onto paper. Not one person in Nettleford had done anything wrong. The practice was correct. The voices were good. Everything was right, and the whole thing was finished, and the Interval is a practice for people who are not finished.
“We should do it for her,” Mira said, that night, at the fire.
She meant the bread-woman. She did not say the name, because none of them could.

It was the ordinary custom. When somebody is gone and there is no grave, the village holds the Interval for them: not sad, not a service, just the two tones held in the air for a person, until the ear gives up wanting them to be one thing. Vellum Reach had done it twice in the two years Riss lived there. The first time, Riss had hated every second of it and had cried at the end without knowing why.
They stood in a circle by the fire and held the two tones.

Nahl held theirs flat and true. Riss sang badly, on purpose, the way the village had taught them, which is the only way it counts. Mira held hers under. Corvath had no voice at all and sang anyway, in a low growl that was more shape than sound. Old Den sang nothing, but he stood in the circle with his arms folded, and that was his way of being in it. Veylan sang as a man sings who has been corrected all his life and has stopped trusting his own ear.
Kael sang last, badly, with the burned hand held up, watching his own fingers.
And the two notes came together, and closed, and resolved.

Riss stood there in the dark with their mouth open and their skin cold, waiting for the thing that always happened at the end: the small unhappiness, the ear’s refusal, the sense of something left unfinished on purpose. It did not come. The chord was clean and finished and it had stopped.
And somewhere in the middle of that, Riss reached for the reason they had wanted it unresolved, and could not find it.

They knew there had been a reason. That was the frightening part. They remembered *having* a reason the way you remember a room you have not been in for years: the shape of it, the fact of it, and nothing inside. The Interval is supposed to end in unquiet. Riss stood in the dark trying to feel unquiet and felt instead a very great calm, and the calm was not theirs.
They looked at the others. Nahl’s face was shut. Mira had both hands over her mouth. Corvath was standing quite still with his head turned, tasting the air.
“It resolved,” Mira said, at last.
“It resolved,” said Nahl.
“I don’t remember why I wanted it not to,” said Riss.
Nobody answered that, because nobody could.
Later, when the others had gone to their blankets, Nahl sat down beside Riss at the fire.
“You wanted it unfinished,” Nahl said.
“I *know* I did.”

“Yes.” Nahl looked into the embers for a while. “That is what they take, in the end. Not the memory. The reason attached to it. A person can lose a name and still be a person. A person who has lost the reason she wanted a thing is agreeable, and agreement is all they have ever needed from anybody.”
Riss put another stick on the fire and watched it catch.

“In my country,” they said, “they never once asked me to agree to anything. That is what I could never explain to anybody here. There was no moment. Nobody ever made me sign. I simply woke up one year and the allowance was lower and everyone thought that was the weather.”
In the morning Corvath went round the village and smelled it.

He did it the way he always did: he walked, and he tasted the air at corners, and he stood in doorways longer than a stranger should stand in doorways. It was one of the few things Corvath did that still embarrassed the company, because the man had spent a century as the thing under the world and had never once learned how to be ordinary in public.
He came back to the fire at noon and sat down and said nothing for a while.
“Well?” said Mira.

“I have smelled this before,” said Corvath, “and I do not smell it now. I told you that in the square, at home. I am telling it you again, and I want it written down, because I do not think you understand what it costs me to keep saying it.”
“Say the rest,” said Nahl.

“There speaks nothing wrong here.” Corvath held his hands out flat, as if testing for rain. “The old hunger, the catalog, the thing that counted: it stank. It stank of closed rooms and wet paper and the inside of a filing-cabinet, and I could find it across a county. I have stood in this village all morning and smelled bread, mud, sheep, wet wool, a bad cistern, and a woman frying onions. That is all. This village smells *clean*.” He said the word the way a man says the name of a disease. “It smells like a sickroom that has been scrubbed.”
Old Den, from the wall, said, “Then it’s not here.”
“It is here,” Corvath said. “That’s what I’m telling you. It’s in the *sound*. Whatever is doing this has got in where the smell can’t reach.”
The girl’s name was Nell, and she was six, and she sang the Interval wrong on purpose.

Riss found her the second evening, at the back of the mill, alone, sitting on an upturned barrow. She was singing: two tones, held, deliberately off. She was making the notes disagree on purpose, in the ordinary childish way, because the Interval is the one song where singing badly is the whole point, and a child who has been told not to will do it the moment nobody is watching.
Riss stood at the corner and listened.
A woman came out of the mill door with a basket and said, kindly, “Nell, love, that doesn’t go like that anymore.”
“It goes like *this*,” said Nell, and sang it wrong again.
The woman laughed and went in and did not correct her a second time.
Riss waited a while, and then came round the corner. “That’s right,” they said. “That’s how it goes.”
Nell looked at them with the flat assessing look children give strangers. “I know,” she said. “They say I’m doing it wrong. I’m not doing it wrong. I’m doing the one where you don’t finish.”
There was nothing Riss could say to that, so they said the only true thing they had.
“You’re the first person in this village I’ve heard do it properly.”
“I know,” said Nell, and went on with her song.
They asked, because that was the whole job, and they asked the questions plainly, and they got answers that made the hair stand up on Riss’s arms.
*When did the Interval start coming out clean?*
Nobody knew.

That was the answer, in six different houses, from six different people, in six different words. The miller thought it had always been like that. His wife said no, when she was a girl it was different, she remembered her mother teaching it. Then she thought about it and could not say what was different about it, and laughed, and said she supposed she had a bad memory.
An old man said it used to leave him unsettled for a whole evening. He said it as a joke. He had just come back from singing it and he was eating his supper and he was entirely content.
*Was it two years ago? Five? Ten?*

They could not find the year. They could not even find the decade. And every person they asked, once they started thinking about it, got a small pleasant expression on their face and changed the subject.
Mira drew the square and wrote nothing on it at all, which was the loudest thing she did all week.

“It isn’t the ledger,” she said, that night. “It isn’t the tally fee. It isn’t the assessor. Those are the doors. This is the *house*.” She put the charcoal down. “Somebody has been in this village for years, and they did not take the bread or the water or the singing. They took the *not finishing*.”

Riss sat by the fire with the plate against their chest and did not sleep. They thought about a room they had carried away. They could not find the reason they had wanted it unresolved, and they knew, for the first time, exactly what the enemy wanted with them.

Mira drew the Interval that night, which was not a thing she had ever drawn before. She made two lines that started apart and came together, and then she looked at it for a while and drew a small closed circle where they met, and wrote beside it: *this is what agreement looks like on paper.* Then she rolled the chart and said nothing else for the rest of the evening.

The shepherds came down out of the western hills on the third afternoon, and they were the same shepherds, or near enough, that the company had been told to look for: four men and a girl, hard as wire, with a dog that had opinions.
They came down for the market and the salt, and they did not talk to anybody about stars, because shepherds do not.

Riss sat with them anyway, because a fire is a fire. They bought bread and gave a little away, which is the way to be allowed to sit at a shepherd’s fire. Nobody asked anything about arithmetic. Nahl had been very clear about that, and Riss had understood.
It was the girl who taught them the count, in the end, without meaning to.

She was about eleven, and she was bored, and she had a stick, and she was pointing at the sky with it the way a bored child points at things. She was counting a constellation the way she had been taught, out loud, to herself: *one, two, three, four*, and she was pointing at the joints of the wing, the way you teach a count to a child, one point per joint.
Riss watched her do it and did not say a word.
Fifteen.
She got to the end and stopped. Then she frowned, and started again from the other end of the sky, which is the oldest check there is, and got fifteen again.
“Fifteen,” she said, to the dog, in an ordinary voice, as if reporting the price of wool.

Her name was Bryn, and she thought Riss was strange, and she said so. They traded a piece of Mira’s bread for a piece of her hard cheese, which is how shepherds and travellers come to an understanding, and they sat together for a while and watched the light go. She said the winter had been long and the lambs had come late and her uncle had a bad knee. She said nothing else about stars, because there was nothing else to say. They were up there every night. They were the ceiling.

Riss counted it themselves, twice, later, alone, with their own pointing. Sixteen joints the shepherds had taught for five hundred years. Fifteen in the sky. One joint of the wing simply was not there. The other fifteen stood in the right places at the right distances, and the shape still read as a dragon, and a child could still point at it and say the name.

Nobody up on the hills was troubled by it. That was the thing. The shepherds had noticed, in the way shepherds notice weather. They had adjusted, in the way shepherds adjust. The adjustment had gone into the teaching. The children were learning fifteen, and in a generation the number would be fifteen everywhere, and sixteen would be a thing old men were wrong about.

They did not say any of this to the shepherds. Nahl had been very clear. The shepherds were witnesses, not interpreters. You do not hand a man your arithmetic and ask him to carry it. You let the count be what the count is.
Riss wrote it in the Leaf’s margin that night, in Halwen’s own style: *fifteen. Confirmed twice, from both ends. Not dim, not fallen, not moved. The teaching is already adjusting.*
The plate went cold on its fire-side at the shepherd’s fire, and then it hummed.

Riss had not asked it to. Nobody had touched it. It was the hour before dawn. Riss was awake with the dog and the last of the embers. The plate lay against their chest under the coat, and the fire-side of it went cold, colder than the night, colder than metal has any business being. Then, from the other side of the cold, it hummed.
A fifth.
Riss sat up very slowly and put their hand flat over the coat and listened with their hand, which is the only way to listen to a thing that hums.

It was not the divided fifth. Riss had lived with the divided fifth for two years and knew it the way you know your own cough. This one came up clean. Two tones, a hair apart, closing into one chord, holding, resolving. It was the exact sound that had come across the fields to them on the road, and out of the square at dusk, and out of the mouths of their own company the night they sang for the bread-woman.
The plate hummed that. Clean. Finished. Agreeable.

Riss sat in the dark with their hand over it and was more frightened than they had ever been. The divided fifth had always meant *something is wrong and I have brought it with me*. A clean fifth meant *something has been settled*. Riss did not know whose settlement it was.

Three paces away, Kael Riven woke up and put his burned hand over his own forearm, where the scar was. The scar had answered the plate for two years, always the same way, always when the fifth was divided.
It answered this one too.
The goat, who had been lying with its back to the fire, got up, turned its head to the west, and stood facing the peaks. It did not move again until the sun came up.
Riss went out of the camp and stood at the edge of the ridge in the grey before dawn, with the plate humming its clean fifth against their chest, and looked west.
The peaks stood up black against the coming light, three of them, and the country under them was not theirs.
And the grey road was already there.

It ran along the top of the ridge, thin as a scratch on glass, the colour of wet ash, going west. It had not been there the evening before. Riss had walked that ridge at dusk with Mira, twice, because Mira did not draw roads she had not walked.
Riss stood and looked at it for a long time.
Behind them, in the village, Nell would be waking up, and would sing two notes that did not fit together before breakfast, and would be told, kindly, that it did not go like that anymore.

The plate hummed. The goat faced west. And out where the road went, past the last field of the counties and up into a country that had not been flown in two hundred years, something enormous had already turned over twice in its sleep before anyone in the world had thought to ask it anything.
Riss put their hand flat on the coat and held the note, and did not know whether they were carrying the plate or the plate was carrying them.
Then the sun came up over the ridge, and the grey road caught the light, and did not shine.

chapters.label: Chapter 4
chapters.title: The Reconstruction
paragraphs: After Nettleford, and the shepherds, and the clean fifth at the fire, they walked two days north to a mill town called Ashenford, and Ashenford kept its books the way mill towns keep them, in two places.

Riss knew that before they arrived, because Riss had grown up in a country of two columns. They knew it the way you know the smell of your own kitchen. There is the column the mill keeps, which is about grain, and there is the column the market keeps, which is about money, and the two of them never meet except in a clerk’s head on a Tuesday.
Mira asked, on the road, why the two columns mattered more than the stamps.
“Because the stamps are what they show you,” said Riss. “The columns are what they *are*. A stamp is a door. The column is the room.”

Ashenford had two mills on one river, and a market square with a stone cross, and a miller’s office on the north side with a proper door and a proper lock on it. It also had an assessor’s table, and a queue, and a wall of CLEAN sacks, because by now the company had stopped being surprised.

They spent the first day doing nothing that mattered. That was Nahl’s instruction and it was a good one. You do not walk into a town with a ledger and ask to see its ledgers. You walk into a town and buy bread and mend a strap and ask where the mill office is, and by the second morning somebody has decided what kind of people you are.
On the second morning, the mill clerk found them.

Her name was Ivet Sallow, and she was about thirty, and she had ink on the side of her right hand and a way of standing that said she had been tired for a long time and had decided not to mention it. She came up to their table in the ordinary way and sat down without asking and said,
“You’re the ones asking about columns.”
“We are,” said Riss.
“Why?”
Riss considered lying and decided it would take too long.

“Because I want to know what happens to a person in a column,” Riss said. “I’m from the Burn. In my country we put everybody in one, every year. I’ve never once seen the inside of the book that does it.”
Ivet Sallow looked at them for a while.
“Nobody’s ever asked me that,” she said. “They ask me what the fee is.”
She gave them the records. Neither Riss nor Nahl ever worked out why.

She did not sneak. That was the strangest part. She walked them into the mill office in daylight, past the boy who swept the floor, and unlocked the press herself, and put two ledgers on the table, and stood there with her hand still on the cover of the second one.

“Market column,” she said. “Mill column. Both from the year the bread-woman’s stall went quiet. I pulled them when I heard somebody up the valley was asking questions about a …” she stopped, and started again. “About a woman who doesn’t have a name anymore.”
“Does it have to go back?” said Nahl.

“No.” Ivet’s hand stayed on the cover. “I’m the one who files them. Nobody has looked at the mill column in this town for four years. If I put them back you’ll never see them again, and I’ll go home, and I’ll think about it for the rest of my life.” She pushed the second ledger across the table. “I want to see what you do with it.”

Nahl stood at the door the whole time. Not blocking it. Standing in it, with the Bearer’s Seal quiet at their chest, which is a different thing, and Ivet Sallow glanced at them twice and went back to the ledgers.
Before she let them start, Ivet asked Riss the question nobody in the counties had ever asked them.
“You keep saying the Burn. What is it? Say it plainly. I’ve heard four versions and all of them are about dragons.”

“There are no dragons in it,” said Riss. “It’s a country with a column and one number. Every year gets a figure. If your holding divides into it, you’re a seed. If it doesn’t, you’re a remainder. Those are the two boxes on the form.”
“Divisibility,” said Ivet Sallow, and something in her face changed, because she was a clerk and it was her own trade being described back to her. “That’s all it is.”

“That’s all it is,” said Riss. “You hand in your year’s figures, the clerk does the sum, and the sum decides which box your children go to school in. Nobody shouts. Nobody drags anybody. It’s a Tuesday.”
It took Riss four hours to lay the figures out.

They did it on the long table in the mill’s back room, with the shutters half closed, because a page of numbers in a window draws the wrong kind of attention. Mira sat at the end and wrote down nothing at all. Kael sat with the slate closed. Corvath stood outside the door with the plowshare against the wall, and Old Den stood beside him, and the two of them took turns being the reason nobody came in. Corvath tasted the air twice through the afternoon. He got the mill’s grain, the river, the oil on the wheel, and the boy who swept the floor. He got nothing else, and said so once, and nobody asked him again.
The market column was about bread. Every seller in the market, every day, and what they sold, and what they were paid. Riss read down it twice and found her.
*Bread-woman. Two loaves. Paid.*
That was the whole entry. Not a name. It was written in the column the way you write a thing you expect to see again tomorrow.
The mill column was about grain. Every sack that came into the mill, and who brought it, and what it was worth, and what the mill gave back. Riss read down it twice and found her.
*Grain-woman. One sack. Paid.*

Same woman. Riss knew it was the same woman, and could not have told anybody how. She came to the market with two loaves on a tray and a laugh you could hear across the square, and she came to the mill with a sack on her back, and in the market column she was a seller and in the mill column she was a supplier, and both columns used the same three words about her, in the same order, in the same hand.
Two accounts. One person. Nothing about her name anywhere on either page.
“They’re both her,” said Mira.
“They’re both her,” said Riss.
“Then add them,” said Mira. “Two accounts is two accounts. That’s more than we had this morning.”
So Riss added them.
They were careful. That was the thing Riss wanted the others to understand afterwards, and the thing that made the whole business so much worse than a theft.

Nobody had made an error. The figures were good. The market column balanced to the penny against the day-slates. The mill column balanced to the pound against the sacks. Riss checked every entry she appeared in, twice, the way Halwen had taught them to check a bad sheet, and the arithmetic was honest from the top of the page to the bottom.

They reconciled the two columns the way a clerk reconciles anything: they lined the year up, month by month, and put the market figures beside the mill figures, and looked for the woman in both. She was in both. Every month. Two entries, one person, sitting side by side on a page for a whole year.

And when Riss added her up, the way you add a person (the loaves and the sack, the money in and the money out, all of it), the sum came out *clean*. The columns agreed. The totals matched. There was not one penny of slippage anywhere in that page.
And the bread-woman was not in the total.
Riss did it again. Slower. Then a third time, writing the working in the margin, the way they would have shown Ness.

The sum was correct. It was correct every time. The woman was in both columns and she did not come out of either of them, and the reason was not a mistake and not a fraud and not a hidden page. The two accounts of her shared a factor. The market column knew her as a seller of two loaves, and the mill column knew her as a supplier of one sack, and everything either column knew about her had gone through that one shared figure in the middle, and a figure that goes through two columns can be taken out of both and leave nothing behind it.
There was no name to be missing. There was no line that had been inked out. There was nothing to point at and say *here, this is where they did it.*
There was just a sum that had been done properly, and a woman who had been divided out of it.
Riss sat back and looked at the page for a long time.

“It’s not taking,” they said, at last. “I’ve been saying it wrong since the square at home. It isn’t taking. Nobody took her. You can’t take a thing that’s still there.” They put a finger on the middle of the page, between the two columns. “This is what’s left of her. This is the whole of it. This is the page after you’ve done the sum honestly.”
The room was quiet. Outside, a cart went past on the stones, and a man swore at a wheel, and the ordinary afternoon went on.
“What do you call that,” said Mira. “In your country. What’s the word for what’s left.”
And Riss said the word, and until that moment they had never once said it in a country that was not their own.
“Remainder,” they said.

Kael Riven opened his eyes. His burned hand was lying flat on the table, and the scar had gone tight and pale along the back of it, the way it went when the plate hummed, and he looked at it and did not say anything, because there was nothing to say that was not already on the page.

Mira wrote it down. One word on a clean sheet, at the top, and under it the two columns in miniature, and a single line from one to the other with the shared figure in the middle, and around the shared figure a small circle.
Then she sat looking at the circle for a while.
“That’s not a person,” she said. “That’s the shape of where a person was.”
“That’s the remainder,” said Riss.
Kael had been quiet all afternoon. Now he pulled the slate out from under his pack, opened it, and set it on the table beside Mira’s sheet, and tried to do the thing he was for.

He was not tracing the woman. There was nothing to trace, and he had known that for a month. He was tracing the *shared figure*: the one in the middle of Mira’s circle, the one that both columns had gone through. If the figure existed, it had been written. If it had been written, it had an edge.
He worked with the charcoal in his burned hand, and he worked slowly, and he took his time, and Riss watched him and did not interrupt.
At the end of it he sat back and looked at the slate, which was empty.

“There’s no edge on it either,” he said. “It’s not a thing that was written and rubbed out. It’s not a thing that was taken.” He closed the lid with his thumb. “There’s an edge on a thing that was kept. There’s no edge on a thing that was added up.”
Nahl came and stood at the end of the table and looked down at the page for the first time.
“Say the rest of it,” Nahl said.

“The rest of it is that we can’t fight this.” Riss put both hands flat on the table. “That is the thing I have been walking to for a month. We cannot fight it. There is nothing to hit. There is no beast. If we go to Ashenford’s assessor and put a knife in him, the columns do not care. They will keep agreeing with each other. Somebody else will sit at the table on Monday and the fee will be the same fee.” Riss looked up. “It has one weakness. It cannot put a person back together, because it never had the parts. But it also cannot take a part away if we keep the part somewhere it can’t reach. So the answer is not fighting. The answer is keeping. Every page. Every song. Every name. Even the ones nobody thinks matter.”
“It’s your rule from the first village,” said Old Den, from the doorway. “The one the Bearer said in the square.”
“It’s the company’s rule now,” said Riss.
Nahl did not say it again. Nahl did not need to. It was already the way everybody in the room was standing.
Veylan was the one who asked the practical question, because that was Veylan.
“Keeping pages is a fine rule,” he said. “But a page is a page. If the counties want to divide us, they’ll divide a page. What does keeping look like, when the thing doing the dividing is a *book*?”

Riss had thought about that on the road for four days, and had not said it out loud, because it had sounded stupid every time they tried it in their head. They said it anyway, on the table, with the two columns still in front of them.
“A wider column,” they said. “You can’t divide a page you can’t get your arms around.”
Mira looked up.
“Tell me that again,” she said.

“The document wins because it’s narrower than the life,” said Riss. “Two loaves and one sack is a narrow account of a woman. It fits in a column. So the column can hold all of her, and there’s nothing left over to keep.” They put a hand flat on the page. “So you make the account wider than the document. Her name. Her mother’s name. The tune she hummed when the dough was slow. Who she lent money to. Who she laughed at. The smell of her stall. Every quarrel she ever had, written down, in her own village’s book, multiplied until no two columns can agree about her neatly anymore.”
“Because the more there is of her, the less she fits,” said Mira.
“Because the more there is of her, the less she fits,” said Riss.
Sancora, who had not spoken since the mill yard, said, “That’s a diagnosis. What’s the treatment?”
“Keeping,” said Riss. “Every village keeps everything, in its own hand, in its own book, and refuses to add itself up for anybody else.”
Mira wrote that down too. She put it under the word *remainder*, and she underlined it once, which was the most excited Mira Solas had been in four chapters.
They gave the ledgers back that afternoon, which cost them more than Riss had expected, and they left Ashenford at dusk.

Ivet Sallow walked them to the yard and shook nobody’s hand, because she was a clerk, and clerks in Ashenford did not shake hands. She said the mills would open at six and that she should get back. She said it twice. Then she went in and closed the door.

The company’s papers went through her office on the way out, the way travellers’ papers did, and she wrote their names in the strangers’ register in her small exact hand, and noted the date and the direction, which was the law. If anybody had been watching her closely they would have seen her pen stop on the last line for about three seconds.
They were not watching closely. They were gathering up their packs in the yard.
The box beside the last name stayed un-ticked.
The grey road was waiting for them beyond the last mill, running north along the riverbank, patient as arithmetic.

They walked out of Ashenford with the light going, and the town behind them showed its evening: windows lit, the mill wheel dark and still, smoke going straight up. Halfway up the hill, in the front room of the assessor’s office, a lamp was burning.
Somebody was still working. It was a small thing to see from a road, and Riss looked at it for longer than it deserved.
The plate hummed against their chest.

Not clean. That was the first thing Riss noticed, and it came with a feeling they could not name: something between disappointment and relief. It had hummed clean at the shepherd’s fire, three nights ago, and had not hummed at all since. Now it had come back to the divided fifth, the two tones held a hair apart and never allowed to close, the sound Riss had lived with for two years the way you live with a cough.
Riss put a hand flat over the coat and held it there, and listened to it, and did the arithmetic on it, because that was the only honest thing to do.

The clean fifth meant a thing had been settled. It had hummed clean at the shepherd’s fire, in a village whose song had been finished, in the same week the count in the sky went to fifteen and the goat turned to the peaks. Whatever had settled out there was still settled. That had not changed.

But the divided fifth was back. And Riss knew what it meant now, which was the new thing, and the bad thing. Two weeks ago the divided fifth had meant only *something is wrong and I have brought it with me*. Now Riss knew what the wrongness was, and where it kept its books, and how it did the sum. They knew the shape of the room the woman had been carried out of.
Riss walked, with their hand over the plate, and could not tell whether they were carrying it or it was carrying them.
Behind them, up the hill, somebody was still working at a desk with a lamp on it, doing arithmetic that balanced.

Ahead of them the grey road ran north, and the gold road came up out of the stones beside it, because it always did, and the two of them went on together through the dark without touching, and neither of them shone.

chapters.label: Interlude A
chapters.title: The Deletion Log
paragraphs: After the mill town with two columns, and the arithmetic that could not put the bread-woman back, and the word *remainder* said out loud for the first time in nine years, the road went on east without them.
North of that road, in a county seat called Carrow, there was a record room.
There is one in every county seat. They are all the same room. A stone floor. A grille on the window. Shelves from the floor to the height of a grown man’s hand. A clerk’s table with a lamp on it.
In the record room at Carrow there was a man of about seventy, and there was one book of his own among the parish copies.

The book sat on the third shelf of the southern wall. It was bound in the same cheap board as thirty others. It was shelved between the third volume and the fifth and it was catalogued with them, in the county’s hand, as *parish copies, unclaimed, south.*
That is what a thing must be if it is to sit on a public shelf in a building that opens at eight and closes at four.
The man’s name was Orphiel. He had been a clerk for fifty years. He had kept that book for forty of them.
He counted it every night.
He counted it in the record room, or in whatever room he was in, and it took nine minutes. It had taken nine minutes for forty years. It was not a superstition and it was not a prayer.

There was one other thing he did in that room, and it was not part of the trade. When he had finished the count he stood at the grille and looked west through it, and if the night was clear he could see the Emberion above the roofs.

Fifteen joints. A piece missing out of the wing. The counties had surveyed it in the fourth year of somebody’s reign and entered it in a volume and taken a fee off nothing at all, and it had gone on turning above the record room for two hundred years and had never once been amended.
It was a count.
He took the book down and opened it flat on the table. He counted the entries made since the last time he counted. Then he added the new ones to the number he carried in his head.
The number was nine thousand and four.
The book has four columns.
**Name. Date. Reason. Line.**
That is all. There is no fifth column. There is nowhere in it to write what he thought about any of them.
That is the whole design, and it is the only design that has ever worked.
A book with four columns is a book with a reason column. A reason column has to be filled. A filled column is a page. A page is a fact. And a fact is a thing a magistrate can be shown.
A deletion is two numbers made to agree.
Nobody outside the trade believes that. It is the whole of the trade.

A person is in two columns. A holding and a household. A market and a mill. A parish line and a fee. If the two figures can be made to agree, the person comes out of both of them at once, and there is nothing left behind.
It is not a burning. It is not a cruelty. It is a subtraction.
It can be done by a tired man at the end of a day with a lamp and a pen, and it leaves no mark on the paper at all.
Nine hundred and sixty-three pages at sixteen to a page.
Orphiel knew that number the way a miller knows the weight of a sack. It was one ordinary year’s work in one ordinary county, and he had done that work for four decades.
Every page of it came to him with the same three words at the top, in the county’s hand.
*At the family’s request.*
He had read that line eleven hundred and six times.
He had not chosen the work.

The ruling came down the shelf, the way everything comes down a shelf. A book that has been written down is a book that has been dealt with. That line was in a margin in a hand older than his own, and it had been copied into three rulings since, and it was the only law the room had.
The shadow of it was never written anywhere. Every clerk in the eleven counties knew it.
A book that is not written down is a book that is not dealt with.

So somebody had to keep the other book. Somebody had to hold the names that came out of the columns. Somebody had to hold them in a hand, on a shelf, in a room, so that the country could go on saying it did not keep them.
That was the post. It was not a rebellion and it was not a vocation.
It was a job with a shelf and a lamp and a table.
Four things make a room.
Orphiel had worked that out over fifty years. He had never written it down. He could say it in his sleep.
A clerk of record. A book. An unwilling person. And a party who can be answered by note.
Take away any one of the four and you have a place where things happen. A place where things happen is worth nothing. Nothing that happens is provable.
He had walked nine record rooms against those four. Only one had ever come close.
He did not put people in.
That was his own rule. It was in no ruling. No supervisor had ever asked him a direct question about it, and that was the whole of how it had survived forty years.
The log holds what has been taken out. It is a register of absences. It is not a register of the living.
A man who writes a living person into a book of absences has done the one thing the trade exists to prevent. He has entered somebody who is still there.

Twice in his life he was asked to. A family in the south, in a bad fever year, who wanted a daughter out of a holding. A magistrate who wanted a name out of a parish line so that a widow could keep her field.
He said no twice, in the same four words.
*I do not put people in.*
His wife had been dead for twenty-two years and she was not in the log.
A man who keeps a book of absences for forty years needs some private arithmetic about his own. That was his.

She had died of an ordinary thing in a bad winter. The parish clerk had entered her in the ordinary way. She had stayed in the parish book, where everybody else was, and no clerk in the eleven counties had ever had a reason to take her out of two columns.
So he had gone on for twenty-two years with a wife who was in the ordinary book and not in his.
He thought about that a great deal. It was the only argument he had ever found that the counties are not the whole of the world.
In the ninth month a page came back up the shelf with an amendment notice on it, and it was not the kind of page that usually came back.
It was a parish copy from a village in the south called Collow. It had gone out to a district office for a query and come back with a notice pinned to it.
*Amended.*
And under that, in the same hand, added later:
*Amended. Again.*
Orphiel looked at that page for a while.

A village amended twice is a village where somebody has been doing arithmetic and has had to do it again. It is not a scandal and it is not a crime. It does not go in any column. It is a clerk somewhere in the south who is tired.
He put the book back on the shelf and wrote nothing down about it, because there was nothing under it to write.
In the same quarter there was a query on his own desk that he could not answer.
That had never happened in forty years.
*A bread-woman. About forty. Two loaves at a market, one sack to a mill, in the south, nine years ago.*
That was the whole of it. It had come up the river from a district office with a request for a line.
Orphiel went to the shelf and took down volume four and turned to the ninth year before the last and looked for it.
The entry was not there.
Not a wrong one. Not an amended one. Not a rounded one. Nothing.
He sat with that for two nights. It was the only page of his professional life he had ever wanted to write a fifth column on.
In the tenth month a man came up from the ridge with a message from the Twelve.
The Twelve do not send for clerks. They have no court and no writ and no seal. They are twelve tired people around a cold fire, and what they have is a practice, and what a practice can do is ask.
The man was a farmer with dirt under his nails. He had no weapon and no letter. He stood in the record room with his hat in his hands.

“There is a party on the road in the south,” he said. “They have found a column with no reason in it. They have kept it and they are going to keep going. The Twelve ask whether there is a keeper who would walk with them and look at it, and say whether it is real.”
Orphiel looked at the man. Then he looked at the shelves.
“I keep what has been taken out,” he said. “I do not put people in.”
“That is not what is being asked,” said the man from the ridge.
“No,” said Orphiel, after a moment. “It is not.”

He tied the cord on his satchel. He did not take the log, and that was the only professional decision of his life he made in nine seconds. He wrote nothing in any book about where he was going or why.
At the door he stopped and looked back once, because he was seventy years old and a man of seventy looks back.

They want me to say whether a thing is real, he thought. They have come to the man who keeps the register of what has been made not to have happened. There is nobody else in the eleven counties whose word on that question would be worth anything at all.
That is the whole of what a witness is.
He shut the door of the record room behind him. It was the last time he was ever in it.

chapters.label: Chapter 5
chapters.title: The Assessor
paragraphs: After Ashenford, they walked three days north, and on the third morning the goat stopped.
It happened at the top of a long rise, with the county seat spread out below them in the flat valley light. Marrowgate was three times the size of Ashenford. It had a wall.
The goat walked up to the place where the grey road met the county road and stopped, and put its head down, and would not come on.

Riss tried first. They took the rope and walked on ten paces. They spoke to it the way you speak to a goat that has decided something, which is to say the way you speak to a wall that is being polite about it. The goat did not move. It was not frightened. Its ears were not back. It simply stood on the grey road with its crooked head turned toward the town, the way it had stood on the *Tin Kettle* when Becks told it to get off.

Then Veylan tried, because he had a way with animals from a lifetime of failing to have a way with people. Then Nahl, who had the patience of a bearer. Then Mira, who made the mistake of explaining to the goat why it should come, and got from the goat exactly the response a reasonable person gets from an unreasonable one.
After an hour they left it.

That was the strange part, and the company felt it more than any of them said. They had never left the goat behind. In Vellum Reach it had come aboard a barge nobody had invited it onto. It had walked the towpath with them, stood in two village squares, faced west on a mountain ridge at dawn. Now it stood on the grey road outside Marrowgate and would not come in, and every one of them understood, without being told, that they were being given a piece of information they could not yet read.
“We’ll come back for it,” Sancora said.
“Of course,” said Nahl.
Nobody said what everybody was thinking, which was that this was a county seat, and that people who went into county seats did not always come back out of them on the day they planned.
Marrowgate had a wall, and a gate, and at the gate a customs house, and the customs house was busy.

It was busy in a way the company had not seen yet. It was busy the way a market is busy, except that everybody in the queue was carrying paper. There were carriers with manifests. There were farmers with stamped tallies. There was a woman with a cart of cloth and a folded sheet of permissions with four different stamps on it. She was arguing, politely, with a clerk, about whether a fifth was required when the cloth had come up the river rather than down it.
The clerk was not unkind. That was becoming a theme of the whole journey and Nahl had begun to write it down: *nobody is ever unkind and that is the method.*

Corvath tasted the air in the customs house the way he tasted the air everywhere now, and got ink, and wool, and wet stone, and a hundred and forty people. He said so once, in a flat voice, and then stood against the wall with the plowshare and was quiet for the rest of the visit. Nobody asked him again. There was no point in asking a man to smell a thing that had got in where the smell could not reach.

They paid the gate fee, which was for the wall. They paid the customs fee, which was for the goods. They declared the tin box, because Veylan insisted. The clerk looked at the tallies inside it for a long moment with an expression that Nahl could not read. Then he wrote the box down in a column and gave them a paper for it.
Then the clerk said, in a pleasant voice, without looking up, “The Assessor’s office is on the north side of the square. Brass plate on the door. He’s expecting you.”
Nahl stopped writing.
“He is?”

“He is, yes.” The clerk stamped something and handed it over. “You’re the company with the tin. Somebody sent word up from Ashenford. There’s been a note on the board about you for two days.” He said it the way you say the weather, and turned to the next person in the queue.
The Assessor’s office had a brass plate on the door, and the plate said:
*ASSESSOR OF HYGIENE · MARROWGATE DISTRICT · BY APPOINTMENT*
The plate was polished. Nahl noticed that, and could not have said why it mattered, so they wrote it down too.

Inside, the office was warm. There was a fire in a grate and a copper kettle on a stand and a window with a view of the wall. There were two desks. At the larger one sat the Assessor of Hygiene. He was a man of about fifty, with grey at the temples, ink on his cuffs, and the shoulders of a man who had been carrying paper for thirty years.
At the smaller desk, in the corner, by the window, sat a girl of about eight, doing sums.
“That’s Pella,” said the Assessor. “My daughter. She comes with me on the short days.” He said it without embarrassment, as a man states a fact. “She’s learning columns. She’s good at it.”

The girl did not look up. She had a sheet in front of her with three ruled columns on it and a slate of working beside it. She was adding a long column of figures with her tongue between her teeth, and she was, Nahl saw, doing it correctly.
“Would you like tea?” said the Assessor. “The kettle’s on. It’s no trouble.”
His name was Corin Quire, and he did not once raise his voice, and he never once stood up.

That was the thing Nahl could not stop noticing. He was polite. He was *actually* polite, not performing it, in the way of a man who has found that politeness costs nothing and settles everything. He offered them chairs. He asked about the road. He asked whether they had eaten, and when it turned out they had not, he sent a boy for bread and did not make a ceremony of it.
Then he asked about their papers.

We do not have papers, Nahl was going to say, because Nahl had been filed once on papers and had a very strong position on the subject. But Riss was already reaching inside their coat, and what Riss brought out was not the plate. It was a folded sheet, gone soft at the creases, and Riss put it on the Assessor’s desk.
The Assessor looked at it for a long time.

It was a form. It was a single page with a broken rule down the middle and two boxes at the bottom. Printed across the top, in a language that was not the language of the counties, was a device Riss had first seen painted on the wall of an office in their own country, and had seen every year of their life since, on a kitchen table.
The Assessor read it. He read it slowly, the way a man reads a document in a language he does not speak but a script he knows, and his eyebrows did the thing eyebrows do when a guess is confirmed.
Then he sat back.
“I’ve seen this before,” he said.
Riss said nothing.
“Not this copy. This *form*. We had four of them come through here in eleven years, all from travellers, all from the same place.” He looked at Riss. “You’re from the Burn.”
Riss did not deny it. There was no version of the next hour in which denying it helped.
“Yes,” they said.
And Corin Quire, Assessor of Hygiene for the Marrowgate District, did the thing that was worse than anything else he did that day.
He said, “I’m sorry. That must have been difficult.”

He was not gloating. That was the whole horror of it, and Nahl wrote that down in the margin that night, in four words: *he was not gloating.* The man meant it. He was sorry. He had read the form, and he understood what the form did, and he was genuinely sorry that Riss had come out of a place that used it, in the way a man is sorry about a flood in a neighbouring county.
And then he said the next thing, which was worse.

“You’ll find ours is gentler,” said the Assessor. “We don’t take children out of schools. We don’t have a single number. We ask, and we pay for what we take, and if a holding doesn’t divide we simply leave the difference where it lies.” He turned his pen over on the desk. “I won’t pretend it’s the same thing. But I won’t have you tell me it’s a different kind of thing either. It’s the same trade. We do it with better manners and a smaller column.”
Riss sat looking at him.
“Why smaller?” they said.
“Because a column you cannot read is a column you cannot argue with,” said the Assessor, “and argument is the whole difficulty of the work.”
Then he did something Nahl had not braced for. He asked about them.

“You’re the bearer,” he said. “The one who carries for other people.” He said it with no particular weight, the way a man notes that a visitor is a smith. “How does that work, exactly? What have you got there?”
Nahl looked at him for a moment.
“A seal,” Nahl said. “It was somebody’s. It’s mine to carry now, not to use.”
“And it’s entered in a register somewhere, is it? With your name against it?”
“No.” Nahl held the Assessor’s eye. “It has never been written down.”

The Assessor’s pen stopped. For the first time that afternoon the man looked genuinely interested, the way he had looked at the woman’s four stamps at the customs house: a column that did not balance, and wanted an explanation.
“Then how do you know it’s yours?” he said.
“Because I’m still carrying it,” said Nahl.
The Assessor wrote nothing. Afterwards, on the road, Nahl decided that was the only point in the entire visit at which the man had lost.
Pella finished her column while the bread came, and Nahl watched her do it.
She checked it twice, from the bottom up, which is the way you check a sum you are proud of. Then she looked up at the room for the first time, and looked at Nahl for a while, and said,
“Are you a man or a woman?”
“I’m a bearer,” said Nahl.
“What’s that?”
“Somebody who carries a thing that belongs to somebody else.”
Pella considered that with the total seriousness of eight years old, and said, “That’s what my father does,” and went back to her column.
Nahl did not answer. Nahl had been carrying the Bearer’s Seal for a long time, and had been filed once, and understood, better than anybody in that room, exactly what the child had just said.
The clerk brought the visitors’ book in at about three o’clock and asked each of them to put a thumb on the page, which was the law for strangers in a county seat.
They did it in order. Riss, Mira, Veylan, Kael, Corvath, Nahl. Sancora was still outside and would put her mark down later. Then the clerk came to Old Den.
Old Den kept his arms folded.
“Just your thumb, sir,” said the clerk.
Old Den said nothing. He had been standing at the window for an hour with his arms folded, the way he had stood through eleven years of mornings, and he did not unfold them.
The clerk looked at the Assessor. The Assessor looked up from his desk, considered Old Den for a moment with no expression at all, and went back to his work.
“Leave it,” he said. “Write refused. That’s his right.”

The clerk wrote it. Nobody said anything else about it. Old Den stood at the window and watched the wall until it was time to go, and it was the only hour of the whole visit in which Riss saw him looking at something that was not a person.
Nahl wrote that down too, and kept the pen on the page a moment longer than the sentence needed.
The wounded man came in at about four o’clock, and he came in the way a delivery comes in.

Two county men brought him. There was a healer with them in the grey coat of the district service, carrying a folder, and the folder had a stamped page in it. The man himself was about forty, a labourer by his hands, and he had a cut in his left forearm six inches long. It had been washed. It had been dressed. There was a clean linen wrap on it, and a stamp on the wrap, and the stamp matched the one on the page in the folder.
He was grey in the face, and he was holding his arm carefully, and he was sweating in a room with a fire in it.
“Routine,” said the healer. “He was on the wall works. Took a fall on a stake. It’s been cleaned and filed. He’s here for the record.”
“Ask them,” said the Assessor, nodding at the company, in the voice of a man being hospitable. “We have a surgeon’s crew travelling through. It’s a courtesy.”
So they asked Sancora.

That was how it happened. Nobody set it up. The Assessor was being polite to a wounded man in the way of a man who is polite to everyone, and the company happened to contain a healer, and a courtesy was offered, and Sancora put her satchels down and went and looked at the arm.
She looked for about ten seconds.

Then she did a thing Nahl had never seen her do. She did not touch him. She stood with her hands at her sides, and she looked at the wrap and the stamp on the wrap, and she looked at the man’s face, and then she looked at the folder with the page in it.

“This cut is six inches long and it is a week old,” she said. “It has been washed and covered. It has not been closed. It has not been drained. He has a fever starting this morning and he can’t hold his own weight on that leg.” She looked at the healer. “It is not healed.”
“It’s been cleaned and filed,” said the healer.
“It is *filed*,” said Sancora. “That’s a different word.”
She picked up her satchels, and she said the thing she had come four hundred miles to say without knowing she was going to say it.

“I’m not going to heal it,” she said. “You have a stamp on it. If I close it, you’ll file my work under yours, and the record will say the district’s healer did it, and next time somebody comes at this man with a stake he’ll be in the same column as before, and it will be *my* stitch in a page that says he was always fine.” She stepped back. “I don’t work under a stamp I didn’t put there. Not with a living arm.”
Then she walked out.

Nobody stopped her. The healer started to say something and the Assessor raised two fingers off the desk, a small movement, and the healer did not say it. Corin Quire looked at the door for a moment, and then he looked at the wounded man, and he said to his clerk, in a completely ordinary voice, “Send for Doctor Rennick. Tell her it’s urgent and put it on my account.”
Nahl watched him do it and understood, then, the thing that had been forming in them since the gate.
He would help the man. He would pay for it himself. And it would change nothing at all.
The Assessor wrote a note at five o’clock.

He did it in the open, at his desk, while they were gathering their packs, and he did it without any attempt to hide it, which was the most frightening courtesy of the whole visit. One sheet. A few lines. He folded it, and sealed it, and rang a little bell, and a boy of about fourteen came in from the yard, and the Assessor gave him the packet and said,
“Fast road, Sunth. Change horses at the bridge.”
“Yes sir,” said the boy, and was gone.
The company stood in the yard and watched him go out through the gate and down the county road, north-west, at a canter.
Mira said, “He’s not sending for soldiers.”
“No,” said Nahl.
“He’s sending a *note*.”
“Yes.”
“To who?”
Nahl watched the boy get small on the road and thought about a note that had been on a board in Marrowgate for two days before they ever arrived.
“To the next one,” Nahl said. “Wherever we go next, they’ll have had the note for a week.”
They left Marrowgate at dusk, and the goat was waiting for them on the grey road, exactly where they had left it, in the same position, as though it had been a piece of the road all along.
It got up when it saw them and walked beside Veylan without being led.

Sancora was quiet. Riss walked with one hand over the coat and the plate under it, humming the divided fifth, which it had done since the gate, louder in the customs house, loudest in the warm office with the fire and the child doing sums. Kael’s burned hand had ached the whole visit and he had said nothing about it, which was how Kael dealt with achings.
Riss looked back once, at the end of the rise, because you look back.

Marrowgate kept its lamps lit late. The wall, the gate, the customs house, the window with the kettle. And on the north side of the square, at the end of the day, the brass plate on the Assessor’s door caught the last of the light.
It did not shine. That was the thing Riss noticed and could not put down.

It was the only piece of metal in that whole town that took the light and gave nothing back, and Nahl, walking beside them in the dark, wrote the line down that night without being asked, because a bearer writes things down:
*It is polished. That is different from shining.*
Ahead of them the gold road came up out of the stones and lay beside the grey, and the two of them went north-west together, side by side, without touching.

chapters.label: Chapter 6
chapters.title: The Twelve
paragraphs: After Marrowgate, they went west for four days into the low limbs of the hills, and on the fourth evening they made camp in a sheep pasture at the foot of a long ridge, because Aureon said he had to go up.

Nobody argued. That was the first surprising thing about the evening and Riss thought about it later, walking. Two months earlier the company would have argued with Aureon about the weather. Now the man said he had to go up a mountain alone and they built a fire and let him.

He took nothing with him. That was the second thing. No pack, no blanket, no knife. He put off the good coat he had bought in Vellum Reach and left it folded on a stone, because you do not carry a coat into a place like that. Riss, watching, understood that Aureon was dressing for something the way other men dress for a funeral.
The goat walked to the foot of the path and stopped.

It did not do what it had done at Marrowgate. It did not stand and face a town with its head down. It simply walked to the place where the sheep track left the pasture and went up into the rock, and stood there, and would not climb.
Aureon looked at the goat for a while.
“All right,” he said. “I know.”
Then he went up, and the goat stayed at the foot of the path with its crooked head turned up the hill, and watched him go until he was out of sight, which is not a thing goats do.
The climb took him two hours and he remembered the war the whole way.

He had not meant to. That was the thing about coming back to the hills: the rock did the remembering for him. There was a place about halfway up where the track bent round a black outcrop. He stood at that bend for a long moment with his hand flat on the stone. That was where he had stood a hundred and forty years ago with eleven others, waiting for the sky to open.

The Ascension War had gone on for nine years, and the Twelve had won it, and nobody had ever once explained to the people below what winning had cost, because the people below had not been told there was a war. That was the arrangement. The gods fought and the farms went on and the harvest came in, and afterward the songs said the summer had been long.
He climbed on. Above him the sky was clear and cold, and the Emberion constellation stood over the western peaks, and Aureon did what he had done since he was a boy and counted it without meaning to.

*Sixteen.* The number came out of his mouth the way an old word does, before his mind arrived. Then his mind arrived, and said *fifteen*, and he stopped on the path in the dark and stood there for a moment with his hands at his sides.
He had been away for two years. He had not known.
He went on up, and he carried no weapon the whole way, because the question he was carrying did not need one.

You do not find the Twelve in a temple. There is no temple. Somebody in Vellum Reach had told Riss that once and Riss had not believed it, and Aureon had agreed with them, because he had been raised in the same stories as everybody else.
They were on the ridge, in a wide hollow of wind-bitten grass, around a fire that had gone cold.

Eleven figures. Some sitting, some standing. All of them in ordinary clothes, dirty at the hem, and all of them tired. There was an old woman with a stick mending a net that had no holes in it. There was a man with a stone in each hand, turning them over and over, and there were nine others scattered round the cold fire in the attitudes of people who had been waiting a long time in a place with a view.
None of them got up when he came. None of them bowed. The old woman with the net looked at him and said, “You’re late,” and Aureon said, “I know,” and sat down, and that made twelve.

They were not corrupt. That was the thing Aureon had known in his bones before he climbed and had needed to see for himself anyway. He had half expected to come up here and find the place gone wrong: the Twelve fat, the Twelve bought, the Twelve asleep on a hoard. He had found twelve tired people around a cold fire, doing the practices they had done for a thousand years.

The old woman’s name for what she did was *keeping the net*, and she had kept it for the fishing villages on the south coast since before the counties had walls. The man with the stones kept the road. Another kept births. Another kept the door in a way that Aureon had never fully understood and had never asked about.
There was one who kept the counting of years. She was very old, and she sat at the edge of the light with her hands folded, and when Aureon looked at her she looked back and did not smile.
That was the one he had come to see, and he knew it before he said a word, and he was sad before he said a word, because he could already see the shape of the answer in her hands.

He put the case to them plainly. He had spent two years learning how to do that, standing in ordinary doorways with ordinary neighbours, and it turned out plainness was the only skill he had ever actually needed.

He told them about the villages. He told them about the stamps and the queues and the ordinary patience of the queue. He told them about the market column and the mill column and a woman who had gone into both and come out of neither. He told them about the interval that resolved in Nettleford and the three hundred people who could not remember why they had wanted it not to. He told them about a child of six singing the Interval wrong on purpose behind a mill, alone, because she had noticed that the song no longer finished and had decided to keep the unfinished one herself.
He told them about the Assessor. He described the kettle and the fire and the child doing sums at the small desk, and the man who was genuinely sorry, and the note going down the fast road to Sunth.
Then he asked for one measure.

“A ruling,” he said. “That is all I want. One ruling from the Twelve, in public, that says the ledger is wrong. That says a person is not a sum. Every village from here to the coast will hear it inside a month. It is a *measure*. You have done it before. You have done it for dogs, and for boundaries, and for a man who wanted to marry a woman in a county that did not like it.”
And the Twelve sat round their cold fire and would not look at him, in the way that people who have to refuse a friend will not look at him until they have found their voice.
The old woman with the net spoke first, and she was kind, which was the worst way to do it.
“We cannot do that,” she said.
“You *can*. You ruled on the dog business in the third year of the war.”
“That was a thing that happened under the sky,” said the man with the stones. “Boundaries happen under the sky. A marriage happens under the sky. What you have brought us is a *book*.”

“We count years,” said the old woman at the edge of the light, and her voice was quiet, and everyone else stopped. “I count years. I have counted them for a very long time. I do not count people. I have never counted people. If I made a ruling about people, I would be making a ruling about a thing I do not keep.” She looked at Aureon and her hands stayed folded. “You are asking us to audit a record we did not write and cannot read. We are not accountants. We are the reason there are songs.”
Aureon said, “Then the songs are wrong.”
“The songs are not wrong,” she said. “The songs are just *not enough*. That is the whole thing you have come up here to hear, Aureon, and I am sorry, because you had to climb a mountain for it.”
One of the others spoke then, and it was the man who kept the door, and he had said nothing all night.

“You want to know how it goes if we rule,” he said. “I can tell you, because we have done it. In the fourth year of the war there was a dispute about the salt rights at Kessel, and we ruled on it. It was a good ruling. It took a year to make and it was read out in eleven market squares.” He turned a stone over in his palm. “Within two years there was a Kessel Ruling in every registry from the coast to the hills, cited twice a year by clerks who had never been north of Sunder. And it had been rewritten, in the copying, so that it said the opposite of what we said.” He looked up. “That is what a book does to a ruling, boy. It eats it and files what is left in a column.”
There was a long silence in the hollow, and the wind went along the ridge, and Aureon sat with his hands on his knees and worked through it.

He did not break. That was a thing he noticed about himself afterwards, and he was not proud of it and he was not ashamed of it. He had gone up with a question and had expected an army, and he was being offered neither.
“All right,” he said. “Then give me an army.”
“No,” said the man with the stones.

“Because an army is a thing that fights,” said the man with the stones. “You have told us what happens when a village fights the fee. The fee goes up. The army would win the square and lose the county, and we would have to come down and stand in the square for a hundred years to hold it. We did that before. We are doing that now, in four places. There is no one left to send.”
“Then a blessing. One blessing for the road. Something that makes people listen to them.”
“No,” said the old woman with the net.
“Why not?”
“Because a blessing is a *gift*,” she said, “and you cannot carry a gift into a room where the man has a ledger. He will ask what it is entered under.”
Aureon sat back on his heels and looked at the cold fire, and understood, fully and without any bitterness, the exact size of the thing he had brought up the hill.
“So that’s the whole of it,” he said. “You can fight a dragon. You cannot fight a column.”
The old woman at the edge of the light inclined her head, which was the only movement she made all night.
“We can *witness*,” she said. “We cannot audit.”
He was rising to go when he asked the last thing, and he asked it the way a man asks for a cup of water, because he had stopped calculating two hours before.
“Then give me a witness.”
The Twelve looked at each other. It was the first time all night that any of them had looked at each other.

The old woman with the net said, “You understand what that means. A witness of ours cannot fight and cannot lie. He can stand in a room and say what he saw. That is all he is for. It will not stop the fee.”

“I know what it’s for,” said Aureon. “It is corroboration. It is one more page that does not agree with their page.” He stood up. “I’ve been two years standing with the people this is happening to, and I have learned exactly one thing up here, and it is that they don’t need a miracle. They need somebody *other* than themselves to say this is real.”
And the old woman at the edge of the light said, “Then take Orphiel.”
Orphiel came down the hill behind him in the dark, and he was not at all what the company expected.

They saw two shapes come off the sheep track in the last of the light. The first was Aureon, in his shirt, carrying nothing, colder than he had any business being. Behind him came a man of about seventy in a good travelling cloak, with white at his temples and a satchel over one shoulder. He walked carefully, the way a man walks who has spent his life on floors.

He was not a warrior. There was nothing about him that suggested a warrior. He had the hands of a man who had held a pen for fifty years. He had the shoulders of a man who had never once been in a fight. When he reached the pasture he put the satchel down on a stone and stood looking at the fire the way you look at something you have not seen in a long time.

The goat had not moved. It had stood at the foot of the sheep track for the whole two hours, and it stood there now. When Orphiel came down the last few paces it turned its head and looked at him for a while. Then it went back to looking up the hill.

Above them, the sky had come out. The Emberion constellation stood over the western peaks, and Riss, sitting by the fire, counted it the way they always counted it and got fifteen, and did not say so.
The plate hummed against their chest. The divided fifth. Kael Riven had his burned hand closed around his own forearm and said nothing, which was how Kael showed a thing.
Aureon came to the fire and sat down and put his hands out to it and said, without any preamble at all, “This is Orphiel. He keeps the deletion log. He is not here to fight anybody.”

Riss watched Aureon’s face in the firelight and looked for the thing they had expected to find there, and did not find it. He was not bitter. He had gone up the hill carrying a large question and had come back down with a smaller answer, and he was sitting with it the way a man sits with a bad field and starts thinking about drainage. Two years of standing in ordinary doorways had done that to him. It had taught him that the useful thing is almost never the large thing.

And at that, out on the western horizon, three of the Twelve stood at the edge of the ridge, a mile up and a mile away, and looked west once, at the peaks, for about four seconds. Then they went back to their cold fire.
They said nothing. It was not a sign. It was a silence, and Riss would spend the rest of the journey deciding which of the two were worse.
Orphiel said nothing for the rest of the evening.

He ate, because they gave him bread and he was polite, and he drank tea. Then he sat at the edge of the fire with his satchel on his knees and watched the company do the ordinary things a company does at night. Mira with the chart. Sancora cleaning a knife she had not used. Veylan checking the seed crate. Old Den with his arms folded. Corvath with the plowshare across his knees. Nahl writing.
At one point he looked at the plate. He looked at it for the length of about three breaths, and Riss felt the look, and looked up, and the old man had already looked away.

Nahl had been looking at the satchel since it came into the firelight. They knew that satchel. They had carried one like it for nine years, tied with the same cord, worn in the same two places, because a bearer’s kit and a vault-keeper’s kit are the same kit, made by the same people, for the same purpose. Nahl did not say so. Nahl opened their own book instead and wrote one short line in it: *he keeps the log. I keep the seal. Neither of us can file anything.*
Then, before the fire went down, Orphiel did the thing that told them what they had actually been given.

He opened the satchel. It was full of ledgers: a dozen of them, small, cheap, well used, tied with cord, the kind of book a shop keeps. He took one out, and set it on his knees, and untied the cord, and opened it to the back, and took out a single blank page which he had kept folded in the cover.

He laid the blank page flat on his knee and took a pen and a small bottle of ink out of the satchel and set them beside him, and then he sat with his hands on his knees and did not write anything at all.
Riss waited. They could feel the fire, and the plate, and the cold coming down off the ridge, and they could feel everybody in the company not saying the obvious question.
Orphiel looked at the blank page. Then he looked up, at Riss, for a long moment.
And then he closed the ink, and corked it, and put the pen away, and folded the blank page back into the cover, and tied the cord, and sat with his satchel on his knees and waited to be asked.
Behind them, at the edge of the pasture, the goat stood up without being asked, and did not move, and faced west.

chapters.label: Chapter 7
chapters.title: The Witness
paragraphs: After the ridge, nobody slept well, and Orphiel was the only one who did.

That was the first thing the company learned about him, and it was such a small thing that Riss almost missed it. They woke before dawn with the cold coming down off the hill, and found the old man already sitting up. He was wrapped in his cloak with the satchel on his knees, looking at the pasture the way a man looks at a room he has just been shown into.
The blank page was still in the cover of the ledger. Nobody had seen him write on it. Nobody had seen him put it away either.

The goat had come up from the foot of the track in the night, and was standing by the fire in the grey light, facing east now, which it had not done in weeks. Nobody knew what that meant and nobody asked.
Nahl found him first, and the two of them had a conversation that the others only heard half of.
It began because of the satchel. Nahl had been watching it since the firelight, and in the morning, with the light flat and ordinary, they finally said something.
“That’s a bearer’s kit,” Nahl said.
Orphiel looked down at the satchel as though he had not considered it in years. “It is.”
“Same cord. Same wear on the flap. Same place the corner goes soft.” Nahl crouched down across the fire from him. “The kit’s made by the same people. It’s the same kit.”

“It is the same kit,” said Orphiel. “There is only one kit. Vault-keepers, bearers, road-wardens, the people who keep the parish books in villages nobody has heard of: it is all the same satchel, because it is all the same *job*, which is to hold a thing that belongs to somebody else and not lose it.”
Nahl was quiet for a moment.
“What do you keep?” they said.

“The log.” Orphiel did not open the satchel. “The names that have been taken out. The ones nobody remembers. When a thing is deleted, by a court, by a county, by a clerk with a pen, it does not go nowhere. It goes *somewhere*, and that somewhere is a shelf, and I sit next to the shelf, and I write down what came off it.”
“How many?”
“Nine thousand and four,” said Orphiel.
Nahl did not say anything for a while. Then they said, “I keep a seal. One thing. A seal that belonged to somebody and now belongs to me to carry, and which I am not allowed to use.”
Orphiel nodded slowly, the way a man nods at a fact he has known for a long time.
“Neither of us can file anything,” said Nahl.
“No,” said Orphiel. “But we can witness.”
“Witness what?” said Nahl.

“Whatever is put in front of us,” said Orphiel. “That is the whole of the discipline. You do not choose the thing you witness. The moment you choose, you are a witness *for* somebody, and then you are a lawyer, and lawyers lose to clerks every time.”

Riss asked the question in the middle of the morning, and afterwards they could not remember deciding to ask it. It came out of them the way a thing comes out of you when you have been carrying it up a hill for a month.
“What do you need to see?”
Orphiel looked at them.

That was all. He looked at Riss, and Riss felt looked at in a way nobody had looked at them since Halwen, because it was the look of a person who was being asked to do their job and intended to do it properly.
“Everything,” said Orphiel. “Not your opinion of it. Everything.”
So they showed him.

Mira cleared the flat stone by the fire and set the chart out on it. Not the whole Wound-Chart, just the one sheet she had made at Ashenford, with the two columns drawn small and the single line from one to the other and the circle round the shared figure.
Riss laid out the copies they had made of the two ledger pages: the market column, which said *Bread-woman. Two loaves. Paid.*, and the mill column, which said *Grain-woman. One sack. Paid.*

Veylan brought the tin box from Collow and opened it, and put three of the tallies out on the stone beside the columns. The old man could see the shape of what a village’s own record looked like. Names, years, births, deaths, the small untidy arithmetic of a place that had kept itself.
Kael Riven put the slate down at the edge of the stone, and opened the lid, and turned it so Orphiel could see the inside, which was empty.

And Riss talked them through it. Not fast. Not clever. They did it the way they had done it at the mill: the two accounts, the same woman in both, the shared factor in the middle, the sum done honestly, the correct total, and the woman not in it.
Then they said the word.
“Remainder.”
Orphiel looked at the stone for a long time.

He looked at the two ledger pages, and at Mira’s circle, and at the tallies in the tin box, and at Kael’s empty slate. That last one was, Riss understood later, the most important thing on the stone. It was the thing a man had tried to trace and could not, and had written nothing rather than write something untrue.

The fire cracked. Corvath stood at the edge of the pasture with the plowshare and watched the old man’s face. Veylan asked, quietly, whether the witness would be wanting a blanket, and Sancora told him to be quiet.
Orphiel did not write anything for a long time.
Then he reached into the satchel and took out the ledger, and untied the cord, and folded the cover open, and took out the blank page, and laid it flat on his knee.
He set the pen beside it. He did not pick it up.
He looked at Riss, and the look was steady and unpleasant and completely fair, in the way a jeweller’s look is fair.

“I have read nine thousand and four names off a shelf,” he said. “I have sat with clerks. I have been in three counties’ record rooms, one of them in the middle of the night. I am telling you plainly, so that you understand me: I have seen nothing in forty years that I could not explain.”
He looked down at the page on his knee for a while.
And then Orphiel, keeper of the deletion log, said the thing that the company had walked four hundred miles to hear and could not have known they were walking toward.
“I can see it,” he said. “This is real.”
The plate hummed.

It was against Riss’s chest under the coat, and it had been quiet enough all morning that Riss had stopped noticing it, which is how you live with a thing. Then it went from nothing to a note, and the note was the divided fifth, and it was *louder*, not louder than the customs house, but louder than it had been in this pasture all week.
Three paces away, Kael Riven put his burned hand flat on his own forearm over the scar, and said nothing, and looked at the old man.
The goat turned its head and looked at the blank page on Orphiel’s knee, and stood there with its head turned for the length of a breath, and then went back to the grass.
Nobody said anything about any of it. That was the company’s way now. Things happened, they were as real as the plate, and the correct response was to write them down and not to make a speech.
Mira wrote one line on the back of the chart.
Then she asked the question everybody had been holding.
“Why not write it down? You’ve got the page out. That’s the whole of what we’ve got, and you’re the only one of us who can say it and make it stick.”
Orphiel looked at her the way he had looked at the stone.

“A log is what came off the shelf,” he said. “That is the only thing I am for. The day I start writing down what I *expect* to be true is the day I become a clerk with a nicer satchel.” He folded the page, and did not put it away. “The page is not for this week. It is for the room. When we are standing in front of somebody who has to write down what was said, then I will write, in my own hand, with my own name under it, and nobody will have to take my word for the shape of it.”
“Then,” said Mira.
“Then,” said Orphiel.
Sancora had been watching him since the fire, and she asked her own question the way she asked all of them, which was after everyone else had stopped.
