“Nine thousand and four,” she said. “How do you keep that and stay in your right mind?”

“I don’t keep them,” said Orphiel. “I keep the *shelf*. The names do the staying. I only do the writing.” He looked into the fire. “It’s easier than what you do. You carry the living ones in your hands and they die anyway. Mine are already gone. Mine cannot get worse.”
Kael Riven had not said a word since the slate went on the stone. He said one now, in the flat voice he used when he was asking something that mattered.
“Can you see the shelf?”
“No,” said Orphiel. “Nobody sees the shelf. That is what makes it a good shelf.”
Kael nodded slowly, as though he had been handed a useful piece of information, and went back to looking at his own burned hand.
Orphiel explained what he could do in about three minutes, and Riss understood, walking afterwards, that the old man had been rehearsing it for years, in case anybody ever asked.

He could come with them. He would come with them, and he would stand in the rooms they stood in, and he would look at what they showed him, and he would say out loud, to whoever was listening, what he saw.
He could not fight. He said this without any apology, as a man states the length of a plank.

He could not audit. He could not add. He would not check their arithmetic in public. If a vault-keeper checked their sums, the whole business became two sets of clerks arguing about a page, and that was a fight the counties won every time. The counties had more clerks.
And there was one more thing, and he said it in a voice that had nothing in it at all.
“I will not file the living,” he said.
Sancora, who had been silent since the mill at Ashenford, looked up.
“What does that mean?”

“It means that when this is over, if we are standing in a room and somebody puts a page in front of me and asks me to enter the company’s names in it, I will not do it. Not even to protect you. Not even to prove we were here.” Orphiel tied the cord on the ledger, slowly, the way a man ties a cord he has tied ten thousand times. “I keep the log. I keep what has *already* been taken out. I do not put people in.”
Riss looked at the old man for a long moment.
“Nine thousand and four,” they said.
“Nine thousand and four,” said Orphiel. “And when I open the log, the first name it takes is mine. That is the arrangement. That is what the job is.”
Riss thought about that for the rest of the afternoon, and what they arrived at, walking, was the thing nobody had said out loud on the ridge.
A witness cannot be protected.

They could stand in front of a company, or a clerk, or a whole market square, with Nahl and Kael and Corvath behind them and everything the company had. It would not matter in the slightest. A witness is a person who says a true thing in a room where nobody wants it said, and there is no formation for that, and no way to stand in front of it. The only protection a witness has is that the room has to remember afterward what it did.
They broke camp at midday, and nobody celebrated.

That felt wrong to Riss for about an hour, and then they understood why it was right. They had gone up a mountain and asked the gods for a weapon, and had come back down with a witness. The witness was an old man with a satchel. The Assessor at Marrowgate was still in his office with the kettle on. The notes were still going down the fast roads. The fee had not gone down by one penny anywhere.
Veylan, who had been quiet all morning, said the practical thing out loud while they were packing, because Veylan always did.

“So what have we actually got?” he said. “Begging your pardon. But we’ve walked into two counties and been polite at both of them, and now we’ve got a man with a book who’s promised to say what he saw.”
“We’ve got a second page,” said Nahl.
Veylan stopped with the seed crate half closed.
“Go on,” he said.

“A page that agrees with ours is nothing. That’s a copy. A page that *disagrees* with theirs is an argument, and they win arguments, because they have more clerks.” Nahl checked the strap on their own satchel. “What we’ve got now is the third thing. We’ve got somebody who was not there and is not ours, who looked at it, and who can stand up in a room and say: *I saw it, and it is real.* That is a fact that does not need to be believed. It only needs to be *said* in front of a clerk who has to write down what was said.”
Mira, who was rolling the chart, said, “Where will we say it?”
“Wherever they’ll let us,” said Nahl. “And then we’ll say it again.”
Veylan asked the other practical question, the one nobody else was going to ask.
“What does he eat? Where does he sleep? He’s seventy.”
“He eats what we eat,” said Nahl. “He sleeps at the fire. He has been walking for forty years, Veylan. He is not the most fragile member of this company.”
“He’s the only one of us who can’t run,” said Veylan.
“Yes,” said Nahl. “That is what a witness is.”

They went west along the base of the hills, because west was where the road went, and toward evening Riss looked back along the line of the company and saw something that made them slow down and look properly.
Orphiel was walking with Nahl.

That was all. But the two of them were walking side by side at the head of the line, not talking, with their satchels on. And their satchels were the same satchel, worn in the same two places, carrying the same kind of weight for the same kind of reason. One of them had a seal that could not be used. One of them had a log that could not be opened. Neither of them could file anything, and both of them were the reason a thing that had been taken might still be said out loud.

Riss watched them for a while and then walked on. The plate hummed the divided fifth under their coat, steady as a cough. The gold road came up out of the stones as it always did and lay beside the grey.

At dusk they stopped in a hollow with water in it and made a fire, and the company did the ordinary things. Mira drew the ground. Sancora went round everybody’s hands. Veylan counted the seed crate twice, which he had been doing more often lately. Corvath sat with the plowshare and said, of Orphiel, in a flat voice,
“He smells of paper and dust. Like a room where nothing has happened for a long time.”
“Is that good?” said Mira.
“It’s the first thing in a month that has smelled like what it is,” said Corvath. “So yes. It’s good.”

Orphiel sat at the fire with the satchel on his knees and said nothing at all. When Riss looked over at him an hour later, the ledger was open on his lap, the cord was tied, and the blank page was still blank.
Riss lay back on the cold grass and looked up. Above them the Emberion constellation stood over the western peaks, and they counted it, and got fifteen, and did not say so.
Then they lay awake for a while, which was ordinary, and thought about paper.

The company’s satchels were full of it. Tally sheets. The chart. The slate. Nahl’s book. The Leaf, with Halwen’s notes in the margin in the small angry hand of a man who had known exactly what was coming. The copies they had made of two counties’ columns. Every scrap of it was written over, crossed out, corrected, added to, argued with. It was the loudest luggage in the world.
And in the middle of all of it, in an old man’s satchel, there was one page that was blank, and had been blank for years, and was going to stay blank until it was needed.
Riss found, lying under the sky, that this was the most encouraging thing they had seen since the stone ring at Vellum Reach.
They had a witness. They did not have a weapon.
Outside the firelight, the gold road and the grey road went on west together through the dark, side by side, without touching, and neither of them shone.

chapters.label: Chapter 8
chapters.title: The Wind
paragraphs: After the witness joined them, the company walked west for six days. On the third day the farms ran out.

It did not happen at once. There was a farm with a good hedge. Then there was a farm with a wall that had fallen in and been left. Then there were two fields with the ridge patterns still in them and nobody working them, and then a mile of nothing with a track through it.
Riss noticed it the way you notice a bruise. Not when it happens. When you press it.
Behind them now were the counties. The queues. The stamps. The tables at the market crosses. The brass plates on the doors of warm offices with kettles on stands. Ahead of them was stone.
Nobody said anything about it for a long way.

That was the first refusal of the chapter, and Riss thought about it afterwards and decided it counted as one. Nobody said *we could turn back*. Six days of walking. Four counties behind them, two of them holding a note with the company’s shape on it. An old man with a bad knee in the middle of the line.
And not one of them said the sentence.

Veylan did not say it. Mira did not draw the road backward on the chart. Sancora, who had said the least since Ashenford, said the least. They simply walked, in silence, and the silence was the decision.
At midday on the fourth day they stopped at a farmhouse, because it was the last roof before the high ground and the cloud was coming down.

It was empty. It had been empty for a while. The door was open and the door had a good hinge on it, and somebody had taken the hinge pins, which is the sort of thing that happens in the first month. The byre was clean. The bread oven in the yard was swept out, which was strange, and Riss stood over it for a while before working out why: whoever left had done the last cleaning themselves. Nobody is tidier than a person leaving a house they expect to come back to.
Inside, on the wall beside the hearth, there were marks.

They were children’s marks. Height marks, cut into the beam with a knife, a hand’s width apart, going up: one set of them, and then a second set lower down, and then both sets continuing year on year with the dates scratched beside them in an unskilled hand. *Annis.* *Perrin.* The last mark on each set was about four years old.
Mira stood in front of it with the chart tube in her hand and did not get the chart out.
“They’re not in a book,” she said. “There is no column with these in it. There is nothing anywhere that says these two people were ever this tall.”
“No,” said Riss.
“So why are they still here?”
Riss looked at the beam.

“Because it’s wood,” they said. “The counties take paper. They take the register, and the tally, and the parish book, and they file them, and the column closes. Nobody’s ever thought to take a wall.” They put a hand flat on the beam. “These are the only records Annes and Perrin have got, and they’re cut into a house, and the house is a thing that keeps.”
Veylan asked the practical question, because the practical question was his whole contribution to the world and it was a good one.
“Should we write them down?”
Riss thought about it for a long moment. The right answer was obvious and the obvious answer was wrong.

“No,” they said. “If we write them down, we’ve written them down *somewhere*, and somewhere is a place a clerk can go. Leave them where they are. They’re safe in the wood.” They took their hand off the beam. “That’s the first thing I’ve learned in four months that I’d actually call a lesson.”

Then they walked on, and two days later the beam and the farmhouse and the marks were behind them, and Riss thought about the marks for a long time afterwards, and about the second set of them, the lower one, and what it meant that both of the sets had stopped on the same year.
The camp that night was on a shelf of bare rock with a spring in it. It was the last water before the high ground.
Veylan asked the practical question while he was counting the seed crate. He always counted the crate when he was worried.
“How far does this go?”
“To the end of the road,” said Nahl.
“That’s not an answer. That’s a saying.”
“It’s both,” said Nahl.
Veylan looked at the crate. Then he looked at the company. Then he looked at the dark hills going up in front of them.

“Because I’ll go,” he said. “I want that written down somewhere. I’m not going to be the man who asks the question and then finds out he was the one who wanted to go home. I’ll go the whole way. I just want to know if the whole way is the whole way.”
“It is,” said Riss.
“Right,” said Veylan.

He shut the crate. That was the whole of the conversation about turning back. They packed the mule. They banked the fire. Nobody made a speech, because a company that has walked for four months has stopped needing them.
Mira was sitting on the rock with the chart tube across her knees. She had not opened it all day.

“I’ve got a gap,” she said. “Two hundred roads and there’s a gap. Everything north of the last county line is a blank, and I don’t draw what I haven’t walked.” She tapped the tube. “So tomorrow I’ll be drawing something new for the first time since Vellum Reach.”
“Does that worry you?” said Riss.
“It worries me that it doesn’t,” said Mira.

Corvath came up out of the dark and sat down by the fire. He had been walking the perimeter, which is a thing he did without being asked, and which had been almost comical a month ago and was not comical now.

“I tasted the ground,” he said. “Out past the spring, up the slope. There’s nothing on it. No farms, no dung, no smoke, no sheep. It’s clean stone.” He put his hands out to the fire. “First place since we left the coast where my nose agrees with my eyes. I’d been starting to think the fault was in me.”
“It is in you,” said Sancora, without looking up.
“Oh, that too,” said Corvath, and that was the closest thing to a joke the company had had all month.
Orphiel asked Nahl about the seal on the fifth day, on the road, which was the first question he had asked anybody about anything.

They were walking in the middle of the line with the mule between them and the wind behind, and the old man said, in the manner of a man checking a figure he has been carrying in his head, “The seal. Whose was it before it was yours?”
“A man called Alder,” said Nahl.
“Where did he get it?”

“He made it. He was a smith, and he made it himself, in a village on the south coast, because the village needed a way of saying *this is ours and not the county’s*, and he did not trust paper.” Nahl walked a few paces. “He used it for forty years. Every lease, every marriage, every will in that village went under it. He cut his own name off the bottom of it the year the counties came, so that it could not be taken as evidence against anybody. That’s why there’s no name on it.”
“And then he died.”
“He drowned,” said Nahl. “In the bad winter. And nobody wanted the thing, because a seal that can’t be used is just a lump of brass.”
“So you took it.”

“I was there,” said Nahl. “It was in the water with him. I got it out.” They adjusted the strap on their shoulder. “I have carried it for nine years and I have never once been able to say why, out loud, in a way that satisfied anybody.”
Orphiel walked on for a while.

“The reason is not interesting,” he said, “which is why you can’t say it. You keep it because somebody has to. That is the whole discipline and it is a boring one, and it is why the two of us are walking up a mountain behind a company of people who are not.”
It was the longest speech Orphiel made in the whole of that chapter.
The unsaid thing got said that night. Riss had not expected that.

They were sitting up late with the fire down to embers. Everyone else was asleep, or folded up in the way of people who have learned to sleep on rock. Orphiel was on his side with the satchel under his head. That is how a man sleeps who has spent forty years deciding the satchel matters more than the neck.

Nahl was awake. That was ordinary. A bearer sleeps in pieces. But Nahl was not sitting the way they usually sat, which was a sentry’s way, facing out. They were sitting facing the fire with their hands around their knees, and they had been like that for an hour.
“Nahl,” said Riss.
“Yes.”
“Nothing. Just checking you were awake.”
“I’m awake,” said Nahl. “And there’s something I want to do. I’ve been not doing it for about a week. So I’m going to do it now, and then we’re not going to talk about it again.”
Riss waited.

“There’s a name,” said Nahl. “It’s mine. It’s not the one on the seal, and it’s not a secret exactly. It’s just that when you carry a seal for nine years, people stop asking. And after a while you stop offering.” They looked at the fire. “If anything happens, the company has to write something. Nahl is what the kit is called. I’d rather you had the other one.”

Riss did not ask for it. That felt important at the time, and felt more important afterwards. Riss did not ask, and did not lean forward, and did not do any of the things a person does when they have been handed something they want.
“Wren,” said Nahl.
Riss did not repeat it.
“I’ll write it,” they said.
“I know,” said Nahl. “That’s why I’m telling you and not Mira. No slight on Mira. It’s that Mira would draw it.”
Then Nahl lay down and went to sleep in about ten seconds, the way bearers do.
Riss sat up with the fire and did not write it down. Not that night. Writing it on the same page as the columns felt like putting it in the wrong column.

Thirteen paces away, on his other side, with the satchel under his head, Orphiel did not move. He slept the whole way through. He never mentioned it afterwards. Riss never worked out whether that was because he had not heard, or because he had, and had decided that a man who keeps a log knows exactly which things do not go in it.
The wind came off the peaks at the end of the night.

It was not a gale. That was the thing nobody was ready for. Riss had been raised on a coast and knew what weather was. This was not weather. It came down off the high ground steady and level, the way water comes out of a sluice. It was cold in a way that had nothing to do with the season.
And it smelled of stone.
The fire went flat, then sideways. The goat stood up.
It did not bleat. It stood up out of its sleep like a soldier and faced west. It did not move. Its coat was standing on end, and the firelight went along the ridgeline of its back.
The plate hummed against Riss’s chest. The divided fifth, and steady with it. Not loud. Not wild. Just present, the way it had been present in the customs house and in the warm office at Marrowgate.
Kael Riven sat up with his burned hand already closed around his own forearm. He breathed through his nose like a man with a cramp. He did not say anything.
Everybody woke. That was the other thing. Nobody had to be shaken.

Sancora came up onto the rock with both satchels on her shoulders, which she had not done in camp since Marrowgate. She stood at the back of the group, and watched the west, and did not put the satchels down.

Veylan went back three paces down the slope and stood over the seed crate. He stood over it the way a man stands over a child in weather, with his shoulders hunched and his back to the wind, and he did not open it, and he did not leave it.

Corvath walked out ten paces to the edge of the rock and stood in the wind with his face up and his eyes shut, tasting it, and he stayed there longer than anybody else, and when he came back he said only: “Stone. Only stone. Nothing alive in it at all,” and it was not clear whether that was a comfort to him or the opposite.
Mira stood beside Riss and did not get the chart out, which was, Riss thought afterwards, the loudest thing that happened all night.

They stood on the shelf of rock in the dark and looked west. What they saw was the peaks, black against a sky that was already going grey at the edge. Above the peaks stood the last of the stars. The Emberion constellation lay along the ridge of the world.
Riss counted it and got fifteen. They did not say so. They understood at last why the old men in the coast villages had stopped finishing the song.

Nobody said the word. Six people, all awake, all looking at the same weather, and not one of them said it out loud. Not the goat. Not the plate. Not the wind off high ground in the wrong season. Not one word about what was up there.
It was the biggest silence the company had ever stood inside. Riss was still standing in it when the sky began to lighten.
Riss thought about the silence afterwards and decided it was not fear, and it was not ignorance, because everybody on that rock knew exactly what they were looking at.

It was arithmetic. In four months, every single time the company had named a thing out loud ahead of time, the name had turned into a paper. The plate was not in a column. The goat was not in a column. The wind off the high ground was not in a column. To say the word would be to *enter* it: to put it on a page in a county’s hand, in a column, with a fee beside it, and to give it a heading that a clerk at the next customs gate could ask about.
So nobody said it. Six people stood in the cold and knew the same thing and kept it where it was safe.
They left it in the stone, the way the two children’s names were in the beam.
Orphiel was awake too.

He had come up onto the rock with the satchel on his shoulder. He stood beside Nahl with his hands folded on the strap, and he looked west for a long time. He looked the way a man looks at a page he has not yet been shown.
Then he did two things. Neither of them was a speech, which was why Riss trusted him.
He put his hand flat on the satchel, on the cover of the ledger where the blank page was folded.
And he did not take the page out.
They were packed before the light.

Nobody had given the order. Nobody had asked for one. The camp came down in the dark, quietly. The mule was loaded. The fire was buried with the last of the water from the spring. Everybody’s pack was on.
Mira rolled the chart and put it in its tube. Then she put the tube in her pack. Then she took it out again and put it inside her coat, which she had never once done.
The wind did not stop. At dawn it was blowing the way it had blown at midnight. Steady. Level. At their backs.

The peaks stood black against the light. The road ran west toward them. It was still the grey road. It had been the grey road all the way from Vellum Reach, and it was the grey road now. Beside it, the gold one came up out of the stones as it always did, and lay next to it, and did not touch it, and neither of them shone.
Riss stood at the head of the line with the plate humming under their coat and looked back once, east.

Behind them was everything the company had walked out of. The counties. The queues. The brass plates. The warm offices. The notes going down the fast roads. The whole enormous well-mannered machine of it, all of it now four days back, and none of it closed down by one hour’s walking.
Then Riss looked at Nahl.
Nahl nodded.

That was all. Nahl was the company’s spine and had been since the river. Nahl nodded, and it meant *go on*, and it meant it the same way it had meant it in the rain at Vellum Reach, and at the market at Collow, and in the yard at Ashenford.
They went west.

The goat walked beside Veylan, which is where it had decided it belonged. Orphiel walked beside Nahl, and the two satchels went up the road together, worn in the same two places. The wind pushed at their backs and did not let up. It came down off the high ground smelling of stone.
Somewhere past the last of the light there was a thing that they did not name, and did not have to name, because every one of them was standing in it.
The dragon was never seen. It was known.
At dusk they stopped, and Riss noticed that the wind stopped at exactly the moment the sun went. It had not gusted once. Not once, in the whole of the day.

chapters.label: Chapter 9
chapters.title: The Sister
paragraphs: After the wind stopped, they went down off the high ground into a valley with a river in it. At the end of the second day they came to a town called Ashgate. Sancora told them, without warning and in a flat voice, that her sister lived there.

She said it the way a person says *there is a stone in my boot*. She said she would go in alone. Nobody argued. Riss, who had learned a few things about the company by then, noticed that nobody ever argued with Sancora about anything to do with hands.

So they made camp in the willows a mile short of the town. Sancora went in at first light with one satchel, and Riss went with her as far as the last hedge, because somebody had to. Then Riss stood at the hedge for two hours with the plate humming under their coat and waited for a healer to come back out of a town.
She had not seen her sister in nine years. That was the fact Sancora carried in, and she carried it the way she carried everything, which was without comment.

Her sister’s name was Neve. Neve was three years older and had married a wheelwright. Sancora had heard about the wheelwright by letter. She had sent a knife as a wedding gift, because in her trade you send a knife. She had heard about the two children the same way.
Then the letters had stopped. That was four years ago.

Sancora had spent four years deciding what the silence meant. She had a healer’s list. Illness. Bad winter. The sort of husband who does not let his wife write. All of it was on the list, and all of it was wrong, and the wrongness was the point of the chapter.
Ashgate was clean.

That was the first thing, and the second thing, and the only thing. It was a market town of maybe four hundred souls. It had a bridge, a mill, and a street of good houses. It had a **Hygiene Hall** on the north side: a long low building of pale stone with a slate roof.
In front of the Hall there was a garden with benches in it. There were people on the benches. The people had cups.

It was the least frightening building Sancora had ever been afraid of. She stood at the end of the street for a while and looked at it and got nothing off it at all. No smell. No smoke. No noise. A garden, benches, cups.
Neve looked well. That was the whole of it.
Sancora stood on the step for a moment doing the arithmetic of *well*, because she was a healer before she was a sister and she could not turn it off.

Skin good. Eyes clear and not too bright. Weight right for her frame. She had been carrying water; the shoulders had the set. She stood on both feet evenly. Her hands were steady on the door. The right one had the wedding ring. The left one had the old break in the wrist, the one from the winter they were girls, when Neve had come off the barn roof. It had been set. Properly. Better than Sancora could have set it at fourteen with a splint and a strap.
“Sancora,” said Neve.
“You know me.”

“Of course I know you. You’re on the wall.” Neve was crying a little, in an ordinary way, the way people cry at weddings. “They keep the family pages at the Hall. I’ve looked at your page every year.”

Sancora had been doing, for nine years, the things a healer does. Somebody had written a page about it. It had gone into a column somewhere. Her sister had looked at it every year, in a bright room, in a town with benches outside.
“Come in,” said Neve. “You’re freezing. You always were.”
Sancora followed her sister down the passage and did the thing she had been doing since she was fourteen, which was to remember the same winter.

She had been fourteen the year Neve came off the barn roof. It was the year their mother started going thin. Neve was seventeen and doing the work of two people because their father was dead by then, and she had gone up on the roof to fix a leak in November.

She had come off the ladder, not the roof. She had landed on the yard with her left arm under her, and she had not shouted either, and Sancora had set the wrist herself with a splint and a strap and a wooden spoon, and she had set it wrong.

Neve’s wrist had healed crooked. It stayed crooked for six years, and Neve never once said a word about it, and she carried water with it crooked, and she butchered with it crooked, and when a travelling bonesetter passed through in the seventh year she had said, *it’s fine, it doesn’t hurt*, and had kept it crooked for the rest of her life.
That was the sister Sancora remembered. A woman who kept a crooked wrist for six years so that nobody would have to say her little sister had set it wrong.
The wrist on the door was straight.
The house was warm and the bread was good and the two girls were at the table. They were six and nine. The nine-year-old was doing sums.
Sancora sat in that kitchen for two hours and did the thing she had come to do. It was not the thing she had thought she was coming to do.

She had come to find a damaged woman and take her out of a town. That was the plan she had been carrying for four years, and it had a shape to it: diagnosis, argument, the walk away through the gate at night. A healer’s plan. Get the patient off the table.
There was no patient.

Neve talked about their mother. She talked about her warmly, and at length, and in the past tense. She talked about the funeral. She talked about the bad year after it. And then she said the sentence Sancora took away and could not put down for the rest of her life.
“It got to be too much for me, and I went to the Hall, and they were very kind, and I got better.”
“Better,” said Sancora.
“Better.” Neve put her hand on Sancora’s arm. “I know what you’re going to say. You’re going to say I don’t remember it right.”
“I wasn’t going to say that.”

“You were. Everyone from outside says it.” Neve smiled. “The first year I did remember. Every hour of it. I remembered it so hard I couldn’t get out of the chair. The girls were tiny. Toller was doing everything. And I thought: *this is what I am now.*” She took her hand back. “So I went to the Hall. And they were very kind. And here I am.”
“Here you are.”
“I *am* here, Sancora. That’s the part people from outside don’t get.” Neve poured the tea. “I’m not a ghost. I’m the one who’s actually here.”
Sancora took her sister’s wrist. She turned it over. She looked at the old break, which had been set better than she could have set it. She put two fingers on the pulse and counted it.
Sixty-two, and regular, and there was nothing wrong with her sister.
Then she did the other thing, the thing she had not intended to do. It was a healer’s trick and it was an unkind one.
“What was Mother’s name?”
“Rena.” Neve said it at once. “Rena of the low field. She had the mole under her left eye, and she sang flat, and she burned the bread once a month like a clock.”
That was all true. It was all correct. Sancora had asked for a specific and she had been given three specific facts and every one of them was accurate.
So Sancora asked for the other kind.
“Who set my hair the morning of the funeral?”
Neve stopped.

It was a small stop. It was two seconds. It was the kind of stop a person makes when they are waiting for a word to come. Sancora watched it happen and watched her sister’s eyes do the thing eyes do when a page is being turned and the line is missing.
“Someone did,” said Neve.
“Yes.”
“It will come. I’m tired. The girls have been …”
“It’s all right,” said Sancora.

That was the moment. Not the song, not the page, not the bridge. She had asked her sister for one small true thing about the worst morning of both their lives, and her sister had everything except the morning.
It had not been taken away from her. It had been taken *out*, like a tooth out of a row. The row still closed. Everything else in that row was still there and still clean and still true.

Sancora sat with her hands in her lap and understood that she had just looked at the wound, and that the wound was a neat hole where a person’s one specific morning used to be, and that there was nothing on earth a healer could do about a hole of that kind.
The youngest one sang the Interval.
That was the thing Sancora could not have prepared for. She had spent four months watching the Interval go wrong in ways that were enormous and structural. She had never once seen it happen small.

They sang at the table, the way a family does. Neve said they had learned it at the Hall, and that the Hall kept it up on Sundays in the garden. The nine-year-old did the counting part. The six-year-old did the two tones.
She did them beautifully.

She had a true ear. She hit both notes cleanly and sweetly. She put a small decent gap between them and finished the song with a little flourish. Neve laughed and clapped. Toller kissed her head. The girl beamed, because she had done well.

There was no discomfort in that kitchen. Nobody winced. Nobody reached for the unfinished note and failed to find it. It was the first time in four months that Sancora had heard the Interval sung the way the counties sang it as a matter of course: by a happy child, for applause, in a warm room.
It was worse than the shepherdess. It was worse than the mill. It was worse than the three hundred people at Nettleford. Those people had been robbed. This child had been *taught*.
Under her coat, on its strap, the plate hummed.
Quietly. Not the clean fifth. Not the loud divided fifth of the customs house. Just the divided fifth, at the volume of a cat, against her ribs, in a kitchen where everyone was happy.
Sancora understood that whatever the plate was doing, it was not doing it for her sake.
They asked her to stay. That was the second attack, and they made it out of love, which is the only way that attack is ever made.
Toller had a workshop. Neve had a room. There was a cot in the back of the Hall’s garden-house for the family of residents. The treatment was free for family.

Neve said all of it in one hopeful rush while she was washing the plates. One of the girls hung on Sancora’s leg the whole time. The other one drew her a picture, and the picture was the four of them with a fifth person in it who was Sancora.

“Just the bad year,” said Neve. “They don’t do the whole thing. You don’t have to forget anything you don’t want to. It isn’t like that.” She wrung the cloth out. “You’ve been carrying something since you were fourteen. I know you. Anybody can see it. You could put it down here.”
Before Sancora could answer, the six-year-old was put on her lap with a chest cough, because that is what happens in a kitchen: the medicine in the room gets found.
Sancora listened to the child’s chest for a minute. She put her ear to the small back and heard the low wet sound in the left side, and she said, “Summer cough. Not the winter one.”
“How do you know?”
“Because the winter one sounds like a door.”

She sat the girl up and got her to breathe on the back of a spoon and looked at the colour of it. Then she gave Neve four instructions: steam in the room at night, no cold water on the chest, honey in the morning, and if the sound changed to a door, send for somebody at once.
It took her nine minutes. It was the only medicine she practised in Ashgate, it was the best nine minutes of the whole visit, and it worked.
The child went back to the table and finished her sums.

Sancora stood in her sister’s kitchen with the plate humming against her ribs and understood exactly what she was being offered. She understood exactly how kind the offer was. She understood exactly what it would cost.
“No,” she said.
“Just …”
“No,” said Sancora. “Not the bad year. Not any of it.”
She dried her hands on the cloth. She dried them carefully, the way she had been taught to dry hands.

“I’m not a person who can put anything down, Neve. That’s the whole of what I am. You take the grief out of me and you don’t get a happy version of me. You get a woman with a very good pair of hands and no reason to use them.”
They let her go, which was the worst thing they did.

That was not fair, and Sancora corrected herself about it on the road afterwards, and made herself be exact, because she had been trained to be exact. They let her go because they loved her and because she asked.
Neve walked her as far as the bridge. They stood there a while in the cold. Neve gave her a jar of preserves and a letter for their aunt and told her to write, and meant it.
The clerk came to the bridge too.

He was a young man from the Hall in a plain coat. He was polite. They were always polite; that was the method, and Sancora had it written in her book by now. He had a page and a pencil, and he explained that because Sancora was a healer of record in the family, the Hall liked to have the family page completed.
“Sign what?”
“That her treatment was received and her condition was good,” said the clerk. “It’s a formality.”

Sancora looked at the page. It said that Neve was well. It had a line at the bottom for a healer’s mark, and the line was empty, and the rest of the record was full. It was, she had to admit, completely true.
Her sister *was* well. That was the fact. There was a page in a hall that said her sister was well, and her sister was well.
“I won’t sign it,” said Sancora.
“It’s a formality,” the clerk said again.

“You’re asking me to put my mark on a page that says she was always fine.” Sancora handed the page back. “She was not always fine. She was ill for a year. Nobody could help her. Then somebody took the year out of her.” She picked up her satchel. “Now there’s a page that says she was fine. If I sign it, the page is right, and the year is nowhere.”
The clerk wrote something down.
“Ask somebody who wasn’t there,” said Sancora. “Ask somebody who hasn’t got a sister.”

She came out through the willows at dusk. The company was waiting with the fire lit. Riss was standing a little way off from everybody, holding a bowl, because Riss always had something in their hands when they did not want to be asked anything.
“How is she?” said Veylan.

“Married,” said Sancora. “Two girls. A good house. A good mill town with a warm room in it and a garden with benches.” She sat down by the fire and put the preserves on the ground. “She’s better than she ever was. She’s the happiest person I’ve seen since we left the coast. There is nothing wrong with her hands or her pulse or her eyes.”
“That’s good, then,” said Veylan.
“It’s the worst thing that has ever happened to me,” said Sancora.
Then she did not say anything else, and nobody made her.
Later, when the fire had burned down and the others were lying down, Orphiel came and stood beside her for a moment before he went to his blanket.
He said one thing. It was the only thing he said about Ashgate, then or afterwards.
“She has been taken out,” he said. “Not away. Out.”
Sancora looked up at him.

“I keep what has been taken out,” said Orphiel. “If you want her written in the log, say the word, and I will write her in it, and her name will sit on the shelf with nine thousand and four.” He waited. “It is what I am for. It is not a favour. It is the job.”
“No,” said Sancora.
“No.”
“She’s alive,” said Sancora. “Her heart’s going at sixty-two and she has two girls and she makes the best bread I’ve eaten in nine years. She’s alive. She’s just not *whole*.”
“Then she is not mine to keep,” said Orphiel, and went to his blanket, and that was the end of it.
After a while she went and sat with Riss by the fire and asked for the Leaf.

Riss got it out of the satchel without asking any of the questions that were available. They handed it over. Sancora opened it at a clean page at the back and took the pen and wrote, in her small square hand, two lines.
*Neve. Alive. Ashgate, on the north side of the bridge.*
Then she sat looking at it.
“Write her girls’ names under it,” she said. “I don’t know them. I didn’t ask. I was too busy being right.”
She held the pen out to Riss.
“You write it. If I write it, it’s a healer’s note. If you write it, it’s a record.”
Riss wrote, in the margin: *two girls.*
Above them the sky was clear and the wind was gone. Out past the willows the grey road went on west along the river. The gold one lay beside it.
Neither of them shone.
“It isn’t taking,” said Sancora, after a while.
Riss looked at her.

“That’s what you said at Ashenford. It isn’t taking. Nobody took her.” Sancora put her hands out to the fire and looked at them, both of them, the way she did before she used them on a person. “Now I know the rest of the sentence.”
“Tell me.”
“Nobody took her. They *improved* her.” She closed her hands. “I could fix a bone. I fixed yours in Collow and I’d fix it again tomorrow. I can’t fix this. Nobody can fix this.”
She looked at the fire.
“That’s why it works.”

chapters.label: Chapter 10
chapters.title: The Clean Grain
paragraphs: After the sister, and the garden with the benches, and the warm room full of people who had been improved, the company came down out of the hills into the flats. On the fifth day they reached a market settlement called Marle. There Old Den found his war again.

Not the old war. He had lost his brother in the old war, and he had stopped wanting it back about sixty years ago. This was the small version. It was worse, because it was made of paper and neighbours and a queue.
And because it happened at chest height, at a market cross, in the middle of the afternoon, with children watching.
Old Den had been a soldier for eleven years and a farmer for forty. He had two rules.

The first rule was that you did not raise your hand to a person. He had made that rule in the fourth year of the Ascension War, standing over his brother in a field. He had kept it for a hundred and twenty years, through three counties and four bad winters and every market in the north.
He had been beaten twice. He had been cheated more times than that. He had never once raised his hand.
The second rule was that you did not put your mark on a page you had not read. He had made that one later, and he did not talk about it.
At Marle they asked him for his mark on a page. Then they took his hand.
The county had a scheme called clean grain, and it worked the way everything worked.

There was a licensed mill at Marle. It had a new wheel and a good road to it. There was a fee for the milling, and a stamp that went into the flour, and a stamped sack sold in the county towns for a third more than an unstamped one.

Unstamped flour could not be sold at the licensed markets. Unstamped flour could not be carried on the county roads above a certain weight. A village that ground its own grain at its own stones and ate its own bread was not, strictly, breaking a law.

But a village that did it for eleven years would find things happening. Its young people could not be apprenticed in the towns. Its carts were stopped more often at the customs gates. The man who came round about the water rates came round twice a year instead of once.
And there was always, always a form.

The company had met clean grain twice before, at Ashenford and at Marrowgate, and had done nothing about it. At that point they had been walking with their hands full of arithmetic and no way to act on it.
At Marle they had a witness. A witness made them brave in a way Riss found interesting and slightly frightening.
It was Veylan who started it, because it was always Veylan who started things by asking a practical question at the wrong moment. It was Mira who gave it a shape. It was Riss who gave it a name.

They were in the mill yard at Marle. The miller’s name was Hesp. He was sixty and tired, and he had been grinding his village’s grain at those stones for forty years. He was going to have to stop, because his son wanted an apprenticeship in the county town, and the apprenticeship forms wanted a clean-grain record for the family.
“So what do we do?” said Hesp.
Riss said the thing they had worked out in a mill’s back room four hundred miles behind them.
“You make the account wider than the document.”

Veylan, who had heard it once before and had spent four months quietly thinking about it, took it further. That was the surprise of the whole business. The trowel man, sixty years old, with a lifetime of being corrected, turned out to be the one in the company who could *build*.
“Here’s what I’d do,” said Veylan. “It’s not clever and it’ll take you a fortnight.”
“Go on,” said Hesp.

“You keep a book. Not one book for the village. Every household keeps its own. The mill keeps the ledger, and the mill’s ledger lists every sack that ever went through these stones and whose it was. The household pages list every loaf and the name of everybody who ever ate it.” Veylan put his hand flat on the mill’s table. “Then the man comes round about the apprenticeship record and says, show me your clean-grain paper. And you show him the book. And it’s got his mother in it.”
Hesp looked at him.
“That isn’t a document,” he said.
“No,” said Veylan. “That’s the point. A document, you can file. A book with his mother in it, you can’t.”
It took them eleven days, and they were the best eleven days the company had had.

Mira drew the columns for the mill ledger and the household pages. She made them big enough to hold the small things, because that was the whole trick: a page with room for *who was at the table*. Riss sat with three families and taught them the difference between a sum and a record. They did it without using the word remainder once. A village in the flats did not need a theory. It needed a ledger with a wide column and somebody to show them how to rule it.
Old Den did the ruling. That was his part, and nobody had expected it.

He had the steadiest hand in the company. The trick of ruling with a straight edge was one he had learned in the war, making maps. He sat in Hesp’s mill for four days with a jar of ink and a rule, and drew lines for eleven households.
He was good at it. He was *content*, which was a thing Riss had never once seen on him.
He said, on the fourth night, in the flat way he said everything: “This is the first useful thing I’ve done since the war.”
The sealer came on the twelfth day.

His name was Tobin Reel. He was twenty-five. He was polite. He came with two men and a cart, and the cart had a screw press on it with a brass plate that said CLEAN GRAIN and a smaller plate with the county seal.

He was not a villain. Riss watched him for a long time from the mill door and could not make him into one, and there was no point pretending. He was a young man from the county town with a good coat and clean hands and a mother.
He had a commission. He had a book to fill in. If he filled it in he got paid. If he did not, he had to explain why not to somebody in an office with a kettle.

He read the notice out at the cross in a clear voice. It said the mill at Marle was to be surrendered to the county for the purposes of the clean-grain scheme, and that the millstones were to be removed for safe disposal, and that a representative of the village should put his mark to the registration.
Nobody in the yard moved.
“Just the mark,” said Tobin Reel. “One of you. Then the paperwork’s done and I can go.”
Hesp said, “No.”
“Then somebody else. It doesn’t have to be you.”
“I mean no,” said Hesp. “I mean nobody’s going to put a mark on it. You can tell them that at the office.”
The young man looked around the yard.
There were maybe forty people in it by then, which is what a mill yard looks like when a village has decided a thing is going to happen. There were children up on the wall of the mill.

He looked at them and Riss watched him do the sum. It was a real sum, and Riss could see the figures going past behind his eyes. No force in the commission. No constable in the village. Eleven miles to the town. And a cart, and a press, and a book to fill in.
Then Old Den stepped out of the mill door and stood between the press and Hesp.
That was all. He did not say anything. He stood there, an old man of a hundred and forty who looked about eighty, with a rule under his arm, and put himself in the way.
“Sir,” said Tobin Reel.
“No,” said Old Den.
“I need a mark.”
“You’ll not get one.”
“Then I’ll have to put the mill out of service,” said the young man. “I can’t do that without the registration.”
Old Den looked at him. Riss saw his face do something and could never afterwards describe it.
“It won’t be,” said Old Den.
It happened in about four seconds.

Tobin Reel took hold of Old Den’s right hand and pushed it under the plate of the screw press. With his other hand he turned the lever one full turn. That was before anybody in the yard had finished understanding what they were looking at.
The press was made for stamping lead. It had a screw and a heavy plate and a brass die underneath, and one turn of the lever took the die down the thickness of a thumb.
Old Den did not shout.

That was the thing the village of Marle talked about for nine years afterwards. Riss wrote it down that night, and Orphiel repeated it in a room in a county town two hundred miles away, word for word, in front of a clerk who had to write it down: **the old man did not shout.**
He made a sound. Everybody makes a sound.
But he did not shout, and he did not pull back, and (this was the thing Riss could not get out of their head) he did not raise his other hand.
He had one hand free and he had been a soldier for eleven years. Tobin Reel was twenty-five and standing right there. Old Den did not raise his hand.
He stood with his ruined hand in the press and looked at the young man’s face. Then he said, in the same flat voice he had said everything in for a hundred and twenty years:
“You’ll want to stop now.”
Tobin Reel stopped. He let go of the lever and stepped back and looked down at what he had done. The look on his face was the look of a man who has just found out the price of his commission.
He was grey.
“You only had to put your mark on the paper,” he said.
Nobody answered him. Riss could have. There were four things a person could say to that sentence, and every one of them was true, and none of them would have helped anybody in that yard.
What happened next in the mill yard was quiet and had four parts, and Riss remembered the order exactly.

Sancora got to Old Den before anybody else. She had been standing by the mill door the whole time with her satchels on her shoulders, which was where she stood now whenever the company went anywhere. She had him sitting on the mounting block with his hand in her lap inside half a minute.

She did not say anything to Tobin Reel. She did not say anything to anybody. She looked at the hand for four seconds. Then she started giving orders about hot water, and about a board, and about a strap, in a voice that had no medicine in it at all, and people went and did what she said.
Hesp said one word, which was the name of the county. Then he stopped and did not say it again, and did not move toward the press or the young man.

Riss would think about that for a long time afterwards. Forty people in a yard with a man who had just broken an old man’s hand, and the forty people did not move. They stood in a ring. They held each other’s arms. They watched, and nobody touched him.
The village of Marle had no hand to raise either.
Orphiel walked over to the clerk.

There was a clerk. There was always a clerk. The young man had brought one, a boy of about seventeen with a book, because the scheme required that everything be written down. The boy had been standing by the cart with his book open for the whole of it.
He had written nothing since Old Den said *it won’t be*. There was nothing in the scheme’s instructions about what to write when this happened.
Orphiel stood in front of him.
“You have a book,” said Orphiel.
“Yes, sir.”
“Then write.”

The old man did not raise his voice. Riss, watching, understood that this was the room. This was the room Orphiel had been waiting for since the ridge. He had not chosen it. He had not wanted it. The whole of his discipline was that he did not choose.
“Write what I say, in my words. Put my name at the bottom of it. Read it back to me when you have done.”
The boy’s hands were shaking.
“What do I write?”
“Write: *The man from the county took the old man’s hand and put it in the press.* Then write: *The old man did not raise his hand.* Then write: *I, Orphiel, keeper of the deletion log, saw it.*”
The boy wrote it. He had to stop twice.
Then he read it back in a shaking voice, and Orphiel listened to the whole of it and said, “That is accurate,” and turned away.
He did not take the page. He did not sign anything. He did not file anything. He did not open his satchel.
The millstones were not removed from Marle.

That was the fourth part. It was the least dramatic and the most important, and it consisted entirely of a thing that did not happen. No cart came back. No constable came. No letter of consequence came.

And the county, which had a page in it now that said a man from the county had put an old man’s hand in a press, did what the county always did when something did not fit its column. It wrote the incident down in a column.

*An incident.* That was the word. The company heard it eight days later from a carrier, who had it from a clerk, who had it from an office. There was an incident at Marle, and the mill had been left out of the registration for the present.
No charge. No hearing. No man’s name against it.

Which meant, Riss understood, walking, that Tobin Reel would keep his commission and lose a year of sleep. Old Den would keep the millstones for the village and lose the use of two fingers and most of a thumb. The county would file it and go on.
And the fee would be the same fee.

That night the village ground its grain. Hesp turned the stones. Eleven households put their bread in the same ovens, and every name went in the books. The ledger at the mill listed every sack of it and whose it was. The last line of it, in Old Den’s straight ruled hand, was forty-one names long.
It did not divide into anything.

Sancora sat up all night with the hand. She saved the fingers. In the morning she told them plainly, standing in the mill door with blood on her cuffs, that the fingers would not straighten and the grip would not come back.
She was not sorry.
“A straight hand is a hand a clerk can sign with,” she said. “A crooked hand is a hand that gets out of the way.”

Tobin Reel was seen once, on the road east, sitting on the tail of the empty cart with the press on it, with his own hands hanging between his knees. Riss did not feel about it what they had expected to feel, and wrote that down too, because it was true.
*He looked like a man who had been filed.*
They went on west the next morning.
The goat stood outside the mill all night facing west across the water. It would not come in. Nobody asked it to.
Old Den walked in the middle of the line with his right arm bound across his chest. Mira offered to rig a sling off the mule and he said no. Veylan offered to carry his pack and he said no.
At the evening halt Riss asked him whether it hurt. He said, “It does.” That was the whole of the conversation.
Then he said, without anybody asking, in the flat voice, looking at the fire:

“I had a brother. He raised his hand.” He put his good hand on his knee. “It didn’t work. That’s all it ever is. That’s the whole thing I could have told anybody, and nobody ever asks an old man anything.”
The plate hummed against Riss’s chest the whole evening. The divided fifth, steady. No louder and no quieter than it had been in the mill yard when the press came down.
Kael Riven sat with his burned hand wrapped around his forearm and said nothing. Above them the Emberion constellation stood over the western peaks with one joint of the wing gone.
Riss wrote the day up that night in the Leaf. They put the forty-one names at the mill at the top of the page, and below them: *the county calls it an incident.*
And under that, in the margin, they found in the morning that Sancora had added one line of her own.
*He did not raise his hand. Write that first.*

chapters.label: Chapter 11
chapters.title: The Vault
paragraphs: After the clean grain and the press, and the mill at Marle, and forty-one names that did not divide into anything, the company went north for six days to a county seat called Carrow, because Orphiel said there was a room there he wanted them to see.
He said it the way he said everything, which was once, plainly, and then he waited.
“What kind of room?” said Veylan.
“A record room,” said Orphiel. “There is one in every county seat. They are all the same room. I have been in nine of them.”
“Will they let us in?”

“They will let *me* in,” said Orphiel. “I have a cord and a card. If you carry the right satchel and you look bored, a record room will open itself. That is the whole of the trick and it is not a trick.”
Nahl walked the last mile into Carrow beside him and asked the question that was actually being asked.
“Why are you showing us this?”
Orphiel did not answer for a while. Ahead of them the town came up out of the flat land: a wall, a gate, a good stone bridge, a tower with a clock on it, and smoke going straight up in the cold air.

“Because you have been four hundred miles asking what the counties do,” he said at last. “You have seen the queues and the stamps and the notes and the warm rooms with kettles in them. You have not yet seen what they do with what they take.” He shifted the satchel on his shoulder. “You should see the shelf, Nahl. Before you decide anything else, you should see the shelf.”
Carrow had a customs house at the gate, and they went through it in twenty minutes, because Veylan had learned exactly which papers to have ready and exactly which papers to say nothing about.

Beyond the gate the town was ordinary. It was bigger than Marrowgate and older than Ashgate. It had a cloth market, two mills, a row of good houses on the north side, and a public garden with gravel walks. There were children sledding on a slope by the wall. There was a smell of bread.
The record room was behind the courthouse, in a long low building of grey stone with a slate roof and two windows too high to see out of.
At the door there was a desk, and at the desk there was a clerk.

He was about thirty-five, thin, with a permanent cough that he kept behind his hand, and he was, Nahl noticed at once, kind. That was the method; Nahl had the sentence written in their own book by now, four months old and still holding. Nobody is ever unkind and that is the method.
Orphiel put the card on the desk.
The clerk looked at it for about two seconds. That was all. Nahl watched his eyes find the right shape on the card and move on, and it was like watching a man read the word *milk* on a churn.
“Vault-keeper,” said the clerk. “South register?”
“It will be vol four.”

“Vol four is in the far room, second gallery, left of the window.” The clerk wrote nothing down, because there was nothing to write down. A keeper coming to look at a keeper’s book was not an event. “Do you want the lamp?”
“Please.”
The clerk gave him a lamp, and then he looked at the rest of them and said, “You’ll be wanting to wait? There’s a bench.”
“Their business is mine,” said Orphiel.
“Right you are,” said the clerk, and went back to his paper, and that was the entire security of the county’s deepest record room.
It was warm inside and it was clean.

That was the first thing and Nahl could not get past it for the whole visit. It was a room full of shelves, and every shelf was full, and there was no dust anywhere. There was a table with blotting paper on it, and a pot of paste, and a set of weights for keeping pages flat. The floor had been swept. There was a stove in the corner with a bucket of coal beside it.

It was not a dungeon. It was not a crypt, or a cave, or a place with chains on the wall. It was better kept than most kitchens Nahl had sat in, and the reason was simple. Paper has to be kept dry, and pest-free, and cool, and if it is not, then the whole object of the exercise fails.
The counties took care of their records the way a farmer takes care of seed.

The shelves went up eleven feet and there were ladders on runners. Somebody had chalked the gallery numbers at the head of each bay. In the far room, second gallery, left of the window, there were four hundred and eleven volumes of parish copies, and vol four was a grey book bound in cloth, about the size of a bible, and it had the county seal stamped into the cover and a catalogue number in ink.
Orphiel took it down and put it on the table and opened the lamp.
Before he opened it he showed them the catalogue, because he wanted them to see the title.
The catalogue was a ledger of its own, ruled in five columns, and it was open on a stand at the end of the bay. Every volume in the room was in it. Entry four hundred and sixty-two read:
*Parish copies, unclaimed, south. Vol 4. Received by transfer, Sallow, 40 yrs. Condition: good. Not to be circulated.*

“*Unclaimed*,” said Orphiel. “That is the word that kept nine thousand and four people on a public shelf for forty years. If you want to hide a book in a county, do not lock it up. Give it a dull title and put it in the catalogue, and every man who reads the catalogue will be satisfied, because a book that has been written down is a book that has been dealt with.”
Kael Riven read the entry twice. He had his slate under his arm the way he always carried it, with the strap in his fingers.
“Does it have an edge?” he said.
That was the only technical question anybody asked in the vault all day, and Nahl did not understand it at the time.

“Every entry has one,” said Orphiel. “That is the fourth column. A thing that was kept has an edge you can follow. A thing that was taken out has an edge too. It is the other kind, and it goes the other way, and it is why you can feel the room.”
Kael put his hand flat on the closed cover and left it there for a moment, and then took it off, and said nothing else.
“This is the log,” he said.
“That’s it?” said Veylan.
“That’s it.”
“It’s a book.”

“It is the most dangerous book in the county,” said Orphiel, “and it is on a public shelf, catalogued, and the catalogue calls it *parish copies, unclaimed, south*, and the clerk at the door has been sitting in front of it for eleven years.” He turned it round so that they could all see. “They do not know what it is. That is not a joke. Nobody in the counties knows what this book is, because the man who made it did not tell them, and because a register that is correctly filed is never opened.”
The log had four columns.
**Name. Date. Reason. Line.**

That was all. No prose. No argument. No commentary. It was ruled by hand in a fine steady hand, and the ruling went all the way down every page, and every page was numbered, and there was no page with anything crossed out on it.
Then Nahl understood what they were looking at, and the understanding came in the same way the smell of the wind had come, which is to say all at once.
The first three columns were the normal thing. They were a record of what had been taken out of a register somewhere in the south of the counties: a name, a date, and a reason.

The fourth column was a single ruled line, drawn across the empty space where the *thing itself* would have been. Every entry had one. Nothing was written in it. It was exactly the width of a name and a household and a life.
Nine thousand and four entries, at an average of eleven to a page, in a hand that had been the same for forty years.
“They’re not hidden,” said Sancora.
“No.”
“Nobody took them away and put them somewhere.”

“They were taken *out*,” said Orphiel, “and I wrote them down, and this is where they are.” He turned a page. “That is the whole of the vault. It is on a shelf. You could walk in here on a Tuesday and read every one of them.”
Riss, who had been quiet, said, “Show me the reasons.”
The reasons were the worst thing in the room.
Nahl read half a page of them and then had to stand up and walk to the window.
*Amended for consistency.* Three words, twice on that page, and beneath them a line drawn the width of a household.
*Not required.* Four times.

*At the family’s request.* That one had a date and no line under it, because the family had come and asked, and the family had wanted it, and the clerk had done it kindly, and it was on the page in the same fine steady hand as all the others.
*Removed to prevent hardship.*
*Duplicated in error.*
*Consolidated.*

There was nothing in the fourth column of any page. In nine thousand and four entries there was not one angry word, not one crossing-out, not one note in the margin. Sixteen entries on a page and every one of them tidy.
Sancora, who had been standing at the end of the table with her arms folded, asked about the kind ones.
“*At the family’s request*,” she said. “How many of those?”
Orphiel turned to the back of the book.
“There is a tally,” he said. “I keep it in the last three pages. Eleven hundred and six.”
“Eleven hundred families asked.”

“Eleven hundred and six,” said Orphiel. “And in nine of those ten, they asked because it was cheaper. That is not a figure I invented; it is a figure I read. When a person is amended for hardship, the fee on the household drops. When a household is consolidated, the water rate drops. The clerk does not have to be cruel. He only has to be helpful.” He closed the tally pages. “The kind ones are the ones I cannot put down. Anyone can carry a cruelty. Nobody can carry a kindness that worked.”
Sancora went and stood by the window for a while after that, facing the wrong way, with her hands on the sill, and did not say anything else in the vault.
“That’s what they’d do to us,” said Veylan, quietly.
“No,” said Orphiel. “That is what they have *done* to nine thousand and four. You are all still in various registers, in the wrong columns, drawing a fee. That is the only difference.”
They looked for the bread-woman.
It was Riss who thought of it, and it took them twenty minutes, because the log is alphabetical by county and then by date, and the woman had been in two counties and neither of them was this one.
When Orphiel found her county he went through it twice, once quickly and once slowly, and then he shut the book.
“She is not in it,” he said.
Riss looked at him. “She’s the whole reason we came west.”

“She is not in it.” Orphiel opened the book again and ran his finger down the column. “Listen to me. This log contains everything that was taken out of a register in the south of the counties in forty years. Every name that came off a shelf is on these pages. Your bread-woman is not on these pages.”
“Then where is she?”
“Nowhere,” said Orphiel. “That is the thing you have to understand, and it is worse than the log. I keep what came *off* the shelf. Nothing came off for her.”
Mira had the chart out on the table, and she was standing over it with both hands flat on the two columns, and she said the sentence that Nahl wrote down that evening and kept.

“She was never on it,” Mira said. “Look at the two pages. The market’s woman sold two loaves. The mill’s woman supplied one sack. Neither page is wrong. Neither page was amended.” Her hands stayed flat. “She was divided out. She wasn’t deleted. There’s nobody to delete. She fell in the gap between two correct pages and there is no clerk anywhere whose job it is to look in the gap.”
Orphiel shut the log, and it made a small sound, and nobody said anything for a while.

“The counties built a machine that only files things,” he said at last. “It is very good at filing. It will file a whole village in one line. It will file a war. But it will not look into the space between two of its own pages, because there is no column for that, and a clerk who looks into a space is a clerk not filling in a box.” He put the grey book back on the table. “Your woman is not hidden. She is *unaccounted*, which in this building is a word with no page under it at all.”
Mira wanted to copy it.

That was the seventh hour of the visit and they had all been quiet for a while, and she had the chart tube out and the cap off, and she said the practical thing in the practical voice, and everybody in the room understood the argument at once because it was a good one.

“Two pages,” she said. “Just the columns and the reasons. Not the names. If nine thousand and four people have been taken out of the south in forty years, then the number of them is the most important fact anybody in this company has ever held. I can draw that.”
“No,” said Orphiel.
“Why not?”

“Because I have already drawn it,” he said. “That is what this book is. A copy of the shape of a copy is a map of a map, and the counties have a room full of those. If you want the shape, keep the shape.” He tapped the grey cover. “The names are the shape. Take the names out and you have got a column, and a column is what they had on the day they started.”
Mira put the cap back on the tube and did not argue, which Nahl noted, because Mira argued about the chart with everybody else in the company and always won on the facts.
“It’s a hundred and six pages of arithmetic and no names,” she said, to be exact.
“Yes,” said Orphiel. “And it has never once been enough, and that is the whole of what I have learned in forty years, and I am not sharing it with you so that you can draw it.”
Nahl found their own village at about four in the afternoon, which was not what they had expected to do when they walked in.

They had not meant to look. They had been reading the reasons, because the reasons were the worst thing in the room and a person keeps reading them, and somewhere in the south section between *Ash* and *Ashby* their eye went past a line and came back to it.
*The village of Lowfield. Amended for consistency. Sixty-two names.*
One line. One date. Forty years ago. Sixty-two names in a village Nahl had not thought about in nine years, and a fourth column, ruled, and empty, the width of a place.
Nahl stood and looked at it for a long time.
They did not say anything to the company. Not then, and not that night.

Nahl was the bearer, and a bearer does not put a thing down in front of six people and ask them to hold it. They knew exactly what it would do to the room. Sancora would ask who was in it. Mira would want the names. Veylan would ask whether anybody had survived. Riss would write it in the Leaf within the hour.
And none of those things would change one word of the page.
So Nahl read the line, and set it down, and stepped back from the table.
That was the difference between the two keepers, and Nahl worked it out standing in front of that shelf, and did not say it out loud for another year.

Orphiel’s book held what had already been taken. Nahl’s seal held one thing that still belonged to somebody. Between the two of them they had one rule, and it was the same rule from both ends: a person is not a thing to be written down by somebody else, even kindly, even to keep them.
Sixty-two names. One line. One date. A fourth column ruled the width of a place, and nothing in it.
Orphiel, across the room, had watched them find it.
He said one sentence, and it was not a question, and Nahl never decided whether it was a kindness or the opposite.
“You can come back and read it whenever you like,” he said. “That is what I keep the room for.”
They came out into the cold at five, past the clerk with the cough, who told them to mind the step.
The goat was outside, standing in the road across from the door, in the exact place it had been standing for four hours. It had not moved. It looked at Orphiel, and then it looked west.

The plate hummed against Nahl’s chest on the way out. The divided fifth, quiet, steady, the same note it had been making since the gate. Kael Riven walked beside them with his burned hand in his coat and said nothing at all, which was how Kael had been carrying things since the mill at Marle.
At the inn that night, Veylan asked the practical question one more time, and this time it was the right one.
“So what did we learn?”
Nahl thought about the clean room, and the swept floor, and the stove, and the paste pot, and the eleven feet of shelves.

“We learned that they’re not monsters,” they said. “That’s what we learned. Monsters, you can fight. This is a building with a stove in it and a man with a cough, and the man is kind, and the room is warm, and every name that ever came off a shelf in the south of these counties is on a public shelf in it, alphabetically.”
“That’s worse,” said Veylan.
“Yes,” said Nahl. “It’s much worse.”
Nahl went up to bed and lay awake for a while and thought about what a bookkeeping system does when it has been running correctly for two hundred years.

It does not need a villain. That was the part the company had been missing for four hundred miles, and it was the part that Carrow had finally given them. Every person Nahl had met in the counties had been polite. The clerk at Marrowgate was polite. The sealer at Marle was polite, and he had a mother. The woman in the queue at Sunth had been served kindly by a young man with clean cuffs.

A machine that must be operated by cruel people would stall at the first good man. The counties had built the other kind. They had built a machine that ran on tidiness and a fee, and any decent person could work it, and most of them did, and went home, and slept well, and never once had to look at what was in the fourth column.
That was the thing Nahl had wanted to know since the river, and now they knew it, and they found that knowing it was worse than not knowing, which was a lesson they were getting used to.
Nahl did not write the village of Lowfield in the Leaf that night.
They wrote three other things, in the order they had happened, in the back of their own book, in handwriting that was smaller than usual.
*The room is warm. There is a stove. The floor is swept.*
*The woman is in neither column and in no log. There is no clerk for the gap.*
*Sixty-two names. One line. One date.*
Then they shut the book and lay down and slept the way bearers sleep, in pieces.

At some point before light, Orphiel got up and went out to sit with the goat. Nahl heard him go, and did not follow, because the two of them had an understanding by then that did not require any words at all.
In the morning they went on west, and Carrow went behind them, and the record room stayed exactly as it was: warm, swept, catalogued, and open to the public.

chapters.label: Chapter 12
chapters.title: The Index
paragraphs: After the vault at Carrow, and the grey book with four columns, and the line ruled the width of a life, the company walked north-west for nine days to the place the note had been sent.

The note was real. That was the thing none of them said out loud for the first three days. At Marrowgate the Assessor’s clerk had written a line on a page and put it in a bag, and the bag had gone down the fast road, and the fast road went to Sunth. So they walked to Sunth, which meant they walked the whole nine days toward a piece of paper that was already there, waiting, with their shape on it.
Veylan said it once, on the fourth morning, in the flat way he said things.
“We’re walking into a town that already knows we’re coming.”
“Yes,” said Nahl.
“And we’re doing it on purpose.”
“Yes,” said Nahl.
“Right,” said Veylan, and counted the seed crate, and that was the end of it.
Sunth was the biggest town any of them had seen.

It had three gates and a wall with eleven towers on it. It had a cathedral with scaffolding on one side, four markets, two cloth halls, a river with barges on it, and a street of offices where every second door had a brass plate on it and every plate had a title on it. It smelled of coal smoke and wet stone and money.
Mira stood at the north gate with the chart tube in her hand and looked at it for a long time before she went in.
“I have drawn two hundred roads,” she said, “and this is the first place I have been that was already drawn.”
The Index was in a public building.
That was the first thing that undid Riss, and it undid them slowly over the course of an afternoon, in stages, so that by evening they were in no doubt at all about what they had walked into.

The building was called the Hall of Records, and it was open from eight to four, six days a week. There was a porter at the door who told them where to hang their coats. There were benches in the front hall and a queue on the benches. The queue was ordinary. A woman with a basket, two men in work clothes, a boy of about twelve running an errand for somebody, a carter, an old man asleep.
At the end of the hall there was a counter with three clerks behind it and a shelf of ledgers on the wall.
The sign above the counter said, in plain letters: **THE INDEX: ENQUIRIES.**

Riss stood in that hall with the plate humming quietly under their coat and worked out, in about four minutes, that they were looking at the machine’s front door. It was not guarded. It was not hidden. There was no fee to look. Any person in the county could walk in off the street, hang up their coat, take a place on a bench, and ask the Index a question about themselves.
They had built the counties so that everybody could check whether they existed, and everybody did, and that was the whole of its power.
The queue took an hour.
Riss spent it listening, because listening was the only thing available and because a person in a queue hears everything.
The woman with the basket was ahead of them. She had a paper in her hand and she was holding it the way you hold a paper you have already read twenty times.
When she got to the counter Riss heard all of it. The hall was quiet, and the acoustics of a stone room are generous.
“I want to correct my son,” she said.
“Name?”
“Bren. He was born in the spring of the year of the long frost. I’ve got the parish line here, look, the priest wrote it.”

The clerk looked at the paper. He looked at it for a while. Then he said, kindly, and he *was* kind, that was the thing, he was a young man with clean cuffs and a good manner and nothing at all wrong with him,
“I’m sorry. There’s no entry for him.”
“There is. Here. The priest wrote it.”
“The parish line is right,” said the clerk. “It’s a good line, and it’s witnessed, and I’ve no doubt at all it’s true. But the Index is the county’s register, and your son is not in it.”
“Then put him in it.”
“I can’t do that,” said the clerk. “I can correct the Index. I can’t add to it. A correction is for a thing that’s recorded wrong. If a thing was never recorded, there’s nothing there to correct.”
The woman stood at the counter with her parish line.
“So he isn’t in it,” she said.
“No.”
“Where is he, then?”
The clerk looked at her, and Riss watched a man search for a sentence that would be true and also kind, and find one, and say it.
“He’s in the parish line,” he said. “That’s a real record. It’s just not ours.”
Then the boy went up to the counter, and Riss watched the whole method operate on a child in under a minute.
He had a slip of paper from his mother. He read it out carefully, in the voice of a boy who had been rehearsed at a kitchen table. A holding, a field name, a name.
Six minutes later he came away with an answer. The answer was good news. He was pleased, and he ran out of the hall with the slip in his fist to tell his mother that everything was in order.
Nothing had happened to him. Nothing had happened to his family. The machine had been kind to him and correct, and Riss stood in the queue and understood how it survived.

It was right eleven times a day. That was the whole trick. A person whose page is in order walks out of the Hall of Records believing the counties are a good thing. The person behind him whose son does not exist walks out with a parish line. Both of them go home and tell their neighbours, and the queue in the morning is as long as it was the day before.
When Riss got to the counter they asked for Collow, because it was the only question they could think of that would not give anything away.

The clerk found it in about ninety seconds, because the Index was very well made. The entry was one line. *Collow. Amended.* And then, in the remarks column, in a hand that was not the clerk’s: *Amended. Again.*
