“That’s odd,” said the clerk, and he sounded genuinely puzzled. “That’s the second amendment. I’ve not seen a village amended twice.”
“What does an amendment mean?”
“It means the entry was brought into line,” said the clerk. “Somebody found a discrepancy and corrected it. It’s a good thing. It means the record’s right.”
Riss asked for two more, because they had to know whether it worked the same way everywhere, and it did. Nettleford. *Amended.* Marle. *Amended.* Vellum Reach. *Amended, and the holding divided.*
And then, because there was no reason not to, they asked for the woman.
The clerk took the details down patiently: a bread-woman, about forty, two loaves at a market, one sack to a mill, in the south, nine years ago.
He looked. He looked for eleven minutes, which was the longest anybody had looked for anything all day, and he went into the back room twice, and when he came out he was apologetic.
“I can’t find her. There’s no entry at all.”
“Not even a wrong one.”
“Not even a wrong one,” said the clerk. “I’m sorry. Was she a relative?”
“No,” said Riss. “She was a person in two columns.”
The correction rule was printed on a card and nailed to the counter, and Riss read it three times.
**A correction may be entered by any person. Find the error. Write the correction. Sign the line.**

That was the whole ceremony. A clerk put a pen and an inkwell down in front of you on the counter. You wrote the correction. Then you signed your name at the bottom of it, and the signature was required. They did not want the correction. They wanted the signature. A correction with no name under it was a rumour, and the Index did not take rumours.
For eleven minutes, with the pen in front of them on the counter and a hundred people behind them in a queue and the clerk waiting with his hands folded, Riss considered writing a line.

There was a line to write. They had it in their head. *Bread-woman. Market at Ashford Green. Two loaves. One sack. Nine years ago. Unentered.* It was true. It was exact. It would put the woman on the county’s register in the only place left.
And below it, on the same page, in the same ink, they would sign: *Riss, of no fixed parish, walked west with six others.*
Riss stood at the counter in the Hall of Records at Sunth and understood, quite precisely, what was being offered.

They had been on the road for four months, and every single thing they had kept was in one satchel. A slate. A chart tube. Some copies of two pages. A brass plate against their chest that no clerk would ever catalogue. The counties had eleven feet of shelves in a clean room in Carrow. They had a public counter in Sunth and a system that would outlive everybody in that hall.
Riss had a Leaf with a spine going. Forty-one names in a dead man’s hand. A page of marks cut into a beam in a farmhouse nobody would ever visit again.
They could be *in the book*. One line. One signature. Proof, in the only register that survives, that they were here at all.
And the price was the thing Nahl had warned them about on the first day, at the river, in the rain, when this had all been arithmetic on a slate.

If Riss signed, the Index would have them. Not as a prisoner. Not as a criminal. As an *entry*. And an entry is a thing that can be amended. Riss had spent four months finding out exactly what the counties do with an entry, and it was the one thing nobody in the company could survive, because there is no defence against a correction.
Riss put the pen down.
“No correction,” they said.
The clerk took the pen back, without any surprise, because that was a thing that happened ten times a day in that hall. “As you like,” he said. “Is there anything else?”
“No,” said Riss. “Thank you.”
Then they asked the last question, because they had come all this way and there was one page left to look at.
The Index had a western section.
It was at the back of the third volume, with tabs on the edge. The clerk brought it out and put it on the counter and opened it at the tab marked **WEST**.
Riss read the page while the plate hummed the divided fifth under their coat and did not stop.

The page was nearly empty, and that was correct and expected. There were eleven villages west of the last river and every one of them had an entry. Above them was the county’s own survey line. Above that, a long empty column ran down the page.
At the top of that column, above the empty part, in a hand that was older than the rest of the book by about two hundred years, there was one line written and nothing else.
It said:
*Beyond the peaks. No entries are to be made.*

That was all. Nine words, in old ink, in a flat clerk’s hand, and under it a small stamp that Riss did not recognise, pressed into the paper once, exactly on the line, the way a seal is pressed onto a ruling to make it final.
No explanation. No date. No *reason* column. Nothing.
Riss stood in the Hall of Records at Sunth with a public queue at their back and read those nine words eleven times.

The counties had walked the whole of the north. They had surveyed rivers and roads and holdings and the height of the land. They had divided every field and entered every name and amended every discrepancy they could find for a hundred and forty years, and where they had not, there was a clerk whose job it was to go and find out.
And at the western edge of the whole machine, in the oldest hand in the book, somebody had written nine words and pressed a stamp onto them.
After that, for two hundred years, no clerk in the Index had written anything there at all.
They knew.

That was the thing Riss took out of that hall and did not manage to say to anybody for the rest of the day. The counties knew it was there. They had always known. It was in the book, at the back, in the oldest ink, with a prohibition on it, and the prohibition had held for two hundred years because the counties do not care what is true. They care what is *filed*.

And a thing that has never been entered is a thing that has never happened. Which meant that for two hundred years the counties had looked west and made the same decision the company had made on the shelf of rock in the wind.
They had left it where it was. In the stone.
Riss came out of the Hall of Records at four in the afternoon, when the porter rang the bell and the whole queue got up and went home at once, in the ordinary way, like people leaving a market.
The company was waiting on the corner with the goat.

Nobody said anything for a while. Veylan had the seed crate on the mule. Sancora had both satchels on. Mira had not opened the chart tube. Kael was standing with his burned hand inside his coat, and Orphiel stood a little apart with his hands on his satchel strap, and waited, because a witness does not ask.
“It’s public,” said Riss.
“What is?” said Mira.

“All of it. The Index. You queue up and ask whether you exist, and they tell you, and if you don’t exist they say sorry, and then the next person steps up.” Riss put their hands in their pockets, because they did not want to be holding anything. “There’s a woman in there whose son was never entered. The clerk was kind to her. He said he was sorry. He said he can correct the Index but he can’t add to it, because there’s nothing there to correct.”
“That’s the whole thing,” said Nahl. “That’s the whole book in one sentence.”
“Yes.”
“And the west?” said Mira. “Did you look?”

“I looked.” Riss looked at the street, and at the ordinary people going home, and at the cathedral, and at the smoke. “It’s in there. At the back of the third volume. There’s a page for west of the peaks with a column down it, and no entries in the column, and one line of old ink at the top.”
“What does it say?”

“*Beyond the peaks. No entries are to be made.*” Riss said it slowly, because they wanted it exact, because exact was the only thing they were going to get out of the day. “There’s a stamp under it. Old. Not in the current seal.”
Veylan said, “What does that mean?”
“It means they know,” said Orphiel.
Everybody looked at him.

“It means they have always known,” he said. “It is not a secret. It is a *ruling*. Somebody with a seal looked at the west a long time ago and decided that the correct thing to do with it was to write nothing down.” He adjusted the strap on the satchel. “That is the only sensible thing about the counties I have ever found.”
Veylan asked the practical question, which was what a ruling was worth when nobody could be made to obey it.

“It means they *looked*,” said Orphiel. “Somebody with a seal and a survey team walked as far west as a man can walk, and came back, and wrote down nothing. Not a description. Not a warning. Nine words and a stamp.”
“Why would they do that?”

“Because the counties write everything down. That is what they are. If they wrote nothing here, it is because writing it down would have made it part of the register.” He shifted the satchel on his shoulder. “They worked out two hundred years ago that the register is the only thing they have, and that a thing which is entered can be divided.”
They took a room over a stable at the north end of Sunth, and Veylan went down to the yard and negotiated for the mule, and Sancora went to buy food, and Mira unrolled the chart on the floor.

She drew the town, because she had walked it. She drew the wall with eleven towers and the four markets and the river. She drew the Hall of Records as a small square, and then she sat looking at the square for a while with the pen in her hand.
Then she drew the Index.

It took her an hour, because Mira drew the way Mira drew and there was no hurrying it. She ruled a page with two columns and made a box at the top for a heading and a long empty column down the left side, and above the empty column, in her smallest lettering, she wrote nine words.
*Beyond the peaks. No entries are to be made.*
Riss watched her do it and understood what she had made. It was the first page of the chart that was not a map of the ground. It was a map of a decision.
“Should I draw that?” said Mira. “It’s a copy of a thing I saw second-hand. You saw it. I didn’t.”
“Draw it,” said Riss. “It’s the most useful thing anybody’s found in four months.”
Upstairs, later, with the lamp down low, Riss got the Leaf out and did the day’s work.

They wrote the Hall of Records, and the queue, and the woman with the parish line, and the clerk who was kind. They wrote the correction rule and the pen and the signature. They wrote that the counties can correct a page and cannot add one. They wrote the nine words from the back of the third volume, exactly, and the stamp under them, and that it was two hundred years old.

At the end of the entry they stopped, with the pen in their hand, in the same position they had been in at the counter seven hours earlier, and considered for a moment whether to write their own name on the page.
It would be true. It would be a record. Riss of the coast road, aged twenty-eight, four hundred miles west of home, witness to a prohibition.
Riss did not write it. They put the pen down and shut the Leaf.
It occurred to them only afterwards that this was the second time that day they had not signed their own name, and that the two refusals were the same refusal said in two different rooms.
The plate hummed under their shirt.

Outside the window, over the roofs, beyond the river and the last of the flat land, the peaks stood up black against the night sky. No books go up there. Nothing has ever been entered. Kael Riven, awake in the dark on the other side of the room, lay with his burned hand closed around his forearm and said nothing, and the goat, down in the yard, stood facing west, and did not lie down.

chapters.label: Interlude B
chapters.title: The Arithmetic of Forgetting
paragraphs: After the Hall of Records at Sunth, and the woman with the parish line, and the pen he was never offered, Orphiel sat up late in the room over the stable and did his arithmetic.
He did it every night. It took nine minutes. It had taken nine minutes for forty years, and it was not a superstition and it was not a prayer.
It was a count.

He took the ledger out of the satchel and untied the cord and opened it flat on his knees. He counted the entries made since the last time he counted. Then he added the new ones to the number he carried in his head.
The number was nine thousand and four.
The log has four columns.
**Name. Date. Reason. Line.**
That is all. There is no fifth column. There is nowhere in that book to write what I thought about it.
I was a clerk for eleven years before I began this. I want that on the record, because the record of me is short, and I would rather it was accurate than flattering.

I was in the county office at Sallow, second desk. My work was registers. I copied entries. I ruled columns. When two pages disagreed I went and found out why, and came back, and told the senior clerk, and he decided, and I wrote down what he decided.
I was good at it. My hand was steady and I did not make mistakes with numbers, and if a thing went wrong in that office it was not me.

In the fourth year of the drought they brought a shelf of registers up from the south and put them in the back room. There were eleven of them. They were parish copies from eleven villages that had been consolidated into four holdings.
I was told to burn them.
That was all. The order came down the usual way, on a slip, with a date on it. The slip said *dispose of duplicates, back room, shelf three*. I was twenty-six years old and it was a Tuesday.
I sat in the back room with eleven registers and a stove.
I did not burn them. I want to be clear about the arithmetic of that decision, because people hear the story and they think it was courage.
It was not courage. Courage is a thing you do when you might be caught.
I was never in the least danger. Nobody was going to check. Nobody has ever checked. That is the whole of the counties: nobody checks.

So I sat there and worked out that nobody would ever know either way. And a person who is not going to be caught is not a hero. He is a man with a stove and a choice. The choice was: either those eleven villages stop existing this afternoon, or they do not.

I copied the names. It took nine months. I did it at nights and at the weekends, and I told my wife I was doing accounts for the chapel. Nine thousand and four names is not a thing you do in a fortnight.
Then I burned the registers, on a Thursday, in front of the man who had asked. He was pleased. He said *that’s the last of it*. I went back to my desk.
That is the beginning. Everything since then has been maintenance.
People ask me what a deletion is. They ask because they imagine a man with a big book striking out a name with a line, and then the person is gone.
It is not like that. A deletion is a thing that is done by making two numbers agree.

That is the whole of the operation. Somewhere in a building there are two pages. One page says a village has sixty-two souls. Another says the village has sixty-two households and pays a fee on sixty-two.
If the two pages ever disagree in public, then a clerk has to go and find out why. A clerk going to find out why is the only real danger the counties have.

So the operation is this. Somebody decides that a person, or a family, or a village, is not to be counted. Then the two pages are brought into agreement, and the agreement is made in whichever column is *cheaper*.
Not truer. Cheaper. It costs less to amend a name than to amend a fee.
And then the pages agree, and there is no discrepancy, and there is no clerk to send, and the machine goes on.

Nobody feels it. That is the thing I cannot get anybody to understand, including the six people asleep in this room. The person does not feel the operation. The village does not feel the operation. There is no moment.
There is a page that was one thing on Tuesday and another thing on Friday. There is a hand that wrote it. There is a slip with a date on it.
Nine thousand and four times, that has happened in the south of these counties in forty years.
I have all of their names, and none of their faces, because I have never met one of them. That is the arithmetic of forgetting, and it is a real arithmetic, and it works like this.
I visit the shelf once a year.
The shelf is in the vault. The vault is a clean room with a stove in it. The log sits in a catalogue with four hundred and ten other volumes.
Nobody has opened it in forty years except me. I have made sure of that by visiting it every year and reading it.

I do not read all of it. Nine thousand and four entries would take a month and I am seventy. I read a county section, or a decade, or a page. I read it out loud. I say each name. Then I close the book and go home.
That is the whole ceremony. There is no candle, and no incense, and no god in it. I would not know how to conduct a service if there was.
I say the names out loud once a year, on a Tuesday, in a warm room with a man coughing at the desk outside. Then I go home. That is the entire religious observance of the deletion log.

It is not enough. I am aware that it is not enough. It is a man reading a list in an empty room and calling it a memorial. Anybody looking in through the window would see a boring old man with a book. They would be right. It would be true.
I would do it again next year anyway.
What it costs is this.
I have written nine thousand and four names and never once written my own.

I am not in a register. I have never been in one, not properly, not since I was a boy in a village that is now a holding. There is no page with my birth on it that survives. There is no page with my marriage on it that survives.
When I die, the man at the desk will write the word *incident* at the top of a form. There is no column for a keeper, and he will have to put me somewhere.

My wife has been dead for twenty-two years and I can no longer see her face when I close my eyes. I can recall the shape of her hands. I cannot recall her face, and I have not been able to bring it back for about nine years.
I have not told anybody. There is a rule about the cost that I made for myself: you do not complain about a job you chose at a stove when you were twenty-six.

That is the price. It is not a dramatic price. It is a slow erosion of ordinary things, and it happens at about the rate of the arithmetic. A man who has spent forty years writing other people’s names has less and less room for his own.
The blank page.

There is a blank page at the back of the log, folded inside the cover. I have carried it for thirty-one years and it is still blank. The company asked me about it once at a fire, and I told them the truth, which is that it is not for this week. It is for the room.
I will tell you what the room has to have, because I have been looking for it for four decades and I know the specification the way a smith knows a hinge.

The room has to have a clerk in it. The clerk has to have a book. He has to be under instruction to write down what is said in his presence. That is the first thing. A room with no clerk is a conversation, and a conversation is worth nothing.

There has to be a superior. Not a villain, necessarily. There has to be a person above the clerk who can be reached by a note. That is the shape of how the counties move: by reference upward. A witness recorded by a clerk who has to report is a witness who has been *entered*.
There has to be at least one person in the room who does not want to be there. That is the most important requirement, and it is not a moral one. It is mechanical.

If everybody in the room is happy, then the room is a ceremony. If one person is unhappy and cannot leave, then the room is a record, because a person who wants to leave a room will remember what was said in it.

And I must not bring my own pen. That is the discipline. If I bring my own pen, then what is written is *mine*, and mine is worth nothing, because a man’s own book is a diary. The book has to be theirs. Theirs is the one that survives.
I will write on the blank page whatever the clerk writes, in their words, at the end. Then I will sign it. The signature is the whole of the work.
The thing I do not know is what I will write.
I know the shape of it. I know it will begin with a date and a place. I know it will have no adjectives in it, because an adjective is an opinion, and the page is not for opinions.
What worries me is this.

When the room comes, there will be an hour, or a minute, in the middle of it, when somebody says something to me and I will want to reply. Not argue. I am not built to argue; that is Riss, and Riss does it better than I have ever seen it done. But there will be a moment when the man across the table says something *untrue*, in a room with a book in it, and the temptation will be to look up.
A witness who looks up has taken a side. A witness who has taken a side is a witness for somebody. A witness for somebody is a lawyer, and lawyers lose to clerks every time.
So I sit with my hands on the strap and I look at the page in front of me. I write down what was said. I do not look up.
That is the whole of the skill. It took me forty years to be able to do it for nine minutes at a time, and I still lose the count when a child is in the room.
I do not file the living.
That is the last rule and the only one I have ever had to defend. I defend it about twice a month, and always against the same argument, which is that it would be *useful*.

The argument goes like this. Write them in. Write the six of them into the log tonight, and the child in the mill yard, and the old man with the hand, and the woman with the parish line. Write them in with the date and the reason *taken by the county*, and then they are *kept*. They are on a shelf. Somebody reading the shelf in a hundred years will find them. They would be safe.
I have thought about it more than I have thought about anything. The answer is no, and the reason is not safety and not sentiment.
The log is a list of what has already been taken out. It is a record of a thing that *has been done*. If I write Riss in it tonight, then I have written that Riss was taken out.
And there is no column in my book for the fact that Riss is not taken out. Riss is asleep on the floor of a room in Sunth with a brass plate under their shirt.

I would be making a true record of a false thing. That is the counties’ entire method. And I would be doing it in my own hand, in my own book, with the reason column saying *taken by the county* and my signature under it.
So no. I keep what is already gone. I do not put people in.
Nine thousand and four.
Tonight, in this room, there are six people and a goat.

I have their names on the paper in my head, all eight of them. I say them the way I say the others. There is no page anywhere with any of them on it, and no column anywhere that will hold them, and that is not a failure of the record.
That is the record working.

The woman with the heavy hands. The trowel man. The woman with the chart. The burned man with the slate. The old soldier who keeps his hand open. The one with the plate under their shirt. And the goat, which I have never once explained and will not.
They are alive. Being alive is not a thing that can be filed.
I did the arithmetic at the end, because I always do the arithmetic at the end. Then I tied the cord on the log and put it back in the satchel.
Then I lay down with the satchel under my head, which is how I have slept for forty years, and which is not comfortable, and which has never been comfortable, and which I am not going to change now.

chapters.label: Chapter 13
chapters.title: The Border
paragraphs: After the arithmetic in the room over the stable, and the eight names Orphiel said to himself and did not write down, the company walked west out of Sunth and did not stop for eleven days.

The first three days were the ordinary counties: farms, hedges, a carrier’s cart, a toll bar, a boy selling water at a crossroads, a village with a new roof on its meeting house. The next three days the farms started getting further apart. On the seventh day they passed four houses standing empty with the doors shut, which is a thing Riss had never seen in a county, because in a county an empty house is a fee and a fee is somebody’s work.
On the ninth day the land went quiet.

Not the way a field goes quiet at night. The way a room goes quiet when somebody in it has stopped talking. There were still fields. There was still a wall. There was a cart track with wheel ruts in it. But there was no smoke anywhere on the whole horizon, and there was no bell, and there was no dog, and Riss walked a whole day without hearing a single human sound except the company’s own boots.
The last village was called Threave.

It had eleven houses. It had a church with no roof on the west end of it. That was the first thing Riss noticed, and it took a while to work out, and when Riss worked it out they had to stand and look at it for a minute.

The church roof had been repaired. The east half of it was sound: new slates, laid within the last twenty years, a ridge line you could read. The west half was open to the sky, with the beams showing, and grass growing in the wall head.
The parish’s repair money had come from the county, and the county had assessed the parish on its eastern holding, and the eastern holding was where the money had gone.
The carter told them there were three families left. He told them the road west was the last road. He told them that after the village there was one house, and after the house there was nothing.
“Do people come back this way?” said Veylan.
“Some,” said the carter. “Not often. Mostly the young men go for a season and come back thinner.”
“Where do they go?”
“West,” said the carter, and pointed, and would not take money for the water.
The customs post was a shed.

That was the whole of the counties’ last apparatus: a shed of planks with a shelf in it and a slate roof and a door that did not close properly. It stood on the east side of the road at the top of a rise, where a checkpoint would go, and it had the county’s board on it with the county’s seal.
There was no gate. There was no barrier. There was no clerk in it.
There was a ledger on the shelf, open, with a strip of ribbon laid across the page.
Riss went in and looked at it, because that was the kind of thing Riss did now without thinking about it.
The ledger was called *Strangers and Goods, West Road Post*. It had four columns: name, parish, date, purpose.
The last entry in it was fourteen months old. It was a man’s name and a parish and one word in the purpose column: *shepherd*.
On the next page there was nothing. Not a line, not a date, not a mark. Fourteen months of a column with nobody at the end of it.
Riss stood in the doorway of a shed on the last mile of the counties and read the headings twice, and then looked at the road, and then looked west at the ridge the road went over.
“How many miles of the counties’ paper stop at that stone?” said Riss.
“All of it,” said Orphiel. “Every form, every column, every fee. It runs out here. You are looking at the end of the counties, and the end of the counties is a shed with a wet ribbon in it.”
“Somebody should take that ledger in before the winter gets it.”
“Somebody stopped sending anybody,” said Orphiel. “That is not the same as a thing being forgotten. It is a thing being *let go*.”
The pen was not there. There was a nail in the wall above the shelf where the pen had hung, and the nail was empty, and there was a pale ring in the dust on the shelf where the inkwell had stood.
“They ran out of ink and never sent any more,” said Veylan.
“Or they ran out of clerks,” said Riss.

Nobody signed it. That was not a decision, and Riss noticed that it was not a decision, and wrote the not-decision down that night because it seemed more important than a decision would have been. There was nobody to receive the signature. There was no column left with a person at the end of it. That is what the last mile of the counties looked like: a shelf, a ribbon, a nail, and no clerk.

The border stone was four feet high and it stood in a low place where the road crossed the ridge, and it had been there long enough that the grass had grown up around the base of it and nobody had cut the grass.
Riss had seen boundary stones all their life, and this one was the same as all of them and worse.

The east face was dressed. It had been worked with a chisel and smoothed. It had the county seal cut into it, and under the seal a line of letters worn down by rain to the shapes of letters, and under that, cut deep, a number: **XI**.
The west face was raw.
That was it. That was the whole of the border.

Somebody a hundred and forty years ago had cut and dressed the east face of a stone. He had put the county seal on it and cut a number into it, and had set it in the gap in the ridge. Then he had walked away and left the other side of the stone exactly as the quarry had given it.
Uncut. Unpolished. Grey, with a chip in it, and no mark of any kind on it at all.
Not blank because it had weathered. Not blank because somebody had erased it. Blank because the counties had never put a chisel to it.
“They stopped,” said Mira.
“They stopped,” said Orphiel.

He was standing on the east side of the stone with his hands on his satchel strap. He had been standing there a while. Riss had watched him walk up to it twice and step back, no matter how many paces short he had started from.
That was the thing Riss would remember about the border: the man who had read about it for forty years taking three tries to get close to it.
“I have never crossed this line,” said Orphiel.

They were at the stone together. The rest of the company had gone on a little way and was standing by the wall, because a company always gives two people a stone’s throw when the two people are standing at a stone.
“You’ve been to the vault,” said Riss.

“The vault is east. Everything I have ever done is east.” He looked at the raw face. “I have read about this line. I have written about this line. Nine words at the back of the third volume, in an old hand, with a stamp under them. I have known that line for thirty-one years the way a man knows the name of a town he has never been to.” He put one finger on the east face, on the seal, without any pressure, the way you touch a book you are putting back on a shelf. “I have never stood on it.”
Riss waited, because Riss had learned by then that when Orphiel said a thing plainly it was because he had decided to say it, and rushing him was the only way to lose it.
“What do you feel?” said Riss.
“Nothing,” said Orphiel.
He said it with no disappointment in it at all. He sounded interested, the way a man sounds interested in his own pulse.

“Nothing at all. Not dread. Not the fear I had at twenty-five, when I first copied the nine words out at the second desk in Sallow and sat looking at them. Not what I have been expecting for thirty-one years.” He took his finger off the stone. “That is the point. There is nothing here to file. I have spent my life in rooms where every object had a page under it, Riss. Every wall, every field, every cow. I put my hand on the east face and I know what it is. It is the eleventh boundary stone of the county, and it is in a catalogue, and it is somebody’s work.” He nodded at the west face. “Put your hand on that one.”
Riss sat on the west side of the stone and looked west.
Nothing happened. That was, Riss understood, exactly what Orphiel meant. There was no hum in the plate, no note in the air, no sense of a thing waiting.
There was a raw rock face with a chip in it in a gap in a ridge. Beyond it, a road going down between two walls. Beyond that, the land went on for a mile and then folded up into the hills.
Behind the hills the peaks stood up in a rank.
“I feel that I’m sitting on a stone,” said Riss.
“Yes,” said Orphiel. “That is the most important thing that will happen to you today, and you will not understand why until you are sixty.”
Kael Riven came up to the stone and did the thing he did.

He came at it slowly, from the east, with the strap of the slate in his fingers, and he put his burned hand flat on the dressed face first and stood with his eyes shut for about ten seconds. Then he stepped around to the other side and put the same hand on the raw face.
He stood there a long time.
“There’s no edge,” he said at last.
“On the west face?”

“On any of it.” He took his hand off and looked at it. “The east face has an edge. Everything in the counties has an edge; it’s been cut off from something. That’s what a boundary is: they cut a thing off and put a number on it. Down the road there’s a post with a ribbon in it, and the ribbon has an edge, and the post has an edge because somebody decided a stranger stops there.” He put the hand in his coat. “The west face has nothing. Not even the other kind. Not the hole and not the cut. There’s nothing to trace, because it was never divided from anything. It’s just rock on the side of a rock.”
“Then how do you find anything out there?” said Veylan, who had come up.
“I don’t,” said Kael. “That’s the part I’ve been dreading since Collow.”
Mira drew the line.
She had walked the whole way from Threave with the tube in her hand. At the stone she unrolled a sheet on the top of the wall and pinned it with four stones of her own.
She drew the stone. She drew the ridge, and the road crossing it, and the wall, and the shed with the ribbon in it, and the last of the county’s hedge.
It took her nineteen minutes, which for Mira was fast.
Then she stopped with the pen in the air above the middle of the sheet.
“Nothing west,” she said. “Not yet. I haven’t walked it.”
“Ours is the first chart to have a blank on it,” said Riss.

“Every chart has a blank on it. That’s what a chart is.” Mira rolled it up without touching the west side of the sheet with the pen. “The difference is that the counties’ charts have a blank east of the line and a *reason*. Mine has a blank because I have not been there yet. That is the whole difference between the two of us and I want it written down somewhere official.”

For the record, she stopped on the far side of the stone, eleven paces west of it, and drew one line: a small circle, and beside it, in her smallest lettering, *stone stopped*. That was all she put on the west side of the sheet that day. One circle and two words, and then she capped the pen and walked on.
Veylan took a handful of the west soil.

He had been doing that since the first village, in a way that was half farmer and half superstition: a handful into a tin from every place the company stopped, and the tin was in the crate with the seedlings and it was half full by then.
He worked the dirt between his fingers for a while at the west side of the stone.

“It’s thin,” he said. “It’s the same rock underneath as the county’s side, but it’s thinner and it’s drier and there’s no lime in it. Nothing’s been put back in this soil for a hundred years.” He put the handful in the tin and closed it. “You can farm it. You’d just have to be there.”
“Are we going to be there?” said Riss.
“Nobody’s asking me,” said Veylan.
The wind came back at the stone, four miles past it, on the west side of the ridge.

It came the way it had come at the farmhouse with the children’s marks in the beam: level, steady, out of the west, not a gust, with the smell of stone in it, and cold enough that Sancora stopped and turned her collar up without being asked.
Corvath stood up into it.

He had been the country’s most ordinary member for four months. Riss had been watching him do it, and had come to understand that a man who says *my sense has failed me* and keeps walking is doing the hardest thing in the company’s whole inventory. He had stopped reporting anything. He had started carrying the wood.
At the stone he lifted his face and smelled the wind for a long time, and everybody stopped and waited, and he said:
“Stone. Stone and cold. That’s all. There’s nothing alive in it at all.”
“Is that bad?” said Veylan.
“It’s the first honest thing this nose has told me in three months,” said Corvath, and picked up the pack he had put down, and walked on, and Riss wrote that down too.
Sancora made them all sit down before they crossed.

That was unexpected and it was completely in character. She put her satchel down on the east side of the line and went along the company one at a time, and checked their boots, and their hands, and the state of their coats, and made Veylan put a second wrap of cloth inside his boot where a seam had gone.
“Twelve days to the settlements,” she said. “There’s no surgeon out there. There’s me, and I’m sixty years of a bad back, and I’m not carrying any of you.”
“There’s the two villages,” said Veylan.

“There are two villages with sheep and a mill and no road to speak of,” said Sancora. “In a county I could be in a town in a day with a clean warm room and a man who keeps his tools sharp. West of this stone you get what I’ve got in these two bags and whatever the weather decides.” She stood up. “That’s the trade. Anyone who wants to go back should go back now, while the choice is still the easy one.”
Nobody said anything.
“Right,” said Sancora, and picked up her satchel, and that was the closest the company came all book to a speech about the border.
They crossed in the afternoon, one at a time, the way a company crosses a thing that matters even when there is nothing to cross.

The goat went first. That was not arranged. The goat had been walking in the middle of the line for four months. At the stone it walked past the whole company, put its head down, went across, and stood on the west side in the wind.
Then it looked back at them.
That was the first time anybody had seen it look back at anything.

Then Nahl. Then Sancora. Then Old Den, with his arm bound across his chest. Then Veylan, then Corvath. Then Mira, who stopped exactly on the line and looked at the west face of the stone from a foot away.
Kael went last but one, and Riss last of all, because Riss was the one who had the plate.

Old Den stopped on the way past. He put his good hand flat on the seal on the east face. He left it there for about four seconds. Then he took it off, and did not say anything about it to anybody, and went across, and Riss, walking behind him, understood that the old man had just said goodbye to the only country he had ever been filed in.
The plate did something.
It came up under Riss’s shirt when they put their foot on the west side of the line.

Not the clean fifth, and not the divided fifth at full voice. A fifth that was split down the middle and louder than it had ever been. Louder than the customs house. Louder than the mill at Marle. Louder than Nahl’s village in a book on a public shelf.
It held one long moment, as if the thing inside it had turned to look west.
Then it dropped back to the hum Riss knew.
Kael Riven, six paces ahead, already had his burned hand closed around his forearm.
Nobody said anything about it. Nobody had said anything about it for four months. That was not a rule anybody had made. It was what the company had become.
“No looking back,” said Nahl, at the top of the rise.
“Why not?” said Veylan.

“Because a person who looks back has already decided what they’re going back to,” said Nahl. “And then every mile after that is a mile they’re farther from something instead of a mile they’re nearer something. The counties do that to people. There’s a whole office for it.”
“About the fees,” said Riss.
“About the fees,” said Nahl, and that was the end of it, and the company walked over the rise and down the long west slope, and not one of the eight of them turned round at the top.
Riss noticed it happening, and noticed it as a thing that was happening *to* them rather than as a thing they were doing.
The ridge behind them, and the stone on it, and the shed with the ribbon. The last wall, the last hedge, the last field. The counties.
All of it going over the edge of the world behind them, unseen, at the exact speed of a walking mule.
Nobody looked. That was the refusal, and it had no words in it, and it was the easiest refusal the company had made in four months and the most expensive.
The wind did not stop that night.
It was the first night the company slept west of the line, in the lee of a wall on the west side of the ridge. The wind came steady out of the west all night. Level, cold, smelling of stone.
Riss lay in it and counted the Emberion constellation through the gap in the clouds.
Fifteen. The same fifteen as the shelf of rock, and the same fifteen as the ridge at Collow, and the same missing joint of the wing.
The peaks were close now. There was nothing between the company and them but two days of hill and a road the counties had never put a stone beside.

And out in front of them, past the hills, in the dark, the wind was coming down off the high ground. It had come down off the high ground for two hundred years, and longer than that, over a line that had a seal on one side and nothing at all on the other.
Riss slept, and the plate hummed, and nobody in the company said the word.
In the morning there was frost on the west side of the wall and none on the east, which is a thing that happens on ridges, and Veylan said so out loud in case anybody needed a reason.

chapters.label: Chapter 14
chapters.title: The Room
paragraphs: After the border stone, and the wind on the west side of the ridge, and the company’s refusal to look back at anything at all, the road ran downhill for four miles.
It ran through country with no wall on it, and it came to a single building.
It was the only roof between Threave and the peaks. Riss had it in the chart by then: one circle, two words, and a long space above the hills with nothing drawn in it yet.
The building was called a waystation, and nobody had named it that.
That was just the word on the county’s last map. The map’s word had gone out of date east of the line. The company kept using it because there was no other word for a building that had no function.
It was stone to the height of a man and timber above. It had one door and one window and a chimney. The door had no lock on it.
There was a rain barrel against the wall, and a woodpile under a lean-to, and a bench, and the shutter on the window swung on a leather hinge.
There was no sign. There was no seal. There was nothing on the building to say who kept it, and nobody in the company was able to find out, because there was nobody there to ask.
Mira worked at it for an hour the first evening, because Mira could not leave a thing unaccounted for.

The woodpile had been split and stacked recently. Not that week, but within a month. The bracken on the bed platform was dry and had been changed at the end of the summer. There was a bucket by the door with a rope on it and a bar of soap in it, and the soap was not county soap, and it had been used.
“So somebody keeps it,” she said. “Four times a year, at least. From the valley. It’s one of the two settlements, or both of them, taking it in turn.”
“Or the road keeps it,” said Nahl.
Mira looked at them.
“That’s not an answer,” she said, and went to bed, and did not draw it.
The inside was one room.
It had a hearth with a crane in it and a sweep. It had a bed platform along the west wall with dry bracken on it, and a table made of a door on two trestles, and a bench, and a stool.
Kael Riven went round the room twice with his burned hand open, and then sat down on the stool by the hearth and said nothing.
“Anything?” said Riss.
“No edge,” said Kael.
“On the plank?”

“On the whole building.” He put the hand in his coat. “On the east side of the stone I could feel the counties the way you feel a wall through a wall. Here there’s nothing. The table was a door once, so the table has an edge, and the door came off a building, so the building had an edge. Everything else in here was made out of a thing that was already out here.” He looked at the fire. “It’s the first room I’ve stood in since Collow where I can’t find out anything about anybody in it. I don’t like it and it’s a rest.”
And it had a plank by the door.
The plank was about four feet long and a hand wide, nailed up at shoulder height, and it was covered in marks.
Nahl stood in front of it for a long time before anybody said anything.
They were not names. That was the first thing. There was not one name on the whole plank.

There were notches. There were initials. There were tally groups of five, and there were small rough shapes that might have been a house or a hand or a bird. There were dates, some of them, cut with a knife.

There were forty or fifty marks at least, in every kind of cutting. Some of them were gouged deep by a man who had worked with tools all his life. Some were a scratch so light it had almost weathered out.

And it was charcoal and it washed off. Whoever kept the waystation (and somebody must have kept the waystation, because the bracken was dry and the woodpile was stacked) had left the plank alone, and the marks on it had been there for years.
Nahl went along it slowly with the lamp, reading what there was to read.

Five tallies in one corner, cut by the same hand. A bird, or a thing like a bird, with a long tail. A shape that was either a small house or a box with a lid on it. Two initials, *A.M.*, with a date under them. Three straight cuts, which in the north country means three days of walking.
And no mark anywhere with an arrow, or a hand pointing east, or a line going the other way.
“All of them are going west,” said Nahl.
“What do you mean?” said Veylan.

“There’s no mark on this plank from anybody coming back,” said Nahl. “Forty marks, years of them, and every one was cut by a person on their way out. Nobody stops here on the way home to say they did it.” They stepped back from the plank. “It’s a ledger of departures with no return column. That’s why the counties can’t read it. It’s got no second half.”
“What is it?” said Veylan.
“It’s a ledger,” said Nahl.
“It’s got no columns.”

“No,” said Nahl. “That’s the point. It’s a ledger with no columns and no names and nobody writing it down. People come through here going west, and they cut a mark, and then they leave, and it stays. Nobody files it. Nobody can amend it. It’s not a register of anything, because a register has to say what a thing is.” They put their hand near the plank without touching it. “It’s the first record I’ve seen in four months that the counties don’t know how to read.”
Mira had her pen out.
“Don’t,” said Orphiel.
“I wasn’t going to draw it.”
“You were.”

“I *was* going to draw it,” said Mira, and put the pen away, and was quiet for a while, and then said, to nobody in particular: “It’s the only page I’ve ever seen that I can’t copy properly, and I don’t like it.”
The carrier came in at dark.

He was a man of about fifty with a mule and four bales of raw wool on it. He had come up the west road from the far side of the hills. He was going through to Threave in the morning and on to the county town after that.
And he did not do anything unusual when he saw eight strangers with a goat sitting around the waystation hearth.

He shared the fire. That was all. He put his mule in the lean-to and took the far end of the bench. He got a piece of bread out of his coat, and he talked about the road, which is what people talk about on roads.
He was coming east. He did that four times a year. He had been doing it for nineteen years.
The company asked him the questions they had been carrying since the border stone.
He answered them the way a man answers a question about his own trade, which is well, and without any idea that it is important.
Was there anything west? There were two settlements, in the big valley, four days further on. Sixty people and forty people. They had sheep and a mill and no road to speak of.
Did the counties take a fee? No. Nobody came. Nothing came.
There was no post, and no tax, and no clerk. The last time he had seen a man from a county office out here was eleven years ago, and that man had turned round at the stone and gone home.
Did nobody come to enter any of it in a book? He looked at them for a while when they asked that, and then he said the sentence Nahl wrote down that night.
“Nobody’s ever asked me for anything out here but salt.”

That was the whole of the unentered land. Sixty people and forty people and a man who had been carrying wool across it four times a year for nineteen years, and in all that time, nobody had once asked him for a paper.
In the morning, before he loaded the mule, the carrier did the decent thing that carriers do, and made the offer.

“I’ll be in Threave tomorrow night,” he said. “Then Wexley, then the county town. Nine days. I take letters for people. Small ones. Nothing heavy.” He tied a cord on the wool bale. “If you’ve got people back there, I can carry word. Nobody charges for it. It’s just what you do.”
That was all it was. It was a courtesy, offered by a man the company would never see again, and there was nothing in it.
And for a moment the whole company stood in the doorway of the waystation with the frost on the ground and their hands in their coats, and every one of them did the arithmetic.

Veylan had a mother in a village in the north, and a sister, and a trowel, and he had left in a hurry. Riss had the Leaf. Sancora had a sister in a town with a garden and benches, who had asked her to write. Old Den had family in the east somewhere, and had never once spoken about any of them. Mira had a house she had not slept in for four months.
Nobody moved.
“I’ve got nothing,” said Kael, first, and that closed it, because Kael had nothing and everybody there knew it was true and knew why.

“I could send a line to my mother,” said Veylan. “She’d know it was from me by the hand. It’d be one line.” He looked at the road going east. “And then for the next year she’d be looking at the door every time somebody walked up the lane, because a letter means the writer is somewhere he can write letters from.”
“They’d have a page with your village on it,” said Nahl.
“They’d have a page,” said Veylan.
Riss put both hands flat on the satchel strap and held it, and did not say anything at all.
Everybody in the company understood that Riss was having the largest argument of the four and winning it.
The Leaf, the slate, the copies, the two columns, forty-one names in a dead man’s hand, four months of days, was not going east for safekeeping.
Because it would be safe. That was the trouble.

Send the Leaf back over the stone with the wool, and in nine days it would be in a place with a roof and a fire and no wind. It would be *safe*. And within a season somebody in a county office would have heard that there was a book that got sent home.
“No,” said Riss.
“Right,” said the carrier, who had no idea what he had just been part of. “Suit yourselves.”
Nothing went east. Not one page, not one line, not one message, not one word. The carrier loaded the mule and went up the road towards the ridge with the four bales on it.
The company stood in the frost and watched him go. Then they went back inside and shut the door.
That was the refusal.
The waystation had four things, and Orphiel went round the room and found all of them in the wrong place.

Nahl watched him do it. It took half an hour. He started at the door and worked clockwise, and he touched everything, and he said nothing for the first twenty minutes, and Nahl followed him with the lamp.

He looked at the table. He looked behind the table, at the wall, for a nail or a shelf or a hook. He opened the little cupboard beside the hearth, and looked in it, and shut it. He looked at the bed platform. He went outside with the lamp and looked along the east wall, and came back in and looked at the west wall, where the light was best.
Then he sat down on the bench and put his hands on his knees.
“It’s not the room,” he said.
“No,” said Nahl. “There’s no book.”

“That is the second item. There are four.” Orphiel counted them off on four fingers, and Nahl understood that this was a specification the man had carried so long he could not describe it any other way. “A clerk. A book. A person above the clerk who can be reached by a note. And at least one person in the room who does not want to be there.”
Nahl sat on the stool.
“There’s no clerk,” they said.
“No.”
“There’s no book. There’s a plank with marks on it and no names.”
“Yes.”
“There’s nobody above anybody. There’s no county on this side of the stone at all.”
“Yes.”

“And everybody here wants to be here,” said Nahl. “Every one of us. Veylan wants to see the peaks, and Mira wants the chart, and Sancora wants to know what happened to people, and Riss wants the answer, and Kael wants an edge, and I …” They stopped for a moment. “I want the thing I carry to have somewhere to go.”

“Then you understand the fourth requirement better than anybody in this company,” said Orphiel. “It is the important one. I have said that to seven people in forty years and none of them believed me.”
He looked around the room the way a smith looks at a doorway that is the wrong size.
“This is a roof,” he said. “It is a very good roof. There is a chimney that draws and a woodpile that somebody keeps up, and I have slept in worse places every winter of my life.”
“But a room is not walls. A room is four people and a book.”
He took the satchel off his shoulder and set it on the floor against his leg.

“Forty years I have been looking for the room. This is the first night of my life that I have been out of the counties. And I am sleeping in a building with no clerk in it, and there will be a cup of water on that table and nobody to sign for it.”
“What if we never find the room?” said Nahl.
“Then I will have walked a long way at seventy for nothing,” said Orphiel.

“And I will have done it in good company, and I will have kept what I had no business keeping. And the nine words will still be at the back of the third volume, where I copied them out at twenty-six.”
“Tell me what you’ll write,” said Nahl, later, when the fire was low.
They were the last two up.

Orphiel had the satchel on his knees with the log inside it, unopened. The folded page was in the satchel too. It had been in the satchel every night for four months without coming out once on the road.
“I will write what the clerk writes,” said Orphiel.
“In their words.”

“In their words. That is the whole of it. If I bring my own pen, then what is written is mine, and mine is worth nothing, because a man’s own book is a diary. It has to be their book and their hand.” He closed his hand on the strap of the satchel. “Then I will sign it at the bottom, and my name under theirs is the entire work of my life.”
“And if they refuse to write it?”
“Then I will not write anything.”
“You’ll have walked all that way …”
“Yes.”
Nahl waited.

“A witness who writes his own book is a diarist,” said Orphiel. “And a diarist is a man talking to himself, and nobody has ever been saved by a man talking to himself.” He looked at the fire. “You keep a seal. You know this. If you stamped it yourself it would be worth nothing.”
“I know,” said Nahl.
“Then you know why the page is still blank.”
“It’s still blank,” said Nahl.
“It’s still blank,” said Orphiel.
They slept in the room without a clerk.
Outside, the goat stood in the frost on the west side of the building, facing west, and did not come in, and did not lie down, and did not turn round for the whole of the night.
Sancora did the hand.

She had been doing it every third evening since Marle, and it took her forty minutes, and it was the only thing in the company’s day that had a timetable. She heated water in the small pan, and she unwrapped the dressing, and she looked at what was under it the way she looked at everything, which was without any expression at all.
Old Den sat on the bench and looked at the wall.

The fingers had gone. Two of them were gone at the middle joint, and the thumb was gone down to the base of it. What was left had healed wrong, and it was going to stay wrong, and Sancora had told him that plainly in the mill yard at Marle and had not softened it once since, because a healer who softens a prognosis is a healer who has stopped working.
The rest of the hand was in good order. That was the thing she was watching now: the palm, and the three fingers left, and the wrist, which the press had not touched, and the arm, which was fine.
“Grip,” she said.
He closed the hand. It closed about a third of the way and it did not hurt him, and she watched the tendons come up under the skin, and she said, “Try again tomorrow.”
“Same answer,” said Old Den.
“Same answer is a good answer,” said Sancora. “Same answer for a month is a hand I can still splint a stick into.”

She wrapped it fresh, and she tied the dressing off with the end of the knot under the thumb, which is the way she had tied it in fourteen villages, and she put the little folding knife back in her satchel, and that was the appointment.
Nahl watched the whole of it from the other side of the fire and did not write it down, because there was nothing in it that a page would hold.
Veylan went out before he slept and stood in the dark with the tin in his hand.

He had been taking a handful of every place the company stopped since the first village. It was half farmer and half habit. The tin lived in the crate with the seedlings and it was three-quarters full by the border, and at the waystation he put the west soil in with the rest, and then stood there turning the tin over.
“Nothing grows here yet,” he said to nobody. “There’s no lime in it and no muck and it’s ninety years behind.”
“Can you fix it?” said Riss, from the doorway.
“You don’t fix soil. You *keep* it.” He put the tin back in the crate. “Nine years of muck and a legume in the rotation and sheep on it in the third year. Anybody could do it. Nobody has.”
“Why not?”
Veylan closed the crate and put the strap on it.

“Because there’s no paper in it,” he said. “You can’t take a fee off a field nobody’s surveyed. That’s the whole reason this side of the stone is empty, and it’s the only piece of luck the company’s had since the river.”
Nahl went out once, near the middle of the night.
The goat was exactly where it had been. The plate was humming quietly under Nahl’s shirt, and past the yard and the woodpile the ground went up in the dark toward the hills.
Riss was awake in the doorway by then, because Riss slept the way the plate let them sleep, and the two of them stood in the cold for a while.
“Fifteen,” said Riss, after a while, looking up.
“Where?”

“The Emberion. There’s a gap in the cloud. Fifteen joints, and the wing’s got a piece missing at the far end.” Riss had their hands in their pockets. “It was fifteen at Collow. It was fifteen on the shelf of rock. It’s fifteen here. It’s going to be fifteen at the top.”
“And that means something.”
“It means it isn’t the counties doing it,” said Riss. “That’s all it means. Whatever took the joint out of the wing didn’t do it with a chisel on the west face of a boundary stone.”

Kael Riven, asleep inside, turned over and put his burned hand around the scar on his forearm without waking up. He had been doing it since the mill at Marle, all night, every night, and nobody had ever mentioned it to him.
In the morning the company ate, and banked the fire, and put the woodpile back the way they had found it, and left the plank with the marks on it exactly as it was.
Nobody cut a mark. Nahl thought about it for a long time at the door with the knife in their hand.
Then they put the knife away and went out into the frost.

A mark on that plank was the only page the counties could not read. Nahl had decided somewhere between the stone and the shed that whatever the company was going to be, it was not going to be a name on a list of people going west.
Then they walked on, and the peaks got bigger.

chapters.label: Interlude C
chapters.title: The Clerk
paragraphs: After the waystation and the plank with the marks on it, and the carrier who took no letters east, the company’s fourth day west of the stone was another day of hill and cold road.
None of them thought about Ashenford.
This is what was happening at Ashenford.
Her name was Ivet Sallow. She was forty-one years old, and she had been a clerk for nineteen years. That was nine years longer than the mill had been in the hands of the family that owned it.

She was the clerk of the mill on the Vellum. That was the whole of her title, and nobody in the world respected it. The job was four ledgers and a box of receipts and a pen she kept in a leather case of her own, because the mill would not buy her one.
She was good at it. That is the first thing to understand about her.
Not clever. Not brave. Not important. Good.

She could add a column of forty figures in her head and be wrong about it once a year. She could look at a page and tell whether a hand had hesitated in the middle of a line. She had a sister in Wexley and a cat named after a man she had never met. She had never in her life done a single thing that anybody outside the mill would call a decision.
She kept her own bottle of ink at the mill, because the mill’s ink was thin. She ruled every column with a straight edge. She had rules about the shape of the number five.
That was the whole woman. Then one day in the spring, four strangers and a goat came to the mill gate and asked to see the books.
What she did, she did in three seconds.
That was the size of it. Three seconds, in a room with four strangers in it and the door half open.
She had the strangers’ register out on the counter. The county required every mill to keep it, and in it the names of visitors and their goods must be put down.

The strangers had a box. The little man with the trowel was carrying it. The woman with the satchels stood in front of it. The old man with the bound hand had already refused to put his thumb in the visitors’ book. And the man from the county office was on the road behind them with a paper in his pocket.
There was a line on her form. **Goods declared: yes / no.**
She put her pen on the *no*.

She un-ticked it. There had been a tick in it. She had made the tick herself, an hour earlier, when she first opened the register, because a visitor with a box is a visitor with goods, and goods have to be declared.
Then the strangers were in front of her, and she put her pen down on the tick and drew a small line through it, twice. That is how a clerk corrects a thing she has decided was a mistake.
Nobody watched her. That was the whole of the dangerous part. There was a man from the county in the yard. He was looking at the old man’s hand. There was nobody at all watching the counter.
Three seconds. Then she looked up, and told them the mill’s hours, and they went away. By the evening they were a rumour in the village. By the end of the month they were nothing at all.
For nine months, nothing happened.
She wants that understood, because there is nobody she can tell, and if she ever does tell somebody she wants the order of it right.
Nothing happened. No letter came. No man came from the county office with a question about a form. No auditor asked why the strangers’ register for that week had an amendment in it.
And there *was* an amendment in it. A soft double stroke in thin ink, over a tick. That is the kind of thing that appears in a hundred registers a year, because clerks are human.
She waited for it. She waited six weeks with her stomach in the wrong place. Then she waited six months with it in the right place again. Nothing ever came.
That turned out to be the worse thing.

Because if a letter had come, then it would have been a thing that happened. She would have answered it. It would have been over. What she got instead was a thing that had *not* happened. A thing that cannot be finished. A thing she was going to carry on her own for the rest of her working life.
She had done one small thing wrong in nineteen years of exact columns. Nobody had checked. Nobody has ever checked.
Nobody checks.
That was the discovery. It was the beginning of everything that happened to her afterwards.
What it cost, in the first year, was sleep.
Not much. She was not the kind of person who lies awake. But she began to wake in the hour before light and lie there doing the arithmetic, and the arithmetic always came out the same.

The company had a box. The box had four things in it, according to everything she heard afterwards. A tin of tallies. A slate with no marks on it. Some copies of two pages. And a brass plate that one of them wore under their shirt and would not take off.
If the box had been declared, the county man would have opened it. That was certain. That was the entire point of the box, and the tick, and the form.
He would have opened it in the yard. He would have looked at the two pages. He would have asked where the copies came from.
Everything that happened to those four people after that day would have happened differently.
That was the arithmetic. Her three seconds, in the yard, unthinking, in a room with four strangers: those three seconds were load-bearing.

And she could not know what they were bearing. She did not know where the box went. She did not know what the two pages were for. She did not know whether the plate under the shirt had ever been anything at all.
All she knew was that she had un-ticked a box, and that the fact of it sat in her like a stone in a boot.
Then the forms came to Ashenford.

They came out of the county in the autumn, in a bundle, with the office’s stamp on the top sheet. Ivet Sallow opened them at the mill counter and understood inside four minutes that she was going to have to be the person who filled them in.
The bundle was the clean grain scheme.

She had heard about it. Everybody in the trade had heard about it, the way people hear about weather in another county. A licensed mill at Marle. A stamp in the flour. A stamped sack selling for a third more in the county towns. Forms, forms, and a scheme.
The bundle she received had a covering letter, and a licence application, and a valuation form for the mill’s stones, and a registration of the mill’s suppliers.
And it had a page headed *Households and Dependants, Verification by Mill Clerk*.
It wanted every household the mill ground for. It wanted them named and counted. It wanted their dependants counted and their daily use estimated. It wanted a column for remarks.
There were four hundred and eleven pages of form and instruction in that bundle. She counted them twice, because she wanted the number to be right.
At the bottom of the verification page, in small print over a line, it said: **to be signed by the mill clerk of record.**
She had a chance to be exact. She took it.
It was the first thing she did in the new matter. She did it the following Tuesday, and she put the whole of her nineteen years of practice into it.
What she did was this. She filled in the form so correctly, and so completely, and in such detail, that no man in the county office would ever be able to read it all the way through.

She listed every household. She listed every dependant. She put in the age of every child and the name of every cow. She wrote the remarks column so full that she had to use the back of the sheet for the last four households, which is permitted, and which is the mark of an extremely careful clerk.
And in the column where the scheme wanted the daily use estimated, she put the true figure. The true figure of what the mill ground for them.
Then, beside each figure, in brackets, in her small even hand, she put what that household had actually been eating.
*0.8 sacks.* (Two loaves a day for six.)
*0.8 sacks, continued.* (One of the six is a neighbour’s child, unenrolled.)
*1.2 sacks.* (Grandmother lives behind the mill. Eats here. No rate page.)
*0.4 sacks.* (The widow rents the west room. The mill grinds hers with the mill’s own, as arranged with the owner. Not in writing.)
She did that on every one of the eleven pages.

It was not the wider column. She had never heard of the wider column. Nobody had told her to do it. It was what came out of her hand when she sat down with a form that wanted a number and a page that had a person on it.
That, and years of practice, and one un-ticked box in her past.

The form went to the county office in the bundle. Six weeks later a note came back. It said the application was *incomplete and under review*. It thanked her for her thoroughness. It asked her to keep the copy at the mill.
She kept the copy at the mill.
The second chance was the widow.

She came in February with the rate book under her arm. She wanted the mill to strike her dead husband off the household line so the rate would come down. She had the certificate from the parish and the letter from the burial.
She was, in every way a person can be, right.
Ivet Sallow did it. She was a clerk, and the woman was right, and the paper was good, and she did it.

Then she sat at the counter for a while with the pen in her hand and the rate book open at the amended line. She did not go back and change it. She has thought about that afternoon about four times a month ever since. She still does not know what she should have done.
Because the amendment was true. There was no dishonesty in it. The man was dead.

But the page now said that the house had been two people and was one. It said it in the same flat shape as eleven hundred other pages in the south of the counties. And a page that says a house was two and is one is a page that can be looked at later, by somebody who is not looking for a widow.

She could have made her own page. That is what she thinks now. A household page, in the mill’s own book, with the man’s name in it, and *buried in February*, and the mill’s own record of the four sacks his household had bought every month for thirty years.
She did not do it. She did not know how to do it that February.
She knows how to do it now.
Here is what she has started. She has told nobody, and there is nobody she could tell who would understand the size of it.
She keeps a page of her own.
It is at the back of the mill’s own account book, after the last of the accounts, on four leaves that were blank when the book was bound.

It is not signed. It is not witnessed. It is not a county form, and it has no heading. If a man from any office in the counties ever opened that book to the end, he would find four pages of names and dates and small remarks in a clerk’s hand.
And he would think. Well. She has thought about what he would think for a long time. The answer is that he would think nothing.

That is the beauty of it. Four pages of names in the back of an account book is not a document. Nobody looks at the end of an account book. Nobody has looked at the end of that account book in nineteen years.
There are eighty-one names on those four leaves now.

Two of them are households that were struck off the rate book in the last year. One of them is the widow’s husband. His entry has the date of the burial and one line under it: *thirty years, four sacks a month.*
The rest are ordinary. They are the household page the mill never had. Who ground what, and who ate it, and who was at whose table.
She does not know what it is for. She does not know who would ever read it. She has never been able to explain to herself why she started it.

Except that she watched four strangers do something at her own counter one spring day. They had a tin of tallies and a printed county schedule, and they filled in the truth on it. Something about that stayed in her hand.
She does not know what she is part of.
That matters, because the reader knows and she does not.

She has no idea that a company of four became a company of eight. She does not know about the vault at Carrow. She does not know about the Index at Sunth. She does not know about the nine words at the back of the third volume, or the border stone with the raw west face.
She does not know that the man who untied his cord in front of her at the counter keeps a book with nine thousand and four names in it.
She thinks she un-ticked one box. She thinks she has been odd about account books ever since.
She thinks she is nobody.
The clean grain scheme came on.

The licensed mill at Marle was in the county paper. There were four more applications in the district. There was a note about a mill in the west whose registration was *suspended pending review*, which is the phrase they use when they do not want to write down what happened.
In the second week of the new year, the bundle came round again at Ashenford. A scheme is never once.
At the bottom of the new verification page, in small print over a line, there were the same nine words as before.
**To be signed by the mill clerk of record.**
Ivet Sallow read it through twice, in her own time, on a Tuesday, at the counter of the mill on the Vellum, with her own pen out of its own leather case.
Then she put the pen down and went and looked out of the window at the yard for a while.
Four strangers and a goat had stood there nine months earlier.
Then she came back to the counter and picked up the pen.
It would take three seconds.

chapters.label: Chapter 15
chapters.title: The Escape
paragraphs: After the room without a clerk, and the plank with the marks on it, and the night the goat stood in the frost facing west, the company walked four days into the hills.
The road stopped being a road on the second day. It became a track. Then it became a line between two walls. Then it became a use-path worn by sheep and nothing else.

The country changed shape. The fields ended and the walls ended. There was grass and rock, and water coming down off the high ground in small cold threads. There was no fence anywhere, and no building, and no smoke.
They were going up. By the fourth day the peaks had stopped being a horizon and had started being weather.
Nine people had come over the boundary stone at the border. Eight of them were the company. The ninth was a witness.

He was not the company’s. He belonged to the room, and the room was four days east of where they were standing, and every mile west made the room further away. Riss had been doing that arithmetic for eleven days and had not said any of it out loud.
Mira found the horses on the third morning.
She had gone back along the track at first light, the way she had every morning since the border. She had learned in the first month that a chart is no use if it is only a map of where you have been.
She came back at a run, which Mira never did.
“Four horses. Shod, fed, and standing,” she said. “They are in the lee of the outcrop a mile back, with a boy holding them.”
“Four horses for how many men?”

“Three men and a boy. Two of the men are wearing town coats.” She put the chart on a rock and pinned it with two stones. “One of them has a leather case across his back, and it is the shape of a book.”
They came up the path in the middle of the afternoon, on foot, leading the horses. That is what a man does when he intends to be civil.

There were three of them and the boy. The oldest was about fifty. He wore a good grey coat with the collar turned up, and a case on his back on a strap. When he came within ten paces he stopped and took his hat off, which nobody had expected.
“My name is Wenlow,” he said. “I am a magistrate of the county of Ash. I have come from Marrowgate on a sealed order, and I am going to ask you to stand still and hear the order read out.”
“That is the form. I have come a long way to read it.”
“Read it,” said Riss.

He took the case off his back and opened it. He took out a sheet with a seal on it and read it in the voice he had been trained to read things in, with the pauses in the right places. It took about two minutes.

It was an order for the production of goods. It named no person. It described, in four clauses, a brass plate and a body of copy sheets and a quantity of tin tallies. It required their surrender to any officer of the county. It required the names of the persons carrying them to be entered in the register of the county. It was valid for ninety days.
Riss listened to the whole of it.
“You are four days west of the stone,” Riss said.
“I am,” said Wenlow.
“Your order is worth nothing here.”

“No,” he said. “This order is worth nothing west of the boundary stone of the county of Ash. The boundaries of Ash end four days east of here. I know precisely where they end, because I have a schedule of them in the case.”
He put the sheet away.
“I said when I left Marrowgate that I would be carrying a document four days past the end of every court that could enforce it. I said it in front of a clerk. It is in the day book.”
“Then why come?”

“Because the alternative was to write a line in the day book saying the matter is closed and the goods are unrecovered.” He looked at them with no anger at all. “I have been a magistrate for twenty-six years. I have never once written that line.”
“I am aware of what I look like. I have had four days on a horse to become aware of it.”
Then he did the thing Riss remembered afterwards. It was worse than the order and worse than the horses.
He had counted them on the way up the path. He said so, in the flat voice of a man reading out a number he had checked twice.
“I make it eight,” he said. “Eight persons, one animal, and a bier of pack loads. I have been counting since the outcrop.”
He asked for the names.
He took out a register. It was a book of the ordinary kind, county stock, pale grey, ruled, with a leather spine. He opened it flat on his forearm and took a pencil out of his coat.

“That is the form,” he said. “Whatever else we settle, I have to enter the names of the persons found in possession. That is the part I can do correctly even out here. Give me the names and I will write them, and then we can discuss the goods.”
“Whose names?” said Veylan.
“Yours. Every one of you. Name and parish.”
“We are not in any parish,” said Corvath.
“Then I will write *none*, which is a correct entry,” said Wenlow.

He held the pencil. He waited. And he did not get a single name out of any of them. He stood in the wind on the west side of the boundary of every county in the world with an open book in his hand and four blank columns in it.
He waited about a minute. It was the longest minute of the four months.
Then he closed the register and put the pencil away.
“Right,” he said. “That is refusal of the first part. I will enter that instead, and I will enter it in the correct column.”
The plate was the problem, and Nahl said it out loud.
“He is going to search us,” said Nahl.
“He has three men and a boy, and he is civil,” said Veylan.
“He has three men, and he is civil because he has not searched us yet,” said Nahl. “Two of us are carrying. Riss has the plate under their shirt. I have the page in the bearer’s kit.”
“He asks for goods. The first thing he does when we say no is examine the loads, because that is the form. He will do it politely. And then it is in his register.”

They looked at Wenlow across the grass. Fifty years old, in a good grey coat, four days from the last court in the world, with a book he had carried over a boundary stone on a horse and nothing at all to write in it.
“We cannot fight him,” said Old Den.
“No,” said Riss.
“We cannot hand over the plate,” said Nahl.
“No.”
“And we cannot hand over the page.”
Riss stood in the wind for a moment and did the arithmetic. The arithmetic came out in one sentence, and Riss said it out loud, because the company deserved to hear it before it was asked of them.

“Then we give him everything that is a copy,” said Riss. “The twelve ledgers. The forty sheets. The tin.
