Everything that can be written again in a season, and everything that is a piece of paper about a piece of paper. He takes the copies back east with his register and he writes his entry. We keep the two things that have never been copies of anything.”
“That is the page and the plate,” said Veylan.
“That is the page and the plate,” said Riss.
“This is the moment where we could hand over everything and walk out of this clean,” said Nahl. “The copies, the plate, the page, the log, all of it. He would let us go. He has no way to hold us.”
“Yes,” said Riss. “That is the thing we are not doing. Everything else can be taken. The page is the witness and it goes with us.”
It was not a fight. It was a search, done politely, and the politeness was the whole of the horror.

Wenlow asked. Riss refused. Wenlow said that in the absence of consent he would examine the loads, and he said it the way a man says he will open a crate of apples. Then he and his two men did it, on the grass, in the wind, while the company stood in a ring and did not move.

They were not rough and they did not touch anybody. They put the packs in a line and went through them with a care that Riss recognised. It was the care of a man who had spent twenty-six years going through other people’s property and had developed a conscience about how it should be done.
They found the satchel.

They took out the twelve cheap ledgers and stacked them on the grass. They took out the forty copy sheets and put them with the ledgers. They took the tin of tallies. They found the slate and looked at both sides of it. Wenlow turned it over twice, because a slate with no marks on it is a thing a magistrate notices. Then he put it back and said that a slate with nothing on it is not a document.
And then they found the log.
It came out of the satchel in its cloth. The man who took it out held it up, and the wind moved the cloth, and Wenlow came and looked at it.
“Father of the counties,” he said, quietly. It was the first time Riss had heard the man’s voice do anything.

He opened it. He stood there in the wind with the book on his forearm, in a hand of sixteen lines to a page. He stood in a column of nine thousand names written on a shelf in Sallow between the age of twenty-six and the age of sixty-nine. He read for about thirty seconds.
Then he closed it.
“This is not on my order,” he said.
“No,” said Orphiel.
Everyone turned round.

The old man had walked up the grass while they were going through the packs. He had the empty satchel in one hand. He was standing in front of the magistrate, and he was out of breath in a way Riss had not heard once in six months.
“I am the keeper of that book,” said Orphiel.
“It is a copy of a register of the parish of Sallow,” said Wenlow. “Made at the instruction of a superior. It is the property of the county, and it goes back east with the rest.”
“It is also the only unamended copy of that register in the world,” said Orphiel.
Wenlow looked at him and did not answer that, because it was true and he was a careful man.
“What will happen to it in the room?” said Orphiel.
“It will be compared with the copy on the shelf at Carrow.”
“And the differences corrected.”
“Yes.”
“Then it will be filed, and there will be one copy again, and it will be the county’s,” said Orphiel. “That is arithmetic, not an accusation. I have known it for forty years.”
He held his hand out for the book.

Wenlow gave it to him. Riss, watching, understood something about the man: he had spent twenty-six years learning when a hand held out is a form and when it is a person, and on this occasion he had not been certain, and had erred on the side of the form.
Orphiel did not open it. He turned, with the book in both hands, and looked at the company standing in the wind. Then he picked the person he wanted out of the middle of them.
He walked the four paces to Nahl and put it into their arms.
“This one goes with the bearer,” he said. “You have the kit and you have the cord. You know what goes against the body. It is not mine to give away to a court, and it never was.”
“It is a copy of a register. The register is the county’s. This copy has been in one man’s hand for forty years, and it is no longer the same object as the one on the shelf.”
“That is not the form,” said Wenlow.
“No,” said Orphiel. “It is what I have instead.”

Nobody moved. Wenlow looked at the book in Nahl’s arms for a long moment. Then he looked at the old man’s face, and then he did the thing that made Riss remember him afterwards as a person and not as an office. He took his hat off a second time and put it back on.
“It is not on my order,” he said. “I will write it as not on my order.”
“Thank you,” said Orphiel.

Then he did the last piece of clerical work of his life. It took him about six seconds and it cost him everything. He bent down. He picked the empty satchel up off the grass and handed it to the second man.
“The copies are the county’s,” he said. “I would take it as a kindness if you would carry them on the horse and not in the cart.”
Then he sat down on the grass, and everybody in the company understood at the same moment that he had not sat down to rest.

Nothing about it looked like a dying speech. That was the thing Riss kept hold of afterwards. Nobody in the company was given anything to be inspired by. There was no lift in the old man’s voice and no hand on anybody’s shoulder and no sentence for the road. He had stood up, and walked fifty yards, and bent over to pick a bag up off the grass at the age of seventy-one. He was four months into a journey he had no business making, and his body had filed its report and closed the file.
The plate hummed the divided fifth.

It came up through Riss’s shirt at the moment the old man went down. Loud. Split down the middle. Louder than either note had ever been. Kael Riven, standing six feet away, closed his burned hand on his forearm hard enough to leave marks in it for two days.
Then the goat walked across the grass. It went past three men and a magistrate and a boy holding four horses. It stood over Orphiel, facing west, and did not move.

Wenlow looked at the goat for a long moment. He had the log in his hands. He had the copies stacked on the grass behind him. He had his register in his coat with four blank columns in it and one word he still had to write.
Riss was already kneeling down.
“Get him up on the packs,” said Sancora, behind them. “Not the litter. The packs. Flat.”
It was the chest and the head, and it was seventy-one years, and it took about forty minutes.

Sancora did everything she had, and there was nothing to be done with any of it. She said so out loud twice, once at the beginning and once in the middle, because she did not soften prognoses and did not start then.
She had the coat open and the collar loosened. She had her hand on the old man’s wrist. She watched his face and she counted, and she did not once say anything hopeful.
The company stood off about ten feet. The magistrate stood off about twenty with his hat in his hand, and did not leave.
Orphiel was awake for most of it.
Riss was holding the folded coat under his head, because it had to be someone, and it turned out that it was going to be Riss.
“The page,” said Orphiel.

“It is with Nahl,” said Riss. “It was never in the satchel when he went through. Nahl has had it against their body the whole time. He has got the copies and the twelve cheap ones and the tin. The plate is under my shirt. He knows about neither.”
“Good,” said Orphiel.
He lay there for a while with the wind going over the grass.
“The clerk,” he said. “In the room. When it comes.”
“Yes.”

“Their words. My hand.” He stopped for a moment and started again, because there was an arithmetic in this and it had to come out in the right order. “He writes it. I read it, and I sign at the bottom, under his name. The two of them together are the whole of it. That is the form. It is the only form I have ever known.”
“And if he will not write it?”
“Then you do not sign,” said Orphiel.
“I will carry it,” said Riss.
“No,” said the old man.

He turned his head, which cost him something, and looked up at Riss properly. This was the last thing he said in the book that was longer than a sentence, and Riss carried it for the rest of their life.

“You will not sign it. You will carry it. That is the difference. I have signed nine thousand names in forty years, and every one of them was on somebody who was not there. Signing is what a clerk does. Carrying is what you do.”

“If they will not write it, then there is no page, and you will still have the thing itself. One of you will have to know the difference between having a document and having a witness.” He closed his eyes. “A document can be amended. Take care of the other one.”

He died on the west side of the boundary of the county of Ash. It was a slope of thin grass above a sheep path, at about nine in the evening, in a steady wind off the western peaks. There was a goat standing over him, facing away from every county in the world.
Sancora laid his head down and straightened up on her knees.
“That’s him,” she said.
Nobody said anything else for a while. Kael Riven said the word *no*, once, at the edge of the light, and did not say it again.

Above them the Emberion stood where it stood. Fifteen joints, and the piece missing out of the wing. The same fifteen it had been at Collow, and on the shelf of rock, and at the waystation. The wind off the peaks came down steady and cold and did not stop.
The magistrate wrote his entry in the last of the light, standing, with the register open on his forearm.

There was no name to write, and no parish, and no consent. He was a man who had come four days past the end of every court in the world on a horse with a book, so he wrote what was true, in the correct column, in a good clerk’s hand.
**Refused.**
Then a date, and his own name under it, and the seal out of the case, and his thumb on the seal, in the wind, on the far side of the stone.

He did not write *deceased*. Riss watched him come to the place on the form where that could have gone, and watched him leave it empty. A man who wrote *deceased* out here would be making an entry about a county subject who had died outside the county. Such an entry cannot be made, because there is no page under it anywhere in the eleven counties.
He gave the register to the second man to carry and put his hat on.

“I will take the books back,” he said. “The plate and the page I never saw. And God help me, I have a wife and a daughter and a pension, and I am not going to write down a thing I cannot prove in a room four days east of here.”
He looked at the old man on the grass.
“He told me to carry it on the horse. I will carry it on the horse.”
Then he said the thing Riss thought about for the rest of the book.

“You will want to know how the fee comes out of this,” said Wenlow. “The twelve ledgers and the sheets and the tin go back east, and they go on a shelf, because that is what happens to a thing that has been recovered. And nothing else happens.”

“There is no trial out here and there is no jury. There is nobody in any of the counties who will ever be asked a question about tonight.” He got up on the horse. “That is the whole of the counties, and I have spent my life in it. The thing that ought to terrify you is not that we are cruel. It is that we are *finished*. We take a thing away and put it on a shelf and consider the matter dealt with. He knew that better than anybody alive.”
“Then why did you come?” said Riss.
“Because I am not finished,” said Wenlow, and rode east in the dark.

chapters.label: Chapter 16
chapters.title: The Burial
paragraphs: After the grass and the register and the four blank columns, and the wind, and the old man on the ground, they carried Orphiel four hundred yards west and up onto a ridge.
Nahl said the one thing about it out loud before anybody else could. Somebody had to say the practical thing first, and it was going to be said badly by whoever said it second.
“Not down there. He died on a slope above a sheep path. If we leave him there, the first thing that happens to him is a flock.”
Sancora agreed and Veylan agreed, and Mira was already walking, and the goat went ahead, which is how the company made every decision worth making.

They made the litter out of two of Veylan’s staves and his coat and Kael’s blanket. Kael and Veylan carried it, and Corvath carried the other end of the load, which was nothing, because there was nothing left in the packs but food and tools.
The twelve cheap ledgers were on a horse going east. The forty copy sheets were on a horse going east. The tin of tallies was in the second man’s pack with the seal and the register.
The log was in Nahl’s arms.
Nahl carried it the whole way up the ridge. They did not once put it in a pack and did not once let go of it. They never explained that to anybody, and nobody in the company ever asked.
The place was in the lee of a wall.

That was the whole of why they stopped there. The wall was long and low and dry-built, laid without a survey and without a fee. It ran the length of the ridge and went nowhere. It had been standing long enough to have a proper footing and a bank of soil built up behind it, and the lee side was out of the wind.

The ground was thin. Veylan put the trowel in it twice and said so. Under the thin soil there was rotten rock, and under that there was solid rock. There was no depth to it anywhere. They were going to be able to get about two feet.
“Two feet is enough,” said Sancora. “He is not a big man and I have wrapped him.”
They dug it together, in the dark, with the lamp on a stone. The wind went over the top of the wall and did not come down into the lee. It took four hours, and they did it badly and correctly.

Nobody said anything while they dug. That was not a rule and it was not mourning and it was not a silence either. There was just nothing to say. Every one of them had spent four months in rooms where people talked, and it had not once changed the arithmetic of anything.
When the hole was as deep as the ground allowed, Kael went down on his knees at the edge with the lamp and looked at the inside of it.
“There’s no edge anywhere in it,” he said. “It’s the same rock as the ridge.”
“That’s because it is the ridge,” said Veylan.
“Yes,” said Kael.
The question of the ground was settled and the question of the body was settled by Sancora, exactly, without softening. The question that took an hour was the log.

It came up because Nahl opened it, in the lee of the wall, by the lamp, while the others were resting. Opening that book in front of the company was the first thing Nahl did as its keeper, and everybody there understood that it was going to have to be done out loud.
Four columns.
The first was the name. The second was the parish. The third was the date, or the range of dates, or the word *unknown*.

The fourth was the reason. It had a heading in a language nobody in the company could read. It was, Nahl understood now, the whole engine of the thing. It was the column where a name went from being a person to being an entry.
The words in it were the same four or five words in the same four or five orders, over and over, for a thousand pages. The hand above them was steady at sixteen lines to a page.
Nahl turned to the end.
The last entry was four months old. It was a name Nahl did not know and a parish Nahl did not know. The reason column said *at the family’s request*. Then the page was blank.
The fourth column was empty, and there was nothing in it about the man who had copied every other line in the book.
“He is not in it,” said Nahl.
“He would not be,” said Corvath.

“He should be,” said Veylan. “He is dead. He is the only one of us who has actually died in this. He was the keeper of the book, and his name should be at the end of the list he kept. That is the whole of it. That is what the book is for.”
“Yes,” said Nahl.
“So write it.”
Nahl sat with the pen for a while.

Riss did not say anything. Sancora did not say anything. Old Den, who had put his own hand in a press rather than let a clerk write his name in a column, did not say anything either, and it was Old Den’s silence that was the loudest thing in the lee of the wall.
Nahl thought about it honestly, out loud, because that was the trade they had. A bearer who cannot explain a refusal to a company is a bearer who will lie to them in about a year.

“If I write his name in this book, then in forty years, or in four, a man with a pen comes to the shelf at Carrow and finds a copy of a register with one entry at the end that does not match the county’s copy. What does he do with it?”
“He writes the correction,” said Veylan.

“He writes the correction, because that is his job and his job is not evil. Then Orphiel is an error in a register. The error gets filed. The last thing left of the man in any book in the counties is a clerk’s neat stroke through his name.”
Nahl closed the book.
“He told me not to. Not in those words. He said a document can be amended. That was the whole of his argument, and it was the whole of his life.”
“So he goes in nothing,” said Veylan. “At all. Anywhere.”

“He goes in Mira’s chart,” said Nahl. “That is one page, in a tube, in a mapmaker’s hand, carried by people who were there. That is not nothing. That is a witness, and he would have understood the difference better than anybody at this wall.”
Nahl did not write it. The fourth column stayed empty. The page stayed blank.
Then Nahl unwrapped the log’s cloth and wrapped it again round the whole book. They tied the cord with the knot the bearers use, gave it to nobody, and kept it.
They buried him two hours before dawn, in the lee of the wall on the ridge, in two feet of soil over rotten rock.
He was wrapped in his own coat and Kael’s blanket and Sancora’s cloth.
The pen went in with him. So did the inkwell, still wrapped in the shop’s paper from Sallow, fifty years old and never once opened.

That was Corvath’s idea and it was a good one and nobody argued with it. A witness is not buried with his book, because the book is not finished. A witness who never wrote a line can be buried with the thing he was going to write it with, and let that be the entry.
Riss asked the company the question out loud, at the edge of the hole, before they closed it.
“Does anybody want to sign it?”
Nobody answered.

Nahl was standing with the log in their arms. Mira had her tube under one arm. Kael had the slate in his fist by the strap. Veylan had the trowel. Old Den had the bound hand across his chest. Sancora had her hands folded in front of her, which she never did.
“That was his page,” said Nahl, after a while. “It has no clerk’s mark on it. It never had one.”
“That’s not what she asked,” said Corvath.
“It’s the whole of my answer,” said Nahl, and that was the end of it, and the page stayed blank.
The mark on the grave took longer to decide than the grave.
Veylan wanted a name cut into a flat stone. He was practically right and he said so twice, and he was not wrong. A grave with nothing on it is a grave nobody can ever find.
Corvath said the thing nobody else wanted to say.
“He is not in any register. He told us that himself. If we cut his name into a stone we make him a page, and a page can be looked at by somebody who is not looking for him.”
Old Den settled it, because Old Den was the oldest person left in the company as of about eleven o’clock that night.

“We do not cut a name and we do not leave it bare,” he said. “Put a mark on it. Not a letter. A mark of the kind people cut who cannot write and do not want to be written about. The same kind of mark as the plank at the waystation. That is the only page in this country the counties cannot read.”
So they marked it with a notch.

Nahl cut it, because it was a keeper’s job. A single vertical cut in the top stone of the cairn, no deeper than a thumbnail, made with the point of the same knife that had not cut a mark on the waystation plank.
Then, on the stone beneath it, Nahl cut five short strokes beside it. A tally group of five.

One mark for the man and five for the company he had walked with. No name, and no date, and no column, and no parish. Nobody in the eleven counties would ever be able to say what the marks meant or who they were for.
That was exactly the specification.
Mira drew it before she slept.

She did it by the lamp in the lee of the wall, with the sheet pinned flat on the grass. It took her an hour and forty minutes. She drew the ridge and the wall and the ridge path, and she drew the cairn in plan and in section, because that is how a mapmaker draws a thing she wants to be findable in the dark.
Then, in the smallest lettering she had ever used on any page of the chart, she wrote his name.
**Orphiel of Sallow. Clerk.**

That was the first human name Mira Solas had ever put on the Wound-Chart. Two hundred roads, a hundred and forty villages, nine county boundaries, and a great empty unbounded west. There had not been a name anywhere on it, because she had always said that a name on a map is a claim.
Nahl sat and watched her do it and understood the whole of what had just happened, and understood it as an arithmetic, which is how Nahl understood most things.

The man had written nine thousand and four names into a book and had never been in one. Now he was in exactly one record on earth. It was not a register and not a parish copy and not a county return, and no clerk in any county would ever see it, and it would never be filed with anything.
It was a name in a mapmaker’s hand on a chart of the country west of the border, drawn by a person who had walked every mile of it.
That was the entire written existence of Orphiel of Sallow. It was on a page in a tube under a woman’s arm on a ridge.
Kael Riven tried the trace that night.

He did not do it secretly and he did not do it for anybody’s benefit. He sat down on the far side of the wall, out of the wind, with the lamp and the slate. He turned the slate over to the grey side and opened his burned hand and put it flat on the stone, and went looking.
Nahl watched him do it and did not interrupt and did not pretend not to be watching.

He sat there for an hour and a half without moving. Then he took his hand off the slate and it was shaking, in a way Nahl had seen once before, in a village called Collow, on a night four months earlier.
“Nothing,” said Kael.
“You tried the grave.”

“I tried the grave, and the cairn, and the ground under it, and the coat, and the pen he never used, and the wall.” He wiped his face with the back of the hand. “And it is not the stone and it is not the gravel and it is not that I have lost it, because I did the wall and Veylan’s trowel and your own boots on the way here, and they are all where they should be.”
“Then what is it?”

“He was never entered anywhere,” said Kael. “That is the whole of the reason. My hand wants an edge. A thing that was cut off from another thing. A man who was never written down was never cut off from anything. He is not on a page, so there is no line to trace him along and no room he was carried out of.”
He turned the slate back over.

“It is the counties’ own method, and I have been carrying it around in my hand for thirty years. They take a person out of the books, and then there is nothing left to find. I cannot trace him because they won.”
Nahl sat down on the ground with their back to the wall.
“They did not win,” they said. “He carried that book up a ridge at seventy-one, in a wind, and put it in my arms, and then he sat down. That happened. I was there. It happened in a place.”
“Yes,” said Kael. “And he is still nowhere. Those two things are both true, and that is exactly what I cannot fix.”
He put the slate inside his coat.

“We cannot win this by tracing. I have spent the whole of this journey finding out how much of what happened is true, so here is the size of the answer, on this ridge, tonight. It does not matter how much of it is true. It matters how much of it can be read. That is the whole difference, and I got it wrong for four months.”
Riss said the unsaid thing at the wall, at first light, with the fire down to its last coal, in the flattest voice they had.
It was the third of the four, and Riss had been carrying it since the river.
“I have a sister.”
Nobody moved. Sancora had her hands out to the fire. Nahl, who had every trade and no curiosity, did not ask a question. Mira, who wanted everything written down, did not reach for the pen.

“Her name is Ness. She is four years younger than me. She is better at columns than I will ever be. She has the best handwriting in our family, and it leans very slightly left at the base, the way soldiers stand at ease. When we were children I used to make her write my name on my slate for me, because mine looked like a wasp had fallen in the ink.”

“I left her downriver two years ago. I did it carefully and I did it in arithmetic. The leaving was going to be for one year, and the year was going to divide better than the one we were in. She wrote back on the back of a form. Three lines. The last line was: *years don’t divide better. Come back when you can say what you took.*”
The fire did what fires do.

“And in the square at Vellum Reach, in the spring, Halwen read out a county schedule with ninety-one names on it in a clerk’s hand. The hand was my sister’s. She was on it. Thirty-first. **Ness Riss.** She wrote the list and she was on the list.”
“What was the third column?” said Mira.

“Nobody could read it,” said Riss. “That is the whole of what I know about my sister’s job. She writes ninety-one names into two columns and a third column in a language she never learned. Then a man in a good coat puts a seal at the foot of it and a box gets ticked. Nine months later a village on a coast road gets a schedule with the truth filled into it.”
Nahl asked the only question that mattered, and asked it once.
“Do you want it in the Leaf?”
No was the answer, and Riss gave it immediately, and it was the same answer they had given to a clerk in Sunth and to a magistrate on this ridge.

“No,” said Riss. “She is alive. The Leaf is for the ones who were taken out. She has not been taken out. She is on a list that has not been worked yet. If I put her in the Leaf tonight I am doing to her exactly what she did to those ninety-one.”
Riss looked at the fire.
“When she is in a book of mine it will be a book she can read. It will have her own hand in it, and she will be able to correct me.”
“That is the first time you have said her name out loud in four months,” said Sancora.
“That is the first time in two years,” said Riss.
They went on west at first light.

Before they left, the company stood at the cairn in the frost. Eight people, and a goat. A log in a bearer’s arms. A chart in a tube. A plate under a shirt. A slate with nothing on it. A folded page with no clerk’s mark on it and no signature at the foot.
Riss took the page out and held it up in the wind for the company to see, because that was the whole of what they had now.
**A page. Blank. No clerk. No book. No signature.**

“Whatever room we find,” said Riss, “there is no clerk in the company any more, and there is not going to be one. If it comes, one of us signs at the foot of it and nobody else. We will decide that when we are standing in it.”
Then the page went back in the satchel, and the company went up the ridge path.
The wall ran beside them for a mile and then stopped, the way the counties’ walls had stopped. After that there was nothing between the company and the peaks at all.
The plate hummed the divided fifth all the way up.
Kael’s scar answered it.
The goat walked in front.
The Emberion was fifteen.
In the west the gold and grey roads ran side by side up into the high country, and neither of them shone.

chapters.label: Chapter 17
chapters.title: The Climb
paragraphs: After the burial in the lee of the wall, and the marks cut in the top stone, and the last four hours of darkness, the company started up.

There was no ceremony about it. The counties had buried people across eleven counties for four hundred years, and they had done it with a clerk and a book and a fee. The clerk read something out of the book and wrote a line in it, and the line was the whole of what a life came to when it was finished.

The company had a wall, a notch, and a tally of five, and Mira’s chart, and no line anywhere in any book. That was going to have to be enough, because there was no other form available west of the stone.
Orphiel had been dead for six hours and nobody had said a word about what to do next.
They climbed instead.

The road up the western side of the ridge was thin, and it was not a county road. Riss could tell within an hour, because there was no wall beside it and no ditch and no stone at the top of the pass with a number cut into it.
It was a track. It had been made by feet and hooves and rain, in that order.

It ran up through the last of the grass and into country that had no grass left in it. After the first thousand feet it became a shelf of broken stone with a use-path along it. After that it became nothing that could be called a road at all. It simply became the place where other people had gone up before.
The wind was steady from the first mile and never once stopped.

Nahl carried the log. It was in the cloth with the cord tied in the bearer’s knot, and it went against Nahl’s body under the coat. Nahl walked with a hand flat on it the way a person walks with a hand flat on a thing that is theirs.
Riss carried the Leaf. It was where it had been for four months, in the flat case against their own body, one strap over the shoulder and one across the chest.
The folded page with no clerk’s mark on it was inside the case now. There was no longer a satchel and there was no longer a clerk, and the page was going to have to travel as what it was.
Two keepers. Two books. Nobody to sign anything.
The practical argument came on the second day, and it came out of Veylan.

Veylan had been carrying the seed crate up a mountain for two days, and had finally started doing arithmetic about it in the open. Here is what he said, and Riss set it down afterwards as the best speech anybody made against the whole enterprise.
“There’s no witness.”
“That’s not news,” said Sancora.

“It’s arithmetic,” said Veylan. “The whole point of going west was that there was a room. The room had four requirements, and one of them was a witness who could stand in it and say what he saw. We had one.”

“He had read nine thousand names and he had the standing of a man who had kept a county register for forty years. He could stand up in a room and say *I have read the log and the column has been amended*, and men would have to listen to him, because he was one of them.”
Veylan shifted the crate on his shoulder.
“He is under a wall on a ridge. So what exactly are we carrying, and who is going to hear it?”
Nobody answered for a while.
Everything he said was true. That was the trouble with Veylan and always had been. He did not argue well. He argued correctly, which is much harder to answer.
“We’re going up,” said Riss.
“That’s not an answer.”

“It’s the only one I’ve got. You want a reason to go back, and I can’t give you one, because you already found the real one. The witness is dead. The page is blank. The counties are four days behind us.”

“And the fee is still going up on every man and woman in the villages we walked through. And the twelve ledgers are on a shelf at Carrow, going into a room where somebody is going to compare them with a copy and write a neat stroke through the differences.”
Riss stopped on the path and turned round.
“You’re right,” they said. “We have got nothing that any room in the world would accept.”
“Then why …”

“Because I have been asked that question four times since the river, and I have never once had a good answer, and I have not once turned round,” said Riss. “That is not a reason either. It is what we do. If you want to go back, go back. I will write in the Leaf that you did it because you were right, and I will date it and sign it.”
Veylan stood on the shelf of broken stone in the wind for a moment.
“I’m not going back down that road,” he said.
He put the crate up on his shoulder again and went on climbing. That was the refusal. Not one speech, and no agreement about what it meant, and eight miles of broken stone.
The goat walked in front the whole way.

That was new. It had walked in the middle of the company since the coast road, and it had crossed the border first, and it had stood over Orphiel facing west. Now it had gone to the front and stayed there, twenty or thirty paces ahead on the shelf, keeping the same pace as the company.
It stopped when they stopped. It never once looked back at any of them.
Nobody commented on it after the first afternoon. It had stopped being a thing worth commenting on about the time it became a thing that was happening.
On the third day above the last grass the plate went quiet.

Not silent. Riss would have noticed silent and would have been frightened by it. It went quiet the way a note goes quiet when it has been sounding in a room for a long time and the room has finally agreed with it.
The divided fifth was still there, under the ribs, at the same split, with the same wrongness. But it was no longer being added to anything. It had no more distance to travel.
Riss stopped on the shelf and stood still for a minute with a hand flat on their chest.
“What,” said Nahl.
“Nothing new,” said Riss. “It has just stopped going anywhere. It has been getting louder since the border, and now it is the same as it was this morning.”
“It has arrived somewhere.”
“Yes,” said Riss. “And I don’t like how much better that feels.”
Kael Riven, ten paces up the path, had his burned hand closed on his forearm the whole time. He said nothing at all and did not need to.
The wind came off the high ground and it did not stop, and it was not weather.

Four months of road had given the company a working knowledge of what wind is. It comes in from a quarter. It rises and falls. It drops at dusk and turns at a valley mouth, and it stops when the land stops pushing it. This wind was none of those things.

It came down the mountain at a steady pressure, all day and all night, from a single direction, with no gusts in it and no lulls in it. The only time it changed was when the company went up a thousand feet, and the pressure came up with them, like a hand leaning on a door.
On the fourth night Nahl said the only thing anybody said about it.
“It’s the same wind as the ridge at Collow.”
“It is,” said Sancora.
“And the ridge at Collow is five hundred miles east of here.”
“Yes,” said Sancora, and turned over.
That was the end of the conversation. Nobody in the company said the word, then or the next day or the day after that.

The Emberion stood over the high ground every clear night. Fifteen joints, with the piece missing out of the wing. It had been fifteen on the shelf of rock at Collow and fifteen on the ridge at the waystation, and it was fifteen now.
Riss had begun, sometime in the last week, to find that comforting in a way they could not explain and did not examine.
The cold was the enemy on this mountain, and Sancora fought it in the open.
She did triage, and she did it out loud, and she did it in front of everybody, and she did not soften a single line of it.

Old Den’s hand came first, every third evening, in the lee of whatever rock they had. A wound that is three weeks old and healing wrong in thin air is a wound that will take a man’s arm if nobody watches it. Then feet, all the pairs, every second day, in the order of who had the worst boots, which she kept in her head and revised without announcing it.
Then, on the fifth night, she reported the general state of the company, standing up, in front of the fire.

“Here is where we are,” said Sancora. “We are eight days above the last grass, and there are eight of us, and I can tell you what every one of us is carrying. About four days of food that anybody wants to eat, and eleven days of food that anybody can eat. Veylan’s chest is bad and it is going to get worse. Mira has lost feeling in two toes. I have got them back, and I will be checking them every day. Old Den’s hand is holding. Kael’s hand burns in the cold, and there is nothing to do about it, and he is not to be asked about it.”
“And Corvath,” she said, “has stopped sleeping.”
“Sancora,” said Corvath.

“He has stopped sleeping and he has not said anything about it. I am telling the company because if he goes down on the shelf above a drop, nobody else in this party is strong enough to carry him. I want everybody to know that now, in the light, while it is a fact about a person and not a decision about a body.”

Corvath did not argue, because there was nothing to argue with. He sat with his back to the fire and his hands round his knees and said the thing that Riss wrote down, because Riss wrote down everything anybody said about being afraid, on the chance that it would be useful in a room at the end of the world.
“I can smell nothing on this mountain,” said Corvath. “Nothing at all. Rock and cold and the inside of my own coat.”
“That was my whole trade for a hundred years under the ground. I could tell you what had been in a room, and who had stood in it, and what they had eaten.”
He looked at the fire.

“I told the company in a village four months ago that my sense had failed me, and you all wrote it down and were very kind about it. It did not fail. It went where the rest of the company went. There is simply nothing up here to smell, because nobody has ever lived on it.”

“I have spent this whole journey complaining that I had become ordinary. It turns out that becoming ordinary was the most useful thing that could have happened to any of us, because I have no gift left to be fooled by. When we get where we are going, whatever it is, ask me first.”
Nobody said anything for a while.
“I will,” said Nahl.
“Write that down,” said Corvath.

That was the whole of Sancora’s practice, and it was the same practice as the hand and the grip. No false hope and no softened prognosis, and the work offered every single day. The company said nothing at all against it, because she was right in every particular, and because a party on a mountain knows the difference between being told the truth and being told a story.
Nahl came to Riss on the sixth night, in the lee of a boulder, with the log in the cloth on their knees.
The two of them had been circling this conversation since the ridge, and both of them knew it.
“What do we do with it?” said Nahl.
“Which one,” said Riss.

“Either one. Both. His.” Nahl put a hand flat on the cloth. “He carried it up the last mile of that ridge at seventy-one and gave it to me in front of a magistrate and told me it goes with the bearer. And I have been walking up this mountain for six days with nine thousand names tied to my chest. Every mile I go up, it gets further from any room in the world that could do anything with it. That is the arithmetic. Up here, this book is worth what it weighs.”
Riss thought about the question for a while, because it was the real one, and because it was the question the whole journey had been narrowing down to since the first village.
“We keep it,” said Riss.
“Keep it meaning what?”
“Keep it meaning the thing it says,” said Riss. “We do not file it. We do not amend it. We do not sign it, and we do not write our own names in it, and we do not tidy it.”

“We carry it up the mountain, and we carry it down the other side. If there is a room at the end of it with a clerk in it, then the clerk writes it in his words, and it is witnessed. If there is no room and no clerk, then it stays exactly as it is for as long as one of us is alive and can carry a book.”
Riss turned their hands over.
“That is all he ever asked of anybody. It is what he did for forty years on a shelf, and he did it with a hole in the ledger the size of nine thousand names, and nobody ever once said thank you.”
“Two keepers,” said Nahl.
“Two keepers,” said Riss. “You have the book that says what was taken. I have the book that says what is left. Neither of us can file anything.”
“No,” said Nahl. “But we can witness.”
They sat with that for a while, in the wind, on the side of a mountain. Then Nahl said the other half of it, which was the harder half.
“And the page.”
“The page stays blank,” said Riss.
“Because a witness who signs his own page is a diarist.”

“Because a witness who signs his own page is a diarist,” said Riss. “That is his rule and it is a good rule, and I have not found a way around it in six days of walking. If you sign it, it is your word about a thing you did yourself. If I sign it, it is mine. And a page signed by the people who carried it is worth exactly what the counties say it is worth, which is nothing. They are right to say so.”
“Then it’s worth nothing.”
“It is worth what a person who was there is worth,” said Riss. “Which is a different kind of nothing.”
Riss looked up the slope at the dark of the high ground.

“It goes to the room blank. That is the whole of the plan. If it comes, we will know it when we are standing in it, and one of us signs it, and it will be one of us. I have been carrying this case for four months so that when it happens there will be a page in the room with no clerk’s mark on it, and a person standing next to it who was there.”
They came up onto the high shelf on the eighth day and saw what the mountain was going to be.

It was a wall of grey stone, three thousand feet of it. The wind came down off the top of it in a steady sheet and the light went flat against it, and above it the rock went up into cloud and stayed there. The shelf they were standing on ran along the base of it like a road cut for a purpose nobody had ever written down.

There was ice in the cracks. There were no birds. There was no grass and no moss and no lichen on the north faces. There was a thin dark line running up the wall from the shelf, which was a chimney, and which was the only way up.
Mira had the chart out and was drawing before she had stopped walking.

She drew the shelf, and the wall, and the chimney, and the ice in the cracks. Then she stopped and stood with the pen up in the air looking at the cloud for about a minute, and did the thing that Mira did, which was to draw the cloud.

Not as a shape. She drew it as an absence. She ruled an area and hatched the edges, and left the chart’s own blank paper in the middle of it, with one sentence in the hatched border in her smallest lettering: **not seen. Not walked. Nothing drawn here is a claim.**
“It is the first time in eleven years I have drawn fog,” she said.
“Is it worth drawing?” said Veylan.

“It is the most important thing on the page,” said Mira. “Everything else on this chart is a place I walked to and measured, and it is true to within a hundred paces, and none of it is worth anything to a person standing on this shelf. That,” she said, tapping the blank middle with the pen, “is what we know about what is up there. It is the only honest page in the whole tube.”
“That’s not a map,” said Veylan.
“No,” said Mira, and rolled it, and put it back in the tube. “That is why I want you to know what is on it.”
Veylan put the seed crate down and stood looking at the wall with his hands on his hips, like a man looking at a field with a bad gradient.

“There is nothing up there for anybody,” he said. “Not a graze, not a spring, not a shelf you could put a house on. I have been walking this country for four months looking at land the way I look at land, and I will tell you what that is: that is a boundary. It is not a place.”
“Somebody put the line out here because the country itself ends here. The counties had the sense not to survey it, and that is the only piece of good judgement I have ever seen out of any of them.”

Old Den, who had been at the foot of the mountains of the Ascension War as a boy of nineteen and had never once talked about it, stood with his bound arm across his chest and said nothing for a long time.
Then he said one thing, in the flat voice that had said *it won’t be* on the river and *write refused* at Marrowgate. Nobody asked him a follow-up question, then or later.
“I went up a mountain once with ten thousand men,” said Old Den. “Two thousand of us came down, and I have never once been able to say what we were doing there.”
He looked up at the cloud.
“That was men. Whatever is coming down that wall at us in the wind is not men, and it has never been men. I want you all to understand that I know the difference, and I am still standing here.”
And the plate hummed, low, split down the middle.
Kael Riven’s scar answered it.
The goat was already twenty paces up the shelf.
It stood where the thin dark line came down out of the wall, waiting for the company the way it had waited at the mouth of the path west of Marrowgate, without any impatience at all.
Above the shelf the wind went on coming down without stopping, at a pressure that had no weather in it, from the one direction, off the high ground, out of the cloud.

Riss stood at the foot of the wall and did not say the word. Neither did anybody else. Everybody in the company knew what was up there and had known it since the first village. The knowing was not the same as a name and did not need to be.
Gold road, grey road, side by side up into the high country. Neither of them shining.
The company started up.

chapters.label: Chapter 18
chapters.title: The Cold
paragraphs: After the marks on the grave, and the last of the grass, and the shelf at the foot of the grey wall, the company went into the chimney.

Sancora had been a healer for nineteen years. She had set bones in a barn. She had delivered two children in a cart. She had once held a man’s scalp on his head while somebody else fetched a needle. She had never in nineteen years been the person who decided whether a company went up or came down.
She was not the person who decided now either. That was the whole of her method, and the mountain was the first thing that had ever tested it.

The chimney went up out of the shelf at the foot of the grey wall. It was not a climb in the ordinary sense. It was a crack in the rock, wide at the base and narrowing as it went, filled at the bottom with old ice and powdered stone.

Four hundred feet, Mira said. She had measured it on the first morning with the chart and a plumb line of knotted cord. The wind pulled the cord sideways the whole time. She had said four hundred feet anyway, with the flat certainty she used for distances.
“That is not a distance,” said Veylan. “That is a verdict.”
The cold on the first day was not the cold of a bad winter. It was the cold of a place that had never once been warm.

Sancora had spent a night in a blizzard north of Ossary. It took a nail off her little toe. She had thought at the time that she understood cold. She had been wrong. That cold had been weather. This cold came down the chimney like water down a drain. It did not shift with the light. It did not let up at noon.
The rules of it were simple and she said them out loud. She stood on the shelf with her two satchels at her feet.

“Hands and feet. That is the whole of the arithmetic up there. A man with a cold hand drops a rope, and a man with a cold foot goes over. Gloves on the rope, and any hand that is not working goes inside a coat, and I want to look at every hand and foot at every stop.”
“No stopping and sitting. Sitting is how people die at altitude. We stop, we eat, we drink, and we go on. If I find anybody asleep at a stop I will put snow in their shirt and I will not apologise.”
“Nobody lies down to rest at the top. We get off the chimney and we keep moving until we have shelter, even if the shelter is a rock and the moving is stamping.”
“And nobody in this company climbs anything on their own. Not the fastest, not the strongest, not the goat.”

“If I tell you to hold, you hold. If I tell you to come down, you come down. I have never once in nineteen years told a person to come down who did not need to come down, and I am not going to start on this mountain.”
Then she looked at Veylan.

“There will be one more thing and I am saying it now, in the warm, where you can all hear it,” she said. “If somebody has to be left, it will not be a vote and it will not be bravery. It will be the weakest leg, and I will say so out loud, and the company will hear it from me and not from a whisper.”
“That is not a threat. That is the reason you brought me.”
Nobody argued, which was the first thing that had gone right all week.
Then she did the rope work. This was the part of the day the company remembered afterwards. It was the last ordinary hour of the whole journey.

She had four lengths of rope, all of them old. Two were bought at Ossary. Two were handed to her by a lock-keeper’s widow at the second river gate. She laid them out on the shelf in the sun and went over every foot of them with both hands. She found one weak place, cut it out, and burned the end with a taper. She threw away a length of eight feet that she did not like.
“Pairs,” she said. “Nobody goes up alone and nobody goes up with the same person twice. If one man goes over, the other man is on a doubled rope against the wall.”
She set the order herself, and she set it by weight and by leg and not by anything else.
Kael first, with the axe and the hand. Riss second, because the plate was under their shirt and Riss climbed badly and would need a rope above them.

Veylan third. Nahl fourth, with the log against the body under the coat. Mira fifth with the tube. Old Den sixth, with the bound hand inside his coat and the other hand on the rope. Corvath seventh. Herself last.
The goat watched the whole arrangement. It had the expression of an animal that had never once in its life been roped.
“Not the goat,” said Mira.
“Not the goat,” said Sancora. “The goat has gone up in front of us since the border stone. If the goat wants a rope it can ask me for one.”
Riss stood at the foot of the crack with a hand flat on the plate through the shirt.
“How is it,” said Nahl.
“Quiet,” said Riss.
“You have said that four times in six days and you say it differently every time.”
“It is quiet the way a room is quiet when the person you came to see is already in it,” said Riss, and that was the end of it, and Sancora turned round and put them all on the rock.
They left the crate at the foot of the chimney.
That was Veylan’s business and he did it himself. He had been corrected about soil his entire life. He had learned to be exact instead of proud.

The crate was four feet by two and weighed, with the seedlings in it, about as much as a small child. It could not go up a four-hundred-foot crack on a rope with a man attached to it. The arithmetic was not close and Veylan had done the arithmetic before anybody asked him to.
He took the tin out of the crate and put it inside his coat.

The tin was the one Veylan had kept his whole life. A flat tobacco tin with a dent in the lid. In it, wrapped in a scrap of sacking, was a handful of west soil taken at the border stone. He had been carrying it for eleven days with a hand on it whenever he sat down.

He opened the crate and looked at the seedlings for a while. There were forty-one of them. They had all come up out of a bad winter. Two of them he had brought through an oven-house in February on the heat of a banked fire.
Then he closed the crate and stacked it in the lee of a boulder, on the flattest ground he could find, with a stone on the lid.
“I will want to know how the frost took it in April,” he said.
“Veylan,” said Mira. “We are not coming back down.”
“No,” said Veylan. “That does not stop me wanting to know.”

He looked at the stack of it, in the lee of the boulder, out of the wind, in the last of the grass. Then he picked the tin up out of the crate one more time and put it back inside his coat. After that he did not look at the crate again.
Sancora kept the company’s numbers in her head, and she was asked twice a day to write them down.
Nahl asked first, on the second evening, on the shelf, with the Leaf open on their knees. Sancora understood the offer and refused it in a way that was not a refusal of Nahl.
“My column stays in my head,” she said. “Put numbers on me and I will start making them agree.”
“Agree with what?”

“With whatever is written next to them. That is how a column works and you know it better than I do. I say the state of the company out loud every evening and everybody hears it. If I have it wrong, they know it inside a day. If I write it down, it will be true because it is written, and then it will be wrong the next morning, and then I will want to keep it tidy.”
“You are telling me a column on paper is a claim.”
“I am telling you that a column on paper is a claim,” said Sancora. “Mira will not draw a road she has not walked. I will not write a number I cannot correct.”
Nahl closed the Leaf and said nothing further about it, then or on any night after.
The chimney took four days.

Sancora would afterwards remember it as one continuous act with no daylight in it, and she was not wrong. The chimney was so narrow that for long stretches there was no sky above them at all. There was only the cold, and the wet of the inner face, and the sound of the wind drawing past the opening they had come in by.
They went up in pairs on a doubled rope. Kael went first on the leading rope, because his hand could tell them where the ice was thin.

That was the discovery of the second day and it was made by accident. Kael had his burned hand out of his glove at a rest, to close it and open it the way he did when it ached, and he put it flat against the face of the chimney to brace himself. Then he took it away and looked at it.
“Here,” he said. “It is thin here. A foot to the left and it is three times thicker.”
“How do you know?” said Veylan.

“Because it burns where the rock is near,” said Kael. “It has been doing it since Collow. It burns when the plate is loud and it burns when there is rock close on the other side of nothing. It is not a gift. It is a nuisance. But it will tell us where to put an axe.”

He did not say anything else about it, and nobody in the company asked. For the next three days Kael went up in front with his bare hand out of the glove, tapping left and right along the ice like a man reading a wall in the dark.
It worked. That was the part that Sancora could never stand to think about afterwards. It worked.
Old Den’s hand held.

That was the biggest piece of luck in the whole climb and it was luck and not judgement. The wound was three weeks old and healing wrong. Sancora had told him on the shelf, plainly, that if the cold got into it he would lose the rest of the hand at the wrist.

He climbed with the bound hand inside his coat and did everything with the other one, and he did not complain once. Somewhere in the middle of the third day Sancora looked at his face at a rest and understood that the man had already spent his decision.
“I have been thinking about it,” said Old Den, when he caught her looking.
“About the hand.”

“About the fact that I will not be carrying anything at the top.” He closed his good hand round the rope. “I have been the oldest man in every room I have been in for nineteen years. This is the first time it has been a fact of any use. Nobody expects anything of me up here and I am not required to pretend.”
“That is not comfort, that is diagnosis,” said Sancora.
“I know,” said Old Den. “I am the one who told you not to soften it.”
The wind in the chimney was the worst thing on the mountain and it was not the wind they had known for eleven days.

Above the shelf it came down the crack in one continuous pressure, without gusts, from the top of the wall. There was nothing at the bottom of it that anybody could name. It did not smell of ice and it did not smell of water. Corvath, who had spent his whole life in rooms under the ground and could read a space by its smell, climbed with his head down and said nothing about it at all, which the whole company noticed and none of them mentioned.
The plate was silent in a way it had never been silent.

Sancora knew that because Riss told her, and because Riss’s whole face had changed on the second day of the climb. For four months the plate had been humming under their shirt: a fifth, split down the middle, a note with something wrong in the middle of it. Sancora had watched it wear Riss down in towns and keep them up at night on the road.
Now it was quiet. It had gone quiet above the last grass, and it had not come back, and Riss said the same sentence about it twice, in the same flat voice, on the second day and the third.
“It has arrived somewhere.”
“Then it should be pleased about it,” said Sancora.
“Yes,” said Riss. “That is what worries me.”
On the fourth day they came out onto a ledge a hundred feet below the top of the chimney, and Mira’s plumb line said so, and they stopped there.

Sancora did the checks. It took her an hour and ten minutes, and she did it out loud, because a cold company is a company that has stopped listening and a healer who works silently is a healer nobody believes.

Two of Mira’s toes were white and had to be brought back with a hand inside a glove, which took twenty minutes and hurt badly and worked. Veylan’s chest was worse and crackling on the left side, and she put her ear on his back and listened to it twice and did not like it. Kael’s burned hand was split in two places across the palm where the scar ran, and she dressed it with the last of the clean linen and told him he would have to keep it in the glove the rest of the way up.
“And the arm?” said Kael.
“The arm is holding,” said Sancora. “Your hand is not your arm.”

Old Den’s hand was intact and ugly and she left it alone and said so. Riss’s hands were fine. Nahl’s hands were fine. Corvath’s hands were fine and Corvath himself had not slept more than an hour at a time in six days.
Then she stood up on the ledge with her back to the wall and gave the company the numbers, which was her last act of the day’s work and the only one she had any real faith in.

“Everybody is up. Everybody has both feet. Nobody has lost a finger, a toe, or a night’s worth of judgement. Wounds: four, all known, all counted, none of them worse than they were yesterday except Veylan’s chest, and I will be listening to it again at dawn.”
“That is the state of the company on the fourth night of the chimney. Tomorrow we finish the climb or we do not, and either way the number tonight is eight.”
Sancora had one thing she did not say to the company, and she thought about it for a long time on the ledge that night, wrapped in her second coat with the goat standing over her out of the wind.

She had been a healer for nineteen years, and in nineteen years she had never once had a body she could not have saved if she had been there in time. That was not modesty and it was not a boast. It was the whole of her professional pride and the whole of her private fear: she had never been tested.

Now she had a company of eight on a mountain with no road down and a chest that was crackling on the left side, and the arithmetic had put a number on somebody for the first time in her life, and she knew exactly which number it was.
She looked at Veylan asleep with his hands round the tin inside his coat.

Then she looked out from the ledge, over the drop, down the chimney. She could not see the bottom of it. The cold had filled it with a kind of standing dust, and the wind was holding the dust inside the crack like water in a drain.
The goat was standing at the lip of the ledge, wide awake, out of the weather, facing up.

Above them the Emberion was where it always was. Fifteen joints, and the piece missing out of the wing, so far up and so much colder than any of them that it looked less like a picture and more like a page.

That was the last night before they came out on the shelf, and it was the coldest of the four, and it was the one the company would have described, if anybody had asked, as the night the mountain stopped pretending.
Sancora took the third watch and sat with her back against the wall of the chimney and her hands inside her coat.

For an hour nothing happened except the wind. The cold came down the crack the way it had come down for four days: steady, from a single direction, without gusts. The dust stood in the air. The ice ticked in the seams of the rock, the way ice ticks on a warm afternoon in the low country.
Then the wind changed pitch for the first time since they had gone into the chimney.

It did not stop and it did not gust. It shifted, by a little, the way a note shifts under a hand that has been pressing it, and the shifted note went on and on above them without any break in it, and the ice in the seams of the wall stopped ticking.
Sancora sat still and listened to it for a long time.

She had spent nineteen years learning what a body sounds like when it is failing: the wet crackle, the shallow pull, the small catch that means a lung is not filling. This sound was not a body and she knew it was not a body and she was a healer, not a woman with opinions, and so she did not say what she thought it sounded like.

She wrote nothing down. She kept the number in her head, which was eight. She sat with her back to the rock in the dark on the fourth night. Above her, at the top of the chimney, something enormous went on breathing in the wind that was not weather.

chapters.label: Chapter 19
chapters.title: The Bone
paragraphs: After four days in the chimney came the ledge and the rest day, and on the ledge, in the ice at the back of it, they found the bone.
Veylan had been corrected his whole life, and he had come to think of it as the trade.

His father corrected him on seed depth. His father’s foreman corrected him on drainage. The mill’s clerk corrected him on the weight of a sack, twice in one morning, with the second correction delivered kindly and the first delivered as if he were an idiot. He had been corrected by an overseer, a priest, a woman at a market who told him he was holding a lamb wrong, and a boy of eleven who knew more about grafting than he did.

He had learned two things from it. The first was that being corrected is free and being wrong is expensive. The second was that a man who digs carefully will be corrected less often than a man who digs fast, and that careful digging is the only dignity available to a person of his sort.
On the fifth morning, on the ledge, Sancora ordered a rest day.
She ordered it after she had listened to Veylan’s back twice with her ear against it, and she ordered it flatly and without apology, the way she did everything.
“Nobody climbs today. His left side is crackling and I want to know what it does over twelve hours.”
“I can climb,” said Veylan.

“You can,” said Sancora. “You would probably make the top. And then you would be a man with wet lungs at the top of a chimney with no way down, and I would be the healer who let you do it because you asked politely.” She sat down against the wall. “Rest day. Eat the good food. Melt ice. I want hands and feet in my lap at noon and I want nobody to move further than the width of this ledge.”
The company spent the day the way they had spent the whole of the journey, which was separately and in the same square of ground.

Mira walked the ledge twice, once in each direction, with the chart under her arm and her fingers spread against the wall, mapping a shelf forty feet long as though it were a county. Then she sat down with the lamp and drew it, and the drawing took her four hours, and there was nothing on the ledge to draw except rock and ice and the shape of the crack above it.

Nahl took the log out of the coat for the first time in six days and put it on a flat stone and looked at the cover of it without opening it. Then they wrapped it again and tied the cord with the bearer’s knot and put it back inside the coat, and Kael, watching from across the ledge, understood that the man had been checking not the book but the knot.

Riss sat against the wall with the blank page out of the case for a while, not writing on it, and then put it away. Corvath slept for two hours in the sun and told nobody whether it had worked. Old Den ate a whole ration on his own, which he had not done since the waystation, and said afterwards that he had done it because he wanted to be worth carrying.

And Sancora sat with her satchels open in front of her. She did the one thing she never let anybody watch. She took every bandage and dressing out of both bags and went over the whole stock by hand, counting it. Then she put it all back in a different order, so that the things she would need first were on top.
She had eleven clean linen strips left and about half a pot of the black salve and no more of anything else.
Eleven, she said to herself, and did not write the number down, because a column on paper is a claim.
So Veylan dug.
That was not defiance. It was the only thing a farmer knows how to do with a day off, and there was a drift at the back of the ledge that had been bothering him since they arrived.

It was old ice packed against the wall of the chimney, three or four feet deep, with grit and stone in it, and it had a shape to it that was not the shape a drift takes when the wind puts it there. It was scooped out at the bottom like the underside of a shelf, and the scoop was full of dark material, and Veylan had looked at it on the fourth night and thought: that is not snow, that is a floor.
He went at it with the trowel because the trowel was what he had. He worked from the top downward and he worked in layers, which is how you dig a hole anybody can trust.

The top layer was fresh ice, maybe a season old. Under that was ice with grit in it, older. Under that was ice with a lot of grit in it and no air in it at all, dense and grey, and it took him an hour to move two feet of it.

Sancora watched him work for a while from her place against the wall and did not stop him. Mira came and asked what he was doing and he said he was digging and she went away and came back with the lamp.
At about the third hour the trowel rang.
Veylan stopped.
He had heard a trowel ring on stone a thousand times. This was not stone. It was a long, flat, hollow sound, like hitting a table with a spoon, and it went on for a moment after the blow.

He cleared the ice away from a patch the size of his hand and looked at it. Then he stood up on the ledge in the cold with the trowel in his hand and said the only word anybody said for the next five minutes.
“Company.”
It was a joint.
That was the first thing anybody could say about it, and it took the rest of the afternoon to say anything else.

It was a bone of the ball-and-socket kind, and it was the size of a boat. Not the size of a big dog’s bone, and not the size of something in a story. It lay in the ice the way a keel lies in a slipway. A length of it ran back into the wall of the drift, with the socket end out toward the ledge. The socket was wide enough that Mira lay down on the ice afterwards to plot it, and could have lain inside it lengthways with room for a pack.

The weathered part was what they saw first. The outside of the bone was grey, cracked, pitted, worn into a shape that had no sharp edges anywhere in it. There was moss on it. There was moss on a bone at four thousand feet above the last grass, in a place no living thing grew.

It was old. Nobody in the company had the training to say how old and nobody was willing to say it out loud anyway. The ice above it was layered the way ice layers over centuries, and the ice above the ice was layered the way ice layers over more.
Veylan got down on his hands and knees at the socket end and looked into it for a long time.
Then he said the thing that made the whole find turn over.
“The inside is clean.”
They all came and looked, one at a time, because Veylan asked them to, and because a company of eight on a ledge knows the difference between a man telling them a thing and a man showing them.

The inside of the socket was white. It was smooth. It was dry. In a bone lying in ice for however many centuries, at the place where a bone is thinnest and weakest, the socket was intact and clean and unmarked.
There were no tooth marks anywhere on it. There were no cut marks. There was no filing, no burning, no break, no hollowing out.
“Something died,” said Veylan, “and nothing ate it.”
“Say the rest,” said Kael.

“Nothing ate it, nothing carried it, nothing broke it open for marrow, and nobody took a piece of it.” Veylan sat back on his heels. “I have dug a lot of middens. I have dug out three burial plots and a plague pit. Anything that dies near people gets a mark on it inside a season.”
“This has been in the ground, or in the ice, or in whatever this was before it was ice, for longer than anybody has been putting marks on anything. And there is not one mark on it anywhere.”
“What it is,” said Sancora, “is the joint of the left leg of something enormous.”
“It is a joint,” said Mira. “One joint. Nothing else. We dug from the wall out to the lip and there is one bone in this drift and no others.”
Kael traced it and found an edge.

He did it that evening, on the ledge, with the lamp, with his bare hand on the bone. And Veylan watched the trace-witness put his palm flat on a thing that had been in the ice since before the counties had names. He had been corrected about soil for forty years and had no gift at all, and he saw the man’s face change.
“There’s an edge,” said Kael.
“Where?”

“Everywhere on the inside of the socket. It is the smoothest thing I have ever touched and it has an edge the whole way round, and it is not the edge of a break.” He moved his hand over the rim, slowly. “It is the edge of a cut.”
Veylan did not understand, and said so.

“I can find two kinds of edge with this hand,” said Kael. “I can find the edge of a thing that was lost, and I have been failing at that for six weeks without any results. And I can find the edge of a thing that was kept.”
He took his hand off the bone.

“This is the second kind. This bone was not lost. It was kept, and it was kept whole. Then at some point a thing that could cut bone the way a cook cuts a haunch took it out of whatever it belonged to. It left the one joint. It did not eat it, and it did not file it, and did not tell anybody.” He looked at the socket. “It is cut off from the thing it belonged to. It has an edge going the other way. Orphiel told me in the vault that a thing taken out has an edge too.”
“And the bone is enormous,” said Riss.

“The bone is enormous,” said Kael, “and it is in no column anywhere, and there is no entry about it in any book in the counties, because there is no book that has ever had a page the size of this animal.”
The company argued about the bone for about two hours, which was longer than they had argued about the crate.
The argument was Veylan’s and he made it well and he lost it, and afterwards he agreed with the losing side, which was the whole of the man.

“Here is my case,” he said. “That bone is a document. It is the only thing any of us has ever handled that a man in a room could not argue with. It is physical. It has weight. You could put it on a table in front of an Assessor and he would have to write something.”
“Go on,” said Riss.

“That is the case. Carry a piece of it east, show it in a room, and every ledger in the county has to move to accommodate it.” He said it the way he said things about land: slowly, in the actual numbers. “I have spent four months carrying a paper that nobody will read. That is a rock that nobody can ignore.”
Then he waited, because a man who has made his case waits.
Mira answered first, and she answered as a mapmaker.

“The chart goes east,” she said. “Not the bone. I can draw it in plan and in section, and I can measure it, and I can write down the depth of the ice above it and the height above the last grass. That is four leaves and it fits in the tube. It is worth more in a room than a piece of the bone, because a piece of the bone is a curiosity and a measured drawing is a fact.”
“A curiosity is a fact with a story on it,” said Veylan.

“Exactly,” said Mira. “And in a room, a story is how a thing gets filed. Give an Assessor a piece of a giant’s bone and he will put it in a case with a label on it and he will write a line about the finder. Give him the measurements and he has to argue with the arithmetic.”
Then Nahl said the thing that settled it, and Nahl said it as a bearer.

“And if we cut a piece of it, we have done the thing that was done to it before.” Nahl had their hand flat on the log’s cloth. “Something big died and everything that has ever touched it either ate it or left it alone. There is nobody in the counties who could have left a thing this size alone. They would have measured it, valued it, taxed it, dug it out and put it in a case.”
“That is what we are proposing,” said Veylan.

“Yes,” said Nahl. “So we are not going to do it. We are going to do the only thing that has ever been done to that bone since it was cut off the animal, which is nothing. We leave it in the ice, and we draw it, and we write down the measurements, and we carry the paper east.”
Veylan sat with that for a while on the ledge in the cold.
Then he got up, and went to the socket end, and put his hand on the rim of it, which was the first time he had touched it with his hand rather than the trowel.

“All right,” he said. “I dug it up and I am the one who is saying leave it. That is a strange day’s work.” He looked at Mira. “Get the numbers right. If this goes east, the numbers are the whole of it.”
Old Den had not said anything for the whole of the argument, which was how he did most things, and he said something afterwards, on the ledge, when the light had gone and the lamp was lit.
“I want to tell you what happened to the other bones,” he said.
“On the mountain,” said Veylan.

“At the mountain. I was nineteen and there were ten thousand of us and the men who came down were two thousand, and I have told you that part twice.” Old Den sat with the bound hand across his chest. “Here is the part I have not told anybody. The counties came up after us. Not an army. Commissioners. They came up with a schedule and a cart and a man with a book, and they went over that ground for four months.”

“And they wrote down every man they found. Name, parish, company, and where he was lying. They had a column for the ground and a column for the state of the body, and they did not miss anybody that could still be told apart, and they took the ones they could carry down in the carts.”
“That is a good thing,” said Sancora.

“It is a very good thing,” said Old Den. “It is the best thing the counties have ever done and I will say so in any room. Nine thousand men got a line in a book and a stone in a churchyard at their own parish. Their mothers got a certificate with a name on it. Every one of those lines is on a shelf today and can be read by anybody who asks.”
He looked at the drift at the back of the ledge.

“And the rest of the bones stayed where they were, because a bone in the high country is not a body and the counties only have a column for a body. The commissioners walked over every foot of that ground and they did not pick up one scrap of what could not be given a name. Not carelessness. There was no line on the page for it.”
“So the counties filed nine thousand men,” said Veylan, “and left the animals.”

“They left everything that was not a man with a parish,” said Old Den. “That is the whole of what a column can do. And that is why there is a bone the size of a boat in the ice behind you, and no scrap of paper anywhere in the world about the animal it came off.”
He put his good hand on his knee, which was the closest he came to a gesture.
“Ten thousand of us went up that mountain,” he said. “I never once saw a bone in a book.”
The goat did not go near the bone.

That was noticed by everybody and mentioned by nobody. The goat had gone to the front on the climb, and it had stood at the lip of the ledge all day out of the wind. Through the whole afternoon of the digging and the arguing it did not come back to the drift, and it did not look at the bone.
On the sixth morning, when they went up the last hundred feet of the chimney, the goat went first, and it went up the crack in the rock at a pace no goat should have needed to use.
Above the ledge, before they moved off, Mira did her measuring.

She did it in the last of the day, with the lamp and the knotted cord. She drew the bone twice: once in section and once in plan, with the socket plotted as a circle and a length running back into the wall of ice. She labelled the drawing in her smallest hand.
She did not write the word bone. She wrote: **one joint. in situ. not entered.**
Then, in the margin, in the same hand, she wrote the only sentence on the page that was not a measurement: **kept, not filed. that is why it is still here.**
Veylan read it over her shoulder before she rolled the chart up, and he stood there in the cold for a moment and then said the only thing he ever said about the bone.
“There is no fee on it,” he said. “That is why it survived. Nobody ever took a fee off a thing that big, because nobody could get a page around it.”

Above them the Emberion stood over the top of the wall, fifteen joints and one piece missing out of the wing. The wind came down out of the cloud without stopping. The plate under Riss’s shirt stayed quiet. The company of eight rested one more night on the ledge, with something the size of a boat lying in the ice two feet behind them: unmeasured by any county, entered in no register, and whole.

chapters.label: Chapter 20
chapters.title: The Wall
paragraphs: After six days of ice and rope came the top of the chimney, and the shelf, and the wall.
They came out of the top of the chimney at midday on the sixth day and Kael Riven was the second man out, which was the highest he had ever been in his life.
The top of the crack opened onto a shelf of ice and stone about forty paces across, with the outer edge running away into white air and the inner edge running into a wall.
That was all there was. A shelf, a drop, and a wall.

The wall went up from the shelf with no ledge and no foothold, into cloud, and it was not rock. It was ice over rock: green-black in the middle, pale at the edges where the wind had carved it, with seams in it that ran at an angle, and the whole face of it was scoured smooth as a chapel door.
The company stood on the shelf and got their breath and looked at the wall, and nobody said anything for a while, because there was nothing to say that was not smaller than the thing.

Kael had spent thirty years looking at surfaces. He had looked at the inside of walls in eleven counties and he had never once been wrong about what he was looking at. He looked at the wall for a long time and understood, in the plain way he understood things, that the wall was not a wall.
It was the side of something.
The wind on the shelf was the worst they had had.

It came over the top and down the face of the wall, not gusting, not dropping, at a pressure that had no weather in it anywhere. There was no snow in it. There was no water in it. It was dry and it was constant and it came from above, and it had been coming from above for eleven days and had not once changed direction.
Sancora moved the company into the lee of a spur of rock at the inner end of the shelf and made them all sit and made them all drink.
Then she did something Kael had never seen her do, in four months in her company.
