She took her glove off and put her hand flat against the face of the wall.
She held it there for a moment, and then she took it away, and then she put it back on the seam below, and then she stepped back and looked at the wall the way she looked at a patient.
“It is warm,” she said.
Nobody answered.

“I do not mean it is warm in the way a rock is warm from the sun. I mean there is no sun on this face and it is warmer than the air by something I can feel through a glove, and it is warmer at the seams than it is at the middle of the slabs.” She pulled her glove back on. “There is heat on the other side of this ice. I am not going to say anything else about it because it is not my trade.”
“Corvath,” said Riss.
“I smelled nothing,” said Corvath. “I have smelled nothing for six days. There is nothing on this mountain to smell, and I told you I would tell you first, and there is nothing.”
Mira found the marks on the fourth hour.

She was walking the shelf the way she walked every piece of new ground, on the inside edge, with her hand on the rock, looking at the wall at an angle instead of straight on. That was a habit she had explained once on the coast road: a mapmaker who looks at a cliff face straight on is drawing a picture, and a mapmaker who walks it at an angle is drawing a map.
She stopped at the inner end of the shelf, twenty paces from where the company was sitting, and stood still for a moment, and then knelt down.
“There is writing on this.”
Kael was the first one up and the first one across the shelf, because that was his trade and because a trace-witness does not wait to be asked.
It was not writing.

It was a ruled form, cut into the face of the ice and into the rock underneath it, in a place where the ice was thin over the stone. The lines were cleaner than any hand he had ever seen, straight, at right angles, in a rectangle about the height of a man and the width of a man’s two arms.
Inside the rectangle there were four columns.
The columns ran from a line at the top to a line at the foot, and each column was cut as a channel: a shallow groove cut to be looked at rather than read.
The first three columns were full.

Kael could not read any of them and neither could anybody else in the company. The characters in the columns were not the county script and not any hand in the eleven counties. They were not letters at all in the way Kael understood letters. They were tally groups, and ticks, and small figures, and they ran down three columns from line to line.
The fourth column was empty.

It was not damaged. That was the thing he checked first, with his palm flat on the ice beside it. It had not been worn away and it had not been broken off and there was no drift over it. There was nothing in it because nothing had ever been put in it.
“Riss,” he said. “You are the one who reads forms.”
Riss came and stood in front of it and read the whole face for a long time without saying anything, in the way they read a page.
“It is a register,” said Riss.

That was the first thing they said about it, and afterwards Kael thought it was the right way round, because it was not a guess. It was a page and it had been made by somebody who had once looked at a register.
“Four columns. The first is a name, or the thing’s name in the place of a name. The second is where it came from or where it stood. The third is a count, or a date, or a number of years.”
“And the fourth,” said Mira.

“The fourth is the reason,” said Riss. “That is the column where a name goes from being a person to being an entry. Whenever a thing is put into a form in the counties, the fourth column is where the taking happens. And it has never once been used.”
“You can read it?”
“No,” said Riss. “I can read what it is for. I cannot read a character of it and neither can you, and neither could any clerk in any of the eleven counties. Which is the entire point of the thing.”
They stood in front of it, the eight of them, in the wind, at the top of a chimney at the end of the world, in front of a form with three columns full and one column empty.
“How old,” said Veylan.

“I do not know,” said Riss. “Older than the border stone. Older than the counties. Older than Tallage, because Tallage is the first thing that ever wrote a boundary down and this was cut into ice before the ice got this thick.” They put their hand on the ruled line at the top. “Older than writing the way we do it. Look at the frame. There is no ornament on it. There is no dedication, no seal, no mark of the county, nothing to say who made it or why.”
“That is not how a register looks,” said Nahl.

“That is exactly how a register looks,” said Riss. “That is what made me sure. Every register in the eleven counties is a form with four columns and no ornament, because a form with no ornament is a form nobody remembers making, and a thing nobody remembers making is a thing nobody has to answer for.”
Kael traced it.

He did it that evening and he did it the way he had been taught, on the ground, with the lamp set on a stone and his hand flat on the surface beside the form. He was not looking for the writing. He was looking for the edge.
And the edge was there.

It came up under his palm within a minute: the edge of a thing that had been kept. The form was cut into the ice and into the rock beneath. The cut was old. The ice had grown over the edge of the cut on both sides without filling it, which is what ice does over a very long time when a thing is left in place.
“It is the same kind of edge as the bone,” he said.
Nobody said anything, so he went on, because he had been waiting six weeks to be able to say something true.

“I have been looking for edges since Collow and I have found three. The slate with nothing on it has no edge. The border stone’s west face has no edge on the far side. The grave has no edge, because the man was never entered anywhere, so there is no line to trace him along.” He moved his palm across the ice. “The bone has an edge. This has an edge. They are the same edge and it is the second kind, the kind that belongs to a thing that was kept.”
“Kept by who?” said Mira.

“Kept,” said Kael, “by nobody. That is what the edge says. A thing that is kept by a person has wear on it. It has a hand-shape on it somewhere, or a strap, or a corner that is worn smooth. There is no hand-shape on this form. It has been left alone, up here, in the ice, for longer than any of us can count, and nobody has come and tidied it and nobody has come and filed it.”
He took his hand off the ice and closed it.

“I have spent my whole life finding the edges of things that people did. This is the edge of a thing nobody has done. There is nothing to find and nothing missing. That is the whole difference and it took me thirty years and a mountain to learn it.”
Then Riss said the thing that the company carried down off the mountain.
“Nobody writes this down.”
Mira had the chart out. She had it out before anybody had finished looking at the form, and the pen was in her hand, and Kael watched her stop with the nib an inch from the paper.
“Say that again,” said Mira.

“Nobody copies this. Not a line of it, not a measurement of it, not a sketch of the frame.” Riss was looking at the form and not at her. “You have drawn everything on this journey that could be drawn. That is your trade and it is a good trade and I am not telling you it is wrong. I am telling you that this is the one page in the world that has never been filed, and a copy of a thing is how a thing gets filed.”
Mira stood there with the pen in the air for a long moment.
“That is the widest column I have ever been asked to keep,” she said.

“It is the practice,” said Riss. “Orphiel refused to copy the log’s reasons, and you took it. You refused to copy the plank at the waystation and admitted you had tried. This is the same rule standing at the top of a mountain. A copy travels. A copy gets carried east into a room and put on a table and compared with something, and then a clerk writes a line and the thing is dealt with.”
“And a witness that nobody has copied is a witness,” said Nahl.
They wrapped the chart and put it in the tube.

Kael noticed that Nahl did not open the Leaf, and that Nahl had not opened it since they came out on the shelf, and that Nahl’s hand was flat on the front of the log under the coat where nobody could see it.
The company sat under the wall at the top of the chimney, out of the wind, and worked out what they had.
They did it the way they did everything, in plain language, with the practical people going first.
“There is something on the other side of that wall,” said Veylan. “It is warm and it is enormous and it has been coming down this mountain in the wind since before there were counties.”
“Say the rest,” said Sancora.

“The rest is that we cannot get over the wall, and there is no road around it, and the wind comes down off the top of it in the same direction every hour of every day.” Veylan put his hands in his coat. “So we are not going over. There is nothing up there for us to do. We have come a thousand miles to a shelf at the top of a chimney and the page we came for is a thing we cannot reach.”
“Then let us be sure of it,” said Mira, “before we say it.”
They spent an hour being sure of it, because a company that has walked a thousand miles is entitled to one hour of looking.

Mira walked the shelf end to end a third time and put the knotted cord against the face of the wall at three places. She read the same number off it every time: forty-one feet of ice at the lowest point, straight up, with no break in the seams that a hand could use. She drew the wall in section and wrote the height on the drawing and put the drawing away, and afterwards she said the only useful sentence she said all evening.
“The wall is not a cliff. It is the outside of a thing. If I had been asked to draw a cliff I would have drawn a cliff.”

Kael walked the shelf with his hand out of the glove and his palm flat on the ice wherever the seams were thin. He found the same edge six times and no route at all: no shelf above, no crack wide enough for a boot, no place where the ice sat over a ledge of rock. He stopped at the eastern end of the shelf and stood there a while and came back and said it plainly.
“There is nothing up there that a person can stand on. Not because it is impossible. Because it was never made for people.”
Even the goat was asked in the only way the company had ever been able to ask the goat anything, which was to walk to the eastern end of the shelf and stand there and look at the way up.

The goat went to the eastern end of the shelf. It stood there for a while in the wind. Then it turned round and came back and lay down against the inner face of the wall, which it had never done before and did not do again.
“Right,” said Veylan. “The goat says no.”
“Yes,” said Riss.
Nobody argued with it, and nobody offered a way over the ice, and that was the first honest hour the company had had in eleven days.
Then Corvath said the thing that nobody else had said, in the flat voice of a man who had spent his life reading rooms.
“So what did we come for?”
Riss thought about it for a long time. Then they stood up and walked to the form and stood in front of it and said the sentence that ended the climb.
“We came for a witness,” said Riss.

“The whole point of going west was that there was a room with a witness in it: a man with a standing and a book who could say what he had seen and be believed. Orphiel was that man and Orphiel is on a ridge four days east of here. We have come the rest of the way with a blank page and no clerk.”

“And then we get up here,” said Riss, “and there is a form cut into the ice older than the counties, with four columns and the fourth one empty, and it has been sitting on this shelf for longer than there has been anybody to file it.”

“It is not a monster. It is not a lair. It is not a hoard and it is not a prophecy. It is a *witness*, and it is the only one on this mountain, and it has been witness to precisely one thing: that a thing can be written down without a taking column.”
The company of eight stood on the shelf at the top of the chimney, in the wind, under a wall of ice they could not climb, in front of a page they had refused to copy.
And every one of them understood, at the same moment, what the journey had actually been.
They stayed one more night on the shelf, because Sancora would not move a company down four hundred feet of ice in the dark.
Kael took the first watch, and he took it standing up, at the lip of the shelf, where he could see down the chimney and out over the drop and up the wall all at once.

Below them the gold and grey roads ran side by side out of the high country and back east across everything, and neither of them shone even in the last of the light, and there was no one on either of them in any direction that a man could see.
Above him the Emberion came up over the top of the wall, fifteen joints, one piece missing out of the wing, so close at this altitude that the gaps between the joints were gaps and not points.
The goat stood beside him at the lip of the shelf, facing the wall, and did not lie down all night.
The plate under Riss’s shirt stayed quiet the whole night through. Kael’s hand burned steadily, the way it burned when rock was near, and he had stopped minding it about six days earlier.

Out in the dark on the far side of the ice, at a distance no man on that shelf could have measured, something enormous went on breathing. It breathed the wind that was not weather down the face of the wall, over the top of the chimney, and out across the eleven counties. It had been doing it since before there were columns. Nobody had ever written it down.

chapters.label: Chapter 21
chapters.title: The Name
paragraphs: After the refusal to copy the form, and the night on the shelf under the wall, and the last of the tallow, the company sat in the open and worked out where they were going.
It took them most of the morning and it was settled in a way that Nahl would think about for years.
The question was not whether they could go over. They had answered that on the first evening with a cord and a goat and a hand on the ice.
The question was what they had come for, and whether they had got it, and what a company of eight was supposed to do with an answer that weighed nothing and could not be carried.
Nahl put the log on the stone in front of them and tied the cord again while the others talked, because a bearer’s hands keep busy when his head has nothing useful in it.
Kael raised the question of the ice because he was the one who had to.
“There is a seam on the north end,” he said. “It runs up the wall at an angle. I traced it twice last night. It is the only place on this shelf where the ice is over rock and not over more ice.”
“Meaning,” said Mira.
“Meaning I could try it. Two hundred feet or so. If the rock holds under the seam, a man could get up there.”
“With a rope?”
“With a rope and somebody holding it.”
Mira had the chart open and did not need to look at it. She had spent the whole of the previous day measuring a wall that could not be climbed and she knew the numbers the way Sancora knew a pulse.

“The rock under that seam is rotten for eleven feet,” she said. “I put the cord against it. It drummed. If you put your weight on that seam you will pull a hundredweight of rock down onto your own head, and everybody below you, and there is no ledge to shelter under.”
“I could go up alone.”
“No,” said Mira.
“No,” said Sancora.
“No,” said Riss.
Kael looked at the three of them and then at his own hand, which was split across the palm and would not close properly, and he did the thing he had done at Collow, which was to agree.
“Then we do not go up,” he said.
“That is the refusal,” said Nahl.
Everybody looked at them.

“Orphiel’s trade was not to file the living,” said Nahl. “Mine is smaller. A bearer does not carry a thing that will not go where it is needed. We have a wall with no way over it, and a seam that will kill whoever tries it, and we are eight people with eleven days of food and one healer.”
“So we are refusing the mountain,” said Veylan.
“We are refusing to force a way where there is not one,” said Nahl. “That is the last refusal in the book and it is the plain one. A company that dies on a shelf leaves nothing to carry east.”
They measured it once more because Mira insisted, and the numbers came back the same, and that was the end of the ascent of the grey wall.

The keeper scene came after that, on the last of the afternoon, and there was nobody near them for twenty paces because the rest of the company had gone down to the lower part of the shelf to melt ice.
Riss had the Leaf out and the blank page out of the case and set the two of them side by side on the stone.
“That is the whole of what we have,” said Riss.
“That is the log, and the Leaf, and a page that nobody has ever put a mark on.”

“We came for a witness,” said Riss. “We found one. Orphiel said the words in a room in Carrow with his hand flat on a ledge and I have been carrying the sentence since the ridge like a stone in a boot. *I can see it. This is real.*”
“We found a form,” said Nahl. “We did not find the thing itself.”
Nahl said it because it was true and because a bearer says the thing that is true before the company gets used to the other thing.
Then Riss said the sentence that Nahl wrote down later in their head, in the private part of their head where a bearer keeps what he cannot put in a book.
“We found the thing that refused to be filed. That is the witness.”
Nahl sat with that for a while and turned it over the way you turn a stone to see what is under it.
“Say the rest,” they said.

“There is a form cut into that ice with four columns in it. The fourth column is the reason column. In the counties, the reason column is where the fee is entered, and the fee is where a person stops being a person and becomes an entry.”
“And on this form?”

“The fourth column has never been used. Not worn off. Not broken. Never used.” Riss put a hand on the ice, flat, where the form was. “Somebody came up this mountain at some point before there were counties, and cut a register into the rock, and the register has three columns full and one column empty, and the reason column is empty because the thing that was supposed to go in it has refused for two hundred years.”
“Why two hundred?”

“Because that is how long the counties have been filing,” said Riss. “Somebody filed something, and this thing has been saying no ever since, and the fourth column is what saying no looks like when it is cut into rock.”
Nahl looked at the empty column, which was a groove in ice with nothing in it, and understood the whole shape of the thing.

The company had come a thousand miles to find a witness who could say what he had seen and be believed. The witness had died on a ridge and had been buried under a wall with a notch and a tally of five on the stone. And the thing they had walked toward for four months was not a monster in a lair and not a hoard and not a prophecy.
It was the one thing on the mountain that had never been entered anywhere.
The sound came at the end of the second night.
Nahl had the middle watch, which ran from the second hour to the fourth, and they had it standing up, out of the wind, at the lip of the shelf with their back to the wall and the log inside the coat.

The night was the coldest of the whole journey. There was no moon above the cloud and there was no dust in the air, and the cold came down the face of the wall the way it had come down for two days, steady, from above.
At some point in the second hour the wind changed pitch, the way it had changed pitch on the fourth night of the chimney, and the ice stopped ticking.
Nahl stood still and listened.

Riss had told them what the plate did when it was loud. They had heard the description four times: a fifth with something wrong in the middle of it, a note split down its own length, a sound that had been stuck under a shirt for four months.
That was not the sound the plate made now.

It made a note. Just one. It was the note that had been missing from the middle of the fifth, and it came up through Riss’s coat and across twenty feet of ice, quiet enough that only the person listening for it would have caught it.
Nahl counted, because counting is the trade.
One. The note held for the length of four breaths. Then it stopped.
Then a sound came off the far side of the wall.

It was not a roar and it was not a voice and it was not made in a throat. It was a long, low, staying sound, the kind a wall makes when something leans on the other side of it, except that the sound had parts.
Nahl counted the parts. It was the only thing they knew how to do and they did it well.
There were eight of them.

The sound came over the ice in eight parts, evenly spaced, in a slow sequence, and each part was different from the one before it, the way words are different, and the whole of it held together into something with a shape.
It had the shape of a name.

Nahl did not understand one syllable of it. Nobody in the company would ever understand one syllable of it, and nobody in the eleven counties could have understood any part of it either, because it was not in any language that had ever been written down.
But it had the shape of a name, and it was said once, and it was said to somebody.
The goat heard it first.

Nahl turned their head at the sound of hooves on ice and saw the goat come up the shelf past the sleeping company, out of the lee of the spur where it had been lying, and walk to the inner end of the shelf where the form was cut into the wall.
It did not run. It walked the way it had walked up the chimney, in front of the whole company, all of them following an animal that had not been asked.
At the form it stopped, and stood facing the ice, and put its head against the wall.
It stood there for the length of the whole sound and did not move once, and when the sound stopped the goat stayed where it was, with its head against the rock, for another long while.
Then it turned round and lay down in front of the form, on the eastern side, which was the side facing home.
Nahl woke Riss with a hand on the shoulder and did not shout and did not shake, because a bearer does not startle a company in the dark.
“The plate,” said Nahl.
Riss was awake at once and had a hand inside the shirt before their eyes were open.
“It is not divided,” said Riss.
“No.”
“It is not clean either.”
“No,” said Nahl. “It is the note that was missing.”

Riss sat with the plate under their palm for a long time on the ice at the top of a chimney at the end of the world, and then said something in a voice that Nahl had never heard from them, which was not wonder and not fear and was closer to recognition.

“It has been waiting for somebody to come and not file it,” said Riss. “It refused for two hundred years. It was not refusing the counties. It was refusing the column. And we came up here with a blank page and no fee and a log with a fourth column we have never used, and now it has said the one thing it has.”
“What did it say?”
“A name,” said Riss. “Its own. In a language with nobody left alive who could write it down.”
They woke the company at first light, or at the hour that passed for it, and Nahl told them about the eight parts.
That was the second shock of the morning and it was harder than the first.
“The sound had eight parts,” said Nahl. “Evenly spaced. I counted them twice and I counted them the second time backwards, which is how you check a tally group. Eight.”
“Eight what?” said Veylan.

“Eight parts. That is all I can tell you. I do not know what a part is in a sound like that. It could be a syllable and it could be a year and it could be a thing that has no word in our language at all.”
Mira had the chart out and was already drawing nothing, which was her habit when she was thinking: she held the pen and left the page alone.
“How long between the parts?”
“Four breaths. Perhaps five. It was regular.”
“Then it counted,” said Mira. “A sound with regular intervals and a fixed number of parts is a count. That is what a count is. That is what a tally is.”
“That is what a tally is,” said Nahl.
Veylan said the thing that everybody was working around, in the plain way he said things about land and weather, which was the reason the company kept him.
“It counted us.”
Nobody answered him for a moment, because he was probably right and because being right about that was not comfortable.
Then Nahl did the arithmetic out loud, because they were the bearer and the arithmetic was theirs.

“There are eight of us on this shelf. There was a ninth and he is buried under a wall four days east of here with a notch and a tally of five on the stone above him.” Nahl looked at the goat, which was still lying in front of the form with its head toward home. “I do not know if the animal was counted. I do not know how a thing like that counts.”
“So it counted the company,” said Sancora.
“It counted the company,” said Nahl. “And then it stopped, and there is no page anywhere with the number on it, and it did not ask anybody for a fee.”

Later that morning Sancora came and sat down beside Nahl on the stone at the lip of the shelf and put the two satchels down in front of her, which was how she announced that she had something to say that was not healing.
“Ask me the question,” said Sancora.
“Whether the count included the goat.”
“Whether the count included the goat,” said Sancora. “It is the only question anybody in this company has asked twice.”
“I do not know how a thing like that counts,” said Nahl. “It had eight parts. There are eight of us. That is all I can swear to and I will swear to it in any room.”
“Then the number is eight,” said Sancora. “And the animal is an animal and it is not in my column, and I have thought about it for an hour and I am telling you the truth about where I put it.”
“Which is where?”

“Nowhere,” said Sancora. “I have never once in nineteen years written a number down that I could not correct. I am not going to start with the only count that has ever been made of us from the other side of a wall.”
She sat with it for a while and then said the second thing, which was the real reason she had sat down.

“I have been going over the descent in my head, because that is what I do on a rest day,” she said. “Eleven hundred feet in four pitches, and a man with a chest that crackles on the left, and two toes that went white once. I have done the arithmetic four times and it comes out the same every time. We get down.”
“You are certain.”

“I am as certain as I have ever been about anything,” said Sancora, “which means I have counted the things that can kill us and I have not counted the things that cannot. That is the whole of medicine.” She picked up the satchels. “I would like it written down somewhere that there were eight of us and we all came down. I do not care whether the writing is a county page or the back of a mill ledger.”
Nahl thought about Orphiel then, on the grass west of every boundary in the world, with the log in both hands.
*This one goes with the bearer.*
*You will not sign it. You will carry it. That is the difference.*

A bearer carries a thing to the person it belongs to. Nahl had said that out loud on the shelf as though it were a rule in a book, and it was not a rule in a book. It was the last thing a dead man had said to them, on a road, with four days of county behind him and the wind going west.

So there was a count of eight with nobody to give it to, and a name in a language nobody could write, and neither of them belonged to a county or a parish or a person. They belonged to whoever would take them, and the company was going to find out who that was.
That was the thing the company understood on the shelf, in the wind, on the third day at the top of the chimney.
It is the sentence Nahl carried down the mountain and would still be carrying years later, in a room, over a page.

The thing on the other side of the wall had refused for two hundred years. It had refused every clerk and every commissioner and every column that had ever been cut into the rock to hold it, and it had refused by remaining exactly where it was and not being written down.
And it had consented once. One time, to one company, on one morning, and the consent was not to be filed.
It was to be counted.

Counting is what you do with a thing you are going to remember. Filing is what you do with a thing you are going to stop remembering. Nahl had known the difference in their hands for twenty years, the way a smith knows the difference between iron and steel, and had never once had it put in front of them as the whole of a mountain.
“You are a bearer,” said Riss.
“I am a bearer,” said Nahl.
“What does a bearer do with a thing like this?”
Nahl looked at the log under their coat and at the blank page in Riss’s case and at the goat lying with its head toward home.

“A bearer carries a thing to the person it belongs to,” said Nahl. “There is nobody alive who owns this. So the bearer carries it to a room, and says what he saw, and lets the room decide what it is worth.”
“And if the room files it?”

“Then the room files it,” said Nahl. “But it will have been counted first, out loud, by somebody standing up. That is the difference between a count and an entry, and it is a difference that can never be undone.”
They went down on the third morning.
Before they started, Nahl did the only formal thing a bearer can do without a form, which was to stand the company in a line on the shelf and count them.
Riss. Kael. Mira. Veylan. Sancora. Corvath. Old Den. Themselves.

Eight. Nahl counted them twice, and counted them backwards the second time, and did not write it down anywhere, because a count that is written becomes an entry and an entry is how a thing stops being remembered.

Above them the Emberion stood over the top of the wall, fifteen joints and one piece missing out of the wing. The wind came down the face of the ice without stopping. Kael’s hand burned steadily, the way it burned when there was rock on the other side of nothing, and he had long since stopped minding it.

Below the shelf, out across everything, the gold road and the grey road ran side by side into the high country and back east toward the counties, and neither of them shone, and there was nobody on either of them in any direction that a man could see.

Under Riss’s shirt the plate hummed the third note: not the divided fifth, not the clean one, but the note that had been missing from the middle of it, quiet and even, the way a person hums when they have finally been asked a question they can answer.
The goat went down behind the company for the first time in a thousand miles.

chapters.label: Chapter 22
chapters.title: The Road Back
paragraphs: After the counting on the shelf, and the goat lying with its head toward home, and the third note under Riss’s shirt, the company went down.

Nobody had said a word about it out loud. They got up on the third morning, packed the bier, ate what there was, and started down the chimney, and that was the whole of the decision as far as any of them made it.
Going down turned out to be worse than going up.

That was the thing nobody had told them and none of them had thought about. A climb is a set of problems you solve in order. A descent is the same problems with the rope above you and your hands going numb on frozen knots, and the company learned in one day what the chimney really was.
Sancora made three new rules on the first morning down and said them standing up, in the wind, with her satchels at her feet.

“The man below goes first, and he goes slowly, and he calls every hold before he takes it. If the man below falls, the man above is on a doubled rope against the wall, and the man above does not let go to catch him.”
“The rope is never off two hands. Not to open a coat. Not to take a drink.”
“And nobody is allowed to be brave. Bravery going down is a man deciding he has one more step in him when he has half a step, and half a step down a chimney is a body at the bottom of it.”
“It is eleven hundred feet to the shelf, in four pitches,” said Mira.
“Then it is eleven hundred feet of nobody being brave,” said Sancora.

It took them two days. Kael led every pitch, bare-handed, tapping the ice. Veylan’s chest was better in the descent than it had been in the climb and worse in every other way, and Sancora put him second in the order so that she could watch him from above.
Eleven hundred feet in two days, and on the second evening they came back onto the ledge where they had found the bone.
They stopped on the ledge because it was the only flat ground in four hundred feet and because the company wanted to look at the bone one more time.
They looked at it for a while in the last of the light, all eight of them, in a rough line, the way people look at a grave they have not decided what to do about.
Then Veylan did the thing he had been carrying down the mountain from the moment he heard what the company was going to do. He did it out loud. That was the whole of his usefulness to the party.
“I want a piece of it,” he said.
Mira looked at him.

“Not for the counties,” said Veylan. “For me. I dug it out. It is the only thing in my life that ever turned out to be more than it looked. I want a piece of it the size of my thumb to put in the tin with the soil.”
“Say the rest,” said Riss.

“The rest is that a man can talk himself into almost anything if he starts with the size of his thumb.” Veylan put his hand flat on the rim of the socket, the way he had on the night he found it. “If I take a thumb, I have cut it. If I cut it, I have done the thing that was done to it before. There is a notch in it somewhere in the counties with my name on it, and the whole reason it survived is that nobody ever did that.”
“Then we leave it,” said Mira.
“Then we leave it,” said Veylan.
They left it in the ice where it had been for longer than there had been anybody to file it, and Mira did not draw it again.
That was the second half of the refusal and it was Mira’s own.

“We have the numbers,” she said, when Veylan asked her whether she wanted a second sheet while the light was on the socket. “Four leaves of it. A second drawing of a thing is a copy of a drawing, and a copy is how a thing starts to travel into rooms it was never in.”
“You said that about the form.”

“I said it about the form,” said Mira. “It is my trade and it is the same rule in both places. I draw a thing once. I write the measurements down. I do not make a second picture of a thing anybody could take.”
The crate was at the foot of the chimney, in the lee of a boulder, under a stone.
They came down to it on the third morning and Veylan went to it first, before anybody could say anything, and lifted the stone off the lid.
The forty-one seedlings were dead.

They had not died of neglect. They had been stacked properly, out of the wind, in the lee of the flattest boulder on the shelf, with a stone on the lid to keep the animals off. The frost had gone into them anyway, the way the frost goes into everything above the last grass. There was a grey film on the top of the soil in every one of the little cloth pots. The stems were soft and black at the base.
Veylan looked at them for a while, and then put the stone back on the lid, and stood up.
“That was the west, in a crate,” he said. “Forty-one of them. Two of them I brought through an oven-house in February on a banked fire.”
Nobody said anything, because there was nothing to say that was not smaller than the fact.
“Put them out of your head,” said Sancora.

“I will put them out of my head at the bottom of the mountain,” said Veylan. “Not before.” He took the tin out of his coat and checked that the sacking was dry round the handful of west soil, which it was. “The tin is what I came for. The crate was a plan.”
They left the crate where it stood, in the lee of the boulder, on the flattest ground on the shelf, with a stone on the lid.
The lower chimney was easier in one way and much worse in another.

Easier because the ice at the bottom was older and thicker and held an axe. Worse because the wind was still coming down it from above. Now they were walking into it instead of pushing away from it. There was no way to get out of it. By the second day the cold had settled in everybody’s hands and stayed there.
They came out onto the shelf at the foot of the grey wall at midday on the fifth day with eight people on their feet and two of them in a state that Sancora did not like.
Riss sat down against the wall of the chimney and took the log out of the case and looked at it, which they had not done since the escape.
Nahl sat down beside them and did not ask for it back. That was the arrangement between the two keepers and it had been the arrangement since the fire.

Nahl had counted the log’s pages at the waystation and at the border stone and on the shelf under the wall, and the count was the same every time. There were four columns in the log, and the fourth column was the reason column, and it had never been used.
“How many names in it?” said Riss.
“Nine thousand and four,” said Nahl. “And not one of them has a reason in the fourth column, because Orphiel would not write one. He said a reason is a fee with better manners.”

Riss handed the log back and Nahl tied it into the coat with the bearer’s knot. Neither of them said the thing both of them were thinking. The two of them were carrying four books between them. The log. The Leaf. The blank page. And a name that had been said once on a shelf at the top of a chimney in a language nobody alive could write down.
Four things, and none of them in any column anywhere in the eleven counties.
The healer and the keeper had their conversation on the last night at the foot of the wall.

It happened because Riss went to check on Veylan and found Sancora sitting up with him instead, her ear against his back and the lamp held low. Riss waited until the breathing evened out. Then they sat down on the other side of the fire with a handful of the bad food and no appetite for it.
“You kept us alive up there,” said Riss.
“I kept the number,” said Sancora. “Eight. That was the whole of my practice.”
“You did more than that.”
“No,” said Sancora. “That was the whole of it. The rest was the company.”

She said it without any modesty in it at all, which was the part Riss never got used to. Sancora did not do modest. She said what she had done the way she said what a wound was doing: flat, and countable, and no more or less than the fact.

“Nineteen years and I have never once had to decide who to leave,” said Sancora. “I said on the first morning that if it came to it I would say the weakest leg out loud. I meant it and it did not come to it and that is not my doing. That is a chest that held and two toes that came back and a man with a burned hand who found the thin ice for us.”
“So what was your practice?”

“Nine days of watching,” said Sancora. “Hands and feet. Every hand and every foot, twice a day, out loud, in front of everybody, so that nobody had to wonder whether they were the one being looked at last. That is it. That is the whole of healing on a mountain. There is no art in it at all and there is nothing else that works.”
Riss sat with that for a while.

“I keep a book,” said Riss. “That is the whole of my practice. I write down what happened and I sign it and I date it, and the signing is the part that matters, because a thing with a date on it can be argued with and a thing without one cannot.”
“I know,” said Sancora. “It is why I would not let Nahl write my numbers in it.”
“And now we are carrying a name that nobody can write, and a page that nobody has signed, and both of them are supposed to go into a room and do something.”
Sancora looked at the fire.

“Then get it to the room,” she said. “I do not care what the room is. I have kept eight alive to the bottom of a mountain and I would like to know what they were kept alive for, and I would like it written down somewhere before I am too old to read it.”
They decided where they were going on the last night before the grass.
They did it the way the company did everything, which was with the practical people going first and the keepers last.
Veylan put the question. “East to the counties, or south to the passes and home?”

“There is no home,” said Riss. “That is not self-pity. The counties have our names on a page at Carrow that says we went west without permission, and every one of us is either a farmer with a seized holding or a clerk with a file that mentions them.”
“Then east to the counties to be arrested is what you are proposing.”
“No,” said Riss. “East to the counties to be witnessed.”
Riss stood up and said the whole of it on their feet, because that was the only way a keeper could say a thing like that and be believed.

“Orphiel told me what the counties need before it will accept anything. A room. A standing. A person who can say what he saw and be believed. That was the whole reason we went west in the first place: to find the one witness in the eleven counties whose word could not be dismissed as a copy.”
“And Orphiel died on a ridge four days east of the stone,” said Mira.

“And there is a room in the counties that is not the Assessor’s office and not the vault and not the counting house,” said Riss. “It is where a page gets entered without a reason column. It exists. Ivet Sallow works next to it at Ashenford and she has been keeping four leaves of her own at the back of a mill ledger for nineteen years because she worked out the same thing we did and had nobody to say it to.”
“You want to walk into a mill and hand a clerk a page,” said Old Den.
“I want to walk into a room with a page and a log and a name, and stand up, and say what we saw,” said Riss. “Not to the counties as a claim. To a clerk as a count.”
Nahl had the log in their lap and did not open it.
“That is a bearer’s work,” said Nahl. “Carrying a thing to the person it belongs to. It has never been done in the counties with a blank page before. I have no idea what happens.”

“Neither do I,” said Riss. “But there is a ridge on the way with a notch and a tally of five on the stone, and the company is going to stop at it, because a witness who is left behind on the road is a witness nobody will believe when we get there.”
The company sat with that for a while, and then Old Den, who had been the oldest man in every room he had been in for nineteen years, said the only thing that needed saying.
“Then we go east,” said Old Den. “I have walked west for four months and I would like to walk in the other direction for a while.”
On the seventh day they came to the old waystation.

It was the same stone shelter with the same hearth and the same plank over the doorway that had been there on the way up, four months earlier, when the company had been nine people and the plate had been loud and the counties had still been close behind them.

The plank had the marks on it. That was all the shelter had ever had to offer: a plank to sleep on and a wall that kept the weather out, and men had been cutting their tallies into the edge of it for a hundred years.
Nahl counted them, because that was the trade.

A notch, and a group of five strokes, and then another group of five, and then a bad winter and three strokes that had been cut twice. Nahl went down the whole edge of the plank twice, forwards and backwards, which is how a bearer checks a tally group.
“Well?” said Riss.

“The same mark,” said Nahl. “Notch, and five strokes to the group. It is the same mark that is on the stone above Orphiel, and the same mark that is in the fourth column of a page in a magistrate’s hand, four days east of here.”
“Somebody cut that on his grave,” said Mira.

“Somebody cut it on the grave,” said Nahl. “And somebody cut it on this plank a hundred years ago, and a magistrate’s clerk copied it onto a county sheet last month, and none of the three of them has ever met. That is what a tally is. It travels without anybody carrying it.”
They stayed the night, and in the morning a carrier came up the road from the west with an empty cart and one horse.

He was an old man with no coat worth the name and he stopped at the shelter for water and did not ask the company anything. He had no letters. He said so himself, without being asked, in the flat voice of a man who had said it four hundred times.
“Nothing to bring east and nothing to take east,” he said. “There is nobody out west to write to.”
Then he asked, as a courtesy and not as a trade, whether anybody in the company wanted anything carried.
Nahl was the one who answered, and Nahl took their time about it.
“No,” they said at last. “There is one thing and it does not go in a satchel. We will carry it ourselves.”

The carrier looked at the log under Nahl’s coat and at the tube under Mira’s arm and at the eight of them sitting in a ruined shelter above the last grass, and nodded, the way a man nods at a thing he has decided not to think about, and went on east with his empty cart.
The grass started on the ninth day of the descent.

It was not a boundary and there was no ceremony about it and nobody in the company was watching for it. They came out of a long trough between two ridges early in the morning. There was turf under the boots, wet and short, with the colour back in it. Mira stopped and put her hand on it and stood there for a while.
That was the last grass, the same grass they had passed on the way up, four months and a thousand miles the other side of the world.

Above them the Emberion was where it always was in the last hour before the light. Fifteen joints, and the piece missing out of the wing, so far up that it looked less like a picture and more like a page with a hole in it.

The wind followed them down. It came off the peaks at their backs all day. It had the same steady pressure it had at the top of the chimney. Corvath said he smelled nothing, and said it twice, which settled it. He had promised to report anything before anybody had to ask.
Kael’s hand burned steadily the whole way down and he had stopped mentioning it, and Riss noticed that he had stopped keeping the glove on the left hand at all.
And the goat walked behind.

That was the thing the company noticed and did not talk about. For a thousand miles the goat had gone in front: over the border stone first, up the chimney first, at the front of the column on the climb and never once looking back. Now it walked at the back of the line, ten paces behind the last person, and twice a day it stopped and turned round and looked back up at the peaks, and then it came on again.
It did not stop looking back until the fourth day, when the peaks were gone behind the weather.

The plate under Riss’s shirt hummed the third note the whole way down. Not the divided fifth and not the clean one. It was the note that had been missing from the middle of it, quiet and even, all day, like something being counted.

Below them the gold road and the grey road ran side by side out of the high country. Neither of them shone. They ran east toward the counties, toward a ridge with a notch on the stone. Past the ridge there was a room with a clerk in it, and a page, and a count nobody had written down.

chapters.label: Interlude D
chapters.title: The Counting House
paragraphs: After the descent from the chimney, and the dead seedlings in the crate, and the goat turning at the back of the line to look up at the peaks, the company walked east into the counties. None of them had ever heard of Maro Holl.
This is what was happening at the counting house.
Maro Holl had been a clerk for thirty years and he had never once questioned the work.

That is the whole of him, and it is not a small thing. He was forty-eight years old, he had a wife called Lira and two boys, and he had gone into the counting house at nineteen as a copying boy with cold hands. He had learned column work from a man named Orrin who had also never questioned the work, and he had learned it well.

He could add a column of nine hundred entries in his head and get it right. He could tell a page written by a tired hand from a page written by a frightened one. He knew the difference between a clerk who has been told to lie and a clerk who has been told to be tidy.
He went home at the sixth hour. He ate with his family. He slept well.

Nobody in the eleven counties had ever had a reason to think about him. If the counties had been asked to name a man who was the system, they would have named an Assessor, or a magistrate, or one of the Twelve. Every one of those answers would have been wrong. The system was Maro Holl.
The system was thirty years of a man doing the arithmetic properly and going home.
The work at the counting house was fees.

Every fee in the county had a column: a column for what was taken, a column for who it was taken from, a column for the ground it was taken off, and a column for why. Four columns, ruled by the printer, forty lines to a page.

Maro Holl’s desk was at the long table on the east side, under the window, and his job was the fourth column: the reasons. When a fee came up the line from the villages with the ground column filled and the reason column empty, it came to him. He wrote the reason in the county’s own words. Then the page was finished, and the file went onto the shelf, and the shelf went into the wall.
Thirty years. Somewhere around four hundred thousand pages.

He was good at the reasons. That was his small pride and it was the only pride he had. There is a way of writing a reason that makes a thing hard and a way that makes it soft, and he had learned to write reasons that were exactly as hard as the law.
He had two rules in thirty years, and he had never broken either one.

The first was: never write a reason that the column could not support. If the ground was not surveyed, the reason was not a fee. He had bounced four hundred pages back up the line on that rule, and been shouted at about nine of them.
The second was: never leave the reason column empty. An empty column is not a decision. An empty column is a mistake, and mistakes are how the file gets cleaned.
The page came in with the Ash bundle on the fourth day of the eleventh month, and it should not have been in the bundle at all.

The bundle was ordinary. It was a seizure inventory from the magistracy at Ash: what had been taken off a party on the western approach, and what had been left, and what had been returned to the parties. Maro Holl had done four hundred of them.

A seizure inventory is the easiest page in the counting house. Nothing comes off a party without being written down and nothing is written down without a value, and a value is a fee one way or another. The Ash bundle was eleven sheets and a cover note, and it took him an afternoon.
The twelfth sheet was the one that did not belong.

It was county stock, pale grey, ruled with the four columns, and it was loose, and it had been folded twice and unfolded badly. On the front of it somebody at the Ash magistracy had gone through a party on the western approach, item by item, in the way the law required.
Three horses, returned to the parish of Ash.
One cart, sold at the county rate, fee entered.
Twelve ledger books, county stock, seized.
Forty copy sheets, seized.
One tin box, contents: soil, returned to the party.
At the bottom of the page, in the row where a party of people would be named and valued, there was a line in a magistrate’s hand. Maro Holl read it four times.
**Party of no account. No names given. Nothing taken. No fee.**
In the fourth column, where the reason was supposed to be written, in the space where Maro Holl wrote four hundred thousand reasons in thirty years, somebody at the magistracy had not written a word.
They had drawn a mark.
A notch, and beside it a group of five small vertical strokes, the kind a farmer makes on a door, and then nothing else on the whole page.
He sat with it for a long time.

That was the first unusual thing, and he noticed himself doing it, which was the second. A page took him a minute. This one he read until the light moved off the desk and the boy came round to light the lamps.
There was no way to file it. He went through the ways, one at a time, the way you go through a calculation.

He could file it as a seizure. But nothing had been seized from the party itself, and the horses had gone back to the parish, and the ledgers and the sheets were county stock coming home. There was no value to enter.
He could file it as an unclaimed page. But an unclaimed page has a query box at the foot, and to run a query he would have to write what the query was, and the query would have to be about something.

He could file it as an amendment to the Ash inventory. But an amendment has to state what was wrong with the original, and nothing was wrong with the original. The original was correct in every column.

And the fourth column of this page had a farmer’s mark in it. It is not a word in the county script. He could not copy it into a file without writing under it what it meant, and he did not know what it meant.
He sat with that for another while and understood the shape of the problem, and the shape of it was this.

Every page in the counties is filed by its fourth column. The fourth column is the reason. A page with a mark in the reason column is not a page with a bad reason. It is a page that says, in the space where the counties keep their reasons, that there is no reason here. There is no file in the building where a page like that can be put. There is no file in any building in the eleven counties.
Maro Holl did the thing that a man does when he has thirty years of doing it properly behind him.
He took the page up the corridor to the senior clerk and asked for a ruling.

The senior clerk was a man called Barden who was fifty-five and had been twenty years at the desk and had never in his life been asked a question like it. He read the sheet twice, and turned it over to see whether there was anything on the back, which there was not. Then he did what any man in the counties does when a page does not fit.
“You file it under the party,” said Barden. “Party of no account. There is a box for that, it goes at the back of the register with the other unattached pages, and you put the date on it.”
“And the fourth column?”
“Leave it as it came. You are not the author of the mark. You are the clerk.”
“I am the clerk,” said Maro Holl. “The clerk writes the fourth column.”
“Then write *no fee*,” said Barden.

“No fee” is a reason. It is a perfectly good reason. Maro Holl had written it eleven thousand times in thirty years, and it always meant one of two things: the ground was not surveyed, or the fee had been waived by the county.
He went back to his desk and sat down with the page and the pen.

He did not write it. He sat there with the nib an inch above the paper until the bell went for the end of the day. Then he did something he had never done in thirty years. He folded a county page twice and put it in his coat pocket and took it home.
He told his wife about it, which was also something he had never done.

Not the details. He did not show her the page, and he did not say the word magistrate. He said that a page had come up from the west that did not fit any column, and that the senior clerk had told him to write *no fee*, and that he had not written it.
Lira Holl had been married to him for twenty-two years and had been watching him do arithmetic at the kitchen table for all of it, and she knew her husband the way a healer knows a pulse.
“Then do not write it,” she said.
“I have to file it. It is a county page.”
“Then file it without writing it.”

“That is not possible,” said Maro Holl. “There is no version of the page that does not have the fourth column in it. The column is on the paper. It is ruled by the printer. You cannot file a page with a column in it that you did not fill in.”
Lira stirred the pot and did not look at him.
“Thirty years,” she said. “You have told me about four hundred thousand pages and every one of them had an answer in it. What is different about this one?”
Maro Holl had to think about that, and he thought about it honestly, because that was the only way he knew how to think.

It was not the missing name. Parties went west without names every year. It was not the party itself, with or without an animal. It was not even the mark in the fourth column, though the mark was what everybody else in the building would have pointed at.
It was the row above it.
One tin box, contents: soil, returned to the party.

Somebody had gone through that party item by item with the law in his hand, the way Maro Holl would have done it. He had found one box of soil. He had written *returned to the party* and had not taken a fee.

Nobody returns soil. Soil has no value. A tin box of soil from beyond the western boundary of the counties is worth nothing at all in any column. The law says everything that comes east is valued. This was valued and returned and not entered.
A county man had stood on the road with a book and had taken nothing off a party that had no names.
And then in the reason column, in the space where the counties keep the arithmetic of everything they have ever taken, the same county man had drawn a notch and five strokes and gone on.
He did not sleep.
He lay in the dark and did what he had done every night of his adult life when there was an arithmetic in front of him, which was to do it properly and see what came out.

The county takes a fee. The fee is a share of what a person makes off the ground. The share is the whole of the arrangement and it is a good one. He had believed all his life that it was the fairest thing any country had ever built. Everybody pays, nobody is spared, and the ones who write it down are the ones who take nothing.
That was the thing he had never once questioned, and it was the thing that turned over in his hands at two in the morning.
The clerks take nothing. The clerks are the ones who write it down.

Nobody files a page for the money. Maro Holl’s salary came out of a different book entirely. It was a county salary, agreed, annual. It had not changed in eleven years and did not depend on a single one of the four hundred thousand pages.
So why did he write the fourth column so well?
Because a page with a mark in the fourth column cannot be filed, and a page that cannot be filed does not exist, and a thing that does not exist has never happened.
He got up at the fourth hour and lit the lamp and took the page out of the coat and read it again, for the fifth time, with his own household book open beside it on the table.
His household book had four columns too, because he had ruled it that way himself at twenty-three and had never seen a reason to change it. What came in, what went out, what was left, and why.
The fourth column of the current page was empty. He paid the county at the end of the month and he had not written the reason yet.
He looked at that for a long time.
Then he took the pen out of the case and did not write in it, and closed the book. He sat in the kitchen with the county page in both hands until the sky came up behind the mill.
At the sixth hour he went to work.

He filed eleven sheets of the Ash bundle in the ordinary way. He put the twelfth sheet back in his coat pocket. He left the day’s query register blank for the first time in thirty years, and went home at the sixth hour, and slept badly. He had no idea that a company of eight was walking east toward him with a log, a Leaf, a blank page, and a name that had been said once on a shelf at the top of a chimney in a language nobody alive could write down.
In the morning the page was still in his coat.

He had not filed it. He had not written in the fourth column. He had not run a query and he had not written a reason. Somewhere in the building behind him four hundred thousand pages sat on their shelves in the wall with the arithmetic of the whole country in them. Every one of them was the same as it had been the day before. One loose sheet of county stock, with a farmer’s mark in the reason column, was out of the wall and out of the file. It was in a man’s pocket, walking around the county on a pair of legs.

chapters.label: Chapter 23
chapters.title: The Ridge
paragraphs: After the last grass, and the waystation with the plank in the doorway, and the carrier with the empty cart, the company walked east for eleven days.
They were going to the ridge.
They did not need the chart to find it. Mira had walked the route on the way out. She had written it down with the cord and the compass, and she was right about it to within an hour of walking.

It was a low ridge. It was not a peak. On the western side it fell away into the long trough the company had come up out of the grass by. On the eastern side it dropped into the country the counties had surveyed and priced and named.
At the top of it there was a low wall. In the lee of the wall, in ground two feet thick over rotten rock, the company had buried a clerk.
The cairn was there.

Nothing had touched it in four months. That was the first thing to notice and it was the only thing on the ridge worth noticing. No snow had buried it. No animals had dug at it. No weather had moved a stone off it.
The stones were heaped the way they had been heaped. The top stone was where it had been set. On the top stone there was a notch and a tally of five.
They stopped a hundred paces short and put the loads down.
That was Sancora’s doing. She did it without being asked, because a company that has walked eleven days into an old grief needs a minute before it walks into the rest of it.
They stood in the wind and looked at the ridge. Nahl did the thing a bearer does at a stopping place. They checked the company and counted them.
Eight. Riss, Kael, Mira, Veylan, Sancora, Corvath, Old Den, themselves.
The goat was already at the cairn.

Nobody had seen it go. It had been at the back of the line for eleven days. It walked ten paces behind the last person and stopped twice a day to look back at the peaks. Now it was standing at the foot of the cairn.
It did not come when Veylan called it. It did not eat the grass at the foot of the cairn. That was the thing that made Corvath speak, and Corvath had not spoken since the last grass.
“Goats eat everything,” said Corvath. “That animal has been eating this ridge for four days. It is standing on the only patch of grass on the whole top of it. It is not eating.”
Old Den sat down on a stone at the hundred-pace mark while the others looked at the ridge.
He had walked eleven days with a bound hand and had not said a word about what the ridge was going to be like. The company had let him have that.
“Twenty-two years,” said Old Den.
“Since the mountain,” said Sancora.

“Since the mountain. There were four hundred funerals in my parish and I went to every one of them. I did not go back up that ground once.” He looked at the cairn. “I have never gone back to a grave. Not one. Fifty-nine years old and I have been walking away from that mountain since I was nineteen.”
“And now?”

“Now there is a clerk under five stones up there with a notch on the top of it,” said Old Den. “I am going to walk up and stand at it and tell him what happened. It turns out that is the whole difference. I could not go back to a grave because there was nobody at it who owed me a report.”
They went up in the afternoon.
Halfway up the western slope Mira stopped and put her hand on a peg.
It was a surveyor’s peg. A foot of dressed ash, driven into the ground to within two inches of its head, and there was a number cut into the top of it in the county script.
“Eighty-four,” said Mira. “That is the peg number. Somewhere in a county office there is a paper with a line on it for this peg, and a man who wrote the line down has never stood here.”
She did not pull it up. She did not move it.
She walked on and left the peg in the ground where the counties had put it, twenty paces below a grave they had never found.

They stood in a line at the cairn. The wind came across the ridge off the western trough. It was the same steady pressure it had been at the top of the chimney, and on the descent, and every hour since. It had not let up once in nineteen days.

The plate hummed the third note under Riss’s shirt. Nahl heard the shape of it in the way Riss stood. It was the note that had been missing from the middle of the divided fifth. It was quiet. It was even. It was present.
Nobody had brought anything to say. That was deliberate. It had been decided on the second day of the walk without anybody deciding it.

Riss put the case down on the flat stone at the foot of the cairn. The Leaf was inside it. Nahl put the log down beside it. Mira put her hand flat on the log’s cloth cover, the way she touched anything she had drawn.
Then the company made the report.
The report was Nahl’s. Nahl had been writing it in their head for eleven days.

A bearer reports. That is the whole of the office. A bearer does not praise. He does not console. He does not improve a thing on its way into a room. He says what was carried, where it came from, and what is left of it.

Nahl stood at the foot of the cairn and reported to a dead clerk on a ridge in the middle of nowhere. The company of eight stood behind them. The goat stood at the other end of the grave with its head down.

“Orphiel of Sallow. Clerk. Keeper of the deletion log.” Nahl said the name once, clearly, and without ornament. “The company that walked west with you has come back east. This is the report of what we carried and what it came to.”
Then Nahl gave each of them their line. A report goes in order of the road.

“Riss. The log, carried to the top of the grey wall and back. Four columns. Nine thousand and four entries. The fourth column is empty from the first page to the last. It will stay empty. A reason is a fee with better manners. That is your sentence, and it is the whole of the log.”

“Kael. Nothing traced. The slate is still in the pack. There is nothing on it and he has not turned it over in nineteen days. There is no edge on the grave. He looked for one. He did not expect one. He is telling you anyway.”

“Mira. One joint of a thing the size of a boat, in ice, above the last grass. Measured, in section and in plan, four leaves, and not entered anywhere. One form cut into the ice, older than the counties. Three columns full and one never used. Read for what it is, and not copied. Nothing drawn here is a claim.”

“Veylan. Forty-one seedlings, dead in a crate at the foot of the chimney. One tin box of west soil, carried up a mountain and back down. It is not staying on your grave, which is the part he wants you to hear. It is going home to the farm. The farm is going to have to take it back.”

“Sancora. Eight persons up four hundred feet of ice and eight persons down eleven hundred feet of the same ice. Two toes that went white and came back. One chest that crackled and held. One hand, cut, bound, carried. She kept the number the whole way, in her head, and she has not written it down.”

“Corvath. Nothing smelled. Nothing on the mountain. Nothing in the chimney. Nothing on this ridge. He promised at Collow that he would say so before anybody had to ask. He has said so eleven times. He is saying it to you now.”

“Old Den. Ten thousand men went up a mountain once and two thousand came down. Nine thousand got a line in a book and a stone in a churchyard at their own parish. The rest of the bones stayed where they lay, because the counties only have a column for a body. He left the war on the mountain. He walked west at sixty-two. He is still walking.”

“Myself. There is a sound off the far side of the grey wall. It has the shape of a name. It came in eight even parts and it was said once, in a language nobody alive can write. I counted it twice and once backwards. I am not going to write it down. Neither is anybody else in this company.”
Nahl stopped there. That was the end of the report of the road.
Then the company said the ninth line. It was not a report of the road. Every one of the eight had agreed to it on the second day of the walk without any of them having to argue.

It was Orphiel’s own line. It was said out loud at the foot of his grave by the bearer, because a witness’s words belong to the witness. The company had carried that sentence four hundred miles. It had no right to keep it.
“I can see it,” said Nahl. “This is real.”
Then the two keepers said the thing the company had walked eleven days to hear them say.
It came out in the order Riss put it in, which was the order of the road.
“We found what we came for,” said Riss.
“We found a form,” said Nahl. “We found a name. We found a count.”
“We found a witness,” said Riss. “He is under this stone.”
The wind kept going. Nahl looked at the top stone with the notch and the tally of five on it, and did not write anything, and did not move toward the pack, and did not ask anybody for a page.
“Say the count,” said Riss.
Nahl said it. Out loud, at the cairn, standing up, in a wind that had not stopped in nineteen days.
“Eight.”
Nobody wrote it. Nahl counted the company on the ridge in their own head one more time, forwards and backwards, and kept it there, where it had been since the shelf.
Kael did what Kael did at every stop on the whole journey. He checked the ground.

He walked the top of the ridge with his bare hand out of the glove. He went over the grass and the stones and the two feet of soil over rotten rock. He did it twice. Then he came back to the cairn and knelt down and traced the top stone itself, slowly, the whole way round the notch and the tally of five.
Then he stood up and said it plainly. The company had expected exactly this and let him say it anyway.
“Nothing. There is no edge on him. I told you there would not be.”
“You said it three times on the walk,” said Mira.
“I said it three times because I wanted somebody to disagree with me,” said Kael. “Nobody did. I was right. I have hated being right about this for four months.”
He put the glove back on. He closed the hand.

“He was never entered anywhere. There is no line from him to anything. So there is nothing to trace and there is nothing missing. That is not a failure. That is the answer. They got what they wanted with him. They rolled him back off the page and buried him in a county plot. The only mark on him anywhere in the world is five strokes cut in a stone by a woman with a map.”
The refusal came after that. It was Kael’s and it was the plainest one the company had made since the shelf.
Veylan had the axe out of the pack.
That was the whole of it. A man who has just walked eleven days to a grave with a mark on it starts thinking about a mark of his own. Veylan was a farmer. Farmers put a stone on a thing.

“I want to cut one more stroke,” he said. “One, for the company. Four of us started at the river. Eight of us crossed the stone. Nine went west. Eight walked back.” He turned the axe in his hand. “And there is nothing anywhere that says the four of us who came out here ever came home.”
“No,” said Riss.
“I know,” said Veylan. “Say it anyway.”

“The mark on that stone is the last thing anybody with a name did for him,” said Riss. “Mira cut it on the night of the burial. She cut it so that a person walking over this ridge in fifty years would know that somebody was here. Add a second stroke and it stops being a mark. It becomes a claim. A claim is something a county can argue with.”
“It is one stroke of a chisel,” said Veylan.
“It is one stroke of a chisel,” said Riss, “and the counties have taken eleven counties with less.”
Veylan stood with the axe in his hand for a while. Then he turned it round and put the handle end on the ground and leaned on it. That is what a farmer does with a tool he has decided not to use.
“Then the mark is the one he got,” he said. “Five strokes and a notch. No column. No name. It will look like a tally off a barn door to anybody who ever finds it.”
“That is what it is,” said Nahl. “That is what all of us are now. A tally group on a barn door that nobody has bothered to count.”
They took nothing and left nothing. That was the other half of the refusal and it was Mira’s.
She did it in the last of the light with her hand on the top stone.
“Say it,” said Nahl.

“There is nothing here that belongs to us,” said Mira. “There is nothing here that we brought for him. He has a pen and an inkwell in the ground. He has a log that never left the counties. He has a mark on a stone. If I take a chip off this cairn to draw, I have made an object out of his grave. If I leave my bad food on it, I have made an offering. An offering is a claim with a story on it.”
“So we leave it as it is.”
“We leave it as we found it,” said Mira. “That is the whole practice. It is the widest column. It is the one nobody can argue with.”
Veylan took the tin out of his coat and opened it once. Inside it, wrapped in sacking, there was a handful of west soil. He had thought about leaving it on the grave for four days of walking.
He closed the tin and put it back inside his coat.
“He would not want it,” said Veylan. “He would want to know what it grows into. And I am the only person here who can find out.”
They camped a mile east of the ridge, in the lee of a stone, on ground the counties had surveyed.

Sancora set the watches. Riss took the first. Nahl took the second. Kael took the third. The goat lay down on the eastern side of the fire and put its head toward the counties for the first time in four months.

Above them the Emberion was where it always was. Fifteen joints, and the piece missing out of the wing. From the ridge, at the last of the light, it looked less like a picture of a creature and more like a page with a hole in it.
Kael sat with his burned hand open on his knee and did not glove it. The wind came across the trough all night from the west, steady, the way it had come down the mountain.
It did not stop.
Sancora did the checks at the fire, all of them, out loud. A company that has been up a chimney does not stop counting hands and feet when it comes down.
Kael had the first watch. Mira had the chart out and did not draw on it. She read the last page she had written instead, which was the bone, and then she put the chart away.
Veylan had the tin out and checked the sacking round the soil twice. Then he closed it and put it back inside his coat.
Nahl sat with the log on their knees and the cord in their hands and did not untie it. There was nothing that needed adding to the log. That was the whole point of the log.

Under Riss’s shirt the plate hummed the third note. Not the divided fifth. Not the clean one. It was the note that had been missing from the middle of it. It was quiet and even, the way a thing hums when the interval it belongs to has finally been closed.
Below them, in the dark on the eastern side, the gold road and the grey road ran down off the ridge and into the counties. They ran side by side. Neither of them shone.

In the morning the company went east. They were carrying a log, a Leaf, a blank page, a spoken count, and a name in a language nobody could write. Ahead of them there was a border stone, and a river, and a mill on the Vellum with four leaves at the back of its ledger and a clerk who had once un-ticked a box.

chapters.label: Chapter 24
chapters.title: The Mill
paragraphs: After the ridge, and the report to a stone, and the refusal to cut a second notch, the company crossed the border stone two days later.

The stone was where it had been. It had a county face and a company face. It was the same stone the company had stood round four months earlier with a hostage-sized secret and no idea what a fee was going to cost them.
They did not stop at it. Old Den put his hand on it going past, the way a man does with a gatepost. That was the whole of the ceremony.
Then they walked east for nine days on the river road. On the ninth day they came to Ashenford.
Ashenford was a mill town. That means it was a road, a bridge, a chapel, forty houses, and a mill.
The mill sat on the Vellum where the river bent and dropped. It was three storeys of stone with a wheel house and a loading yard and a wall with iron hooks set in it for the barges.
It was the biggest building Veylan had been inside in eleven years.

He had come to it once before and it had cost him four hundred crowns off the top of a harvest. He had written a letter of complaint about it. The letter had gone to the county and the county had answered with a form.
He said nothing about any of that to the company. A man does not explain why he does not want to be somewhere when there is work in front of him.
He did say one thing, in the yard, with his hand on the cart.
“I will be outside if anybody wants me.”
“You will be inside,” said Sancora.
“I will be inside,” said Veylan.

The woman who came out to meet them was forty-one years old. She wore an apron over a good coat and she had a leather pen case in her hand, because she had been working when the boy came in to say there were eight strangers in the yard.
Her name was Ivet Sallow. She was the clerk of the mill on the Vellum. That was the whole of her title and nobody in the world respected it.
She looked at the company for a long time and did not ask them anything.

Then she did a thing Veylan noticed, because he had spent his life noticing what practical people do under pressure. She looked at the company. She looked at the road behind them. She looked at the company again and counted them, and her mouth moved slightly the way a mouth moves when a person is finishing an arithmetic they do not like.
“You are the eight,” said Ivet Sallow.
That stopped the yard.
“Which eight?” said Riss.

“The party that went west in the spring,” said Ivet. “There was a carpenter’s cart, and a goat, and a man in a good coat who did the talking. You came through in the third month and you went over the bridge. You were supposed to be written in the strangers’ register. Every party that comes through Ashenford West with a cart is written in the strangers’ register. It is the mill’s book and I keep it.”
“And were we written in it?” said Riss.
“No,” said Ivet.
She said it without any emphasis at all, the way she said everything. Then she stood in the yard in the rain with the pen case in her hand and waited to be arrested, or thanked, or asked.
She took them inside, because it was going to rain and because eight people standing in a yard is a thing a town notices twice.

The office was one room. It had two windows, a stove, and a long counter. Behind the counter there were four big ledgers on a shelf. Each of them was two inches thick and had been in the same place for eleven years.
Veylan stood at the back with his arms folded and looked at the ledgers. They were grain ledgers. They had the same four columns in them as the page that had cost him four hundred crowns.
Ivet put the pen case down on the counter and said the rest of it without being asked. Veylan came to understand that this was the whole of the woman.

“Nine months ago a bundle came up the river from the county office with a note on it. The note had nine words. I know them off by heart because I read them four hundred times. *Verification of departures over the western boundary, by party.* There was a list with four parties on it. The fourth party had no names at all.”
“And the box,” said Riss.
“There was a box at the foot of the page,” said Ivet. “It said *verified*. Beside it there was a line for the clerk’s name and the date and the mill’s mark.”
“Did you verify it?”
