“I ticked it,” said Ivet. “I signed my name and stamped the mark and sent it up the river. The party went down as departed west. That is the last anybody in the county ever looked for them.”
Veylan looked at Riss. Riss looked at Ivet.
“Then why are you telling us you un-ticked it?” said Riss.

“Because I un-ticked it,” said Ivet. “Nine months and four days later there was a second bundle. Same nine words. There was a note asking the mill to confirm that the fourth party had left the county, and stating that no return had been recorded, and requesting a confirmation of the original verification.”
“And?”

“And the box was already ticked,” said Ivet. “So there was nothing to do but sign it again. It was the easiest thing on the desk that morning. It would have taken me a minute. Nobody would ever have read it.”
She reached under the counter and brought out a book.
It was a mill account book, ordinary stock, ruled, four hundred pages of grain in and grain out. She put it on the counter and opened it at the back.
Past the last ruled page there were four leaves of good writing paper stitched in against the board.
Every leaf was covered in names in her own hand. They were small and neat and column-straight, with a date beside each one and a note of where the person had come from.
There were eighty-one of them.

“These are the strangers,” said Ivet Sallow. “Four years of strangers coming through Ashenford West with no papers, or papers taken off them at the bridge, or papers with the wrong name on them. The register is supposed to hold them. The register goes up the river at the end of the year. The names get sorted into the county’s lists. A person with no papers goes onto the list of persons of no account. Once you are on that list you cannot hold ground. You cannot sign a contract. You cannot be entered in a parish book. You cannot be buried in a parish yard.”
“Eighty-one of them,” said Mira.
“Eighty-one in four years,” said Ivet. “I keep them here instead. It is the back of a mill ledger. Nobody has ever looked in the back of a mill ledger.”
They slept in the loft over the loading bay, on straw, under a roof, for the first time in four months.
Veylan was up before the light with his hands full of nothing to do. Old Den was awake because he always was. The two of them stood at the loft door and looked down at the yard.
“You keep looking at those ledgers,” said Old Den.

“I have a page in one of them somewhere,” said Veylan. “Four hundred crowns off the top of a harvest. A letter of complaint that went up the river and came back as a form. The harvest went into this building in sacks and I stood in that yard and asked a clerk what the mill paid for oats, and the clerk said the mill paid what the mill paid.”
“And now?”

“Now a clerk in this building has eighty-one names stitched into her own ledger,” said Veylan. “She has not sent the county a return for four days. I do not know what that is. It is not a fee. It is not a claim. It is the other thing.”
Old Den nodded at the yard.
“It is a page that cannot be filed,” he said.
“That is what I said.”

“No,” said Old Den. “You said it is not a fee and not a claim. I am telling you what it is. I have spent fifty years watching the counties file things. I have never once seen a page they could not put somewhere.”
The keeper and the clerk had their conversation in the yard, in the rain, under the loading hoist.

It happened because Riss went out to bring the goat in out of the weather and found Ivet standing under the hoist with her arms crossed, watching the goat. The goat was in the middle of the yard with its head down. It would not be moved.
“He will not come in,” said Ivet.
“No,” said Riss. “He does not come into buildings. He has been outside every building we have slept in since the border stone.”
“He is a very reasonable animal.”
“He is the most reasonable person in the company.”
They stood in the rain for a while. Then Riss said the thing that needed saying, and said it flatly, because a keeper says a thing once and says it exactly.
“You un-ticked a box.”
“I did,” said Ivet.
“Why?”
“Because you were standing there,” said Ivet Sallow.
Riss did not say anything.

“I was at the counter and the boy came in and said there were eight of you in the yard with a cart and a goat. So I got the register out, because that is what the register is for. Then you came in. One of you asked me what the mill paid for oats. One of you stood at the door with a goat and asked whether the bridge was good to the far bank. A very old man with a bound hand sat down on the bench by the stove and went to sleep.”
“And?”

“And I looked at the list of four parties,” said Ivet, “and I thought: that is a party of people going somewhere on purpose. And I thought: if I write their names in this register, the names go up the river at the end of the year and get put on a list, and a person on that list cannot hold ground.” She shrugged in the rain. “So I ticked the box and signed it and put the register away. I did not write your names in it. That was nine months ago.”

“You are the reason we got out of the counties,” said Riss. “The counties were behind us for eleven days. Every gate and bridge and mill between the river and the mountains had the same nine words on it. Not one of them had our names. The one clerk on the road who had us standing in front of her did not write them down.”
Ivet looked out at the yard.
“That is not a thing that matters,” she said.
“It is the whole reason we are standing here.”

“No,” said Ivet. “It is one box on one page. There are eleven counties and four hundred thousand pages and a hundred clerks doing the arithmetic properly. One un-ticked box is a hole in a fence. It does not stop anything.”
“You do not believe me,” said Riss.
“No,” said Ivet. “I do not need to. It was nine months ago. I did it because you were standing there. If I had written the names down I would have done that because you were standing there too.”
The refusal happened at the counter on the second morning. It happened in the plainest possible way, which was that Ivet got the strangers’ register down off the shelf.
The company had been eleven days on the road and two days in a mill yard. They had slept in the loft over the loading bay.
Ivet came in with her pen case and her keys. She set the register on the counter and opened it at the current page. Every one of the company in the room understood exactly what was about to happen.

“There is a difficulty,” said Ivet. “You are strangers in Ashenford West with no papers and no names on any list. You have a cart and an animal. You have been in the yard two days. Every day you are here I am breaking the register. The carrier comes twice a week and the carrier talks.”
“So you want to write us in,” said Riss.
“I want to write you in,” said Ivet. “I have thought about it half the night. It is the safe thing and it is the easy thing and it is what I would have done in my first year at this counter.”
“And now?”
“Now I am forty-one and I have eighty-one names at the back of a ledger,” said Ivet Sallow. “I am not going to write down any more.”
She closed the register.
“I un-ticked it once,” she said. “I am not going to write it down now.”
“That is the refusal,” said Nahl.
“That is the refusal,” said Ivet, “but do not make it larger than it is. It is not courage. I am not brave. I am tidy, and I have worked out which way round the tidiness goes.”
The arithmetic of the room was done that afternoon on the office table with the rain on both windows.
Mira put it in three sentences.

“We have come a thousand miles in both directions to find a room that can take a report. Orphiel gave us the specification before he died. It has four parts and none of them is a courthouse or a vault.” She counted them off with a finger on the table. “A clerk with a standing to write in a book of record. A book of record. A person present who does not want to be there. And a superior who can be reached by a note, because a clerk who cannot be overruled is a clerk nobody answers to.”
“Say the four,” said Old Den.
Ivet answered, because it was her room.
“I am the clerk,” she said. “I have the standing to write in the mill’s books of account and in the register of strangers. The county office takes my pen on a mill matter without asking twice.”
“The book,” said Mira.
“The ledger at the back of which eighty-one people have been kept alive for four years,” said Ivet.
“The person who does not want to be there,” said Mira.
Everybody looked at Veylan.
“I do not want to be here,” said Veylan. “I want that entered too.”
“And the superior,” said Mira.

“The mill belongs to a family,” said Ivet. “They are four miles down the river at the big house and they do not come here. There is a carrier goes that way twice a week. I can put a note in his bag on Thursday and have an answer back by Monday. They will answer. They have had four hundred notes from me and they have never once refused to answer one.”

Then she did the thing Nahl remembered afterwards. She got out a single sheet of paper and ruled it by hand in four columns, because there was no printed county stock in the mill and she was not going to use grain paper for this.
She put the sheet on the table in front of the company with the fourth column empty.
“Then that is the room,” said Ivet Sallow. “Bring me the books. I will write the note to the family tonight.”
That was the ninth day east of the border stone. It was the first day in nineteen that there was no wind.

Veylan noticed it before anybody else. He was a farmer and he had spent the whole of the walk listening to it. It had come down off the peaks and followed them across the trough and off the ridge and down to the county road. It had been in every fire and every conversation and every night’s sleep for four months. In the mill yard at Ashenford it was gone.
The plate hummed the third note under Riss’s shirt the moment they came through the mill door. It hummed all day, quiet and even. Nahl saw Riss put a hand inside their coat twice and leave it there.
Kael’s hand burned in the mill office the way it burned on a mountain. He said so once and then left it alone. A man does not ask a mill for anything.

The goat stood in the yard in the rain for two days and would not come in. On the second evening it walked round the whole building once, slowly, the way a person walks a boundary. Then it lay down against the mill door with its back to the road.

Above the mill there was nothing to see. Rain, and the county sky, and the Emberion somewhere behind it, fifteen joints and a piece missing out of the wing, invisible for the first time since the river.

Out beyond the yard the gold road and the grey road ran side by side down to the bridge and across the water and on into the counties. Neither of them shone. There was nobody on either of them in any direction that a man could see.

chapters.label: Chapter 25
chapters.title: The Room
paragraphs: After the mill yard, and the note that went down the river in the carrier’s bag on Thursday, and the four days of waiting, the answer came back on Monday morning.
It was three lines long.
Ivet Sallow read it standing in the office with her coat still on. Then she put it down on the counter and read it out loud, because a clerk reads a document to the people the document is about.

*To the clerk of the mill on the Vellum. If the matter is not a fee and is not a claim, and no part of it is owed to the family or to the county, then it is nothing, and the clerk may enter it as nothing and keep the record in the mill’s books. Signed, for the family.*
“Nothing was taken and no fee is due on any part of it,” said Ivet. “So it is nothing, and I may enter it as nothing.”
She folded the answer and put it in the ledger at the back with the four leaves.
“That is the fourth requirement met,” she said. “Whatever you have carried a thousand miles, this room can take it.”
They set the room that evening.

It was the back room of the mill, past the office, where the grain weights were kept and where the men ate in bad weather. One window. One door. A long table with a seam down the middle and eight chairs that did not match.
Ivet lit two lamps and put them at the ends of the table. The room came up yellow and small.
Then she did the thing the company had come a thousand miles for. She did it as a piece of office work, which was the only way it could have been done.
She sat at the head of the table with her pen case open and her keys beside it.
Down the length of the table, on the cloth, Nahl laid out the three books the company had carried out of the counties and back into them.
The log. Brown, heavy, worn at the corners. The county’s columns marked in another hand on every page. Nine thousand and four entries. A fourth column empty from the first page to the last.
The Leaf. Small, plain, cheap. Riss’s own notes in small writing and a strip of cloth round the spine to hold it.

The blank page. White, unsized, expensive paper, folded three times. No rule on it. No clerk’s mark. No signature at the foot. Nothing written on it anywhere in either direction of a thousand miles of road.
Ivet Sallow looked at the three of them for a while in the lamplight.
Then she pushed the mill’s paper aside, because she had brought a fresh sheet up from the office and did not use it, and she put her hand flat on the blank page.
“This is the page,” she said.
“It is the only one of the three with no marks on it,” said Riss.

“It is the only one of the three a clerk can write in without crossing out somebody else’s work,” said Ivet. “The log belongs to a dead man. The Leaf belongs to you. This is a page. It is nobody’s. That is what a page is supposed to be before it is entered.”
She took her rule and her pen and ruled it by hand, down the long way, in four columns. The ink went on clean, because the paper was good.

Four columns. Forty lines. It was not county stock and it was not printed. No office in the eleven counties had a plate for it. It was as square and as plain as anything Maro Holl would have ruled himself.
Then she looked up the table at the company.
“Now,” said Ivet Sallow. “Who signs?”
The keeper scene happened across the table, in front of everybody, and it took less than a minute.
“You carry the log,” said Nahl.
“I carry the Leaf,” said Riss.
“Neither of us can file anything.”
“Neither of us can file anything,” said Riss.
“Then who signs?”
“The clerk,” said Nahl.
They both looked at Ivet, who had already uncapped the pen.
Then Riss made the refusal, and made it on the page and not in a speech, which was how the company made the ones that mattered.

“Not us,” said Riss. “Nobody in this company puts their name at the foot of that page. We are the witnesses. A man who signs his own account of himself is a diarist. A diarist is a person with an opinion, and an opinion is the easiest thing in the world to file.”
“Orphiel’s rule,” said Nahl.

“Orphiel’s rule,” said Riss. “He told me in a room at Carrow with his hand on a ledge. A witness who signs his own page has already been dealt with. The clerk signs. The witnesses stand up and say what they saw, and then they stand back.”
Ivet Sallow looked round the table once, slowly, at all of them.

“I have signed four thousand documents,” she said. “Every one of them was read to me by somebody who wanted something. This is the first one I have been asked for.” She put the pen down on the rule. “Say the report. I will write it.”
Nahl said the count the way a bearer says a count, which is standing up.
That was the shape of the whole evening, and afterwards the company could never describe it to anybody without sounding like a meeting.

The eight of them stood in a line along the long table. Riss, Kael, Mira, Veylan, Sancora, Corvath, Old Den, and Nahl at the end nearest the lamp. Ivet sat at the head with the blank page ruled in four columns in front of her and the pen in her hand.
Nahl reported.

“A company came off the western boundary four months ago. There were more of us going out than came back. We came back by the ridge, the last grass, and the border stone. We stopped at a grave on the way and said the report to a stone. Now we are saying it to a clerk in a room, standing up. That is the report of the road.”
Then Nahl counted them.
“Forwards,” they said. “Riss. Kael. Mira. Veylan. Sancora. Corvath. Old Den. Myself. Backwards. Myself. Old Den. Corvath. Sancora. Veylan. Mira. Kael. Riss.”
“Eight,” said Nahl.
The room was quiet. The two lamps did what lamps do in a small room. The rain had stopped outside and there was no wind on the mill at all.
Nahl said the number one more time. Out loud, standing, in the room where a book was open. And did not move toward the table.

“Eight. That is the count of this company. It was counted three times on the mountain and once into the wind at the top of the grey wall. It is not going into your page. The reason it is not going into your page is the whole reason we walked here.”
Ivet Sallow had not written anything.
She sat with the pen a little above the paper and watched the man at the end of the table. Then she said something no county clerk would have said, and that no county clerk would have needed to say.

“I was not going to write it,” she said. “A number with nothing under it is not a count in a book. It is a claim. If I put a number in a column I have to put a value beside it and a ground under it and a reason across from it. Then there is a fee at the foot of the page and a list at the end of the year. Then the company stops being a company and becomes an entry.”
“That,” said Riss, “is the whole reason we walked here.”
Then there was the name.
That part took longer. It was harder than the count. It was the only part of the evening that nobody in the room ever told anybody about afterwards.
Riss asked Nahl to say it. Nahl said they could not. Riss asked Kael, and Kael said it was not a thing a hand could hold.
So Riss tried to say it.
They stood at the table in the lamplight and said the first part of the sound. Then they stopped, because there was nothing in a human throat that could turn it into the second part.

Riss tried it three times. The third time was the worst of the three. The first part came out right. The second part came out as a county word, ordinary and flat, a word with nothing to do with anything. Riss heard themselves say it and stopped, and put both hands down flat on the table.
“It is not that I have forgotten it,” said Riss. “A name in that language does not fit through a face like mine. I have known that since the shelf. I wanted to be wrong about it in front of a clerk.”
Ivet Sallow did not write anything then either. She asked the only question left, which was the right one.
“Where does it go?”

“Nowhere,” said Riss. “There is no column in your page for a name that cannot be written. There is no column in any page in the counties for it either. A clerk who writes down a sound is a clerk writing down a claim. So it does not go into the page. It goes into the report as a thing that happened.”
Ivet looked at the empty first column of the page for a moment.
“I can write one thing about it that is true,” she said.
“Write it,” said Riss.
Mira raised the risk after that, and she raised it because somebody had to.
“Before she writes anything,” said Mira, “ask her what happens to her.”
Ivet looked up.

“Say it plainly,” said Mira. “You have eighty-one names at the back of a ledger and no authority for a single one of them. Now you are going to stitch in a page about a party off the western boundary and a count and a name. What happens when the county comes up the river and opens that book?”
“Then I am a clerk who kept private records in a mill ledger,” said Ivet Sallow. “It is not a hanging matter. It is a dismissal matter. Thirty years of my life and no pen case of my own ever again.”
“We can take the page with us,” said Riss. “We have carried it a thousand miles and we can carry it further. Then there is nothing in your book and nothing for them to find.”
“No,” said Ivet.
“Think about it.”

“I have thought about it for four days,” said Ivet. “The page stays. It is a mill record and it goes in the mill’s book with the other four leaves. If I am going to be a clerk who keeps pages, then I keep the page in my own book and I take what comes with it. A page in a satchel is a rumour. A page stitched in a ledger is a record.”
She looked at Mira, and then at the whole line of them.
“You walked a thousand miles to find a clerk with a book,” she said. “Do not walk out with the page in your hand. That would make the whole of it nothing at all.”
That is how the page was written, on a hand-ruled sheet of fine white paper that had come off a mountain in a tube.

Ivet Sallow wrote it slowly in her own hand, in the four columns she had ruled herself. She read every line of it aloud as she wrote it, because that is what a clerk does when the people the document is about are standing in the room.
In the first column, where a name goes: **one company, off the western boundary, no names given.**
In the second column, where the ground goes: **the grey wall, above the last grass.**

In the third column, where the value goes: **one log of entries. one leaf of notes. one count, spoken in this room and not written here. one name, said once, off the far side of the wall, and not written here, and not written anywhere.**
In the fourth column, where the reason goes, and where every page in the eleven counties turns a person into an entry, Ivet Sallow wrote:

**nothing was taken and no fee is due on any part of it. this page is entered because a report was made, standing, out loud, in my hearing, in this room, by witnesses who came here on foot to make it.**
Then, in the row where the value of a party is totalled, she wrote the other thing.
**present and unwilling: one. he said so himself in the room, and asked that it be entered, and it is entered here, because a room without an unwilling person cannot hear a report.**
Veylan read it over her shoulder. He did not say anything for a while, and then he said one thing.
“That is the first time in thirty years that anybody has wanted that written down.”
Then Ivet signed it. Name, the day of the month, the century, and the mill’s mark. She blotted it and left it open on the table to dry.
The page went into the back of the ledger with the four leaves.

Ivet did it at the end of the evening while the company stood and watched. There was no ceremony in it at all. She opened the mill’s account book at the back, took the needle and the thread out of the drawer, and stitched the new page in against the board beside the eighty-one names.
Five leaves in the back of the mill’s ledger. Four years of strangers, and a company.
Nahl counted them, because that was the trade. Riss said it out loud, standing at the end of the table with a hand on the closed cover.
“Five.”
“Five on the stone above him,” said Nahl.
“Yes,” said Riss.

Nobody said anything else about it. Mira took her hand off the chart and put her pen away. She did not draw the back of the ledger. Veylan went out to check the cart. Old Den, who had been standing the whole time because his knees did not do a chair well any more, sat down at last in the chair at the end of the long table.
The carrier came on Thursday.

That was four days after the page went in, and it was the day the river road filled up with carts and people, because Thursday was the day the carrier took the mill’s post down to the bridge and on to the county office.
Ivet came into the office with the bag. She opened it on the counter and did the thing she had done every Thursday for nineteen years.
She put nothing in it.

The company watched her do it from the doorway, the whole of it, the four seconds of office work. She looked into the bag, and she looked up at the shelf where a bundle of mill business would have gone on any other Thursday of her working life, and she closed the bag, and she handed it to the carrier at the door, and the man went off down the road with an empty bag.
Nahl understood the whole of it, because a bearer notices what a person leaves out of a delivery.
She had not sent a note to the county office in four days. There was nothing in that bag that could be read by anybody at the other end of the river.
“What did you not send?” said Riss, in the office, after the carrier had gone.
“The monthly return,” said Ivet Sallow. “Four columns. Grain in, grain out, fees entered at the foot, and the mill’s mark at the bottom, and my name. It was due on Thursday.”
“And?”
“And I have left the query register blank all week,” said Ivet, “and this morning I looked at the return and I did not write it.”
“Why?”

“Because I could not see a way to write the mill’s numbers,” said Ivet, “with that page four leaves behind them in the same book. I will write it next week. Or I will not. I do not know yet. That is the truth of where I am and I am telling it to you once.”
The plate hummed the third note the whole night.

In the morning the company was still there. Nothing had been signed by any of them. The count had been spoken and it was still spoken. The name had been said and it was still a sound. The page had been ruled, written, signed, and stitched in by a clerk of a mill, and there was no fee anywhere on it and no value in any column.
Outside, the goat was lying against the mill door with its back to the road.
Kael’s burned hand had stopped burning in the night, for the first time since Collow. He did not mention it to anybody. He kept lighting it up in the dark of the loft to check.
Above the mill there was nothing to see. Rain again, and county sky, and the Emberion somewhere behind it, fifteen joints and the piece missing out of the wing, invisible for two days now.

Down at the bridge the gold road and the grey road ran side by side across the water and into the counties. Neither of them shone. There was nobody on either of them in any direction that a man could see.
And in the back of a mill ledger in Ashenford West there were five leaves of writing that no list in the eleven counties was ever going to get, and one of them was a count.

chapters.label: Chapter 26
chapters.title: The Query
paragraphs: After the page was stitched into the mill ledger, and the carrier went down the river with an empty bag, and three weeks went by, a query came up the river from the county office.
It was not a magistrate. It was not an Assessor. It was a clerk.
His name was Maro Holl. He was forty-eight years old and he had been a clerk for thirty years. He had asked for the mill route himself.

That was unusual and nobody in the counting house thought about it twice. A clerk asking for a route is a clerk who wants three days on the road instead of three days at the desk. It happens. The senior clerk signed it and forgot it.
The reason was in his coat.
Maro Holl had the twelfth sheet of the Ash bundle folded twice in his inside pocket, and he had carried it there for three weeks.

He had shown it to one person. Lira had looked at it on the kitchen table at two in the morning and had not asked him to explain it. He had gone to work the next day and filed eleven sheets and left the query register blank, and he had not written the reason in the fourth column, and he had not written *no fee*.
He had not been able to say why. Or rather, he could say why and it embarrassed him.

He was the fourth column. Thirty years and four hundred thousand reasons. He could write the reason on any page in the eleven counties, and if the reason was not there to be written, he could write the one that made the page go away.

That was the whole of his trade, and he had never once questioned it, and now a county man on a western road had drawn a notch and five strokes where the reason was supposed to go, and Maro Holl could not copy it and could not improve it and could not file it.

So he had asked for a route that would put him in a mill office forty miles upriver with the sheet in his coat. And on the fourth day of the tenth month he got on the carrier’s cart at the sixth hour and went.
The official reason for the route was on the paper in his bag and it was perfectly good.
The mill on the Vellum was four weeks late with its monthly return.

That had never happened. Maro Holl knew that because he knew every return in the county the way a man knows his own stairs. The mill on the Vellum had sent a return in the same week of every month for nineteen years. Four columns, grain in, grain out, fees at the foot, the mark, the clerk’s name.
Ivet Sallow. He knew the name off the leaf, the way he knew four hundred names off leaves. He had never wondered anything about her.
Now a return was four weeks late and a mill clerk’s name was on the last one that had come in, and Maro Holl was going up the river to ask her why, and that was the whole of the official business.
He was aware that this was not why he was going. He made himself admit that at the second milestone, because a man who does not admit the thing at the second milestone will lie about it at the tenth.
The road came into Ashenford from the south. The mill came up on the left, three storeys of stone with a wheel house and a wall with iron hooks set in it for the barges.
Maro Holl got down off the carrier’s cart in the yard at the middle of the afternoon with his bag in one hand and his coat on and the twelfth sheet against his ribs.
The first thing he saw was a goat lying against the mill door with its back to the road.

It did not get up. It did not move its head. It was a goat in a mill yard, which is not remarkable in a county town. It was the position that was wrong. The animal was lying flat against the door of a working mill at the middle of the afternoon with the whole yard and the whole road available to it.
Maro Holl looked at it for a moment and then went in, because a clerk does not make an entry about a goat.
The office had two windows, a stove, and a long counter. There were four big ledgers on a shelf behind the counter and each of them was two inches thick.

The woman behind the counter was about his own age, with an apron over a good coat and a leather pen case open in front of her. She looked up when he came in and read his coat and his bag in about a second and a half, which is the speed a working clerk reads another clerk.
“County,” she said.
“County office,” said Maro Holl. “Counting house. My name is Maro Holl.”
“Ivet Sallow.” She did not offer her hand. He did not offer his. Clerks do not. “You have come about the return.”
“I have come about the return.”
“It is four weeks late,” said Ivet Sallow.

“It is four weeks late,” said Maro Holl. “There is a query on the ledger at the office. In nineteen years it has not happened once, and there is a query on the ledger, and I have been sent to ask you why.”
“That is fair,” said Ivet. “Ask me.”
He asked her. He asked her properly, with the query open on the counter and his pen in his hand, because that was his trade and he did it well.
And she gave him nothing to write.

She answered him in the flat, level voice of a clerk who has decided what she is going to say. The mill’s grain had not been counted to the day. The mill’s fees had not been totalled. The family had been notified and had not objected. The return was in hand. It would go up the river on Thursday.
“On which Thursday?” said Maro Holl.
“On a Thursday,” said Ivet Sallow.
He wrote that down. There was nothing else to write, and he wrote it, and he sat looking at a query page with four lines on it and a large amount of empty paper underneath.
Then he asked the question that was on the paper in his bag and not on the paper on the counter.
“I would like to see the mill’s books.”
That was a legitimate request and both of them knew it.

The county had a right to query a return. The family had a right to inspect its own books. And a query about a return is answered by the return, so a clerk who queries a mill’s numbers may properly be shown the mill’s ledgers up to the point where the numbers stop.
Ivet Sallow looked at him for a while.

“The mill’s books are the mill’s,” she said. “The family has the right to inspect. The county has the right to query. The county does not have the right to seize a mill’s account book without a warrant from the assize, and there is no warrant in that bag.”
“There is no warrant in this bag,” said Maro Holl.

“Then you may read the books at this counter,” said Ivet, “with me standing here, and you may not take one off the shelf, and you may not copy a page of one, and if you ask me to leave the room the answer is no.”
“That is correct procedure,” said Maro Holl.
“I know it is correct procedure,” said Ivet Sallow. “I have been a clerk for nineteen years.”
She got the four ledgers down herself, one at a time, and set them on the counter, and opened the first one at the current page.
He read the grain for an hour.

It was good work. That is the first thing to say about the mill on the Vellum and Maro Holl said it to himself inside five minutes. The columns were straight. The totals were carried forward correctly. The fees were entered at the foot with the ground stated and the dates in order.
Whoever did this had been taught properly and had never once written a number to make a page look better than the ground it came off.
“You are three days off on the spring total,” said Maro Holl.
“The spring total is three days off,” said Ivet. “I know.”
“It is the only error in nineteen years of ledgers.”
“It is the only error in nineteen years of ledgers,” said Ivet Sallow, “and I have not corrected it, because the correction would be a second page and the second page would be a claim.”
Maro Holl put his pen down on the counter.

Clerks do not often meet. They are alone in their trades like men in separate cells. When two of them do meet, they find out in about ten minutes whether the other one is a proper clerk, and this one was a proper clerk, and he had not expected that when he got on the cart.
“I want to ask you something that is not on the query,” he said.
“Ask.”
“The three-day error. Why did you leave it?”

“Because it is true,” said Ivet Sallow. “The mill lost three days of water in the spring and I wrote the numbers as they came. If I go back and fix the number, I have written a page that says the mill never lost three days of water. A clerk’s whole value is that his wrong numbers are the wrong numbers that happened.”
Maro Holl stood at the counter and understood that he had just been told the whole of his own trade by a woman in a mill.
He saw the leaves at the back of the fourth ledger because she gave him the fourth ledger and he opened it at the back.
That is how it happened. There was no drama in it and he was not searching. He was checking the ledger’s condition, which is a thing clerks do, because a ledger is only as good as its stitching.
At the back of the fourth ledger, past the last ruled page, there were five leaves of paper stitched in against the board.
Four of them were covered in names in small, neat, column-straight writing, with a date beside each one. There were eighty-one names. He counted them twice because that is the trade.
The fifth leaf was finer paper and it was ruled by hand in four columns, and it had been written recently, in the same hand.
He read it.
He read the four columns the way he had read four hundred thousand pages: left to right, top to bottom, and with his pen down.
The first column, where a name goes, said that a company had come off the western boundary and had given no names.
The second, where the ground goes, named a wall above the last grass.

The third listed what had been carried back. A log of entries. A leaf of notes. A count that had been spoken in the room and was not written, and a name that had been said once off the far side of a wall and was not written anywhere either.

That third column was the one that made Maro Holl put his pen down on the counter. He was a clerk of values. A column of value that contained no value in it was not a column. It was a list of things that had refused to be turned into a number.
Then he read the fourth column twice.

It did not claim a fee and it did not claim a ground. It said that nothing had been taken and that no fee was due on any part of the page, and it said that the page had been entered because a report had been made, standing, out loud, in the clerk’s hearing, in that room, by witnesses who had come there on foot to make it.
Below that, in the row where the value of a party is totalled, somebody had written one more line.
**present and unwilling: one.**
There was no fee at the foot of the page. There was no ground valued. There was no column of numbers anywhere on it.
Maro Holl stood at the counter of a mill office with his hand flat on a leaf of fine paper and did not write anything, because there was nothing on the page for him to write.
The plate hummed while he stood there.

He had heard it when he came in and he heard it again now: a note in the room, quiet, even, coming from somewhere behind the counter. It was not the stove and it was not the wheel. It was not a bell and it was not a horn.

It was one note, and it was the note that a fifth is missing. He could not have said that. He had no words for it. He was a clerk of numbers and not a man of music, and he heard a sound in a mill office and put it down as a sound in a mill office.
Behind him, in the doorway, a man with a burned hand stood watching him read. The man said nothing at all and did not move, and Maro Holl finished the page anyway, because a clerk finishes the page.
“I have written four hundred thousand reasons,” said Maro Holl.
He said it out loud in the office, to the leaf of paper, in the voice a man uses when he has just done an arithmetic that will not come out.
“I have never once seen a page with no reason in it.”
“There is a reason written there,” said Ivet Sallow. “You read it.”

“I read it,” said Maro Holl. “It is a reason for nothing. There is no ground under it and no value beside it and no fee at the foot. It is a page that says a report was made by people who walked here on foot. I have been a clerk for thirty years and I do not have a file in which that page can be put.”
“No,” said Ivet. “You do not.”
“And you have stitched it into a mill account book with eighty-one names.”
“I have,” said Ivet Sallow. “At the back, past the ruled pages, where nobody looks.”
Maro Holl took his hand off the page.
“You kept a page,” he said.
“I did,” said Ivet.
“Why?”
“Because it was true,” said Ivet Sallow.

Maro Holl did not understand that. He stood in a mill office with a county query open on the counter in front of him and a county sheet folded twice in his coat, and he did not understand what a clerk meant by keeping a page that was true, and he was too honest a man to pretend that he did.
So he asked her the other question instead, and it was the one he had actually come up the river to ask.
“And the mark in your fourth column,” he said. “Your page does not have a mark in it. Why not?”
Ivet Sallow looked at him.
“Because the page I wrote is about a report,” she said. “The mark is not mine to copy. I have never seen the stone it is cut in. There is a man in your county who has.”
He did not file it. He did not seize it. He went back down the river.
That is the whole of what happened, and it took four days to do and about ten minutes to tell.

He wrote the query up in the office in a fair hand: the mill’s return is in hand and will be sent. He did not write anything about the fourth ledger or the leaves at the back of it. He did not put the twelfth sheet from his coat on the counter, and he did not hand it to her, and he did not ask her whether she had a mark with a notch and five strokes anywhere in her books.
He asked one more question instead, at the door, with his bag in his hand.
“The party on that leaf,” said Maro Holl. “The one that came off the western boundary. Did they come from the mountains?”
“They came from the mountains,” said Ivet Sallow.
“And where are they now?”

“They are in the yard,” said Ivet. “There are eight of them and one animal and they have been here three weeks. They are waiting for somebody to do something. I do not know what I am waiting for either.”
The man with the burned hand was standing by the mill door when Maro Holl came out with his bag.

He was a big man and he was not doing anything. He had his left hand open on the wall, palm flat, the way a man rests a hand on a stove to see whether it is warm, and there was a scar across the whole of the palm.
Maro Holl went past him and out into the yard and the man said nothing at all, and the hand stayed flat on the wall.

It had hurt the whole afternoon, that hand. It had hurt from the moment the county clerk came into the mill, in the same place, in the same way, and it kept on hurting until the cart went out of the gate and turned south. Kael Riven told the company about it that night, once, and then did not mention it again for a week.
There was no wind in the yard. That was the second thing Maro Holl noticed on his way out and it was the thing he thought about on the road. It was the tenth month and there was no wind on a river.

Above the mill there was rain and county sky, and behind the rain there was nothing to see. The Emberion was somewhere up there with its fifteen joints and the piece missing out of the wing, and it had not been visible since the day the company came into the town.

Down at the bridge the gold road and the grey road ran side by side across the water and away south into the counties. Neither of them shone. There was nobody on either of them in any direction a man could see.
Maro Holl went out into the yard with the twelfth sheet still folded twice in his coat, unfiled.
There was no boat and no cart going south until the morning. He took a room at the inn above the bridge for one night and put his bag on the chair and sat on the edge of the bed with his coat on.
Behind him, in a mill office on the Vellum, the plate hummed the third note until the gate was shut and the cart was out of sight.

chapters.label: Chapter 27
chapters.title: The Second Witness
paragraphs: After the county clerk read the fifth leaf at the counter, he took a room at the inn above the bridge. Then he sent word through the mill boy that he would like to speak to the party before he went south. The company sat in the back room and waited for him.
They did not discuss what to say. That was deliberate too.

Ivet Sallow lit the two lamps. She set out the long table the way she had set it out three weeks earlier. She put the fourth ledger at the head of the table with the page in it. Then she sat down at the end nearest the door and folded her hands and did not speak.
Nahl had the log on their knees and kept the cord tied.
“He is a clerk,” said Riss.
“He is a clerk,” said Nahl.
“Then say to him what you would say to Orphiel.”
He came at the eighth hour with his coat buttoned and his bag left at the inn.

He was a small, square man of forty-eight. His hands were grey and he had a careful way of standing in a doorway. He came into the mill’s back room like a man expecting to be asked to explain himself.
The first thing he did was look at the eight of them.
The second thing he did was count them.
Nahl watched him do it. It was not a hostile count and it was not even a curious one. It was the way a man counts anything, the way Nahl counted a tally group, and it took him about four seconds.
“Maro Holl,” he said. “County office. Counting house.”
“Nahl.”
“Riss.”
He did not ask for the rest of the names, and none of the rest of them offered one, and he did not write anything down.
“May I sit?”
“You may sit,” said Ivet Sallow.
He sat at the long side of the table, facing the window, which is where a clerk sits if he has been in rooms with clerks before, and put his hands flat on the wood.
“You have not filed it,” said Nahl.
“No,” said Maro Holl.
“Why?”
Maro Holl looked at the log on Nahl’s knees and at the Leaf on the table and at the ledger at the head of the table with its five leaves stitched in the back.

“Because a page with a mark in the fourth column is not a page with a bad reason,” he said. “It is a page that says there is no reason here. There is no file in the building where a page like that can be put.”
Nahl let that sit in the room for a moment, because it was the whole of what the company had walked a thousand miles to hear a county man say.
“Show me the log,” said Maro Holl.
Nahl untied the cord and put it on the table and let him look.

The county clerk went through it the way a clerk goes through a book, which is not reading. He put his thumb on the top corner and turned pages in blocks. He checked the fourth column of every block he turned, the whole way through. It took him four minutes. He did not hurry once and he did not skip a page.
“Nine thousand and four entries,” he said, at the end, without being told.
“Nine thousand and four.”
“There is no reason in any of them.”
“No,” said Nahl. “He would not write one. He said a reason is a fee with better manners.”
Maro Holl put both hands on the closed log and sat looking at the corners of it, which were worn the way a county book is worn and not the way a private book is worn.

“Do you know what this is?” he said. “This is the only book in the eleven counties that a clerk cannot use. It has everything in it. Names, dates, grounds, parishes. Nine thousand and four. And it is worth nothing at all in any office, because there is not one fee in it and not one reason, and a book with no reasons in it cannot prove that anything in it ever happened.”
“That is what he intended,” said Nahl.
“I have been a clerk for thirty years,” said Maro Holl, “and I have never once seen a book that a man built on purpose so that it could not be filed.”
“Say the rest of it,” said Nahl.

“The reason column is the engine,” said Maro Holl. “I have understood that for three weeks and I cannot make it stop being true. The counties do not take a man’s ground because the counties are cruel. They take it because there is a column, and the column has to be filled, and a filled column is a page, and a page is a fact. Every fee in eleven counties has a reason beside it. Nine hundred clerks write reasons all day. I am one of them. I wrote reasons before you were born.”
“And the mark on the sheet in your coat.”

“There is no reason beside it,” said Maro Holl. “There is a notch and five strokes. It is the only page in the county in thirty years that has come across my desk with a mark in the fourth column, and the mark is not in any script, and I am not the author of it.”
“And you did not write *no fee*.”
“I did not write *no fee*,” said Maro Holl.
“Why not?”
Maro Holl put his hands flat on the table.

“Because *no fee* is a reason,” he said. “If I write *no fee*, the page goes into the file and the file goes onto the shelf and the thing that happened out west stops being a thing that happened and becomes a line in a book that nobody reads. And there is a man who drew that mark in the knowledge of what it would do to me, and I have never met him, and I am not going to erase his work.”
Then Nahl told the county clerk the trade.

That is what it came to, and Nahl did it deliberately. On the road east the company had worked out that there are two trades in the world that never meet. The whole of the counties is built out of the gap between them.

“A bearer carries a thing to the person it belongs to,” said Nahl. “He does not write it down and he does not improve it and he does not sign it. He says what he was given and where he got it and what is left of it, standing up, in front of the person it belongs to, and then he stops talking.”
“And a clerk writes it down,” said Maro Holl.
“A clerk writes it down,” said Nahl.
“And if the thing cannot be written down?”
“Then the bearer carries it anyway,” said Nahl. “That is the whole of my trade and it is the reason I have a log under my knees that belongs to a dead man and no page anywhere with his name on it.”
Maro Holl looked at Nahl for a long time.

“In the counting house,” he said slowly, “there is a man in every chair who would have written *no fee* on that sheet. Barden, who is senior to me, told me to write it. Barden is not a bad man. He is a proper clerk and he is right, and if the twelfth sheet had gone into the file I would have been right too.”
“Then why are you here?”
“Because I did not do it,” said Maro Holl. “And because when a man does not do a thing, he has to find out what it was, or he cannot sleep in his own house.”
Then Nahl made the refusal in front of the second witness.
It was the same refusal the company had made on the page in the mill, and it was made again because it had to be made in front of the county.

Ivet Sallow brought the ledger over and opened it at the back. She put it in front of the county clerk. Maro Holl took the fifth leaf between his fingers and looked at it. Then he looked at the eight of them standing in the room.
“Somebody has to sign this,” he said.
“The clerk has signed it,” said Riss.

“The clerk has signed it as the clerk,” said Maro Holl. “The party has not signed it. In the counties, a page without a party’s mark on it is a page about nobody. If it ever goes up the river without a name at the foot of it, the first thing the office will ask is who the party was and why they will not put their hand to their own account.”
“Then the office will ask that,” said Nahl.

“There is no name to put,” said Maro Holl. “I understand that. The log belongs to a dead man and the Leaf belongs to you. But somebody in this room has to write his own name at the foot of that page or the page is nothing.”
“No,” said Nahl.
“Why not?”

“Because a witness who signs his own page is a diarist,” said Nahl. “That was Orphiel’s rule and it is the last rule he gave this company, and it is the reason none of us has written anything for a thousand miles. A witness says what he saw. The moment he signs his own account of himself, he has become the subject of the account, and then there is a page with one man on it and nothing behind him.”
Maro Holl sat with his hands flat on the table.
“Then I will not sign it either,” he said.
“No,” said Nahl.
“I am a clerk,” said Maro Holl. “A clerk does not witness. A clerk files.”
He closed the ledger himself, carefully, with both hands, and pushed it back across the table to Ivet Sallow, and did not file anything, and that was the whole of his refusal.
They worked out the shape of it that night, in the back room, over the third pot of the mill’s tea.
Mira did it, because Mira did the arithmetic in that company and had done it since the first road.
“He is not a witness,” she said. “Say that first, because it matters.”
“He saw the page,” said Veylan.

“He saw the page and he read it and he did not file it. That is not witnessing. Witnessing is standing up in a room and saying what you saw and having somebody write it down against your name. He has nothing to say. He never went west. He has never stood on the ridge and he has never seen the wall.”
“Then what is he?” said Old Den.

“He is the second read,” said Mira. “That is the whole of it. The page exists in a mill ledger and one clerk in the county has read it and not filed it. That is a different thing from a witness and it is worth more than a witness to the counties, because a witness can be dismissed and a read cannot.”
“Say that again,” said Riss.

“A witness can be dismissed,” said Mira. “The counties dismissed four hundred witnesses in the war and never lost a page. But a clerk who has read a page and not filed it is inside the machine. He cannot dismiss himself. He will go back to his desk and he will be sitting in it, every day, with the sheet in his coat.”
Nahl looked at the county clerk, who was sitting at the end of the table with a cup he had not drunk from and his coat still buttoned.
“Then we do not need him to do anything,” said Nahl.
“No,” said Mira. “That is exactly what I am saying. A second read does not do anything. It just is. One clerk at a time.”
The county clerk took the sheet out of his coat.
He did that near the end of the evening, and he did it without any prompting, and it was the only thing he did that nobody in the company had expected.
He unbuttoned his coat and took out a county page, folded twice, and opened it on the long table, and put his hand on it, and pushed it across to Nahl.
“That is the twelfth sheet of the Ash bundle,” said Maro Holl. “It came into the counting house four weeks ago. Eleven sheets of it were ordinary. That is the twelfth.”
Nahl looked at it.

It was county stock, pale grey, ruled in the four columns. On the front of it, in a magistrate’s hand, somebody had gone through a party on the western approach, item by item, in the way the law required.
Three horses, returned to the parish of Ash.
One cart, sold at the county rate, fee entered.
Twelve ledger books, county stock, seized.
Forty copy sheets, seized.
One tin box, contents: soil, returned to the party.
Party of no account. No names given. Nothing taken. No fee.

And in the fourth column, in the space where four hundred thousand reasons had been written by Maro Holl in thirty years, there was a notch and a group of five small vertical strokes, cut into the page with the nib in an angry hand.
Nahl sat and looked at it for a long time.
“That is the mark on the stone above Orphiel,” they said at last.
“I do not know who Orphiel is,” said Maro Holl.
“He is the man the mark belongs to,” said Nahl. “It is a tally. A bearer’s tally. A notch and a group of five, which is how a man counts something he is going to remember and not write down.”
Maro Holl looked at the page.
“Then the magistrate copied a tally,” he said.

“The magistrate copied a tally,” said Nahl. “Or he cut one of his own. It travels either way. The same mark is on a plank at a waystation above the last grass, cut a hundred years ago by somebody nobody has ever heard of. It is on the stone of a grave on the ridge. It is now on a county sheet on a mill table.”
“Three men who never met,” said Maro Holl.
“Three men who never met,” said Nahl.
Then Nahl folded the sheet, along the fold that was already in it, and pushed it back across the table.
“It is yours,” they said. “Keep it in your coat.”
“What do I do with it?”

“Nothing,” said Nahl. “That is the difference between your trade and mine and it is the whole of what I have to give you. Do not file it. Carry it. I have carried a log a thousand miles and I have never once signed it, and the man who gave it to me said the same thing to me on a grass road four months ago. You will not sign it. You will carry it. That is the difference.”
Sancora did the other thing, which nobody else would have thought of.
She got up before he left and stood in front of him and looked at his face and his hands the way she had looked at eight people on a mountain twice a day for nine days.
“Your hands are cold,” she said.
“They are always cold,” said Maro Holl.

“Your face is grey and your hands are cold and you have been awake about a week,” said Sancora. “You will go back down the river tomorrow and you will sit at a desk with a page in your coat and you will not sleep, and in about four months your chest will start to hurt on the left side and you will tell nobody, because you are a clerk and clerks do not report themselves.”
Maro Holl stood in the doorway of the mill’s back room with his coat buttoned and his bag in his hand and did not answer her.
“Report yourself,” said Sancora. “That is my trade and it is the whole of it. Go home and tell your wife that your chest hurts, and do it in the first week, not in the fourth.”
He went south at the sixth hour on the carrier’s cart.

The company stood in the yard and watched him go. That is what a company does with a man who has read its page. The mill boy put his bag on the cart. The goat lay against the mill door with its back to the road and did not look up.

Ivet Sallow stood at the office door with her arms crossed and watched until the cart was out of the gate. Then she went back inside to her counter. The mill had grain coming in at noon, and a clerk does not stand in a yard.
The plate hummed the third note under Riss’s shirt all morning.

Kael’s burned hand stopped hurting at about the time the cart crossed the bridge. He did not say so. He stood with the hand open at his side and looked at it once, the way a man looks at a tool that has finished a job.

There was still no wind in Ashenford. There had not been for three weeks and a day, and the county paper would have called it weather, and Corvath called it the second thing he had ever smelled that he could not explain.

Maro Holl went down the river with a county page folded twice in his coat and nothing written anywhere about what he had read, and the company had a second witness, and neither side of it was ever going to be a document.
Above the mill there was nothing to see. Rain, and county sky, and the Emberion somewhere behind it.

Down at the bridge the gold road and the grey road ran side by side across the water and away south into the counties. Neither of them shone. There was nobody on either of them in any direction that a man could see.

chapters.label: Chapter 28
chapters.title: The Road East
paragraphs: After the county clerk went south with a page in his coat, and the mill went back to its grain, and a week went by, the company had to decide what to do next.

They had done what they came to do. That was the difficulty. For four months there had been a thing in front of them that had to be carried somewhere and given to somebody, and now it had been carried and given.

The page was stitched in. The count had been spoken. The name had been said. A clerk of the county had read the page and had not filed it, and had gone back to his desk with a mark in his fourth column and no intention of writing it up.
There was nothing left on the list.
They worked it out in the yard over four days, in the way the company worked everything out, which was slowly and with the practical people first.
Veylan started it, because he was the one who had been standing in the yard from the beginning.
“We cannot stay here,” he said.
“No,” said Riss.

“I am not saying it because I do not like the mill. I am saying it because I have watched this town for four weeks and the town has watched us. There are eight people with no papers and one goat and a county clerk has been up the river and read a page in the ledger. Every day we stand in this yard we are eight more reasons for somebody to ask Ivet Sallow a question.”
“Say the rest,” said Riss.

“The rest is that I would like to see the farm before the turn of the year,” said Veylan. “I have a tin of west soil in my coat and forty-one dead seedlings in a crate at the foot of a mountain, and if I am going to try a season on the high field I need to be there before the frost is out of the ground.”
“That is west,” said Mira.
“That is west,” said Veylan. “But I am not going alone and I am not going today, and I have walked enough to know what I am asking.”
Then the others said their pieces, in turn, which is what a company does when it cannot decide.
Sancora said hers standing up, because she always stood when she said a thing that mattered.

“It is written down,” she said. “That is mine and I am taking it and I will say it once. On the mountain I said that I had kept eight alive and that I would like to know what they were kept alive for, and that I would like it written down somewhere before I was too old to read it. It is written down. It is four columns on a leaf of paper in a mill ledger behind a counter, eleven feet from where I am standing, and I have read every word of it twice.”
“Does it say what they were kept alive for?” said Nahl.
“No,” said Sancora. “It says a report was made by people who walked here on foot. That is what it says. That is what there is.”
Mira said hers with the chart on the table.

“I am not putting the mill on the chart,” she said. “Not the yard and not the room and not the ledger. The chart has roads and villages and boundaries and one grave on it, and if I start drawing the insides of buildings it stops being a chart and becomes a diary. The mill goes in the Leaf as a place we were, with a date, and nothing else.”
“What about the count?” said Veylan.
“The count goes in the Leaf as a count that was spoken and not written,” said Mira. “That is the only entry I am making this month, and it does not have a number in it, and I will not put one in.”

That evening Riss made the entry herself, at the mill’s long table, with both lamps lit and the company round the table. The Leaf is a keeper’s book. A keeper writes it in the room where the thing happened.
She wrote four lines.
Tenth month, fifteenth day. Ashenford West. The mill on the Vellum.
A clerk kept our page. Her name is Ivet Sallow. She has kept eighty-one names of her own at the back of a ledger for four years.
She has never sent them up the river.
The page is stitched into the mill’s ledger, behind the ruled pages, with her other leaves. Nothing was taken from us and no fee is due on any part of it.
The count of this company was spoken in that room, standing. It is not written here and it is not written anywhere.
She read it back to them and nobody corrected anything.
Then she asked the one question a keeper asks at the end of an entry.
“Does anybody want to say anything to the Leaf?”
“Say that the man who read it did not file it,” said Nahl.
Riss wrote that in as well.
Kael said his in about six words, because he had been saying less and less since the ridge.
“My hand has stopped,” said Kael. “I do not know what I am for now.”
“You are for the next thing,” said Riss.
“That is what I am afraid of,” said Kael, and that was the whole of it.
Corvath said his, and his was the shortest and the strangest of the eight.
“I can smell this place,” said Corvath.
Everybody looked at him.

“I have not smelled anything since the river,” said Corvath. “Not the chimney and not the ice and not the goat. This morning I came down into the yard and I could smell bread and wet stone and the river. It is the first thing I have smelled in four months and I would like somebody to write down the date.”
“It did not use a column,” said Riss.
“It did not use a column,” said Corvath. “I am telling you anyway.”
Then Old Den said his, and Old Den had been the oldest man in every room he had been in for nineteen years, and he said it like a man making a plan.

“I came west to see the end of a thing,” said Old Den. “I have seen it. There is a wall at the top of the world with a form cut in the ice and a dragon behind it that counted us and did not file us, and I will be dead inside ten years and I would like those ten years to go east.”
“East is the counties,” said Mira.
“East is everything,” said Old Den. “West of this mill there are mountains and no roads and one grave. I have done all four months of west that a man of sixty-two has in him. I am going east.”
Then Nahl said the thing that settled it, and Nahl said it last because a bearer speaks after the company has spoken and not before.
They had the log on their knees while the others talked, and they had not opened it and did not open it now.

“I have carried this log for four months,” said Nahl. “Nine thousand and four entries and a fourth column that nobody has ever used. It belongs to a dead man and there is no page anywhere with his name on it, and I have not found a room in the eleven counties where a book like that can be put.”
“And you have stopped looking,” said Riss.

“I have stopped looking,” said Nahl. “That is the whole of what the mill did to me. A room with a clerk is not a place where a thing gets filed. It is a place where a thing gets said out loud and written down by somebody else and left standing. The page in that ledger is the only page in the counties with the truth in the fourth column, and it is behind eighty-one names in a mill account book, and Maro Holl has gone south with a mark in his coat that he will never write up.”
“So where does the log go?” said Veylan.

“East with me,” said Nahl. “And when it wears out I will not copy it, and when somebody asks me for it I will not give it, and when I die it will go wherever bearers’ things go, which is nowhere. That is not a failure. That is the trade.”
The keeper and the clerk had their conversation on the loading bay, in the last of the light, on the evening before the company went.
It was Riss’s doing. Riss went up to the office at the end of the day with the Leaf in the case and stood at the counter and waited until Ivet had closed the day book.
“Sit down,” said Ivet. “You are making the counter nervous.”
“I have one thing to say and then I have two questions.”
“Say the thing.”
Riss put the Leaf on the counter between them.

“It did not occur to any of us until we were three days on the road,” said Riss, “that a clerk in Ashenford West had already put her hand up for this four months before we got here. You un-ticked a box in the third month. You started keeping names at the back of a ledger four years before that. There is not one of us who has done anything you had not already done, and you did it alone in a mill office with no company and nobody to tell.”
“Say the questions,” said Ivet Sallow.
“You kept the page,” said Riss.
“I kept the page,” said Ivet.
“What happens now?”
Ivet Sallow looked at the closed ledger on the shelf behind her for a while.
“I do not know,” she said. “I have never kept a page before.”
Riss made the offer then, and it was the only offer the company made in the whole of the four months.
It was short and it was practical and it was made on the loading bay because Riss had already worked out that the office was a room where a clerk could not say no.

“Stay,” said Riss. “Not the eight of us. Me. I keep books. I can add a column and I can write a fair hand and I have kept a signed account of a company for eleven years. You have a mill and a counter and eighty-one names and a page five leaves deep, and one clerk on the river road. When the county asks its next question you will need somebody in this office with you who has already been asked one.”
Ivet Sallow stood with her arms crossed and looked at the yard.
“No,” she said.
“You have not thought about it.”

“I have thought about it for three weeks,” said Ivet. “That is why the answer is no. Do you know what you have done? You have carried a log a thousand miles. You have stood at the top of a wall and been counted by something that nobody has ever seen and you have kept the number in your mouths the whole way home. You have a page in a ledger with the truth in the fourth column and a county clerk with a mark in his coat. There are eight of you and there is nobody else in the eleven counties, and if the two of you keepers both stop walking in a mill in Ashenford, the whole of it is one page in one book.”
“That is enough,” said Riss.
“No,” said Ivet Sallow. “It is enough in fifty years. It is not enough now. You have carried this a thousand miles. You do not stay. You go. I keep the page. That is the room.”
The refusal took two people to make and both of them made it, which is the only way a refusal of that kind holds.
It came up because Riss asked the wrong question at the wrong moment.
“Would you let us take a copy of it?” said Riss. “Not the leaf. A copy. Four columns on a sheet, in my hand, for the Leaf, so that when we are east and you are here there is one page in two places.”
“No,” said Ivet Sallow.
“I can copy it exactly.”

“That is exactly the problem,” said Ivet. “A copy of a page is a page. If you copy that leaf, then there is a sheet of fine paper in a satchel going east, and a sheet of fine paper in a ledger staying here, and in six months there are two pages and nobody can say which one is the record.”
“Then we take the leaf,” said Veylan, from the doorway, who had been listening and had opinions. “She can write the page again later and stitch the new one in. We take the original east with us.”
“No,” said Ivet Sallow, and this time she said it to the room.
“Why not?” said Veylan.

“Because a page in a satchel is a rumour,” said Ivet. “A page stitched in a ledger is a record. The whole value of that leaf is that it is in a book with eighty-one names in front of it and a mill’s mark on the counter underneath it, and that anybody who ever wants to know whether it happened can walk into this office and ask to see it and I will have to get it down.”
“And if the county takes the book?”

“Then the county takes the book,” said Ivet, “and the page goes with it, and it is a page in a book either way, and it will have to be dealt with by somebody, and somebody is where I want it. A page in a pocket is where a thing goes to die.”
So the company refused to take the page and Ivet refused to let them, and the page stayed in the ledger at the back, five leaves behind the ruled pages, and neither side of it was ever written down.
They went on the fourth morning.

Ivet Sallow gave them nothing. That was deliberate on both sides and it was the last piece of procedure in the whole affair: no letter, no pass, no character, no line in the register, no discount on the mill’s oats. She came out into the yard with her keys on her arm and stood by the cart while Veylan loaded it, and did not help and did not say anything about the load.
The company’s property, when it was all on the cart, came to this.
One log, brown and heavy, cord tied, nine thousand and four entries, carried by the bearer.
One small Leaf in a case with a strip of cloth round the spine, carried by the keeper.
One tin box of west soil in a farmer’s inside pocket.
One coil of cord and a compass and a chart in a tube, carried by a mapmaker.
Two satchels of linen and knives and dried roots, carried by a healer.
One slate in a pack that had nothing on it in nineteen days.
One pair of good boots that had been worn out twice and mended twice by an old man of sixty-two.
Nothing else. No page. No paper with a number on it. Nothing with any of their names at the foot of it anywhere in the world.

“Do not come back through the counties in daylight,” said Ivet Sallow, at the gate, in the flattest voice in the world. “The carrier comes up on Thursdays and I read the road book every week, and the assize sits in the spring.”
“We know,” said Riss.
“I am not a fool,” said Ivet. “I know the two of you know. I am saying it because I will worry about it otherwise, and I do not have room to worry about it.”
Then she went back inside, because the mill had grain coming in at eleven and a clerk does not stand at a gate.
The goat walked ahead.

That was the thing the company noticed and did not talk about, the same way they had not talked about it on the descent when it walked behind. For four months, out and back, it had walked in front of the column on the way out and behind it on the way home. In Ashenford it had lain against the mill door with its back to the road for four weeks.

On the fourth morning it stood up before the cart was loaded and walked out of the gate. It waited on the road, facing east. When the company came out it went on ahead of them down the river road at the same steady pace it had used on the climb.
It never looked back at the mill, and it never looked back at the peaks, and it did not look back once in the whole of the first day.

The plate hummed the third note under Riss’s shirt all morning. Not the divided fifth and not the clean one. It was the note that had been missing from the middle of it, quiet and even. It hummed the way a thing hums when it has finished being an interval and has become a key.

Kael’s burned hand did not hurt. It had not hurt since the county clerk went south. He kept the glove off it and kept looking at it. That worried Sancora and did not worry Riss. Riss had seen the same look on a man who has finished a job he is not sure he was right to do.
There was no wind.

There had been no wind in Ashenford for three weeks and four days. The company walked east out of the town with the river on their left. The county road ran on ahead of them into the interior and the goat walked in front. Nobody in the eight of them said a word about a home, because none of them had one. They had a mill and a clerk and a page and a count and a name. That was the whole of what they had carried out of the west and back into the counties.
Above them the sky was county sky, and behind the rain the Emberion was up there somewhere with its fifteen joints and the piece missing out of the wing and nobody had seen it in four weeks.
At the bridge, where the road crossed the Vellum, the gold road and the grey road ran side by side out of the town and on to the east. Neither of them shone.
There was nobody on either of them in any direction that a man could see.

chapters.label: Chapter 29
chapters.title: The Road East
paragraphs: After the company left Ashenford on the fourth morning, they walked east on the river road for nine days. The page stayed behind them, stitched in a mill ledger. Nothing anywhere had their names at the foot of it.
There was nothing on the list.

That was the strange part of the ninth day and it kept being the strange part of every day after it. For four months there had been a thing in front of them. A wall. A form. A bone. A grave. A mill. A clerk. A page.
Now there was a road. The river was on the left. The county road ran ahead of them into the interior. The goat walked in front and did not look back.
The company walked in the same order it had walked out of the counties in the spring.
The goat first, because the goat had decided that.
Then Nahl, with the log in the pack and the cord tied.
Then Riss, with the case that held the Leaf.
Then Mira with the chart in its tube, then Sancora, then Corvath, then Veylan with the tin inside his coat, then Kael with the empty slate, and Old Den last, at his own pace, with his boots.
Nobody had told them to walk in that order. It had happened on the first day out of the mill gate and nobody had changed it since.
The log was the weight.
Nahl worked that out in the first three days and then stopped thinking about it, because a bearer does not complain about a load. But it was the log, and it was not the log’s two pounds.

A bearer carries a thing to the person it belongs to. That is the whole of the office and it is a clean trade. A letter goes to a woman in a village and you put it in her hand and you are done. A summons goes to a man at a gate and you wait for the mark and walk away. There is a person at the other end of it every time, and the end of the walking is always the same, which is a hand out in front of you and something leaving your care.

The log did not have a person at the other end of it. The log’s clerk was under five stones on a ridge four hundred miles behind them. There was no hand to put it in. There was no office in the eleven counties that could take a book with nine thousand and four entries and no reason in any of them.
So Nahl carried it the way a man carries a stone from a beach: because he had picked it up, and because putting it down somewhere would be a claim about who it belonged to.
The country east of Ashenford was smaller than the country west of it.

That was Mira’s observation on the sixth day and it was exact, the way her observations were exact. West of the river there were long fields and low walls and the grass running up to the last grass and then the mountains. East of the river there were hedges, and gates, and lanes that went nowhere, and every field had a name cut into a stone at the corner of it.

The counties had been surveyed out here for two hundred years. Every hedge was a boundary and every boundary had a paper behind it, and the papers had gone to the assize and the assize had ruled on them, and out of the rulings the county books had been made.
“It is all columns out here,” said Mira, at the sixth day’s stop.
“Say the rest of it,” said Riss.

“There is no land in this country that is not in a book,” said Mira. “That is what the wall was for. That is what the mark in the reason column was about. We came out of the only place in the world that nobody ever wrote down, and we are walking into the place where everybody did.”
The fingerpost came on the ninth day.

It stood where three lanes met, on a rise, with a stone under it and a hedge on two sides. It was a county fingerpost. A dressed oak post eight feet high, with arms bolted to the head of it. Each arm was painted and lettered in the county script.
The post had four arms once. Nahl could see where the fourth had been, because the bolt holes were still there and the paint under the eastern holes was darker than the paint next to it.
“We are not going to talk about the east arm,” said Riss.
“We are not going to talk about the east arm,” said Nahl.

The three surviving arms said **Rowan Cross** and **Carden** and **Whitbridge**, and each of them had a small carved number under the name, which was the mileage, and a small carved mark beside the number, which was the parish.
Nothing on the post named the east.
Veylan stood in front of it for a while with his hands in his coat and read all three arms twice.
“Which road are we taking?” he said.
“The east one,” said Mira.
“There is no east one. There are three arms and none of them points east and the fourth one is gone.”
“There is a road,” said Mira. “It is the one the hedge lets through. It goes east. Nobody has put a county arm on it.”
The refusal came out of that post and it took the company the whole of the afternoon. It was the first refusal they had had to make since the ridge. The shape of it was new.

The difficulty was simple. A company on a road with no destination has to say something when a man asks where it is going. It has to say something to itself when it stops for the night. It has to say something to the boy at the tollgate and the woman at the well.

The easy answers were all names. The next town. The coast. The mountains. The next county seat. Veylan said three of them out loud at the post, and each one was better than the last, because Veylan was a farmer and a farmer on a road is a farmer thinking about a field.
Then Nahl said the thing, and the company stood in the road at the foot of a fingerpost and agreed to it.

“We do not name the room before we find it,” said Nahl. “That is the whole of it. A destination is a claim. If I stand on a road and say we are going to Carden, then we have made a page in our own heads about where this company belongs, and that page has a name at the top of it and a place at the foot of it, and the first man who asks us whether we got there has put us in a column.”
“So we do not say,” said Veylan.

“We do not say,” said Riss. “We walk east. If the road bends north we walk north, and if a village is in front of us we stop in it, and if there is a room with a clerk in it we sit in the room. And we do not write the name of the next place anywhere, and we do not say *we are going to* anything, because the moment a company says where it is going, somebody can meet it there.”
Veylan looked at the post.
“And if somebody asks?”
“Then we say the truth,” said Nahl, “which is that we are walking east.”
The keepers had their conversation an hour after the post, on the long straight piece of road where the hedge on the left had a gap and the river showed through it.
It was short and neither of them felt the need to dress it up.
“What do we do now?” said Riss.
“We carry it,” said Nahl.
“Carry it where?”
“East,” said Nahl. “Until we find the next room.”
They walked east and the road let them.
