That is worth saying plainly about the day after the fingerpost, because the company noticed it and talked about it that night around the fire. The eastern lane was not on any arm and had no name on any post, and it was in better repair than the roads on the post. It was drained. It had been metalled in the last twenty years and the metal had been rolled and the edges had been cut. It ran between two hedges and through three gates that all opened, and at every gate there was a stone with a name cut into it, and the name was always different and never a place: they were people’s names.
“Who mends a road that is on no post?” said Veylan.
“Somebody who uses it,” said Old Den.
“Who uses it?”
“People who do not want to be on a post,” said Old Den, and would not be drawn further, because he was sixty-two and had spent his life on roads that were on no post.
They met a tollgate on the tenth day and it was the first time in four months that Nahl had to use the trade on a stranger, because a gate is a place where a man keeps a book.

The gate stood across the lane with a bar and a chain and a small stone house beside it, and the gatekeeper was an old man in a coat with two buttons and a ledger on the sill of the window, and he came out and put his hand flat on the bar and looked at the company the way a man looks at a thing he has to write down.
“Names,” he said.
“We have none to give,” said Nahl.
“Then I cannot open the gate,” said the gatekeeper. “The book has a line for every party that comes through and I have kept it for eleven years. It is four crowns a cart and a penny a person.”
Veylan put the toll on the sill, in coin, and the gatekeeper counted it twice and put it in his pocket and then stood looking at the ledger with the pen in his hand.
“There is a line here for the names,” he said. “What do I put?”
“Nothing,” said Nahl.

“I cannot put nothing. There is a printed box and the box has a heading and the heading is *party*. If I put nothing in the box then the line is not a line and the four crowns are not in the book, and the four crowns are in the book because this gate is audited twice a year.”
“Then put what you like,” said Riss, from the cart. “It cannot be worse than what the counties have already put.”

The gatekeeper thought about it for a while with the pen in his hand. Then he wrote four words and closed the book and went to the bar and lifted it, and the company went through, and Nahl, who was last, looked back at the sill and the open ledger and read the line upside down.
*Party of no account. Nothing taken. Nothing owed.*

It was the same line the counties had written on a seizure sheet in the ninth month of the year, in a magistrate’s hand, with a mark in the fourth column. The counties had written it to make a company disappear. The gatekeeper had written it to make his day’s arithmetic come out.
They meant the same thing on the page and they meant two entirely different things under it, and Nahl carried that down the road for a mile without saying it out loud.
They met a carrier on the eleventh day and it was the first time in four months that Nahl had to use the trade on a stranger.

The carrier was a thin man with a good cart and a bad mule, going west toward Ashenford with three crates and a mail bag. He stopped in the middle of the road and looked the company up and down. That is what a carrier does.
“Are you for hire?” he said.
“No,” said Nahl.
“What are you, then?”
Nahl stood in the road and considered the question, because a bearer answers questions and does not dodge them.
“We are a company walking east,” said Nahl.
“With a goat and eight people and no load worth carrying?”
“That is the whole of it.”
The carrier looked at the pack on Nahl’s back and at Riss’s case and at Veylan’s coat.
“There is a mail bag on this cart,” he said. “For Ashenford. Do you want to put a letter in it? It costs four crowns and it will be there in two days.”
“No,” said Nahl.
“Nothing at all?”
“Nothing at all,” said Nahl. “There is one thing and it does not go in a satchel. We carry it ourselves.”

The carrier shrugged and clicked at his mule and went west. Nahl stood in the road for a moment after he had gone. A bearer’s trade has one weakness in it and this was the weakness. A bearer who will not put anything in anybody’s bag is a bearer who will never be believed.

At the eleventh day’s end there was a farm gate with a woman standing at it with a pail, and she offered them a hot meal in exchange for an hour’s work, framing the shocks, because her man’s back was out and there were four rows standing wet in a field.
The company refused the work and paid for the meal, and the woman thought that was strange and said so.

“You have eight pairs of hands and a cart,” she said. “There is a field behind me with four rows of shocks in it and my man cannot bend. An hour of your time is a meal for all of you and a bag of oats for the animal.”
“We do not take work,” said Mira.
“What is wrong with work?”

“Nothing at all,” said Mira. “But a man who works for a day is asked for his name at the end of it, and a man whose name goes in a farm book is a man the parish can find, and the parish is the county’s last mile. Your field is a good field and your offer is a fair one and I am telling you the truth, which is that we cannot be in a book.”
The woman looked at the eight of them, one at a time, and then at the goat.
“You are running,” she said.
“We are walking,” said Nahl. “That is the whole difference and it is the only thing I can give you.”

The woman gave them the meal anyway for the toll-money and would not take more, and the company ate it standing at her gate with their backs to the field, and Mira did not draw the farm and did not put it on the chart, because a chart is for roads.
The road went east for six more days.

The autumn went the way autumn goes in the counties, which is all at once. The hedges turned and then thinned. The days came in shorter and the mornings came in white. Sancora put the company onto two cooked meals a day and made them all sleep four to a bedroll. When Veylan complained about the bedrolls she told him exactly what a man his age dies of in a cold field. She said it in the flat voice she used for a diagnosis. He stopped complaining the same day.

Kael’s hand was quiet the whole way. He walked with the glove off it and kept it out of his coat. He looked at it every morning before the company started, the way a man checks a tool. It was quiet. He said so on the fourteenth day, with a kind of wonder in it that nobody in the company liked.

Corvath smelled everything. That was the other change and it went the other way. He had not smelled a thing for four months. Now he smelled the rain coming two hours before it came and the smoke of a fire on the far side of a hill. He told them at every stop, unprompted, in the flat voice of a man reporting a fact.
“It is a nuisance,” said Corvath. “I have four months of nothing to make up for and I am doing it all at once.”
The plate hummed the third note the whole way.

Under Riss’s shirt, every day: not the divided fifth and not the clean one. It was the note that had been missing from the middle of it. It hummed from the mill gate to the hedge lane to the gap where the river showed through. Quiet. Even. Present.

Riss listened to it the way a person listens to a kettle in another room. Not at all, most of the time. Then all at once, four or five times a day, with a small cold start that never turned into anything.
There was no wind.
Above them there was county sky and rain and, somewhere behind it, the Emberion with its fifteen joints and the piece missing out of the wing, and nobody in the company had seen it since the mill.

At the gap in the hedge the gold road and the grey road showed at the bottom of the valley, running side by side across the water and away north and south. Neither of them shone. There was nobody on either of them in any direction that a man could see.

At the end of the fifteenth day the company stopped at a village on the road with a tavern and a church and a ford. Nahl looked at the village for a while before they went down into it. Then they said the thing that had been building for six days.
“There is a room in that village,” they said.
“There is a tavern in that village,” said Veylan.
“There is a room in that village with a book in it,” said Nahl, “and I am going to find out whether it can hear us.”

chapters.label: Chapter 30
chapters.title: The Next Room
paragraphs: After the seventeenth day on the road east, with the frost coming down out of the north and the hedges bare and the goat walking in front, the company came into a village called Odder.
It was a small place and it was a complete one. That was what struck Mira first and she said it out loud at the top of the hill.

A church with a squat tower. A ford where the lane crossed a stream. A green with a well on it. Fourteen houses, eleven of them with smoke. A tavern with a painted sign hanging off an iron bracket. Two fields of winter wheat with a low wall around them. A mill, but a small one, a water mill of two storeys with the wheel not turning.
“There is a book in that village,” said Mira.
“There is always a book in a village,” said Nahl.
“Yes,” said Mira. “But that one has a tower and a stone wall round the churchyard, and a book with a tower is kept by somebody who does not move.”
The tavern was called the Bell and it had a fire and a table long enough for eight.

They paid for the night and got two rooms and a place in the barn. The woman who kept the tavern warned them about the goat. Then she gave up on the goat, because it lay down against the door with its back to the road and would not move.
They ate at the long table. Sancora made sure of the food first and then let the company eat it the way a company eats when it has had fifteen days of cold rations: fast, and without much talk.
The plate hummed under Riss’s shirt. The fire was hot. Corvath said it smelled of wood smoke and bacon and wet wool, which it did.

And the man at the end of the room by the window kept looking at them over the top of a book. He was not a tavern keeper and he was not a farmer. Mira worked out what he was in about ten minutes. She had been in rooms with clerks since the spring.

His name was Anselm Reed. He was seventy-one years old and he had been the parish clerk of Odder for forty-nine of those years. He came down to the Bell for his supper six nights a week. His wife had died in the third year of the war and he did not like cooking.
He came over to the table with his book under his arm after the company had eaten, which he did after half an hour, and stood at the end of the table and looked at all of them in turn.
“You are from the west,” he said.
“We are from the west,” said Mira.

“Nobody comes from the west,” said Anselm Reed. “There is nothing out there. That is what they teach us. There is a line of stones on the border and after that there is grass and then nothing at all.”
“That is close to the truth,” said Mira. “There is grass and then a mountain.”
He sat down with them because there was a fire and because a company of strangers in Odder was the largest event of Anselm Reed’s year.
The churchyard walk happened the next morning, before the company left, because Mira asked for it and Anselm Reed took her.

It was a cold bright morning with the frost going off the stones and the two of them went round the tower on the north side, where the wall ran along a hedge and the ground behind it fell away toward the stream.

The wall was knee-high and old and there was a row of stones in the grass against it, flat stones, no names, no dates, no cut letters. Nineteen of them in one run and eleven more beyond a gap where the grass had not been cut.
“Thirty,” said Anselm Reed. “That is the whole of it. They lie in a row because a row is how you dig when you have no names to keep them apart.”
Mira went down the row and did what she had done at the outcrop above the last grass, which was to put her hand flat on the ground and think about what was under it.
Then she stopped, because there was nothing here to measure.

That was the whole of it and it took her a moment to understand what had happened to her trade. On the mountain above the last grass there had been a form cut in ice, three columns full and one never used, and she had measured it in section and in plan and refused a copy, and her measurement had been worth something to the company because a measurement is a thing that can be carried.

Here there was a row of thirty people with no names, and the only measurement that mattered was the distance from the wall to the hedge, and that was a measurement of the place a person could not be entered, and it did not need her. It had been the same number for two hundred years and it would be the same number in two hundred more.
“Do you want to know their names?” said Anselm Reed.
“There are none,” said Mira.

“There are names,” said the parish clerk. “I know eleven of them and my father knew nineteen. They are not written anywhere. That is the difference between a name and an entry, and I have been a clerk for forty-nine years and I have never once been able to explain it to anybody.”

Mira did not draw the row. She drew the church, and the ford, and the lane, and left the north wall off the chart, because a chart with a row of nameless graves on it would be a chart that made a claim about them.
And that is when Mira asked for the book, and got it, and asked the questions that made the rest of the evening.
“You keep the parish book,” said Mira.
“I do,” said Anselm Reed.
“What do you keep in it?”
“Names,” he said. “Births. Deaths. The things that happen.”

He put the book down on the long table, which took both hands, because a parish register is a heavy thing. He opened it in the middle where the current leaves were. There they were: four ruled columns and a date column and a page number, in three different hands.

Christenings in the first column. Marriages in the second. Burials in the third. And beside the burials, in the fourth column, in a smaller hand and a different ink, a set of short entries: *with whom*, and then a name.

“That column only gets used when there was somebody at the grave who asked for it,” said Anselm Reed. “It is used nine times in forty years. The county wants it used always. Two of the last three vicars tried to make it the rule and could not, because a man standing at a grave with his hat in his hands does not want to be asked who the dead one belonged to.”
Mira looked at the book for a while. Then she asked the question that she had actually come down the road east to ask.
“What about the things that don’t happen?”
“What kind of thing?”

“A person who dies in this parish and is not in that book,” said Mira. “A stranger. A foundling. A man who came off the road with no papers and no parish and no name that anybody was willing to write at the top of a page.”
Anselm Reed sat back in his chair.
“There is no column for that,” he said.
Then he told them the whole of it, because he was seventy-one and there was a fire and nobody had asked him this question in forty-nine years.

“There are thirty people in the ground behind that church who are not in this book,” he said. “I dug six of them myself and my father dug nineteen of the rest and the vicar’s man dug the others. There is a corner of the yard behind the wall on the north side, where the ground is soft in a row, and that is where a person goes who cannot be entered.”
“Cannot be entered,” said Mira.

“Persons of no account,” said Anselm Reed. “That is the county’s phrase, not mine. If a man dies with no papers and nobody to stand up for him, the parish cannot put him in the book, because the book is for the parish and a person of no account is not the parish’s. It is not cruelty. It is arithmetic. There is a column and the column has a heading, and if the man’s name cannot go under the heading, then the man does not go in the book.”
“And he goes in the ground anyway.”

“He goes in the ground anyway,” said Anselm Reed. “That is the part the county has never worked out. The book is not where a person is. The book is where a person is remembered. Those are two different places and they have never been the same place, and I have spent forty-nine years standing between them with a pen in my hand.”
Then Riss asked the other question, and it was the one the whole company had come down the hill for.
“What would you write in that book if we asked you to enter us?”
Anselm Reed looked at the eight of them and at the goat at the door.

“Nothing,” he said. “I cannot. You are not of this parish and you have no papers and no names that I have been given. If I put eight strangers in that book under the burials column, I would be a parish clerk writing a story.”
“Then you will not write us in,” said Riss.
“I will not write you in,” said Anselm Reed.
And the company made its refusal on the other side of the same sentence, which is what they had learned in the mill and had carried east.
“We are not here to be entered,” said Nahl.
“Then what are you?”
“We are here to be counted,” said Nahl.
They did it in the tavern, in front of the fire, with the parish clerk of Odder sitting at the end of the long table and the tavern keeper’s wife stopped in the doorway with a cloth in her hand.
Nahl stood up.
The company stood up with them, in a line along the table, in the order they walked on the road: Riss, Kael, Mira, Veylan, Sancora, Corvath, Old Den, Nahl at the end by the fire.
“A bearer reports,” said Nahl. “That is the whole of the office. This is not a report. This is a count.”
Then they counted.
“Forwards. Riss. Kael. Mira. Veylan. Sancora. Corvath. Old Den. Myself. Backwards. Myself. Old Den. Corvath. Sancora. Veylan. Mira. Kael. Riss.”
“Eight,” said Nahl.
Nobody wrote anything down.

Mira watched the parish clerk’s hands the whole time, because that was her trade and she watched everything that could be measured. Anselm Reed had a pen in his coat and a book open on the table in front of him and forty-nine years of the habit of writing down a thing the moment it was said out loud.
And his hand went to his coat, and stopped, and came back to the table.
That was the whole of what Mira had come east to see and she watched it happen and did not draw it.
The parish clerk asked Nahl one more question, at the end, with the book closed and his hands flat on it.
“Why is it not written anywhere?”

“Because the number belongs to the company,” said Nahl. “A count that is written down becomes an entry, and an entry is how a thing stops being remembered. If I write that number on a page and give it to a man, then the man has it and I do not have to hold it. I would rather hold it.”
“For how long?”

“Until I die,” said Nahl. “And then the company will hold it after me, if the company is still walking, and if it is not, then the number is lost, and that is the trade. That is what a bearer is for. A bearer is a person who holds a thing that no page will hold.”
Anselm Reed sat and thought about that for a while with his hand flat on a book of forty-nine years of the things that happened.

“I have written the things that happen in this village for half a century,” he said. “There is a corner of my yard where thirty people lie who could not go under a heading. And here you are in my tavern, with the goat at my door, telling me that the number is not the entry and the book is not the person.”
“That is the whole of it,” said Nahl.

“Then you be careful on the road,” said Anselm Reed, “because there is nothing in any of my books that will remember you, and I am the only clerk in this parish, and you were inside my door for one night.”
They went on in the morning.

The company paid for its two rooms and its place in the barn. It left nothing behind in the tavern and took nothing away. The tavern keeper’s wife gave them a bag of bread and would not take money for it. Sancora accepted it, because a healer does not refuse food on a cold road.

Anselm Reed came out to the green in his coat and his hat while Veylan loaded the cart. He stood there with his hands in his pockets. He did not offer to put them in the book and he did not ask where they were going.

“They did it in the Bell,” said the tavern keeper’s wife at the door, to nobody in particular. By the time the company was over the ford the whole of Odder knew. Eight people with a goat had stood up in the tavern and been counted out loud, and nobody had written the number down.

Mira did not draw the book. She had the chart out that evening on the road. She put the village on it as a village, with the ford and the church and nothing else. A chart with the inside of a building on it stops being a chart.
They were three miles east of Odder when the tavern keeper’s wife’s bread ran out, and Mira said the thing she had been holding since the churchyard.
“That village talked about us before we were over the ford,” she said.
“Villages talk,” said Veylan.

“It is not the talking. It is what they had to talk about. There is nothing in that village to show that we were there. No name, no entry, no line in the book. What they have is a story about eight people who stood up in the Bell and were counted.”
“That is the practice,” said Riss.

“I know it is the practice,” said Mira. “I am telling you what it looks like from the outside, because I am the one who looks at things from the outside. They will tell it wrong within a year. The number will be eleven by the time it reaches the next parish. Somebody will say we had a bell.”
Nahl laughed at that, which happened about twice a month.

“Then that is the room,” said Nahl. “A room with a story in it that nobody wrote down. That is the widest column there is. It cannot be seized, and it cannot be corrected, and it goes out of the parish on its own feet.”

The company did the other thing the practice required of a room, which was to leave it alone. Nobody in Odder was going to get a letter. Nobody was going to get a copy. Nobody was going to be asked to remember anything and nobody was going to be asked to forget.
Later that day Sancora gave her opinion, which nobody had asked for and everybody needed.
“Two rooms, a fire, bread, and a man of seventy-one who keeps a book,” she said. “That is the best night this company has had since the mill, and I want it said, because I am the one who counts.”
“You have counted,” said Riss.

“I have counted. One night in a village. Nobody wrote anything. The old man asked the right questions and the company answered them standing up. If the whole of the practice comes to anything, it comes to that. Two nights would have been a farm and a fire and a hand out for our names.”
“One night,” said Riss.
“One night,” said Sancora. “That is the rule. I made it because of the frost and not because of the philosophy, and it turns out the philosophy is the same as the frost.”
Veylan said something under his breath about healers and philosophies, and the company went on east.
The plate hummed the third note the whole of the next morning.

The goat walked in front and did not look back at Odder once. There was still no wind. The frost held the hedges white until the sun was over them. Corvath said it smelled like iron and reedwater and snow coming, which it did.
Above the village the sky was county sky and the Emberion was behind it somewhere with its fifteen joints and the piece missing out of the wing.
Down in the valley the gold road and the grey road ran side by side away north and south with nobody on them in any direction that a man could see.

chapters.label: Chapter 31
chapters.title: The Count
paragraphs: After Odder there were two more villages and then three weeks of frost on the hedges. At the end of the eleventh month the company was on a road that had no name on any post.
They had done it four times by then and they had it down to a practice.

That is the word the company had arrived at by the end of the second village. Riss wrote it in the Leaf once and never wrote it again. A practice is not a plan and it is not a trade. A plan has an end and a trade has a customer. A practice is a thing you do because it is the thing you do, and it does not have a column for results.
The practice, as it stood at the end of the eleventh month, had nine parts.
Walk in at the end of the day and pay for what you take. Bread, bed, barn, grain for the goat, and money on the counter before anything is eaten.
Give no names, and take no work, and accept no paper.
Do not stay two nights in a village unless there is snow on the ground or a person is ill.

Find the clerk first, before the tavern. Every village has one. Sometimes it is the priest. Sometimes it is the person who keeps the parish book. Sometimes it is the woman who keeps the accounts for the mill. Every one of them can be found in an hour by asking who keeps the book.
Sit in a room with the book in it and say the count standing up.
Write nothing, and let the clerk write nothing.
Leave in the morning, and leave nothing behind, and take nothing away.
And when somebody asks where the company is going, say that the company is walking east.
Two of the four villages had heard it and two had not.

That was the arithmetic of the practice and the company had learned to expect it. In Odder the whole tavern had stopped and the parish clerk’s hand had gone to his coat and come back to the table. In Gorse the tavern keeper had wiped the same spot on the counter for the whole of the count. Then he charged them for the bread like nothing had happened. Neither of them could have said why.

In Marden it had gone the other way and it had gone badly for a quarter of an hour. There was a constable’s man in Marden who had watched the company come in. He had asked for their names in the street before they had found the tavern. Nahl had given him the trade’s answer, which is that a company walking east does not have names to give. The constable’s man had taken that exactly the way a constable’s man takes it. He had gone away and come back with a parish book and a demand. The company had stood in the road with their cart and refused him three times in flat voices. Then they had left Marden at dusk and walked six miles in the dark and slept in a barn.

Nobody had followed them. That was the whole of it. Nobody ever followed them. A company with no names in any book and no work and no paper is a company that a constable’s man cannot do anything about. That is a hard thing for a constable’s man to accept. He does accept it in the end, by doing nothing.
A girl at a well asked them a question at the end of the eleventh day. The company had stopped at that well to water the goat.
“What are you doing?” she said.
“Counting,” said Nahl.
“Counting what?”
“Counting us.”
The girl looked at the goat and at the cart.
“Are you going to write it down?”
“No.”
“Then how will you know?”
Nahl thought about that for a moment, because a child asks the real question and the trade has to have an answer for it.

“Because I will say it again tomorrow,” said Nahl. “And the day after that. And at the next well. A number you say every day is a number you keep. A number you write down once is a number you have given away.”

The girl considered this and took it as the truth, which is what children do with an answer that is not an insult. Then she went and told it in her house. By the morning the whole village had heard it. Eight people with a goat were counting themselves out loud and had no intention of writing anything down.
“Say the count,” said the girl, at the gate, when the company went out.
So they said it at the gate. Standing up, on the road, with a child watching them and nobody writing.

The snow came on the twelfth day and the company spent two nights in a farm’s hay barn with the door barred and the goat in with them, and on the second of those nights Sancora told Old Den the truth about his chest, because he had been coughing for nine days and had stopped hiding it.
They were at the far end of the barn with a lantern between them and the others asleep at the other end.

“You have a cough that is in the lung and not in the throat,” said Sancora. “That is the one I do not like. It will go off when the weather turns and it will come back next winter and it will be worse. You have two more winters in you at this rate, on the road, in the cold.”
“I know,” said Old Den.
“I want to say the rest of it plainly, because I say everything plainly and you can stop me if you want to.”
“Say it.”

“If you sat in a cottage by a fire for the whole of a winter you would have four winters in you instead of two,” said Sancora. “That is the arithmetic. It is not a guess. I have watched eleven men die of it and I have never been wrong about the first part.”
Old Den sat with his bound hand on his knee and looked at the lantern for a while.
“Eleven men,” he said. “I have watched two thousand.”
“Then you know what I am telling you and you know why I am telling you and you do not need the rest of it.”
“I will not be sitting in a cottage,” said Old Den.
“You will not be sitting in a cottage,” said Sancora.

“I want it entered somewhere that I chose the road,” said Old Den, “and I want you to be the one who has it, because you are the only person in this company who writes anything down that matters, and I know you write nothing down, and I am asking you anyway.”

Sancora sat with the lantern between them and did not write anything down and did not promise to, and Old Den did not ask her twice, and in the morning they went on east with the snow on the cart and the goat breaking the crust in front of them.
The county rider came at them on the fourteenth day of the eleventh month, at a ford, going the other way.

He was young and he was on a good horse. He had a leather bag across his back with the county’s mark burnt into the flap. Riss saw the bag before she saw the man and understood the whole of what he was in about two seconds.

A county rider carries notices. Every notice has four columns on it and a place for the parish to write at the bottom. The rider goes from parish to parish and puts up what the assize has ruled. He takes down what the parishes have answered. He does that twice a month in a county and he knows every road and every gate on it. He is the single most useful person in the eleven counties to a county office.
He stopped in the middle of the ford and looked at the company.
Riss watched the whole of it happen. She watched it with a keeper’s eye. The questions got asked and answered in the ordinary way.
“Bound east?”
“Bound east.”
“Any of you with business at Sessions?”
“No.”
“No papers, then.”
“No papers.”

The rider looked at the goat and at the cart. He looked at the eight of them standing in the water in the middle of a November ford. Riss could see the arithmetic being done in his head. Eight people, one animal, no names, no papers, no work, no load, a good cart, and every one of them fit and none of them frightened.
“That is an odd party,” said the rider.
“It is,” said Riss.
“What are you?”
“A company walking east.”

The county rider took that away with him. What Riss noticed and did not say out loud was this. He did not reach into his bag once. There was no form in that bag for a company walking east with no names. There was a notice about strays. There was a notice about the spring sessions of the assize. There was a reward notice for a horse and a notice about the boundary of two parishes on the far side of the county. Not one of them had a column in it that would take the company.
Riss thought about the assize that night, by the fire, in a ditch on the far side of the ford.

The spring sessions. That was in the notice and it was in the world. The world contained a mill on the Vellum with a page stitched into a ledger behind eighty-one names. It contained a clerk called Ivet Sallow who had not sent a return in four months. It contained a county sheet in a counting house in a coat, folded twice, with a mark in the fourth column.
“He is going to have to answer something in the spring,” said Riss.
“He is,” said Nahl.
“Which one?”

“Both of them,” said Nahl. “That is the arithmetic of a cracked system. There is a mill clerk with a page and a counting-house clerk with a sheet. They are four hundred miles apart and neither of them filed anything. The spring sessions will bring the county’s attention to the mill on the Vellum, because the mill has not sent a return. That is the whole of the counties’ machine. It is not a hangman. It is a calendar.”
They did the count on the last day of the month, on a hill, at a milestone.

It was cold and clear and there was no wind. The milestone was a county stone. It had the name of a town on it that none of them had ever been to. It had a number on it that was the mileage. The company stood in a line beside it in the order they walked.
Nahl did the whole of it properly, because that was the trade.

“A bearer reports. I have a log under my arm that belongs to a dead man and a count that belongs to nobody, and I am standing on a county road in the eleventh month with a company of eight and one animal and no papers and no names in any book anywhere in the eleven counties.”
Then the count, forwards and backwards, and then the number said once, out loud, standing, on the top of a hill.
Then the name.

Nahl did that part too and did it the way the company had agreed to do it, which was in the parts and not in the whole. They said the first part of the sound, which was a sound a throat could make. Then they said the second part, which was not. Then they stopped and said the third part and the fourth and the fifth. Then the sixth and the seventh and the eighth, one at a time, with a breath between each one. What came off the hill was not a name. It was a tally of what a name had been made of.
The goat stood at the milestone with its head down and did not eat.
Then they said Orphiel’s line, all eight of them, out loud. Standing up, on a county road, four hundred miles from a ridge with a notch on a stone.
“I can see it. This is real.”
The two keepers had their conversation on the hill after the count, in the flat cold. The company stood off a little way to give them the room.
It was the shortest exchange the company had ever had and it was the whole of what the next ten years were going to be.
“We will do this again,” said Riss.
“Yes,” said Nahl.
“At the next room. And the next.”
“Yes.”
“Until we die.”
“Yes.”
The refusal came three days later, at a village called Harlow Green. It was made to a good offer. That is the only kind of offer worth refusing.

The company had been four days on ice-hard roads and Old Den had a cough that Sancora did not like. Harlow Green had a farm with a cottage on it and eighty acres of grass. The farmer was sixty and had no sons and was willing to talk. He came to the tavern himself on the second night with a jug and a proposition.
A place to winter. Work for eight. A cottage for the old man. Straw in the barn for the animal. Wages in coin, or in kind if the company preferred it.
Veylan listened to the whole of it and did not say anything. Veylan was a farmer. Every word of it was a word he had said himself once to a man with land.
Then Riss refused it, and she refused it in front of the company, so that the refusal belonged to all eight of them.
“We are not a parish,” said Riss.
“I am not asking you to be a parish,” said the farmer. “It is a job of work and a roof and a fire.”

“And in the spring there would be a row of crops with our hands in it,” said Riss. “By the second spring there would be a row of crops that we had a right to. By the third spring somebody in this village would have written our names in a book in order to leave us the field. That is how a company stops being a company. It is not a betrayal and it is not a failure. It is a cottage and a wet winter and a man of eighty acres who is being kind to us.”
The farmer looked at the eight of them.
“Then what are you for?” he said.
“We are for the next room,” said Nahl.
Veylan said his piece that night, on his own, with the tin out. It was the only time on the whole road east that the company heard him come close to asking for something.

“I want the high field,” he said. “I have said it since the mill and I will say it once more and then I will shut up about it. In the spring I am going west to my own ground with a tin of soil from the top of a mountain. If any of you want to be standing in that field when the first thing comes up green, then you will be there. That is not settling. That is a farmer planting a field, and after it is planted I will walk out of it with you and go east again, or wherever the road is, and the field can do what it likes without me.”
“You will not stay,” said Riss.

“I will not stay,” said Veylan. “I have four hundred crowns in a county book and a complaint in a county file. I am not going in front of a magistrate in a hat. The only thing I have ever wanted since the spring was to find out what a handful of that soil grows in a proper field. Then I will know, and then I will go.”
They went east out of Harlow Green on the fourth morning with the frost on the cart and the goat in front.

The plate hummed the third note the whole of the day. Kael’s hand was quiet in the cold. He had stopped looking at it every morning. He had started looking at it once a week. Sancora took that as an improvement and said so.
Corvath smelled snow two days before it came. The company dug in at a farm and were fed for two days. The farmer’s wife would not take money for the second day.
Old Den walked last and coughed and did not complain and kept up.
Above them there was nothing to see. The Emberion was up there with its fifteen joints and the piece missing out of the wing. Nobody in the company had seen it in two months.

Below them, in the valley, the gold road and the grey road ran side by side across the frozen water and away north and south. Neither of them shone. There was nobody on either of them in any direction that a man could see.

The company was on the road. It had a log and a Leaf. It had a tin of soil, a cord, and a chart. It had a blank slate and one pair of twice-mended boots between the eight of them. It had a count that was spoken and a name that was a sound. It had a page in a mill ledger behind eighty-one names and a clerk in a mill office who had kept it. It had a counting-house clerk with a sheet in his coat who had read the page and not filed it.
And it had a practice. That was the whole of what it had, and it was enough, and it was going east.

chapters.label: Interlude E
chapters.title: The Long Column
paragraphs: After the company went east out of the mill yard, and the carrier took an empty bag down the river, and the winter came, and the wheel froze twice and was broken out twice with crowbars, six months had gone by.
It was the fourth month of the year. The river was up.

The Vellum came down off the high country in the fourth month every year and it came down fast. The mill ran day and night for eleven days. Every man in the yard was on the wheel house and the lights were on all night.
Ivet Sallow worked sixteen hours a day at the counter and did not go home for two of those nights. She slept on the bench by the stove with her keys on her arm.
That was the mill’s year. Grain in. Grain out. Fees at the foot. The mark at the bottom. The clerk behind the counter with her pen case open.
The page was in the back of the fourth ledger and Ivet read it once a week.
Sunday evenings were her own. The men went home at the sixth hour and the mill went quiet. She would bank the office fire and take the fourth ledger down off the shelf and open it at the back.
She did it with one lamp and the door shut. It took ten minutes. She had never told anybody.
There was nobody to tell. She lived alone in a small house at the end of the lane behind the chapel. Her mother had been dead eleven years. She had no sister.
The only person in Ashenford West who knew about the fifth leaf was the boy who had carried the family’s answer back from the big house.
She read the four columns the way she read any page she had written. That is to say she read them for errors, and there were none.
One company, off the western boundary, no names given.
The grey wall, above the last grass.
One log of entries. One leaf of notes. One count, spoken in this room and not written here. One name, said once, off the far side of the wall, and not written here, and not written anywhere.

Then the fourth column. It said that nothing had been taken and no fee was due on any part of it. It said that the page had been entered because a report had been made standing, out loud, in her hearing, in that room, by witnesses who had come there on foot to make it.
Below it, in the row where the value of a party is totalled: *present and unwilling: one.*
Ivet Sallow read it. Then she read it again. Then she wrote nothing.
Three more names had gone in at the back of the book since the fourth month.

That was the part of the practice nobody outside the mill would ever have understood. She had tried to explain it to herself on a long Sunday in the first month and had failed, and had stopped trying.
A stranger came through Ashenford West with no papers. There was a register for strangers. The register went up the river at the end of the year.

So instead of the register, Ivet took the person’s name and where they had come from and the date. She wrote it in small neat column-straight writing at the back of a mill account book, on the fifth leaf’s side of the stitching.
Three of them since the company left.
A man off a barge who had been put ashore for fighting and had no parish.
A girl of about fourteen who had come up the river road with a bundle and had gone on east.
A woman with a child of two whose papers had been taken off her at the bridge two counties down, and who had stayed four days and worked in the loading yard for her bread and gone on.
In the fourth month of the year the clerk of the mill on the Vellum had eighty-four names at the back of a mill ledger and no authority for any one of them.
She had thought about the arithmetic of it all winter. It came out the same way every time.
Past the ruled pages there was now one long column.

That is how she had come to think of it. It was the only way she could make it hold together. Four leaves of names and a page about a company, and every line of it was a person or a party the county’s books would not take.

It was not a file and it was not a register. It was a column, ruled once, by nobody, going down the back of a working mill’s ledger. It had been running four years and it would run as long as she kept the counter.
The county’s second question came up the river on a Thursday in the fourth month.
It came in the carrier’s bag on a good sheet of county stock with the office’s stamp at the head of it. Ivet opened it at the counter with her coat on, because that was the habit of nineteen years.
A clerk opens the day’s post standing up.
It was three paragraphs and she read all three twice.

The first paragraph was ordinary. The mill’s monthly return was six months in arrears. No return had been received since the ninth month of the previous year. A query report had come in at the tenth month stating that the return was in hand and would be sent. The office now required the return within fourteen days.
The second paragraph was not ordinary. Ivet read that one four times.

*Further, in accordance with the standing instruction of the fourth month, the office requires from every mill and every merchant holding county contracts a certificate as follows: that no person has been entered in the books of the said mill or merchant who is not a party to a mill or merchant transaction, and that no record has been kept other than records of trade.*
At the foot of the sheet there was a box for the clerk’s name. There was a box for the mill’s mark. There was a line for the date.
It was not signed by a magistrate. It was signed *for the office, senior clerk*, and the hand was not Maro Holl’s.
She sat with it for the whole of the afternoon and worked out what she could write and what she could not.
She did that properly, in the way she did everything. A blank sheet. A pen. The two documents side by side on the counter.

She could write the return. That was the first thing and she was honest with herself about it. The grain had been counted. The fees had been totalled. The columns were straight and the totals were carried.
The three-day water error was still in the ledger where it had been for nineteen years, uncorrected. A correction would be a second page. A second page would be a claim.
She could write the return in two hours. She could have it in the bag on Thursday and the mill would be in good standing by the end of the month.
She could not write the certificate.
That was the second thing and it took her less time to work out than the first.
The certificate asked her to state, in her own hand, under the mill’s mark, that no person had been entered in the mill’s books who was not a party to a mill transaction.

Eighty-four names were stitched into the back of the fourth ledger. Five leaves deep in that same book there was a page about a company that had never bought a sack of the mill’s grain in its life and never would.
The two documents were on the same counter. They were in the same room. They were in the same book.
She could send the return and be in good standing by the end of the month. The certificate was the sentence at the bottom of the page.
A clerk who signs the sentence at the bottom of a page has signed the page.
So she did the arithmetic the way she did every arithmetic. She looked at the two of them and she put the pen down.
She did not send the return. She did not write the query register. She did not answer the second question.
That is the whole of six months in one sentence. It took six months to say, because it was not one decision.
It was a decision taken once a week, on the Thursday, in the four seconds of office work between opening the bag and handing it to the carrier.
She looked into the bag. She looked up at the shelf where a bundle of mill business would have gone on any other Thursday of her working life.
She put nothing in the bag. She handed it to the carrier at the door.
He went off down the road with an empty bag, twice a week, all winter.
After the third week he stopped making a joke about it. After the sixth week he stopped asking.
The second question went into the drawer under the counter with the other papers. In the drawer, with the string on them, there were four.
The first answer from the family.
The family’s note from the tenth month.
The query report she had written out in the tenth month and never sent.
And the certificate, with its box for her name and its box for the mill’s mark, unmarked.
The family had said nothing.
That was the other half of it and it was the half that kept her standing up behind the counter.

The agent’s note from the tenth month was one of the four papers in the drawer. It said only that if the matter was not a fee and not a claim, and no part of it was owed to the family or to the county, then it was nothing, and that the clerk might enter it as nothing and keep the record in the mill’s books.
The family had been sent no return for six months and had said nothing about it. The county had asked twice and the family had said nothing about that either.

There was a mill on the Vellum that had not answered the county office in half a year, and the people who owned it had answered a letter from their clerk in four days and then let the whole matter lie.

Ivet had thought about that a good deal in the winter. She had come to the conclusion that a family four miles down the river, with a house and a name and a seat in two counties, had worked out exactly what she had worked out.
A mill that is quiet is worth more than a mill that is argued about.
If a clerk in their office wanted to keep a page, then that was the clerk’s business and the mill’s book. And neither of them had ever been asked a question they could not answer by saying nothing.
She did not know whether that was courage or arithmetic. She suspected it was arithmetic. She was a clerk, and she took it.
On the Sunday of the fourth week of the fourth month she did the thing she did every Sunday.
It was the whole of her practice and it took ten minutes behind a shut door with a lamp.
She banked the fire. She took the fourth ledger down off the shelf. She opened it at the back.
Four leaves of names in small neat writing. The fifth leaf, ruled in four columns. And the long column, running down the back of a working mill’s book for four years and getting longer every year.
She read the page. She read the fourth column. She put her hand flat on it the way a person checks whether a stove is warm, and left it there for a moment.
Then she closed the ledger and put it back on the shelf. She hung the lamp on its hook and locked the office and walked home down the lane behind the chapel in the dark.
There was no plate in Ashenford West.

That had never been hers. There was a case of notes and a piece of old metal in it, and it had gone east on a cart with a keeper. Whatever note it hummed, the clerk of the mill on the Vellum had never heard it and would never hear it.

There was no goat either. The goat was on a road somewhere east with its head down. What the mill had was a cat that slept in the wheel house, and a drake on the pond behind the loading yard, and the noise of water.
The mill was quiet in the fourth month. The river was up and the men were busy and the office door was shut.
The desk was clear except for the day book and the week’s letters and the four papers in the drawer under the counter with the string on them.

Nobody in the eleven counties had written anything about Ivet Sallow and there was no reason why anybody would. She was the clerk of the mill on the Vellum, nineteen years at the same counter, four hundred documents a year, and her name was at the foot of every one of them.
None of them had ever been questioned.

Above the mill there was county sky and rain. Behind it the Emberion was up there with its fifteen joints and the piece missing out of the wing, and nobody in Ashenford West had seen it in six months.

Down at the bridge the gold road and the grey road ran side by side across the water and away north and south into the counties. Neither of them shone. There was nobody on either of them in any direction that a man could see.
And in the back of a mill ledger in Ashenford West there were five leaves and one long column, and a clerk who kept it, and a count that was not written in it and was not written anywhere.
One clerk at a time was still the whole of the arithmetic.

chapters.label: Chapter 32
chapters.title: The Visit
paragraphs: After Harlow Green, and three more weeks on ice-hard roads, and the turn of the twelfth month, the company came into a village called Carden.
That was the first thing the company noticed about it and the company noticed it at the top of the hill.

Carden had been on the fingerpost six weeks back, on the north arm, with a mileage under it and a parish mark beside the mileage. Nobody had said the name out loud at the post. Veylan had wanted to and had been told to hold his tongue.
And now here they were, walking into it, and nobody had ever said the word until the sign over the tavern said it for them.
“That is the whole of why we do not name the room,” said Riss.
“It is,” said Nahl. “We have been walking to Carden for six weeks and we did not know it. If we had said the name at the post, somebody would have been waiting for us here.”
Carden was bigger than Odder and colder.

It had two inns, a market cross with a stone step, a church with a proper spire, three streets, and a river wide enough for a barge. It had a fulling mill and a tannery and a rope walk. It had forty houses, and eleven of them had shutters closed, which meant the people in them had the money to shut out the weather.
It was the twelfth month and the market was out of season and the town was quiet.
The company took rooms at the second inn, which was the cheaper one, and paid for them first, which was the first of the nine parts and the easiest.
Mira counted the room when they came in, because that was her trade.

Fire in the middle of the floor. A long table at the far side with benches. Two men on one bench with a jug between them. A woman behind the bar with a ledger open on the counter, which meant she was the one who kept the accounts, which meant she was the clerk.
Eleven people in the room. A dog. A boy carrying plates.

And the plate under Riss’s shirt, which had been humming the third note all day, went up a note when the company came in. Mira did not understand what had happened. Then the door opened again three minutes later and a woman came in out of the dark.
The woman was about forty-five years old.

She was dressed for the road and dressed well for it. A plain good coat. Boots that had been mended by a man who knew his trade. A leather case on a strap, and a hat with a band. She had come in on a hired horse and the boy took the horse into the yard. She paid the boy in coin and thanked him by name. That meant she had been here before, or she was the kind of woman who learns a name in ten seconds.
She had no servant. That was the thing Mira noticed and could not stop noticing.
A woman of that coat and those boots, travelling alone in the twelfth month. On a hired horse, with a case on a strap. No servant and no man. And a face that told you nothing at all.
She stood in the door for a moment and looked at the room. She looked the way a clerk looks at a page.
Then she came in and put her case down and sat at the end of the long table, four feet from the company, with her back to the window and her face to the fire.
She did not look at any of the eight of them for the whole of an hour.
That was the other thing Mira noticed and it was the thing that made her sit up.
A stranger walks into a tavern with eight people in it and one goat at the door, and a stranger looks. It is not manners and it is not curiosity. It is what people do.
This woman looked at the fire. She looked at her hands. She looked at the woman behind the bar and ordered bread and beer in a low voice that carried no further than the counter.
She did not look at the company once.
Kael’s hand answered her.

Kael had not had a hand answer anything since the county clerk went south. He had his left hand flat on the table and it began to hurt. It hurt in the place where the scar was, in the old way, the way it had hurt on the ridge and in the mill office. He did not say anything to anybody. He turned the hand over and put it in his lap and looked at the fire.
And the plate under Riss’s shirt hummed the third note as though a thing had been found that had been missing.
The eight of them did the same thing back, and Mira noticed that too, because it was exact.

Nobody in the company looked at the woman for the first quarter of an hour. Veylan looked at the fire. Sancora looked at her own hands, which she did when she was deciding something about a person. Kael looked at the door. Nahl looked at the table in front of them, which is what a bearer does with a page that is not his.
It was not rudeness on either side. It was the two of them measuring each other at arm’s length, the way two clerks do in a room with a counter between them.
The woman ate her bread and drank her beer and then she came over.

She came over without any fuss in the world. She picked up her case and walked the four feet and put the case on the bench and sat down on the opposite side of the long table from the company, all eight of them, square.
She looked at all eight of them then, one at a time, and she took her time about it.
“You are looking for a company,” said Riss.
“I am looking for a mill,” said the woman.
“The mill is west,” said Riss. “Two hundred miles west. On a river called the Vellum.”
“I know where the mill is,” said the woman. “I am looking for the people who were in it.”
Her name was Serle.
That was the whole of what she gave them, and she gave it the way a person gives a thing they have decided not to argue about. No first name. No house. No county.
“I am the family’s woman of business,” she said. “I keep the accounts at the big house at Vellum Reach and I have kept them for nine years.”
“Then you are a clerk,” said Mira.

“I am not a clerk,” said Serle. “I am a woman who does accounts. A clerk keeps a book that goes to a county office. I keep a book that goes to a family, and a family’s book stops at the door of the house, and that is the whole difference between me and every clerk in the eleven counties, and it is the reason I am sitting here.”
“You read the page,” said Nahl.
“I read the page,” said Serle.
Then she told them the whole of it, and she told it in the flat voice of a woman giving an account, which is a thing Mira recognised.

She had been sent to the mill in the eleventh month to inspect the books. The mill’s return was five months late. The family wanted to know what was going on before the county got any further with its questions.

She had read the four grain ledgers in one day. She had found the three-day water error and had written nothing about it, because a woman who inspects books for a family knows better than to correct a clerk’s page.
She had found the leaves at the back of the fourth ledger on the second day.

“The fourth leaf of names was nothing new to me,” she said. “I have known about those names for three years. The clerk has been keeping her own list at the back of a mill book since the war and I have never written a word about it, because it has never cost the family a crown and because a mill clerk who keeps the names of strangers is a mill clerk who does not lose barges.”
“And the fifth leaf?”
“The fifth leaf was new.”
Serle took hold of her beer and did not drink it.

“I read it four times,” she said. “I sat on the stool in that office with the clerk standing at the end of the counter not saying anything, and I read the four columns of that page four times, and then I closed the book and went home.”
Mira asked the question that mattered, because a measurer asks the question that matters.
“You wrote a report.”
“I wrote a report,” said Serle.
“And the family answered it.”

“The family answered it in four days,” said Serle. “The answer was one line. If the matter is not a fee and not a claim and nothing is owed to the family or to the county, then it is nothing, and the clerk may enter it and keep it in the mill’s books.”
“That is word for word what the agent’s note said in the tenth month,” said Riss.
“It is word for word,” said Serle. “I wrote both of them. It is my sentence. I have written that sentence on four hundred matters at that house and every time I have known exactly what it meant.”
“And what did it mean this time?”
Serle looked at the fire for a while.

“This time it meant that I did not know what it meant,” she said. “That is the whole of the reason I am on the road in the twelfth month on a hired horse with nobody with me. I have been the family’s woman of business for nine years and I have never once written a sentence I could not explain to the family, and I wrote that one and it was true and it was exact and it was correct, and it said nothing at all about a page with the truth in the fourth column.”
Then she said the thing that told the company the whole of who she was, and she said it without any drama in it at all.

“I copied four lines out of that leaf and I put them in my coat,” she said. “I did it on the last night, in the office, after the clerk had gone home, with the lamp turned down. I have carried them for six weeks. I have read them on the road most nights, and I have not written anything else about that page, not one word, from the eleventh month to this one.”
“That is why you have not filed your report,” said Nahl.
“I have not filed my report,” said Serle.
“Why not?”

“Because if I file it, it goes in the family’s file, and the family’s file is a column in the counties’ book,” said Serle. “The moment a page about that leaf goes into a file at the big house, the leaf stops being a thing that happened in a mill. It becomes a line in a book that a magistrate can be shown. And I am not going to be the woman who turned a page with no reason in it into an exhibit.”
The company had one question to settle before it did anything else, and Riss asked it out loud in the way the company asked everything on the road.
“Do we run?”

That was the whole of it. Eight people, one animal, no papers, no names. And a stranger in a tavern in Carden who had been sent west in the twelfth month to ask why a mill had not answered. Who had read the page and had not filed her report, and had come east on her own time.
The company had been running since the border stone. They had walked east for three months and changed roads twice for men with paper.
Nobody in the eight of them wanted to run.

“There is a difference,” said Nahl, “between a man with a form and a person with a question. A form is the county asking. A person asking is a person asking. If we walk out of this tavern tonight, then we are telling her that we are afraid of one woman with a slip of paper in her coat, and that is not true, and it is worse than anything she could write in a file.”
“We sit,” said Riss.
“We sit,” said Nahl. “We answer. We do not lie. We do not sign. We do not give names. And when she has asked, we finish our beer and pay for the beds and go east in the morning.”
So they sat.
And the stranger asked questions, and they answered them, and Mira sat at the end of the table and counted every one of them because that was her trade.
Serle asked how long they had been on the road. Nahl said four months west and three months back, and Serle wrote nothing down.
Serle asked whether they had been inside the mill. Nahl said they had, in the ninth month, for one night and one day, and that they had bought nothing and sold nothing and taken nothing.
Serle asked what they had brought back from the west. Nahl said a log that belonged to a dead man, and a leaf of notes, and a chart, and a tin of soil, and a blank slate, and a pair of boots.
“What is in the log?” said Serle.
“Nine thousand and four entries,” said Nahl.
“And the fourth column?”
“The fourth column is empty,” said Nahl. “It is empty on all nine thousand and four of them.”
Serle sat with that.

“I have been in the counties for nine years,” she said, “and I have read forty thousand pages. In every one of them there is a reason in the fourth column. Every reason is a fee or a claim or a duty. I have never seen a book where the fourth column was empty. I did not think it could be done. It is the one column you cannot lie in because it is the only column that has to be true.”
“It is the only column that gets you taken off your ground,” said Riss.
“It is,” said Serle.
Then Mira went to the door and looked out at the yard and the town. It was the twelfth month and Carden was quiet, and she wanted to know what a quiet town looked like from the inside.
There was no wind. There had not been any wind since the mill, four months back, and Carden was cold and still and the smoke went straight up from forty chimneys.

The goat was standing at the tavern door with its back to the wall and its head up. It did not lie down at Carden and it did not sleep. It stood in the doorway the whole night, between the company and the street. It had stood at the mill door for four weeks like that. It had walked in front for three months.

Above the town the sky was county sky and there was nothing in it to see. The Emberion was up there with its fifteen joints and the piece missing out of the wing, and nobody in the company had seen it since the tenth month.

Where the Carden road crossed the river, the gold road and the grey road ran side by side away north and south into the counties. Neither of them shone. There was nobody on either of them in any direction a man could see.
Mira went back in and sat down at the table and said nothing about any of it.
Serle took a room at the inn for the night, which was the thing that told the company what was going to happen next.
She did it without asking them, and without a hint that she expected anything of them. She went up the stairs at the tenth hour with her case on her strap and her hat in her hand.
At the top of the stairs she stopped and looked back down at the long table.
“I have four lines in my coat,” she said. “I have read them most nights for six weeks. Tomorrow, if you will, I would like to hear what is not in them.”
Then she went up to her room and shut the door.
Nothing in the room had been written down. Mira checked that, because it was her trade, and she checked it twice.
The woman behind the bar had her ledger open at the counter and had put nothing in it about the company, because the company had paid in coin and a tavern’s day book takes money and not names.
The two men on the bench had gone home at the ninth hour.
The boy had swept the floor and put the stools up and gone to his bed over the stable.

And the stranger had a case on a strap and a slip of paper in her coat and had written nothing at all in two hours in a public room. There was no line about the company anywhere in that inn except the coin in the drawer and the two rooms paid for.
Mira banked the fire with the boy and paid for the beds, and the company sat up a while longer in the dark, and nobody said very much.
“We will hear her out,” said Riss.
“We will hear her out,” said Nahl. “And then we will see whether the book has a third read in it.”

chapters.label: Chapter 33
chapters.title: The Third Read
paragraphs: After the woman called Serle took a room at the inn and went up the stairs with her case, the company sat up late in the dark. The boy banked the fire. The four of them who were on watch that night slept in the taproom with the door barred and the goat outside it.

In the morning the innkeeper gave them the back room. It was the twelfth month and the taproom had a market crowd coming in at noon. Riss paid him for the room in coin and asked for it the way a person asks for a thing they expect to pay for.
It was a good room. Two windows, a table, a settle, a fire that smoked, and a door that shut properly.
Serle came down at the eighth hour with her case and her coat and her hat. She asked the innkeeper for tea. Then she sat down on the far side of the table from the company with her case on her knee.
“You read the page,” said Nahl.
“I read the page,” said Serle.
“Why did you come?”
Serle opened the case.

She took out a slip of paper, folded twice, and put it on the table between them. It was a small slip, the kind a person tears off the edge of a page, and it had four lines on it in a small, neat, business hand.
“I could not stop thinking about the fourth column,” she said.
The four lines were in her own writing.
Nahl read them without picking the slip up, because a bearer does not put his hand on another person’s page until he is asked.
They were not the words of the leaf. That was the first thing Nahl noticed and it was the thing that decided everything that came after.
They were what a woman of business had written down for herself after reading a page she could not explain, and she had put them in the order she could hold them in. Four lines, one for each column.
The first line named a party with no names in it.
The second named a wall and the last grass above it.
The third said, in her own shorthand, that the value of the page was a log and a leaf and a count that had been spoken and not written.

And the fourth line said this. *No fee is claimed on any part of this page. The reason entered above is a report made standing, out loud, by witnesses who came on foot, and it is the only reason I have ever read that is not a fee.*
Nahl read the fourth line three times, the way the company had learned to read everything since the ridge, and then looked up at the woman across the table.
“You wrote down what the clerk meant,” they said.

“I wrote down what I understood,” said Serle. “It is not the same thing and I am not a person who confuses the two. If I had written down what she wrote, I would have made a copy, and a copy of a page is a page. I wrote the thing in my head instead, and I have carried it for six weeks, and I would like to know whether I have got it right.”
They told her.
That is the whole of what happened in the back room of an inn at Carden on the second morning of the twelfth month, and it took the company about two hours, and nobody wrote anything down.
Nahl told her about the log first, because the log was the thing she had come for and because a bearer reports before anything else.

Nine thousand and four entries. Every one of them a person, a date, a ground, a parish. A fourth column ruled from the first page to the last and empty from the first page to the last. A dead man’s book that no office in the eleven counties could take, because a book with no reasons in it cannot prove that anything in it ever happened.
Then Riss told her about the mill, because Riss was the keeper of that part of it.

The four requirements. A clerk with standing. A book of record. A person present who did not want to be there. A superior who could be reached by a note. And the page written in four columns by hand, and signed by the clerk, and not signed by anybody in the company.
Then Mira told her the arithmetic, because that was Mira’s trade.

Two reads and not one. Maro Holl at the counting house, who had read the page and filed nothing. Serle at the big house, who had read the page and filed nothing. A page in a mill ledger. A mark in a fourth column on a county sheet. A slip of paper in a woman’s coat. And a count spoken in a room in Ashenford and never written anywhere.

“That is the whole of the system,” said Mira. “It is not a rebellion and it is not a movement. It is one clerk at a time. One read at a time. That is what a cracked system looks like from the inside. Nothing is broken and nothing is fixed, and one page at a time the arithmetic stops coming out.”
Then they did the thing the practice required of a room and it was harder in front of a woman of business than it had been in front of a parish clerk.
Nahl stood up.
The company stood up with them, all eight, in the order they walked on the road, facing the fire.
Nahl said the opening of it, because the trade requires the opening, and then said what it was not.
“A bearer reports. That is the office and it is not what this is. This is a count.”
Then they counted. Forwards, in the order of the walk. Backwards, from the last to the first.

Then the number, said once, standing up, in a room with a book in it. The inn’s day book was on the counter through the wall, and the company had checked that before they began. That was the fourth part of the practice and it had to be kept exactly.
Then the name.

Nahl did that in the parts and not in the whole, the way the company had agreed to do it on the road. The first part of the sound, which a throat can make. Then the second, which it cannot. Then the third and the fourth and the fifth. Then the sixth and the seventh and the eighth. One at a time, with a breath between each. What came into that back room was not a name. It was the tally of what a name had been made of.
Then Orphiel’s line, all eight of them, out loud, standing up.
“I can see it. This is real.”
Serle sat at the table with her hands flat on the wood and did not write anything and did not sign anything and did not say a word for the whole of it.
She asked the questions afterwards and they were the questions of a person who had come two hundred miles for an answer.
She asked whether the count could be written down. Nahl said no.
She asked whether the name could be written down. Nahl said that the name could not be said, let alone written, and that what the company had was a tally of the parts of it.

She asked whether the page in the ledger said the number. Nahl said that the page said a count had been spoken in the room and not written there, and that the number itself was in eight heads and in nobody’s book.
She asked the question a woman of business asks, which is the one that costs money.
“Then what holds it?”

“Nothing holds it,” said Nahl. “That is the whole of the design and it is not a design, it is what there is. There is a page in a mill ledger and a mark on a county sheet. There is a slip in a coat and a tally in our heads. There is a parish clerk in Odder who has watched a hand go into a coat and come back to the table. None of it can be seized and none of it can be copied and none of it can be filed. And every one of those things is a person, and there are six of them now, and there were two six months ago.”
Serle sat with that for a while.
“That is the worst thing I have ever heard,” she said. “It is also the only thing I have ever heard that a county cannot get at.”
Then the company made its refusal, and it was made twice. The woman across the table was not a stranger by then. A refusal made to a stranger is a different thing from a refusal made to a person.
She asked, at the end, to be given something to take back.

Not the log. She was careful about that and she said so out loud, and it was the reason the company trusted her with the rest of it. She asked for a copy of the page’s four columns in Nahl’s hand. Or a short letter from the company. Or the tally of the name written out. Or anything at all that could be put in her case and carried west as an account of this.
“No,” said Nahl.

“I have carried a slip of paper with four lines on it for six weeks,” said Serle. “It is a poor thing to hand the family and it is worse to hand nobody at all. Give me one page and I will keep it in my coat the way I have kept this, and I will not file it, and I will not show it to a magistrate, and I will not copy it.”

“No,” said Nahl again. “And it is not because we do not trust you. You have the page in your head. That is enough. A thing in a case is a rumour and a thing in a head is a read, and we have spent four months finding out which of those two the counties can take away from a person.”
“So I go back with nothing.”

“You go back with the count and the name and Orphiel’s line and a slip of paper with four lines on it,” said Nahl. “That is more than I had when I came out of the mountains in the third month. That is the whole of what a bearer carries and it is the reason a bearer is a poor man.”
She asked one more thing before she went, and it was the thing the company could not refuse her because it was not a page.
“Will you let me read one page of the log?”
Nahl thought about it for a moment and then got the log out of the pack and untied the cord and put it on the table. They opened it at the first page.
Serle read the first page. It took her about four minutes. She read the four columns and then she read them again, and then she put her finger under one entry and looked at it for a while.
Then she turned the page.
“No,” said Nahl.
Serle stopped with her hand on the leaf.

“One page is a read,” said Nahl. “Ten pages is a copy. You have read one page of the log of Orphiel of the Nine, and that is a read, and there is now a person in the county who has read a page of that book. If you turn the leaf, then you have begun to hold the whole of it in your head, and by the spring you would be the only person west of here who knew what was in it, and you would have to decide every day whether to say it, and it would eat you the way the fourth column ate Maro Holl.”
Serle took her hand off the leaf.
“I will not turn the page,” she said.
She went west at noon.

She had a hired horse and a case on a strap and a slip of paper with four lines on it. She stood in the inn yard in the cold with her hat on. Then she said the last of what she had to say to Riss and Nahl, who had come out to the yard with her.
“I am going back to the mill first,” she said. “I want to see the clerk again before I go home.”
“That is your trade and not mine,” said Nahl.

“I know it is. I am not asking permission. I am telling you where I am going, because you are the only people in the eleven counties I have ever told anything true, and I have not decided what I am going to say to her.”
“Then do not decide it now,” said Riss. “That is the whole of what we know and it took us four months and a mountain to learn it. Do the day in front of you.”
“And if she asks me whether the page is safe?”

“Then say what you saw,” said Nahl. “Say that a company of eight walked east into the counties and gave no names and took no work. Say they were counted out loud in a room. Say that you were in the room, and that nothing was written down. Say that. It is true, and it is the whole of it, and a true thing said in a room does not go into a file.”
Serle put her hat straight.

“There is one thing I want to say before I go,” she said, “and then I will not say anything else about it for the rest of my life. I was sent west in the eleventh month to find out why a mill had not answered a letter from a county office. I have ridden two hundred miles east and sat in a country inn and heard a count spoken by people with no names, and I am going back west to a family and a house and a book that stops at the door, and I will not file my report, and I will not write another one.”
“You will carry it,” said Nahl.
“I will carry it,” said Serle.

She got on the horse and went out of the yard and turned west on the Carden road. The company stood in the yard and watched her until she was out of the gate. That is what a company does with a person who has read its page.
The plate had hummed the third note the whole of her visit and did not stop when she left, and Riss noticed that and said nothing about it.
Kael’s hand was quiet again by noon.

The goat had stood at the door of the inn for the whole of the two days. It had not eaten much and had not moved. When the company went out of the yard it stood up and walked into the road and turned east without being told.
Mira wrote the village in the Leaf that night, and the entry had four lines in it and no number.
Twelfth month. Carden. A woman of business called Serle, sent west, and the reason she came east.
She read the page. She filed nothing.
She copied four lines into her coat and carried them six weeks.
The count was spoken in the back room of the inn and there was a book behind the wall.
She read one page of the log and put her hand down. She went west with nothing at all and everything she needed.
Riss read it back and nobody corrected anything, and Nahl asked for one line to be added, and it was added.
“Say that she will not file it,” said Nahl.

Above the town the sky was county sky and there was nothing in it a man could see. The Emberion was up there with its fifteen joints and the piece missing out of the wing, and the company had not laid eyes on it since the mill.

Down where the Carden road crossed the river the gold road and the grey road ran side by side away north and south into the counties. Neither of them shone. There was nobody on either of them in either direction.
There was no wind.

The company went east out of Carden in the middle of the afternoon. A page was stitched in a ledger two hundred miles behind them. A mark was on a county sheet four hundred miles behind that. A slip of paper was going west in a woman’s coat, and a count was not written anywhere, and a third read was walking away from them up a county road on a hired horse.
