The company talked about her for a mile down the road and then stopped, because there was nothing to decide.
“She will file it,” said Veylan. “Anybody would file it. She has a report and a desk and a family that pays her.”
“She will not file it,” said Mira.
“You cannot know that.”

“I can know the arithmetic of it,” said Mira. “She has carried a slip in her coat for six weeks and told nobody. That is a read. A read is a thing a person does alone and cannot undo. If she files her report, then the report is the last page in the matter and she becomes a woman who wrote it, and she will have to live in the house with the family and pass the door of the office every day with that in her.”
“So?”
“So she will not file it,” said Mira. “Not because she is brave. Because it is the cheaper of the two ways to live.”
Veylan thought about that for half a mile.
“You people have one arithmetic,” he said, “and you apply it to everybody.”
“It is a very good arithmetic,” said Mira. “It is the only one I have ever owned.”
“One clerk at a time,” said Mira.
“One read at a time,” said Riss.
They walked east.

chapters.label: Chapter 34
chapters.title: The Road
paragraphs: After the woman of business went west out of the inn yard at Carden, the company went east out of the same yard in the middle of the afternoon. They walked four days to the end of the twelfth month.
It was the hard end of the winter and the roads were iron.

They walked in the order they always walked. The goat first, because the goat had decided that in the first week out of the mill and nobody had ever questioned it. Then Nahl with the log. Then Riss with the Leaf in its case. Then Mira with the chart in its tube. Then Sancora. Then Corvath. Then Veylan with the tin inside his coat. Then Kael with the slate in his pack, and Old Den last, at his own pace, with the boots.
Nobody had arranged it. It had happened in the first mile of the road east and it had held for three months.
They brought the year in on the road, and it was the plainest thing the company did.

There was no drinking in it and no speech. That was decided by Sancora, who made the decisions about anything to do with the body. Her ruling was that a company with a cough in it does not spend a night on a cold road with a jug.

At the last light of the last day of the year the company stopped at a milestone on a rise with a hedge behind it. It was out of the wind. They built a small fire with wood they had bought at a farm gate.
Then Nahl stood up and the company stood up with them, and they counted.
Forwards: Riss, Kael, Mira, Veylan, Sancora, Corvath, Old Den, Nahl.
Backwards: Nahl, Old Den, Corvath, Sancora, Veylan, Mira, Kael, Riss.
Then the number, said once, out loud, standing, in the dark, on a county road at the turn of a year. Then the name in its parts. Then Orphiel’s line.
Then the company sat down and ate bread and dried roots and went to sleep in a row with the goat in front of the row.

“A year is a count,” said Nahl, before they slept, because Veylan had asked what the fire was for. “That is the whole of it. A year is a count of days that somebody else keeps, and we do not keep it in any book, so we say the count out loud when the year turns and then we lose it. Tomorrow it will be the first month and nobody will know how many of them there have been.”
The first month went on and the practice went on with it.

They did it twice more in the first three weeks of the year. Once at a hamlet of nine houses where the clerk was the priest and the room was the church porch, because the tavern had no room with a book in it. Once at a village on a hill where the clerk was a woman who kept the accounts for the wool merchant and who heard the count standing behind her own counter with the ledger open under her hand and wrote nothing in it.

The second one was the better of the two. The company paid for the beds and said the count and said the name in its parts and said the line, and the woman with the ledger stood there for the whole of it with her hand flat on the book, and afterwards she asked one question and it was the right one.
“What do I do with it?” she said.
“Nothing,” said Nahl. “That is the whole of your part. You heard it and you wrote nothing and you will remember it or you will not.”
“I will remember it,” said the wool merchant’s clerk.
Then the company went on east and left her standing behind her counter with the ledger and the answer.
Three days into the first month the parish came to see them.

That is how Riss described it afterwards and it was exact. A village called Wend. Twenty-one houses, a church without a tower, a green with a pond, and a tavern with two rooms above it. The company had done the practice there properly. Paid first, no names, no work, the count spoken standing up in a room with a book in it. And the clerk of the parish, a thin man of about thirty with a bad chest, had watched the whole of it with his hand on his book.
The company had done the count in the tavern. The parish clerk had been in the tavern and had heard it, and had gone away, and had come back in the morning with two other men and a piece of paper.
The paper was the offer and it was a good offer, and Riss stood in the yard of that tavern for a quarter of an hour and understood exactly what she was being offered.

It was a settlement paper. The parish would take the company in. Not as paupers, the parish clerk said, and he said it twice. As a party of labour without a place, which was a thing the county law had a form for. The counties had found over two hundred years that a party of moving people was less trouble in a book than a party of moving people out of a book.

Twenty-four words on a county sheet and a box for the heads of a household. The party could be entered at the bottom, as a company, without the individual names going in at all. The parish would take the standing and the county would take the paper. The company would be persons in the eleven counties. Nobody could seize them or demand their names at a gate or move them on with a constable’s man at dusk.

“There have been four of you turned away in this county in the last two months,” said the parish clerk. “I am not saying the county is hunting. I am saying it is the winter and the roads are bad and there is a tavern with two rooms in it, and a paper would make the whole of it easier for everybody, including me.”
The company took an hour over it in the tavern, with the door shut, which is the only time in three months that the company shut a door.

Veylan was for it. That is worth saying plainly, because Veylan was a farmer and every farmer in the eleven counties would have taken that paper. He argued it well. He argued it like a man who had been in the room where such decisions are made.

“It is not a name,” he said. “That is the thing. It puts the party in and leaves us out. Twenty-four words and no names in the book and the county stops looking at us. In the spring I go west to my field and the rest of you go east, and no constable’s man ever asks you anything again. Where is the harm?”
“The harm is the first line,” said Mira.
“Say it.”

“The first line is the name of the party as entered. Somebody has to write something in it. A party has to be *called* something in that box, because a county form cannot have a blank in it. So the parish clerk writes *the company off the western boundary* or *the eight of the road* or *the travelling party of Wend*, and the moment it is written there is a name in a county book with our count in it, and a name in a book is a thing a magistrate can argue with.”
“That is thin,” said Veylan.
“It is exact,” said Mira. “It is the only thing I have ever been good at.”
Riss made the refusal to the parish clerk in the yard, in the cold, with the two other men standing off to hear it. A refusal has to be said in front of the people who have to live with it.
“We are not going to take the paper,” she said.
“It costs you nothing,” said the parish clerk.
“It costs us the fourth column,” said Riss.
The parish clerk looked at her.
“I do not understand that,” he said. “There is no fourth column on that sheet.”

“There is one on every sheet in the eleven counties and there is one on the page in the book you heard us counted against,” said Riss. “The fourth column on your form is the reason. The reason for taking your paper would be that we wanted a room and a fire and a name on a list of a parish. Once that is written we are a party that was settled. And a party that was settled is a party the county can put its hand on whenever it likes, for as long as it likes. We are not a parish. We are not a mill. We are not a county. We are a practice, and a practice does not take a paper, and I know exactly how that sounds standing in a yard in the first month with the roads iron and my oldest man coughing.”
The parish clerk stood there with his form in his hand.
“You will not be here in the spring,” he said.
“No,” said Riss.
“Then God go with you, and I mean that,” said the parish clerk, and he folded the paper and put it in his coat and went back inside, and the two other men went with him.
Old Den had something to say about the paper that evening and he said it in his own way, which was to say it as though it were arithmetic.
“I am the one who would have gained the most,” he said. “You know that. A cottage and a fire and a parish list and a man of my age on it is the whole of what a settlement paper is for.”
“You did not ask for it,” said Riss.

“I did not ask for it,” said Old Den. “I have been on the roads for nineteen years and I have taken a paper twice, and both times it was a wet winter and both times I was gone by the spring, and both times I signed nothing and gave a name that was not mine, and I have never been able to say the name out loud since without feeling it in my mouth like a piece of tin.”
“Then you are the only man in the company who has ever been entered,” said Mira.

“I am,” said Old Den. “Twice. And I can tell you what it is, because none of the rest of you have ever done it. It does not feel like a roof. It feels like being counted for something you did not do. Some clerk writes you into a column and then you are a person who can be looked up, and every time anybody looks you up they find the wrong thing and you cannot correct it, because the page is not yours and the pen is not yours and the clerk is twelve miles away.”
He coughed, and it took him a while.

“That is why I asked the healer to have it entered somewhere that I chose the road,” he said. “Not the county. Not a parish. Nowhere with a pen in it. I know she did not write it and I know she did not promise to. I asked anyway, and I would ask again, and that is the whole of what I have to say about papers.”
They were four miles down the road that afternoon when the keepers had their conversation, on the long straight piece where the hedge on the left had a gap and the river showed through it.

It was the same conversation they had had at the fingerpost six weeks before and it was the same answer. Riss noticed that and did not remark on it out loud. A thing that is the same twice a day is not an event. It is a practice.
“What do we do now?” said Riss.
“We carry it,” said Nahl.
“Carry it where?”
“East,” said Nahl. “Until we find the next room.”
Behind them, when Riss did the arithmetic at the end of the first month, the whole of it came to this.
A page in a mill ledger at Ashenford West, stitched behind eighty-one names, with the truth in the fourth column.

A clerk called Ivet Sallow who had not sent a return in six months. Who had not written her query register. Who had not answered the county’s second question, because the second question had a certificate under it that she could not sign.
Four papers in a drawer under a counter with a string on them.

A county sheet in a counting house, folded twice, with a notch and a tally of five where four hundred thousand reasons had been written in thirty years. It was in the inside pocket of a clerk who had read it and filed nothing.
A woman of business two hundred miles west with four lines in her coat and a report she was never going to write.
A parish clerk at Odder who had watched a hand go into a coat and come back to the table.

And the assize, which sat in the spring, and which would bring the counties’ attention back to the mill on the Vellum on a calendar and not on a warrant, because that was how the machine worked. Not a hangman. A calendar.
Riss put all of it in the Leaf one evening and read it back to the company, and the entry had four lines and no number in it.
Ahead of them, when Riss did the other arithmetic, was this.
The road, which had no name on any post east of the fingerpost.
Whatever room came next, with whatever clerk and whatever book, and a count to be spoken standing up with nobody writing it.

Veylan’s field in the west, in the spring, with a tin of soil at the top of his coat and forty-one dead seedlings in a crate at the foot of a mountain. And a promise that he would walk out of the field after it was planted and go east again, or wherever the road was.
Kael’s hand, quiet, and Kael himself without any idea what he was for.
Corvath, who had not smelled anything for four months and could now smell the iron in the frost and the smoke of a village four miles off, and who said so every day.
Old Den, who walked last and coughed and kept up. Two winters in him by the healer’s count, and four if he sat in a cottage. He had asked twice that his choosing the road be entered somewhere.

Eight people and one goat, and no names in any book anywhere in the eleven counties. A log that belonged to a dead man. A Leaf. A count that was in their mouths and a name that was a sound. And the practice, which had nine parts and did not have a destination.
There was no wind.

That was the thing that had been true every single day since the tenth month and it had stopped being strange, which was the strangest part of it. The winter passed without a gale. The smoke went up straight out of every village they came to. The hedges held the frost and the frost did not blow off them.

The plate hummed the third note under Riss’s shirt every day. Not the divided fifth and not the clean one. The note that had been missing from the middle of it, quiet and even. Riss had long since stopped trying to find a word for it. Some time in the eleventh month she had started to notice the days when it was not there, and there were none of them.

Above the road the sky was county sky. Behind it the Emberion hung with its fifteen joints and the piece missing out of the wing, and nobody in the company had seen it since the mill. Nobody in the company expected to.

And down in every valley where the roads crossed, the gold road and the grey road ran side by side with nobody on either of them in any direction a man could see. Neither of them shone. They had not shone since the border stone, four hundred miles west of the road the company was on, in a country nobody had written down.

They came to the end of the first month on a road that ran east out of a village with a well on the green and a ford below it. In the evening they stopped on a low hill at a milestone. It had a town’s name on it and a worn number under the name.
The town was four days east and none of the eight of them had ever heard of it and none of them said its name out loud.

Nahl put the log down on the stone and sat on the wall by the milestone. The company stood around in the last of the light in the order they walked. Riss looked at all eight of them once, the way a keeper counts a row.
Then the count was said.
Forwards and backwards. Standing up, on a county road, in the first month of a year nobody in the company was keeping.
Then the name in its parts, one at a time, with a breath between each.
Then the line, all eight together, on a hill, in the cold.
“I can see it. This is real.”

Then they picked up the log and the Leaf and the tin and the chart and the slate and the boots and went on down the hill, with the goat in front and Old Den last. There was nothing in front of them on that road except a village they had never seen. And a room with a book in it somewhere beyond it.
The page stayed in a mill ledger behind eighty-one names. The count stayed in eight mouths. The name stayed a sound.
There was no destination and there was a practice, and the practice was the point, and the company walked east.

chapters.label: Interlude F
chapters.title: The Third Column
paragraphs: After the turn of the year at the milestone, and the count said out loud and lost, and the road going on east out of the counties, four hundred miles back down that road there was a clerk at a counter with a pen in her hand.
The clerk was twenty-four years old. She had the best handwriting in her family and it leaned very slightly left at the base, the way soldiers stand at ease.
Her name was Ness Riss.
She was good at columns. That was the first fact of her life and the only one she had never had to defend.
She had been in that office two years and nine months.
She had written one thousand nine hundred columns in the county tongue. She could write it faster than she could read it. She had never once been able to read a line of what she wrote.
A person who writes a column in a language she does not read learns to care about other things.

The width of the letters. The height of the figures. Whether a four sits on the line or stands in the box. Whether the rule at the top of a page is drawn with the straight edge on the left and taken off to the right, or the other way about.
There is a right way. Ness found it in her first month. Nobody had ever told her what it was and nobody had ever improved on it since.
The third column is the reason column.
That is true of most forms in the eleven counties, and it is not true of hers.
The county’s forms have four columns. Every column has a heading. The headings are in the county tongue.
The heading on the third column is nine words long. It has been the same nine words on every form in the eleven counties for two hundred years.
Ness Riss could write those nine words in four seconds. She wrote them about eleven times a day. Her hand knew the shape of them the way a hand knows a door.
She did not know what they said.
She asked, once, in her third week. She asked a senior clerk with nine years in the building. He looked at her the way a man looks at a question that has never once occurred to him.
“I don’t know,” he said. Then, after a moment: “Nobody in the building knows. The heading comes with the form.”

So the heading came with the form. The form came with the district. The district came with the county. And somewhere in the eleven counties there was a man who could read the nine words, and nobody had asked him a direct question about them either.
Nineteen hundred columns.
Ness kept that number in her head and checked it from the bottom up, which is how her family did arithmetic. It came out the same every way she did it.
Nineteen hundred columns. Not one line of any of them readable by the woman who wrote them.
She had one private sentence about the whole of it, and she had never said it out loud to anybody.
*A hand is not a person.*

A hand can be excellent. A hand can be the best in the district. A hand can be given a column and a straight edge and a pen cut to its own grip, and it will turn out the most exact work in the building for two years and nine months.
And at the end of it, the hand has written nineteen hundred columns and the person does not know what any of them says.
The county runs on people who are useful in ways they cannot check.
She had un-ticked a box once.
It was in the spring, two years ago, in a market square. It was a county schedule with ninety-one names on it in her own hand.

The box was at the foot of the sheet. It is the box the office ticks when the names are taken. A form with a box at the foot of it is not a finished page until the box is ticked, and a finished page is what a district gets paid for.
Ness left the box un-ticked.
She could not have said at the time why she did it. She put the pen down with the box in front of her and went on to the next line of the work, which was an inventory.
A supervisor came along at four o’clock with the day’s sheaf and ticked sixty boxes in eleven minutes and did not look at one of them. That is what a supervisor is.
Somewhere in that ninety-one names was her own.
Thirty-first. **Ness Riss.**

She had been made to write her own name on a county schedule with her own hand, in the best handwriting in the family. Then somebody else had ticked a box over the top of it, and the box is the part that counts.
A person who writes her own name into a column and then watches a box be ticked over it learns something a clerk should not know.
The writing is not the thing. The tick is the thing.
The note about the party came up the river on the Thursday. It was one line on the corner of a bag.
*Party of no account, east road, one animal. Watch and note.*
That is the whole of the county’s interest in a company of eight that had been on the road for five months.

It was not a levy and it was not a warrant and it was not a pursuit. It was a line on the corner of a bag. It went to the gatekeepers and the ferrymen and the two parish clerks. Every one of them would note it daily for a fortnight and then stop. The district would know exactly where eight people with a goat had been and exactly nothing else.
Ness read the line twice.

She knew what a party of no account was. Every clerk knew the phrase. It is the phrase a seizure sheet uses for a thing that has no page under it, and the county uses it the way arithmetic is kind, which is to say without malice.
She knew something else, and she had not said it to anybody.
The company on the east road had a goat in front of it and a party of eight, and the county’s own note had been using their phrase since the ninth month of the year before last.
There had been a schedule at Vellum Reach in the spring of that year with ninety-one names on it in her hand.
The thirty-first one had been hers.
And the party on the east road was the only other thing in the eleven counties that had come out of that square with nothing on it.
Her sister’s sentence was in the drawer of her desk. It was in a letter that had been answered and not sent.
It was nine words long. Ness had written it in the blank space on the back of a household form.
*Years don’t divide better. Come back when you can say what you took.*

She had thought about it for two years and nine months. She had written four answers in her head and never put one on paper, because the whole point of the sentence is that it cannot be answered by a person sitting down.
Over the ridge, past the border stone, out on the nine hundred miles of the road, her sister was walking east with a log and a page and a name no throat could say and a count written nowhere.
And Ness Riss was in a warm room at a counter with a lamp and a pen and one thousand nine hundred columns.
Her sister had taken a year. That was what Ness had.
It was not a grievance. Ness was better at columns than Riss would ever be, and she had done the arithmetic of it long ago, and the arithmetic was correct.
*They left. I stayed. Both were the careful choice. Only one of us ended up with a page under her name.*
The item came onto the calendar in the second month.
*Unentered animal, north meadow, present since the fifteenth day of the first month. Disposition required.*
Ness read it on the board on her way in, on a Tuesday, in the cold. Then she went upstairs and did eleven columns.
The office talked about it for a week, the way offices do.

The senior clerk said the item would go to an entry, because you cannot remove a thing that cannot be removed. A counter clerk said his brother-in-law had seen it from the north road and that it was the size of a barn and a half. A woman in the copying room said the counties ought to have a form for it, and everybody laughed, and it was not an unkind laugh, and Ness laughed too, because she was liked in that building.
Ness Riss said nothing at all about the mechanic.

She had worked it out in the first week. It is not difficult. An entry needs a correction. A correction needs the third column. The third column is hers. So it would come down to her desk, and somebody in the office would assume she would do it in the ordinary way, because she did everything in the ordinary way and because she was the fastest hand in the district.

They would assume it because there is no person in the eleven counties who can write a column in a language she cannot read, eleven times a day, for two years and nine months, be excellent at it, and then refuse.
The refusal of a clerk like that is not in the county’s experience of its own clerks.
She did the arithmetic one more time on the Tuesday evening, with the lamp lit and the last of the sheaf in front of her.
She was the clerk of record. She could write the correction. She could not sign it.
The card on the counter said *find the error, write the correction, sign the line.* There was no error. Everybody in the building knew there was no error.
A person who writes a correction and does not sign it has left a page in a working register that the register cannot answer.
That is a lapsed item. It was the only sentence she had, and she had had it for a fortnight, and she was not going to write it down.
On the last evening of the second month she was the last one in the room, which was usual.
She closed the ledger and put the pen away and drew the cover over the counter, the way she did every night.
Then she went out and stood in the market for a minute in the cold.
Her sister was on the east road somewhere with a goat in front of her and would be here in three weeks. Neither of them had said one word about it in two years.
Ness Riss looked at the board with the district’s business on it, and at the item at the bottom of it, and at the two lamps at the corner being lit by a boy.
Then she looked up, because the night was clear and the town was full of people who did not.

The Emberion stood over the county town with its fifteen joints and the piece missing out of the wing, the way it stood over every town in the eleven counties, and every person in that market was walking home under it without once lifting their head.

At the far end of the street, past the customs house, the two roads came in through the gate side by side. The gold one and the grey one. They ran together for a hundred yards at the crossing and then they went east out of the town, and both of them were ordinary road in the lamplight, and neither of them had ever been entered in any book that Ness had ever written in.
Then she went home, because a clerk with a desk in the morning goes home.
She had decided about the box in the first week.
She did not know it yet, but so had her sister.

chapters.part: Act V · The Return and the Counting
chapters.label: Chapter 35
chapters.title: The Return
paragraphs: After the turn of the year at the milestone, and the settlement paper at Wend, the company walked east with winter in it. The last refusal of the book had been made in a yard in front of two men who had to live with it.
They walked for three weeks.

The practice went with them, all nine parts, exactly as it had been written down on the hill. Pay first. Give no names. Take no work. Never two nights. Find the clerk before the tavern. Count standing up. Write nothing. Leave nothing. And when somebody asks where the company is going, say that the company is walking east.
Nine parts, and no destination, and that was the whole of the machine they carried. It weighed nothing. It had no page under it anywhere in the eleven counties.
On the fourth day of the first month they came to a village with a mill and two streets. Nahl went to find the clerk first, as the practice says. The clerk was already standing in his door.
That was the thing that had changed, and it took the company a week to see the size of it.
The clerk knew the shape.

He was a thin man of about forty with a book under his arm, and he did not ask them anything. He stood in the doorway of his house and looked at the eight of them and at the goat in front, and he said one sentence before Nahl had opened their mouth.
“Party of no account,” he said. “Eight persons, one animal, no names given.”
“Not yet,” said Nahl.
“The county’s had the line since the ninth month,” said the clerk. “It came up the river with the quarter’s papers. Party of no account, nothing taken, nothing owed. I have it in the end of my book.”
Nobody said anything for a moment.
“Then you know how we do it,” said Riss.

“I have read how the counties do it,” said the clerk. “That is a different thing and you know it is. You are the eight that walked west and came back with a log.” He shifted the book under his arm. “Come in or do not come in. If you come in, stand in the room with the book and say your number out loud and I will hear it and write nothing, the same as the last clerk did, and I will go to bed afterwards and be a man who heard a count.”
“That is the practice exactly,” said Nahl.
“I know it is,” said the clerk. “It went through the trade like a fire.”
They did the room that night, properly, and the count was spoken standing up, and the clerk wrote nothing.
But Nahl lay awake afterwards, and the arithmetic of the thing would not come out.
A practice that goes through the trade like a fire is a practice that is in the trade’s books.

Not in a county book. In the trade’s. In the way a man at Ashgate tells a man at Sunth that the eight are on the road. What they will do when they arrive. How to behave. What to write down, which is nothing. The counties had not caught the company. The counties had learned it.
They were still unfiled. They were, at the same time, expected.

Nahl lay in the dark with the log under their head and worked it out the way a bearer works a page. There was no line about the company anywhere in the eleven counties. That was true, and it would stay true. But there was now a *way to receive them*, and a way to receive a thing is a kind of entry, and an entry is a thing that can be amended.
That was the fourth part of the year turning, and Nahl carried it for a week without saying it.
The valley opened out on the eleventh day.
It stopped being one road between hedges. It became three roads and a river with two bridges. On the far bank there was a town with a wall on the low ground and smoke standing straight up out of it.
Mira stopped at the top of the rise and took the chart tube out of her pack and did not open it.
“That is the county town,” she said.
“Which one?” said Veylan.
“The one they meant,” said Mira. “It is on the fingerpost. It was on the county rider’s bag. It is where the assize sits.”
Riss came up beside her and stood looking down at it for a while.
“How far off?”

“Eleven miles,” said Mira. “Eleven and a bit. There are four roads coming into it and a wall with a gate on the north side, and the water at the bottom is the Vellum and the river goes east out of the town, which is the way we are going.” She put the tube back. “I am not drawing it.”
“You walked it.”
“I will walk it,” said Mira. “When I have walked it, I will draw it. That is the rule and it has not changed because the town is the last one.”
They camped that night in a beech wood two miles short of the gate, out of the wind, because Sancora would not have them walk into a walled town at the end of a day.
The fire was small and the company sat around it in the order they walked, and Riss said the thing that had been waiting for eleven days.

“The assize sits in the third month,” said Riss. “That is six weeks. Before it sits, there is nothing in that town that decides anything. When it sits, the counties spend nine days finishing their year.”
“Finishing their year,” said Veylan.

“Every return, every query, every certificate in the district comes up to the assize in the third month,” said Riss. “The mill’s page comes up. The clerk at Odder comes up. The surveyor’s peg comes up. All of it has to agree, and when it agrees, it is the year.”
“And?”

“And there is not one line in any of it about the eight of us, and there never will be, because that is the practice, and the practice has been working since the ninth month.” Riss put another stick on the fire. “But the thing we are carrying is not in the practice. It does not have a part. It has been on the road behind us for three months and it does not fit in any of the nine.”
The company sat with that.

It was the first time any of them had said it out loud in a sentence. The sentence had a shape to it that everybody in the circle recognised. They had all been carrying it the same way. Something had been walking behind them since the high ground. Nobody had said so. Nobody had looked at it directly, the way a person does not look at a thing on the far side of a hedge until they have decided what is going to be done about it.
“You have all seen it,” said Riss.
“A shape on the road,” said Sancora. “Twice. At evening.”
“The goat has been walking behind since the descent,” said Kael.
“Nothing,” said Corvath.
Everybody looked at him, because that is what the company did now whenever Corvath said anything about the air.

“I can smell rain on a hide and smoke and wet stone, and I can smell a mill from a mile off,” said Corvath. “That is what I have got back and I am not going to pretend to more. The thing on the road behind us has no smell. That is not the same as there being nothing there. It is the same as there being nothing there *for me*. I have been fooled by that once already, on the mountain, and I am telling you plainly so that nobody counts on me.”
“Nobody is counting on you,” said Sancora. “You are a man at a fire. That is all any of us are.”
Kael said the other thing that had been waiting, and he said it to the fire.

“I tried the trace on it at first light. There is no edge. Not the kept kind and not the added-up kind. It is not a thing that has been taken out of anything, and it is not a thing that anybody has added up. I have nothing to say about it and that is my whole report.”
Sancora made them all sit down in a row and did their feet, because that is what she did before a town and she had done it before every town for five months.

She did it in the light of the fire, with the kit open on a flat stone, and she did not ask anybody whether they wanted it done. Hands first: the knuckles, the tendons, the two fingers on Kael’s left hand that had gone a little stiff since the ridge. Then feet: the heels, the nails, the space between the toes. She cut Veylan’s nails with a knife and made him swear at her for it and told him to hold still.

“Kael’s left hand is worse than it was at Odder,” she said. “It will hold for a town. It will hold all spring. After that it wants a proper man to look at it and I am not a proper man, I am a woman with two satchels.”
“Noted,” said Kael.
“Old Den’s feet are better than the rest of him,” said Sancora. “The chest is the chest and I have said what there is to say about it and I am not going to say it again at a fire.”
“Noted,” said Old Den, in exactly the same voice, and the company laughed, and the fire moved, and it was the last easy hour they had before the town.

Old Den was sitting on the outside of the circle as he always did, with his back to a tree. He said the practical thing, because he was the only one in the company old enough to say it without it being a question.
“Then what do we do with it?”
Nobody answered at once.
“The practice says walk east,” said Veylan. “I am not in favour of re-writing it on the last night before a walled town. It has kept us for four months.”

“Then we walk east with it,” said Riss. “That is my answer and it is the same answer. But we do not walk east past the gate the way we have walked past eleven villages. The thing behind us does not fit in nine parts and it never will. The room that decides what a thing is in this country is in that town, and it is open six days a week, and the assize sits in the third month.”
“You are saying we take it in.”

“I am saying we stop walking away from the only room that can be told the truth,” said Riss. “We have carried a page a thousand miles and the page has not moved. The page cannot move. It is stitched in a ledger at Ashenford and it will be there when the roof comes off. We are the only thing in this company that moves, and we have been moving in the wrong direction since the ninth month.”
That was as long a speech as Riss had made since the ridge, and the company took it the way they took everything Riss said, which was to check it against their own trade.
“Farmer’s answer,” said Veylan, after a while. “If there is a field at the end of a road and the field has to be ploughed, you do not plough the road.”
“No.”
“So we go in and we plough,” said Veylan. “All right. When?”

“Four days,” said Nahl. “We go in on the fifteenth, which is the day after tomorrow and then two days. We take a room. We find the clerk before the tavern, which is the practice and I am not minded to break it because the town is bigger. And then Riss and I go and look at a door.”
The thing came out of the high ground on the fourteenth day.
It did not come at them. That is worth writing down plainly, because a person who has heard the stories would expect the other thing, and the other thing did not happen.

The wind came first, in the afternoon, from the west, which is where they had come from. It was the same wind as Collow and the same wind as the grey wall. Every blade of it went the wrong way for the season.

The plate under Riss’s shirt hummed. It hummed the divided fifth, quiet, the volume of a cat. Then it moved up and found the third note. That was the note that had been missing from the middle of the divided fifth. It had first hummed it on the shelf of rock above the last grass.
Riss stopped walking and stood in the road with a hand flat on their chest.
The goat came back.

That was the second thing and it was the thing that made Nahl’s mouth dry. The goat walked back down the company’s own line. Past Nahl, past Riss, past all eight of them. It went and stood in the road facing west with its head up, and did not bleat, and did not lie down.
The company stood in the road and waited, because there was nothing else that could be done with a goat on the grey line.
Then the high ground behind them, which had been the same brown ridge for three days, was not the same brown ridge.
It came down off the shoulder of it and out onto the flat.

It was the size of a barn and a half and it was built the way a hill is built. It had a wing folded along its back, and there was a piece missing out of the wing. It came down the road at the pace of a person walking a horse. It did not hurry and it did not slow.
Kael’s burned hand opened on its own and closed again.
Old Den, who had gone up a mountain once with ten thousand men, did not say anything at all, which was the worst thing anybody in the company heard that day.

Nobody ran. Riss thought about that afterwards for years and never found a better reason than this. The practice has nine parts and none of them says run. And a company that has spent four months teaching eleven villages a form does not get to break the form in front of the eleventh.
It came up the road and it stopped at the goat.
It stood over the goat for a while.
Then the goat turned around, without any fuss at all, and walked back east up the line to the front, and took its place in front of the company, and stood there.
And the thing followed it.

That was the whole of the transaction, and it took about nine minutes, and nobody in the company ever managed to describe it afterwards in a way that satisfied anybody else. Veylan tried it once, in a room, and said: “It is like being met at your own gate by a man who has no letter and wants nothing. You do not know what to do with your hands.”
It walked behind them.

It did not attack. It did not speak, on the road, then or on any of the days that came after. It did not ask for anything and it did not give anything and it did not come between the company and the town. It stayed about two hundred paces back. That is the distance a man walks in a day when he is following a party he does not wish to be part of and does not wish to lose. It walked the way it had come down the hill, which was the pace of a person walking a horse.

The goat walked in front. The company walked in the middle. The thing that had never been entered walked behind, and the wind came with it the whole way, and the plate hummed the third note, quietly, for eleven miles.

They stopped on the rise a mile short of the north gate. Mira wanted to look at the wall in the light and Sancora wanted to look at everybody’s feet before a town. And they all wanted one minute in which the thing was behind them, and the town was in front of them, and there was nothing in between.
Mira counted the towers. Seven, and the signboard at the gate said three markets, a bridge, and a customs house.
“Well,” said Veylan.
“Well,” said Nahl.

The company stood in the road in the cold with the town below them and the thing on the road behind them. Then Riss looked at Nahl and Nahl looked at Riss, and they said the exchange the two of them had been saying since the ridge. The others had learned to leave it alone.
“What do we do now?”
“We carry it.”
“Carry it where?”
“East,” said Nahl. “Into the room.”
“Until when?”

“Until we are told no,” said Nahl. “And we will be told no. That is what the room is for. Everything in this country that says no is in that town, behind that wall, on a form, and the form has a box on it, and the box is where the no lives.”
Riss looked down at the town for a moment.
“Then let us go and be told no,” they said.

The goat walked down the hill. The company followed it. Two hundred paces back, at the pace of a person walking a horse, the thing that had never been entered came down the road after them and out of the last of the light. The wind went into the streets ahead of all of them and pushed the smoke of the county town sideways.

chapters.part: Act V · The Return and the Counting
chapters.label: Chapter 36
chapters.title: The County Seat
paragraphs: After the north gate of the county town, and the wall with seven towers on it, and the bridge over the Vellum with a mill under the arch, the company did what the practice says. In a town, find the clerk before the tavern.
The clerk was at the gate.
There was a gatehouse, and there was a desk in the gatehouse, and on the desk there was a book.

The book was for strangers. That was the law in a county seat. The law was old and had been written by people who had long since been filed and forgotten. Any person not of the town who came in through a gate should put a thumb on the page.
The gatekeeper was a man of about sixty in a coat with a county badge on the shoulder. He was polite. He had a pot of ink and a cloth and he had been doing the job for thirty years.
“Thumb,” he said.
Nahl looked at the book. It had a page ruled into columns. The columns had no headings. The page held about eleven thumbs and a date at the top in a clerk’s hand.
“What is the column for?” said Nahl.
“That is the county’s business,” said the gatekeeper.
“I am a bearer,” said Nahl. “I ask because it is my trade to know what a page is for before I put anything on it.”
The gatekeeper looked at Nahl for a moment with the tired patience of a man whose desk has heard every argument there is.

“It is for the thumb,” he said. “I do not write anything. I take the thumb. The page goes up to the office at the end of the month and a clerk counts the thumbs, and if the count is right the page is initialled and filed, and if the count is wrong there is a query, and I have had two queries in thirty years and both of them were mine and both of them were arithmetic.”
“And what happens to the thumbs?”
“Nothing,” said the gatekeeper. “They are a count. That is the whole of the law.”

Old Den, who was at the back of the line, said the thing he had said at Marrowgate two years before. He said it in exactly the same words, which is what a man does with a sentence he has decided to keep.
“Write refused,” he said. “That is his right.”
The gatekeeper looked up.
“Whose right?”
“Ours,” said Old Den. “We are eight strangers in a county seat and we are not putting anything on the page.”
And here is the thing that Riss put in the Leaf that night, because it was the whole of the day and it was worth being exact about.
The gatekeeper wrote it.

He took his pen and wrote, in the margin of the page, in a hand that was not a clerk’s hand, three words. *Refused. Eight. Party.* Then he blotted it and closed the book and put it back on the desk and said, “Keep your hands off the ink and the rest of it is no business of mine.”

Nobody was arrested. Nobody was sent for. The gate opened. The company walked into the county town of the district that had been sending them papers for two years. The only trace of them in the town’s own law was three words in a margin and a blotted page.
That was the counties. Riss had known it since Marrowgate and it still took the breath out of the day every time.

A thing that has been refused is not a thing that has been entered. And a thing that has not been entered has not happened. And there is no form in the country for a company of eight that is on the road.
The town had three markets and a customs house and a street of offices with brass plates on the doors.

They took rooms over a stable in the yard of an inn called the Bell and Crown, two streets back from the river. The landlord looked at the goat for a while. Then he put the company in the wing by the yard, which was what landlords did with anybody who had an animal.

The goat walked the yard’s boundary, once, all the way round, with its nose down. Then it lay at the door of the wing, which was what the goat did, and which the company had long since stopped discussing.
Then they all did the thing each of them did in a town.

Veylan went to the market to look at the seed, because a farmer in a market is a farmer doing arithmetic. Sancora took the satchels and went to find a chandler and a physician’s shop, because a healer in a town is a healer replacing what she has used. Kael went to the river, because Kael had spent four months finding edges in things and a working river has a great many of them. Corvath walked the streets with his nose up and said nothing to anybody for three hours and came back reeking of fish and smoke and said, “It is all there. All of it. I could tell you what the man at the end of the lane had for breakfast.” Mira sat on the step with the chart tube across her knees and did not open it, because she had not walked the town yet.
Mira went out at two in the afternoon and walked the whole town, and it took her the rest of the day.

She walked the wall from the north gate to the east gate and counted seven towers. She walked the two bridges and stood at the mill under the arch for a quarter of an hour, because a mill is a place where a river is made to do arithmetic. She walked the three markets and the street of offices and the lane by the river where the barges come in, and she came back up through the customs house yard, where a clerk was chalking sacks, and out at the north gate again.
The chalk was red and the sacks were counted in sevens, and a boy stood behind the clerk with a slate and wrote nothing, because a number called out in a yard is not a number in a book.
Then she sat on the step of the Bell and Crown with the tube across her knees and unrolled the paper and drew the county town.

It took her an hour and a half. She drew the wall and the seven towers and the two bridges and the mill and the three markets and the river going east. She drew the Hall with its garden and its benches, and she drew the office door with the two brass plates on it and did not write anything on either plate, because she had not read one of them. She drew the meadow to the north with a mark in it and no shape.

Then she rolled it up and put it back in the tube, and that was the end of it. One sheet. One town. No copies. Riss came past and looked at the tube and did not ask, because the rule had held for five months and nobody was going to break it in the last town before the assize.
“Anything you did not draw?” said Riss.
“The inside of the Hall,” said Mira. “I have not been in it and I am not going to put the inside of a building on the sheet. That has been the rule since Marle.”
And Riss and Nahl went to look at a door.
The Hygiene Hall stood on the north side of the third market, and it was the same building as the one at Ashgate, to the width of a hand.

That was the thing that Riss could not get over, and had not been able to get over since the first one. Long. Low. Pale stone. Slate roof. A garden in front of it with benches in it, and people on the benches, and the people had cups.

It was the least frightening building in the town. Nobody there was doing anything wrong to anybody. That was the whole method, and it worked the same in the last town and it would work the same in the next one.
The door had two brass plates on it.

The upper one said, in plain capital letters, ASSESSOR OF HYGIENE. The lower one was in the county tongue, in smaller letters: three words that Riss could not read. Riss had never been able to read them. But Riss had seen them once before. They had been at the foot of a page at Vellum Reach, in the spring, on a schedule with ninety-one names on it.
Nahl read it, because Nahl had traded in six counties and read the tongue.
“It says the office is open,” said Nahl. “Eight to four. Six days.”
“Then we have come on the right day,” said Riss.
“We have come on a Thursday,” said Nahl. “Thursday is the day the bags go out.”
There was a board at the side of the door with the county’s business on it, and the county’s business covered four sheets of paper.
Riss stood in front of it for a quarter of an hour and read the whole thing. By the end of it, Riss knew more about the district than they had known in four months on the road.

The assize would sit on the ninth day of the third month. It would sit for nine days. Every return, query, certificate, seizure, survey and correction in the district was on that calendar. Anybody could read it. It was the district’s business and the district had a right to know what was going to be decided about it.
There were a hundred and eleven items on the list.

Riss read them all, because they were the shape of the thing Riss had been walking toward for five months. One of them was about a mill on the Vellum at Ashenford. One was about the return of a clerk at Odder. And one was about a surveyor’s peg on the western slope below a cairn. The county described it in its own words. *Marker, unclaimed, no parish, sixty-one miles west of the last surveyed line.* There was a query against it in the sixth column. The query said: *who is at this mark.*
“Well,” said Nahl, reading over Riss’s shoulder.
“Well,” said Riss.
“They have been to the stone.”
“They have been to the stone,” said Riss. “It took them four months and it is a query and it is item eighty-four.”
And then Riss turned around, and looked through the open door of the Hygiene Hall, and saw their sister.
Ness Riss was twenty-four years old and she was standing at a counter in a room of desks.

She had her sleeves rolled and she was writing. She was writing a column. The column was in a book that lay flat on the counter. She wrote with her left hand held flat along the page and her right hand moving small and quick. Riss knew the movement the way a person knows the sound of a house at night, from before words.

There was a queue of three at her counter. She dealt with all three. She was quick and she was correct. Two of the three went away satisfied. The third went away with a query slip and a date on it, which is what you get in that building when the answer is no.
Riss stood on the pavement in the cold on the other side of the third market with the plate humming quietly under their coat and did not cross the street.

That is the whole of it. There is no better way to write it. Riss had walked eleven hundred miles and had been counted on a shelf of rock. Riss had carried a log and a page and a name in eight parts, and a brass plate that no clerk would ever catalogue. And Riss had come at last to a town with their sister in it, at a counter, thirty feet away. Riss did not cross the street.
Riss stood there for nine minutes. Then the door of the Hall opened and a clerk came out with a bag of post and went off down the lane toward the river. Riss turned around and walked away.
Nahl, who had stood at their shoulder the whole time without saying one word, walked away with them.
They went down to the river and stood on the bridge for a while. Riss had something to say, and a bridge is a good place for a sentence with a person you have walked with for five months.
“She is better at columns than I ever was,” said Riss.
“Yes,” said Nahl.
“She has the best handwriting in my family. It leans very slightly left at the base, the way soldiers stand at ease.”
“I have heard you say that once before,” said Nahl.
“At the cairn,” said Riss. “On the ridge, in the wind. I said the whole of the thing to a stone because I could not say it to a person.”
“And now she is thirty feet away and there is a counter in between.”
“There is a counter in between,” said Riss.
Nahl said nothing, because a bearer’s trade is knowing when a page has been turned and the sentence under it is not written yet.
Riss looked at the water for a while.

“When the year divides better,” said Riss. “That is what I told her. I left her downriver in the spring and I did it carefully and I did it in arithmetic. One year. Then the year would divide better and I would send for her.”
“And the year did not divide better.”

“No.” Riss put both hands on the parapet, because a person with their hands on a parapet does not have to do anything with them. “She wrote back on the back of a form. Three lines. The last line was: *years don’t divide better. Come back when you can say what you took.*”
“And can you say what you took?” said Nahl.

Riss was quiet for a long time. Below them the Vellum went under the bridge with the last of the winter in it. It was the same water that went past the mill at Ashenford four hundred miles west. It was the same water that went east out of the town past Vellum Reach, nine miles down, where a market square had a post-boat and a trough and a woman with two loaves.
“No,” said Riss. “I can say what I kept. I cannot say what I took. Those are two different sentences and I have spent five months learning the difference.”
They came back through the market at dusk and Riss looked at the board again. The board was the district’s business, and the district’s business was the only map of the thing Riss was inside of.
There was one new thing on it.

It was a small sheet, pinned in the corner of the fourth frame, and it was new enough that the ink was still black and not grey. It was a notice of the kind that goes up when something unusual happens that the counties have no form for. It said four lines. It was signed by a clerk of the office and addressed to the market constables, the gatekeepers, the ferrymen, the two parish clerks, and the man who did the county’s cartage.
*Unentered animal, present in the north meadow since this day. No return is to be taken. No fee is to be charged. No person is to interfere. Watch is to be kept and noted daily.*
Riss read it twice.
“No return is to be taken,” said Riss.
“They have had a look at it,” said Nahl, “and they have made the only ruling they can make, and the ruling is the same nine words the Index has at the back of the third volume.”
“*Beyond the peaks. No entries are to be made.*”

“The counties have looked at a thing they cannot file,” said Nahl, “and they have written nothing down about it except that nothing is to be written down. Which is the only sensible thing about this country that I have ever found.”
Riss looked at the notice for a while longer.

“It is going to be a problem for them,” said Riss. “It is in the meadow and it is on the calendar of the mind of the district. They cannot put it in a column and they cannot move it on, and a thing that cannot be moved on has to be *done about*, and doing something about it is the one thing their own law does not allow.”
“Yes,” said Nahl.
“And the assize sits in the third month.”
“The assize sits in the third month,” said Nahl. “Three weeks.”

Night came down and the office across the market kept a lamp on in the front room until eight. Then the lamp went out. That is what lamps do in a building where a clerk has finished for the day and gone home to a house with children in it.

The company ate in the inn, and everybody was tired, and Mira wrote one line in her notebook and closed it, and Old Den went out to the yard at ten to look at the goat and came back and said, “It is at the door and it is awake.”
And Riss lay in the dark over the stable of the Bell and Crown and did the thing Riss did every night. The day went into one sentence so that it could be carried.
The sentence was: *we have come to the room, and the room is open at eight.*

chapters.part: Act V · The Return and the Counting
chapters.label: Chapter 37
chapters.title: The Office
paragraphs: After the counter at the gate, and the board with the district’s calendar on it, and the sister at her counter thirty feet away, Nahl went to the office at eight in the morning on the Friday. The practice says find the clerk. And a bearer does not send for a clerk. A bearer stands in the room and waits to be asked.
Nahl went alone, and that was deliberate, and the company agreed with it.

A party of eight in a public office is a demonstration. A party of one is a person with a question. The practice has nine parts and no part of it says how many of you go in. That is because the answer changes with the room. And the company had learned in five months that the man who writes the room’s answer is usually the one who came in by himself.
The room was the same as every room in the county that deals with people.

A counter. Three clerks. A shelf of ledgers on the wall. A queue of six on the benches, in the ordinary way, with baskets and papers and one child asleep on a coat. A sign above the counter that said ENQUIRIES, and under it, in the county tongue, four words that Nahl could read and most of the queue could not.
Nahl took a place on the bench and waited an hour and ten minutes, which is the whole of what a bearer is for in a public building.

The queue talked, because queues talk, and Nahl listened, because that is the trade. A man two benches down was querying a fee on a mill race. A woman at the counter was asking for a copy of a page about her father. The clerk was explaining, kindly, that the page was in a volume that was at the bindery and would be back in nine days. A boy of about twelve was there for his mother, with a slip in his fist, and he got his answer in four minutes and ran out pleased.

That was the machine at work and Nahl had seen it before, and there was nothing in it that was cruel. It was a room full of people being helped by a system that was correct nearly all of the time. That was the thing Nahl had learned on the road and could never manage to write down properly in the Leaf when it was Riss’s turn to have the pen.
When Nahl got to the counter, Nahl said the true thing.
“I want to make an entry for a thing that has never been entered.”
The clerk was a young man with clean cuffs. He was polite and he was quick, and he was the fourth man of that exact description that the company had met in this book.

“That is not a thing this office does,” he said. “The office enters parties. Names with accounts against them. Mill transactions. Holdings. You want the Hall of Records at Sunth for corrections, and even there …” He stopped. “What is it that you want entered?”

“An animal,” said Nahl. “It is in the north meadow. Your own notice is on the board at the side of this building. Unentered animal, present in the north meadow since Thursday. No return is to be taken.”
The clerk’s face did the thing that faces do in offices.

“That is the Assessor’s own notice,” he said. “I cannot help you with it. Nobody at this desk can help you with it.” He looked at Nahl for a moment, and then did the thing that Nahl had been counting on, which was that a good clerk does not want a question to sit unanswered on his own desk. “I will take it through to the inner office.”
The inner office was a room with a window and a fire and two desks.
One desk was a working desk: papers in three trays, a blotter, an inkwell, a pen, a pair of spectacles folded on a page.
The other desk was small and it was at the window, and a child was sitting at it doing sums.
Corin Quire, Assessor of Hygiene, was fifty-six years old and had ink on his cuffs and thirty-one years of paper behind him.

He came round the desk himself and shook Nahl’s hand, which the county did not require of him. He remembered Nahl. He said so at once, and he said the true thing about where they had met, and he did not pretend it had been pleasant for anybody.

“Marrowgate,” he said. “The customs house. You are the bearer. You gave me no name and I did not insist, and I have thought about that more often than I have thought about most pages I have written since.”
“There were nine of us then,” said Nahl.

“I know,” said Corin Quire. “I have heard. I get the trade’s word on things the county does not write down.” He went back to his chair. “Sit down, bearer. This will take a quarter of an hour and you are entitled to sit through it. This is my daughter Pella. She does sums on short days.”
The girl at the small desk looked up and said, “Good morning,” in the way a child says it when she has been taught to say it to everybody who comes in, and returned to her column.
“Do you want to tell me about the animal,” said the Assessor, “or do you want to ask me a question?”
Nahl had thought about that for eleven days of walking. It had come to the same thing in the end, and the same thing was the reason Nahl had come in alone.
“A question,” said Nahl. “And then I will answer anything you ask me, including the things I will not tell you.”

“That is a fair trade,” said Corin Quire. “It is the fairest trade anybody has offered me in this office in nine years, and it is offered by the only man in the district who is not on the calendar. Ask.”
“What is a person for?”

The Assessor did not laugh and he did not look away and he did not ask what Nahl meant. He thought about the question. He was a man who thought about questions, and Nahl, watching him, understood why the counties had got as far as they had. This was not a stupid man and it was not an evil one. It was a man who had spent thirty-one years making an answer and had never once been asked the question.
“That is not a question the office answers,” he said at last. “We are not licensed to it. There is no column for it.”

“I know,” said Nahl. “I sat in your queue for an hour. I watched you be right four times out of five. You are correct nearly all of the time and the whole building runs on it.” Nahl put both hands on their knees, because a bearer reporting says it with the hands still. “I am asking the man, not the office.”
Corin Quire looked at the fire for a moment.

“A person is a party,” he said. “That is what we have. A party is a name with an account against it. Land, fee, duty, holding, return, birth, death, marriage, mill transaction.” He said the list without looking anything up. “A person who is a party can be helped. We can correct her page, we can pay her, we can free her from a fee, we can find her son’s line and tell her it is a good line. That is not nothing. That is a great deal, and I have watched it change lives in this district for thirty-one years.”
“And a person who is not a party?”

“A person who is not a party is not a person in this office,” said Corin Quire. “I do not say that to be cruel. I say it because it is the only true sentence I have. We cannot help a thing with no column under it. There is nowhere to put the help.”
“That is the answer,” said Nahl. “That is the whole answer.”

Then Nahl asked the second question. That was the one the company had written out on the road. They had decided that Nahl should ask it with Riss in the room and nobody else. Nahl asked it alone, which was a departure, and Nahl took responsibility for it in the Leaf that night.

“There is a thing in the north meadow that your district has looked at and cannot enter. Your notice is on the board. In three weeks your assize sits and the district finishes its year, and every item on your calendar will be disposed of, and this one cannot be, because your own law says no entries are to be made beyond the peaks and your own Index says the same in two-hundred-year-old ink.” Nahl waited. “What does the office do with an item it cannot dispose of?”
Corin Quire was quiet for a moment.
“You have read my board very carefully,” he said.
“I have read every line of it,” said Nahl.

“Then you know item eighty-four as well as I do.” The Assessor turned a page on his desk, without needing to, because it was a page he had been turning for four months. “A surveyor went west on the county’s order in the ninth month, at the request of this office. He came back with a mark on a slope and four names of people he never met, and a stone with a tally on it. And a query in the sixth column that reads *who is at this mark*. I put that query there myself. I have written four hundred thousand corrections in my life and that is the only query I have ever written that I cannot answer.”
“Because the answer is not in a book.”

“Because the answer is in a book in my district and not in my office,” said Corin Quire. “There is a page at Ashenford with a fourth column that says no fee is due on any part of it, and it is stitched into a working mill’s ledger, and it is not mine, and if I pull it out I have committed the only crime this country has, which is making a record untrue.”
Nahl said nothing, because there was nothing to say and because the man was not finished.

“As to the meadow,” said Corin Quire, “the office does nothing. That is the answer and I will say it plainly. It is the same answer the counties gave two hundred years ago, when somebody with a seal walked west and came back and wrote nine words and stamped them. The office does not enter it. The office does not remove it. It stays in the meadow and it is watched and noted daily, and in the third month it comes up at the assize as an item requiring disposition.”
“And then?”

“And then the assize does what an assize does,” said the Assessor. “It disposes. A thing that has been entered can be amended and a thing that has not been entered does not exist, and to make the item go away the assize has exactly two ways. It can order the animal entered. Or it can order the animal removed.”
“It cannot be removed,” said Nahl.

“No,” said Corin Quire. “I have seen it from my window on the north road and I am not going to pretend to a professional opinion about a thing the trade tells me walks the pace of a person on a horse. It cannot be removed.”
“Then it must be entered.”

“Then it must be entered,” said the Assessor. “And to make an entry, the register must be corrected, because the register says no entries are to be made. The correction rule is printed on a card and it is the same card in every office in the eleven counties. Find the error. Write the correction. Sign the line.”
He put his pen down.

“So the question is not what the office does,” he said. “The question is who signs. The signature is required. There is no disposition of that item in the third month unless a person takes a pen and writes a correction and puts a name under it, and the name will be a name in a column, and it will be *his* name, and he will be a party to it from that day to the end of his life, and the counties will know exactly who he is.”
The child at the small desk had finished her sums.

She came over with the page, because she had been told not to interrupt and had also been told to show her work. She stood at her father’s elbow and waited to be noticed. The two men waited with her. There is no room in the world in which an eight-year-old with a page is not more important than a question.
“Nineteen,” said Pella Quire.
Corin Quire looked down the column. He checked the last four figures first, from the bottom up, which is how a clerk checks, and which was where the girl had learned it.
“Again,” he said.
She took it back to her desk and found the place and did it again, and brought it back, and said, “Nineteen. It was nineteen the first time.”
“It was,” said her father. “You are right and I was wasting your time. That is what I do when I want to be sure.”
Pella looked at Nahl then, all the way up and all the way down, in the frank way of a child who has not yet been taught that a person on a bench is a party to something.
“You don’t have a name on the board,” she said.
“No,” said Nahl.
“Everybody has a page,” said Pella. “Papa’s got a whole shelf of them at home. Do you want to see mine? It has my sums on it and my height in the margin every year.”
“No, thank you,” said Nahl.
She nodded, without any offence at all, as if a refusal were the most ordinary kind of answer in the world, and went back to her desk.
Nahl watched her go and understood exactly what was in the room, and did not say it, then or ever.
Then the Assessor did the thing that Nahl had been dreading for four months and had not once managed to guess the shape of.
He made them an offer, and it was sincere, and it was the best offer anybody in the counties was capable of making to a person who has no page.

“I can enter you,” said Corin Quire. “Not the animal. You. The eight of you. As a party of labour without a place, on the district’s own motion, this office’s request to the assize. Twenty-four words. No individual names. A standing, a parish to answer to, and a route. You would be persons in the eleven counties by the third month.”
Nahl sat in the chair.

“You would be able to walk into any office in this country and ask for something,” said the Assessor. “You could put a child in a school. You could be seen by a doctor at the district’s cost. If one of you is injured on a road in a county that is not mine, there is a page with his standing on it, and a man with a standing gets looked at.” He folded his spectacles. “And the office would stop, bearer. That is the part I am asking you to weigh. If you are on a page, then you are not a question any more, and every clerk in this district can go back to the ordinary work of finishing the year.”
The fire moved in the grate.
“No,” said Nahl.
“I would like a reason.”

“The reason is the same twenty-four words,” said Nahl. “A party of labour without a place is a form, and a form cannot have a blank in it, and the first blank in that form is a name, and the second is a count. You would take the eight out of our mouths and put it in a box, and then there would be a page in a county book with our number on it, and a page can be corrected.” Nahl stood up, because a bearer stands when he has decided. “We are a count that is only ever said out loud. That is the whole of what we are. It is the only thing we have that your office cannot amend.”
Corin Quire looked at Nahl for a long moment.
“You understand what I am doing,” he said.
“I do.”

“I am not threatening you. I want that written down somewhere, whatever comes of this. I have no levy and no warrant and no man at the door. I am offering the only thing this country has ever had, which is a page and a doctor and a school and somewhere to be looked at.” He put the spectacles down on the page in front of him. “You may take it or not take it. Refusals are honoured here. They are honoured by *people*, and I am one.”
“I know,” said Nahl. “That is what makes it hard.”
Nahl was at the door when the Assessor said the last thing, and it was said quietly, and it was not a threat either.

“Bearer. If the assize orders the animal entered, the correction goes up from this district to the Hall of Records, and a correction has to be written in the hand of a clerk of record, in the ordinary way, and signed by the person who finds the error.” Corin Quire had not looked up from his page. “There is one clerk in this district who writes the third column. That is the column your correction would go into. It is written in the county tongue and she writes it better than anybody in the eleven counties and she has been writing it for two years.”
Nahl stood with a hand on the door.

“I am telling you the mechanic,” said the Assessor. “It is not a tactic. If nobody in this district signs that line, the item is disposed of in the third month without a disposition, and the office calls that a lapsed item, and a lapsed item is what this country does with weather.”
“And if somebody signs it?”

“Then your creature is in the register,” said Corin Quire, “and the counties have a page about the thing west of the peaks for the first time in two hundred years. And the west is divided like everything else is divided. And I do not know what that does. I am not a man who pretends to know what a thing that size does. I only know the mechanic.”
Nahl came out of the office at twenty past ten in the morning.

The market was busier than the day before. The board with the district’s calendar on it had two people in front of it. One of them was an old woman with a basket, and she was reading the assize list out loud to a man who could not read. That is the ordinary way a county tells itself what it is about to do.
Riss was waiting at the pump across from the Hall, because it was Riss’s turn and Riss had not argued about it, and because a bearer who goes in alone should come out to somebody.
“Well?” said Riss.
Nahl told it exactly, in order, the way a bearer reports, and it took nine minutes.
When it was finished Riss said the thing that Nahl had already worked out on the walk back across the market.
“It is her,” said Riss.
“It is the mechanic,” said Nahl.

“It is her handwriting on the page,” said Riss. “It has been her handwriting since Vellum Reach in the spring. She wrote the ninety-one names and she was the thirty-first one, and now the column in the correction is the third column and it is written in the county tongue in a hand that leans slightly left at the base, and there is one clerk in this district who does that, and it is my sister.”
“Yes,” said Nahl.
“And I have to go and ask her,” said Riss.

“You have to go and ask her,” said Nahl. “And when you do, remember that the practice has nine parts, and that none of the nine has ever had a name in it, and that the county’s whole answer is a signature, and that we have said no to that four times now in four rooms.”
Riss looked across the market at the Hall with its benches and its cups and its long pale stone front, and at the garden, and at the people sitting in it who had nothing wrong with them at all.
“Five rooms,” said Riss. “This is the fifth.”
“Yes,” said Nahl.

“And this time it is not a form and it is not a magistrate and it is not a parish clerk and it is not the Index. It is a page in a hand I have known since before I could write.” Riss put their hands in their pockets. “Nahl, I am going to ask her for the one thing I have never asked anybody for, and the whole book has been walking toward it since the river.”
Nahl, who had carried a log for nine months and had written nothing in it that mattered, said the thing that a bearer says.
“Then go and ask her,” said Nahl. “And whatever she says, say it out loud afterwards, because I will be writing nothing down and one of us has to be able to carry it.”

chapters.part: Act V · The Return and the Counting
chapters.label: Chapter 38
chapters.title: The Counting
paragraphs: After the office, and the offer, and the refusal in the chair, Riss went to ask their sister.
It took four days to get the asking done. Riss had spent five months thinking about one sentence of nine words. It took four days of standing in a market to say it.

The town was full of clerks. The office was open from eight to four and again from six to eight in the last weeks before the assize, and the queue stood out of the door and along the pavement in the cold. Everybody in it knew that the person in front of them was in the same position. That is what the third month is in the counties.
Riss went to the Hall four times.

The first time there were nine people at the counter and Ness was writing. The second time Ness was at the back with a bag of returns and did not come out. The third time Riss asked for a copy of a page, because it was the only question that gave nothing away, and was told the volume was at the bindery, which was true.
The fourth time Riss waited on the pavement at four in the afternoon for a door to open, the way a person waits outside a school.
Ness came out at ten past four with a coat over her arm and a bag on her shoulder. She stopped.
Nobody in that market looked at the two of them. Nobody in a market looks at two people standing still.
“You are on the road,” said Ness.
“Yes,” said Riss.
“Since when?”
“The ninth month of the year before last,” said Riss. “Five months and eleven days.”
Ness did the arithmetic in her head, and it was the same arithmetic Riss had done on the first page of the Leaf.
“That is longer than a year,” said Ness.
“Yes.”
“I said *come back when you can say what you took.*”

“I know,” said Riss. “I read that about a thousand times. It was written on the back of a form for a household in the south with two names on it and a stamp in the corner. You crossed it out and wrote on the other side, and you used the county’s ink.”
Ness looked at Riss for a long moment.
“You are in the county town and the assize is in eleven days,” she said. “Do not pretend this is a visit.”
“No,” said Riss. “A paper is coming and it will come to your desk. I have come to ask you to do the trade.”

They walked. That is the whole of what happened next. It took about an hour, round the town twice, and ended at the river where it is quiet. It is the only hour in this account that nobody in the company was present for.
Riss said three things first.
What the company had done at Ashenford. The page, the four columns, the fifth leaf, no fee due on any part of it, and the clerk who kept it.

What the company had lost. A keeper of the deletion log, about seventy, who sat down in the grass west of a border stone with a satchel in his hand. His name was on no page in the eleven counties. His grave had a notch and a tally of five on it.

And what the company found above the last grass. A form cut into the ice in four columns, three full and the fourth never used. A sound off the far side of a wall in a language nobody alive could write, in eight even parts.
And Riss said the sentence the whole book had been walking toward.

“I left you downriver. I told you the year would divide better and I would send for you. I did it carefully and I did it in arithmetic and it was the worst thing I have ever done to a person. I took the year. That is what I took. I took a year out of your life and I put it in a column of my own and I rounded it. You are better at columns than I will ever be. It was still me who did it.”
Ness stopped walking and stood with her hands in her pockets and looked at the water.
“Two years,” she said.
“Two years,” said Riss.
