“On the twenty-ninth day of the fourth month I will have been in that office two years and eleven months. I have written one thousand nine hundred columns in the county tongue. I can write it faster than I can read it, and I have never been able to read a line of it. I am the fastest hand in the district in a language I do not know.”
Riss said nothing, because the trade is knowing when the page has turned.

“I read one word of it,” said Ness. “One. It is in the heading of the third column. It is the same word on every form in the eleven counties and it has been the same word for two hundred years. I asked a senior clerk with nine years in the building what it meant. He did not know. He said nobody in the building knows, and that the heading came with the form.”
Ness looked at the water.
“So I write it eleven times a day. Nine words. And under it I write figures.”
“What is the word?”
“I do not know,” said Ness. “That is the point. That is the whole of what I have been doing for two years and eleven months.”
Then Ness said the thing Riss had not asked for and had not expected. It took two sentences.

“There is a paper coming,” said Ness. “Everybody in the office knows what is on it. There is one animal in the north meadow and there is no form for it. The assize must dispose of it in eleven days. The office has decided the disposition will be an entry, because the other option is removing a thing that cannot be removed. So the correction will be made and the entry will be made, and it will come down to my desk, because the third column is mine.”
“And?”
“And I will not tick the box,” said Ness.
Riss stopped.
“I did not ask you that.”

“You did not have to,” said Ness. “You asked me to do the trade. I have done the arithmetic. I am not going to tick the box. I am telling you now because you are my sister, and because I know what you would have said if you had thought of it, which is that the office asked a clerk to lie. I am not going to lie. I am also not going to refuse loudly. I am going to do the trade exactly. I will rule the page and write the heading and set the columns out square. I will write every figure that is true. Then I will leave the box at the foot of the page un-ticked.”
“That is a lapsed item.”

“That is a lapsed item,” said Ness. “It is the one thing a clerk of record can do that the register cannot answer. It is not a refusal and it is not a resignation. It is a page that is not finished. It will be in a working ledger with my hand on it, and when the assize closes the year the machine will have to carry it forward.”
The assize sat on the ninth day of the third month, and the company was not in it.
That is worth writing plainly. Eight people with no names on them did not walk into a court and put a case.

The court sat in the assembly hall by the market: two magistrates, a clerk, and a table. The list was a hundred and eleven items and it took nine days. The mill on the Vellum at Ashenford came up on the third day and was fined two pounds and eleven shillings, and nothing was said about a certificate.
Item eighty-four came up on the seventh day. *Marker, unclaimed, no parish, sixty-one miles west of the last surveyed line. Query: who is at this mark.*

The court heard the surveyor, a plain man who had walked west and come back with a drawing. It recorded that the mark is a county peg above a cairn of stones with a tally of five cut into the top stone, and that no parish claims it and no name can be attached to it. Then it ordered the mark entered as *marker, unnumbered, no parish, no name,* and the clerk wrote that down, and the year, and the court’s seal under it. Orphiel of Sallow remained, on the county’s own record, a mark.
The company heard about that in the evening, and Veylan went out to the yard and sat with the goat for a while.
The meadow item was the last item of the ninth day, and it was heard in the way the whole town had known it would be heard.
*Unentered animal, present in the north meadow since the fifteenth day of the first month. No return is to be taken. Disposition required.*

The court did what the office had told the company it would do. It found that a thing present in the district should be entered, and directed this office to make the entry, and directed the clerk of record to write the correction of the register’s western page. Then it put the item over to the close of the year. The clerk of the court wrote the direction in the book and initialled it, and the counties had finished their year.
They did it in the Assessor’s office on the twelfth day of the third month, at four in the afternoon, with the light going.

There was no ceremony and no crowd. Corin Quire was there because it was his office and his page. A senior clerk was there with the register. There was a cleared table, and a lamp lit early because of the light, and eight people standing.
Ness Riss came in last with the portfolio under her arm, in her work coat, with a pen she had cut herself.
She did not look at Riss. Riss did not look at her. That was their arrangement, made by the river in four sentences, and it was kept.

The window was open, because the Assessor had opened it himself an hour before. It looked out over the last of the town and the north road. Out in the meadow, at about two hundred paces, standing at the pace of a person on a horse and going nowhere, was the thing that had never been entered.
The Assessor did it exactly by the book, because the book was the only thing he had, and because kindness has a procedure in an office.

He read the direction out loud and said what the page was. The register’s western section. The column. The nine words in the oldest ink in the book, written two hundred years ago, with a stamp under them.
Then he said the correction rule, which is printed on a card nailed by every counter in the eleven counties.
*Find the error. Write the correction. Sign the line.*

“The error is the nine words,” said Corin Quire. “The register says that beyond the peaks no entries are to be made. There is now a thing beyond the peaks standing in the north meadow of this town, present and unwilling, and the district has watched it and noted it daily since the fifteenth day of the first month. The nine words are no longer true. The correction of a page is the ordinary work of a clerk of record. Here is the page, and here is the clerk.”
He said all of it without any drama, which was the worst of it. Then he stood back from the table, because it was not his hand.
Ness ruled the correction in six lines with a straight edge, under the nine words, in the county tongue, in the hand that leans very slightly left at the base.
She wrote four things.

She wrote that the western section above was entered by hand in the year of the long frost and that no entry had been made under it in two hundred years. She wrote that a thing had been present and unwritten in the district since the fifteenth day of the first month of the present year. She wrote that this sheet was the correction of the section so as to make the register true. And she wrote that no number and no name were entered, because there was no number that was true and no name that any living hand could write.

The company watched a clerk of record do the most exact work any of them had ever seen. Riss understood, for the first time in five months, what the counties had and why they had lasted, and how much of the world’s weight is carried by a person who writes small and square and never rounds.
Then Ness dipped the pen for the last line, and stopped, and put the pen down, and did not write it.
That was the signing line. It was ruled, and it was empty, and it was at the foot of the correction, and the box beside it was un-ticked.
The office waited about four minutes.
The senior clerk moved first, and what he did was look at the Assessor, which is the whole of a senior clerk’s job in a room like that one.
Corin Quire came back to the table and read the page, and checked the last four figures first, from the bottom up, the way he had learned it and the way his daughter did it.
“You have not signed it,” he said.
“No,” said Ness.
“It is the rule.”

“It is the rule,” said Ness. “I can write the correction, because I am a clerk of record and the hand is the office’s. I cannot sign it, because the signature is not the office’s. The card says *sign the line,* and the person who signs it is the person who found the error. I have not found an error. Neither has anybody in this building. We have found a thing in a meadow.”
The Assessor was quiet.
“You understand what you have done,” he said.

“I have left an unfinished page in a working register,” said Ness. “It will go forward into the next year. It has no disposition on it and no name under it. The office cannot finish it and cannot remove it, because the page is true, and the only thing this country has is that its pages are true.”
“That is a lapsed item,” said the senior clerk, from the side, in the voice of a man watching a wall come down. “In the western section.”
“It is,” said Ness. “And it is true. It will be true next year. You will have to put the item on the calendar again, and there is no column you can put it in.”
Then Corin Quire did the last of what the counties could do. It was not cruel and it was not loud. It was the most frightening thing in the book.
He asked the form’s question.
“The entry requires a purpose,” he said. “It is the fourth column. It is empty. I cannot close this page without it. What is the party for?”
He said it politely, in the tone of a man asking for a figure he knows is somewhere on the desk.
The company stood in a row in the order they walked. The goat was at the door, the lamp was on the table, and the thing in the meadow was at two hundred paces, going nowhere.
And the remainder answered.
“To be counted,” said Nahl. “Once. Standing up, in a room with a book in it. That is the whole of the trade, and it is the only thing I have ever been asked for that I could do.”
“To keep the measurement,” said Mira. “One sheet for one thing and no copies.”
“To sit with what cannot be fixed,” said Sancora. “Somebody has to be in the room after the hands have stopped. That is not healing. It is the rest of it.”

“To smell the rain come back,” said Corvath. “There was nothing in the air at all for two books, and then there was bread and wet stone and a river. I am the man it all came back to, and somebody had to be that.”

“To stand where the wall is and find the edge of a thing that was kept,” said Kael Riven. “There is an edge on a thing that was kept and no edge on a thing that was added up. I have spent five months on that. It is the only sentence I have got and I am content with it.”

“To hold a soil and put a seed in it,” said Veylan. “I have four seedlings alive in a tin by the grace of a healer and a pot. I have a field of my own that I promised to plant in the spring, and when I have planted it I will walk out of it and go east with these people. That is not a settling, and I have thought about the difference for a year.”

“To say no in front of witnesses,” said Old Den. “I said it at Marle and a young man took my hand and I lost what I lost. I have gone back over that day more than any other day and the answer is the same every time. It was not the counties that did it. It was a person. That is the whole of what I know at sixty-two.”
And Riss said the last one, with the plate humming the third note under their shirt and their sister four feet away with a pen in her hand and an unsigned page in front of her.
“To come back when you can say what you took,” said Riss, and did not look at Ness, and Ness did not look at them. “And to say it out loud, in a room with a book in it, and have it entered nowhere.”
Then the thing in the meadow did the last thing it ever did in this book.

It came up the north road at the pace of a person on a horse and stopped in the market, and it stood at the window of the Assessor’s office with the lamp on inside and eight people and a goat, and it did not come in.

The goat went out to it. The goat walked out of the door and across the market yard and stood in front of it, and neither of them did anything at all. Then the goat came back and lay down on the line of grey stone at the office’s threshold, which is the line the surveyors cut into every public building’s step, and it did not move for the rest of the hour.
And then it said its name.

I have tried to write that sentence four times. This is the fourth. It said its name once, out loud, in a room with a book in it and witnesses on their feet. It went into the room whole and it did not come out of anybody’s mouth the way a name comes out. The plate under Riss’s shirt answered with the third note and something under the third note. Kael’s burned hand opened and closed and ached for the first time in six months. The senior clerk, who had seen everything the eleven counties could do to a person, did not write one character of it.
Then the light in the room moved, and Riss looked at the eye.

It was the size of a mill wheel and it was not looking at anybody in the room. It was polished, and polished is not shining, which is a thing Riss had learned at a customs house two years before and had never once been able to put down.

The pen was in Ness Riss’s hand. The line was ruled and the box was at the foot of a true page in a working register. There was no column in the book for what had just happened and no name that any hand in the eleven counties could write.
Ness did not tick the box.
The company went out at ten past six and stood in the market. The thing had gone back down the north road. A boy was lighting the two lamps at the corner.
Corin Quire came out after them with his hat and his bag, because he had a house to go to and a daughter who had done her sums.
He stopped beside Nahl.

“The item is in the register unfinished,” he said. “It will be on the calendar next year. My office will be queried about it in the fourth month, and every fourth month after that, until I am dead. My clerk will answer the query. The answer will be that the correction is written, that the entry is made, that the box is un-ticked, and that the district cannot finish the page and will not remove it.”
“Yes,” said Nahl.

“That is the first time in thirty-one years,” said Corin Quire, “that I have watched a thing go through this office that the counties cannot do anything about.” He put his hat on. “I would like to thank you for it. I am aware that this is not a thing a man is supposed to want.”
“Nothing was taken,” said Nahl. “No fee is due on any part of it.”
“No fee is due on any part of it,” said the Assessor of Hygiene, and went home to his children.
They walked east out of the county town on the fifteenth day of the third month.
It was a mild morning and the smoke stood straight up out of the chimneys, which is the county’s sign for a fine day. The goat walked in front.
Nahl stopped at the mile stone and looked back once, because a bearer counts a row when he leaves a room. The company stood in the road and let them look.
Then Nahl said the exchange the two of them had been saying since the ridge. The whole company heard it. It was the last time anybody said it in this book.
“What do we do now?”
“We carry it.”
“Carry it where?”
“East,” said Riss. “Until we find the next room.”
“And the next one after that?”
“We carry it there too,” said Riss. “And the one after that. We do not put it down. We do not file it and we do not sign it, and the counties can go on finishing their year without us.”
The goat walked on. The company followed it.

Above the road the sky was county sky. Behind them the register was on its shelf with an unfinished page in the western section and an un-ticked box on it. Ahead of them the road went east out of the stones of the gate. For a hundred yards at the crossing there were two roads side by side, the gold and the grey, running together and then apart, and both of them going east.
Neither of them shone.
The plate under Riss’s shirt hummed the third note, quiet, at the volume of a cat, and did not stop.

chapters.label: Epilogue
chapters.title: The Counted
paragraphs: After the winter turned and the roads opened, the assize came to the county town in the third month. It sat for nine days and went away again. Then the mill on the Vellum went back to its ordinary Tuesdays.
It was the fourth month of the following year. The river was up.

The Vellum came down off the high country in the fourth month the way it had come down every fourth month of Ivet Sallow’s life, and the mill ran day and night for eleven days. The wheel house was lit. Every man in the yard was on the loading floor and the office door was open from the sixth hour to the fourteenth.
The office door was open and the clerk was behind the counter. The day book was on the desk. The ledger shelves were behind her. The fourth ledger was on the shelf where it had always been.
The fine had come out of the assize and it was two pounds.

Ivet could have told anybody the whole of it in four sentences. She had written it down four times that week for the family. A clerk who has to explain a fine explains it in the same words every time.

The mill’s monthly return was fourteen months in arrears at the third month of that year. The office at the county town had required the return, and had required a certificate, and had received neither. The family had been summoned, as the county’s contracting party, and the family’s woman of business had attended in the family’s place and had answered for the family.
The court had fined the mill two pounds and eleven shillings in costs for the return in arrears, and had ordered the return brought up to date, and had said nothing at all about the certificate.
That was the fourth sentence and it was the one that mattered. Ivet had written it out four times and read it four times. She had never once been able to make it stop surprising her.

The office had stopped asking for the certificate in the fourth month. That was what the man who came down the river on the county’s business told her, and he told her in the flat way that a man tells a clerk something the office is tired of. The standing instruction had been withdrawn for mills and merchants, on the office’s own motion. Four hundred of them had been unable to produce it. And a requirement that cannot be met is a requirement that makes the office look foolish.
Ivet had asked him one question and it was the question of a clerk who wants the arithmetic exactly.
“Did any of them sign it?”
The man from the office had looked at her and had understood the question perfectly, because he was a clerk too.

“Nine did,” he said. “The other four hundred and some did not, and every one of the four hundred said the same thing, which is that they keep the trades’ books and not their neighbours’, and the office did not want to be in front of the assize arguing about what a certificate means.”

The certificate was in the drawer under the counter with the string on it. Unanswered. Unsigned. It had stayed there through the assize, and after the fourth month of the year it was a piece of paper with a heading on it that the counties were no longer interested in.
Ivet Sallow had not signed it, and she never would, and the mill had been fined two pounds and eleven shillings, and the page was still in the ledger.
Serle came up the river road on the fourteenth day of the fourth month.

She came on the barge from the bridge and walked up from the landing stage. She had a case on a strap and a plain good coat and a face that told you nothing at all. The loading men knew her by sight and one of them took his hat off.

She stood in the doorway of the office for a moment with the light behind her. Ivet looked up from the day book with her pen in her hand and knew the whole of who it was. She had been told in the third month who had stood up in the county court and answered for the family.
“You read the page,” said Ivet Sallow.
“I read the page,” said Serle.
“And you did not file your report.”
“No,” said Serle.
“Neither did I,” said Ivet.
They did not embrace and neither of them cried.

That is worth saying for the plain reason that it is what two clerks do. The woman in the doorway and the woman behind the counter had between them about nine hundred documents and forty years of accounts. They had a settled dislike of any display in a public office.
Ivet put the pen down and closed the day book and pushed the money drawer shut, because a clerk with a guest does not leave the drawer open.
Serle put her case down on the end of the counter and did not open it.
“I have an hour,” she said. “The barge goes back at the fourth hour.”
“Then sit down,” said Ivet. “I will put the kettle on the office stove. The loading floor has one and the men are at the wall.”
They sat on the two stools at the end of the counter, one on each side of it, because that is how two clerks sit in an office. They drank tea out of the two office cups.
Neither of them went into the back room, and that was deliberate on both sides and neither of them said so.
Serle did not ask about the fine. Ivet did not ask about the court. There was nothing to ask about either of them, and both of them had read the same papers.
They talked about the page.
Ivet took the fourth ledger down off the shelf after the tea and put it on the counter between them, and opened it at the back, and did not turn it toward Serle or away from her.
There were five leaves.
Four leaves of names in small neat column-straight writing, eighty-seven names now, three more since the fourth month of the year before, no authority for any one of them.
Then the fifth leaf, ruled by hand in four columns.
Ivet read the fourth column out loud, in the voice that a clerk uses for a page she has read four hundred times in a doorway with the light behind it.
“Nothing was taken and no fee is due on any part of it.”
Serle listened with her hands around the tea.
Then Serle said the four lines.

She did not get the slip out of her coat. She had never needed it to say the lines, and they were in the order she had made for herself. She said them the way she had said them at the counters of the counties for the whole of the year.

The fourth line was the one about the reason. It said, in her own words, that the reason entered above was a report made standing by witnesses who came on foot. It said that this was the only reason she had ever read that was not a fee.
Neither of them wrote anything down.
Then they did the count.

It was not the company’s count. That count was in eight mouths and it was four hundred miles east. It had never been written anywhere. Neither of the two women in that office had ever heard it, and neither of them ever would.
The count they did was the count of the page. It was Serle’s idea and she said it plainly, because she was a woman of business and a woman of business counts things.
“How many people have read it?”
“Let us find out,” said Ivet.
So they counted the reads, out loud, sitting on two stools in a mill office in the fourth month of the year, and it took them about four minutes and neither of them wrote it down.
“One,” said Ivet. “The clerk who wrote it. I read it every Sunday evening with the door shut and I have written nothing about it in fourteen months.”

“Two,” said Serle. “The county clerk who came down the river in the ninth month and read it at this counter with you standing there, and went back up the river and filed nothing. He had it in his coat for a month and he never put it in a file.”
“Three,” said Ivet.

“Three,” said Serle. “The woman of business, who read it four times on the second day of the eleventh month and copied four lines into her coat and has carried them for a year, and has not filed her report and is not going to.”
They stopped there, because there were two of them and they had counted three, and both of them understood the arithmetic of what was left.
“Four,” said Serle. “There will be a fourth.”
“There will be a fourth,” said Ivet.
“Who?”

“I do not know,” said Ivet. “That is the whole of it. That is the thing about a page with no reason in it. It does not circulate. It does not get copied and it does not get posted. It sits in a ledger in a working mill and somebody reads it, one person at a time, and the only way it moves is that a person who has read it cannot stop thinking about the fourth column.”
“And then what?”
“Then that person walks into a room and asks somebody a question,” said Ivet. “And the count goes up by one.”
They did not write the four down.
There was one thing Ivet wanted to say and she said it near the end. The cups were empty and the barge was still an hour off. She said it in the flat voice she used for a page she was checking.
“I never heard the name.”
Serle sat with that for a moment.
“Neither did I,” she said.

“They said it in this room,” said Ivet. “That was in the report and the report is true and I signed it. They said it in this room in the ninth month of the year before. It did not come out of a human throat. What went into the fourth column was that a name had been said and not written down. That is all I have.”
“I have less than that,” said Serle. “I have a slip of paper with four lines on it in my own hand, and none of them is a name.”
“So between the two of us,” said Ivet, “there are a page and a slip of paper and eight people’s worth of a name, and not one of us has it.”
“One page and four lines,” said Serle.
“One page and four lines,” said Ivet.
The page stayed in the ledger and the ledger stayed on the shelf.

That was the whole of the refusal. It was made in the ninth month of the year before and it was made again in the fourth month of that year. Neither of the two women in the office had to say a word about it.
Serle did not ask to copy it and Ivet did not offer.
Serle’s report was not written and was not going to be written. The family had not asked for it in a year. A mill that answers the county and pays its fine is a mill that needs no report.

And Ivet did not sign the certificate, and the certificate stopped being asked for. The return went up the river in the fourth month with the current figures in it. There was no covering sentence at the foot of that page that was not a trade figure.
That was the arithmetic and it was the same arithmetic it had been for a year, and it came out the same way.
Two pounds and eleven shillings.
A page in a ledger.
Nothing written down.
The company was not at Ashenford West and had not been for seven months.
Where they were was east. That was the whole of what anybody in that office knew about it, and it was all that Serle had been given in the tavern at Carden, and she had asked twice.
There was no plate in Ashenford. There never had been. There was a case of notes with a piece of old metal in it and it had gone east on a cart in the ninth month of the year before.

There was no goat in Ashenford, either. The goat was on a road, or in a barn, or standing in a doorway somewhere east somewhere between here and whatever town has the next book in it, and it was in front of eight people.
There was no wind in Ashenford and there had not been any for more than a year. Nobody in the town had remarked on it. A town does not notice a thing that only stops.
Ivet Sallow had walked down to the bridge in the second month and had stood on the parapet in the cold, because she had wanted to see what it looked like from there.

There was nothing to see. The gold road and the grey road ran side by side across the bridge and away north and south into the counties. Neither of them shone. There was nobody on either of them in any direction a man could see.

The Emberion was not visible above the mill. It had not been visible for a year. It was up there somewhere with its fifteen joints and the piece missing out of the wing, behind county sky, and nobody in Ashenford West was looking for it and nobody in Ashenford West was going to.
The practice was still running four hundred miles east and it had nine parts and they were the same nine parts.
Pay first. Give no names. Take no work. Never two nights. Find the clerk before the tavern. Count standing up. Write nothing. Leave nothing. Say the company is walking east.

A girl at a well in a village with a name nobody in Ashenford had ever heard had been told one thing. In the first month of the year she had been told that a number you say every day is a number you keep.

An old man at Odder kept a parish book and had watched a hand go into a coat and come back to the table. He had told the whole of his tavern about it. Eight people with a goat had stood up in his taproom and been counted out loud, and nobody had written the number down.

A parish clerk at Wend had a settlement paper in his coat with a box on it that nobody had put a name in. He had gone home and told his wife about it. His wife had said something about it in the market in the next village.

And the eight of them were on a road somewhere east of all of it. A log under a bearer’s arm. A Leaf in a case. A tin of soil in a farmer’s coat. A chart in a tube, a slate in a pack, and one pair of twice-mended boots between them.
None of it was written anywhere. That was the whole of the design. It was not a design. It was what there was.
Serle went back down to the landing stage at the fourth hour with her case on her strap.

She stood in the office doorway for a moment before she went. The two of them looked at each other the way two clerks look at each other at the end of a transaction. Thoroughly, and once, and without any talk.
“Write to me,” said Serle.
“No,” said Ivet.
“No,” said Serle. “Quite right. There is nothing to write.”
“There is nothing to write,” said Ivet. “That is the whole of the trade. You have four lines in your coat and I have five leaves in a ledger and neither of us has a thing that can go into a bag.”
Serle put her hat on.
“The fourth read,” she said.

“The fourth read,” said Ivet. “Somebody will come into this office in a year, or five years, or ten, and ask me a question about the back of that ledger, and I will hand them the book and stand at the end of the counter the way I did in the eleventh month, and they will read it four times and go home.”
“And then?”

“Then nothing,” said Ivet. “That is what the page is for. It is not for a county and it is not for a family and it is not for a rebellion. It is for the next person who cannot stop thinking about the fourth column.”
Then Serle went out of the door and down the lane to the river, and Ivet Sallow went back behind the counter and opened the day book and picked up her pen.
The mill at dusk at the end of the fourth month, and the office lamp lit, and the loading floor quiet with the last of the barges gone down.
Ivet Sallow at the counter with the day book open and the money drawer shut and the pen in her hand, adding up a column of tonnage for the fourteenth time that month.
Serle in the doorway with her hat on and her case on her strap, saying nothing at all, which is what she had come two hundred miles east to do, and which she had done.

The ledger on the shelf with the fourth ledger’s fourth leaf open at the back where it always opened. The page in the ledger. The count in the room, which was three and would be four. The name a sound that neither woman in that room had heard and neither of them would.
The gold road and the grey road running side by side across the bridge and away north and south. Neither of them shining. Nobody on either of them in any direction that a man could see.
The page stayed in the ledger. The count stayed in the room. The name stayed a sound. And the road went on east.
